causes_en: Sun load sensor failed

causes_en: Ambient air temperature sensor failed
Wiring or connector fault
B0158.desc: The HVAC control module has detected an implausible signal from the ambient air temperature sensor used by the climate control system. Symptoms include incorrect outside temperature display and erratic automatic climate behavior.

causes_en: Outside temperature sensor failed
Wiring or connector fault
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

causes_en: In-vehicle temperature sensor failed
Aspirator fan or duct blocked
B0160.desc: The HVAC control module has detected an implausible signal from the in-vehicle temperature sensor — typically an aspirated sensor in the dashboard. Automatic climate control regulates cabin temperature using this signal.

causes_en: Sun load sensor 2 failed
Wiring or connector fault
B0162.desc: The HVAC control module has detected an implausible signal from the second sun load sensor. Dual-zone systems use two solar sensors to detect side-asymmetric sunlight and adjust left/right airflow temperature.

causes_en: Temperature sensor failure
Wiring short or open

causes_en: Inlet door actuator failed

causes_en: Recirculation door actuator failed

causes_en: Blower motor worn or seized
Cabin filter heavily blocked
B0186.desc: The HVAC control module has detected that the front blower motor does not run at the commanded speed. Possible causes include a worn motor, blocked airway, or driver module fault.

causes_en: Rear wiper motor failed
Tailgate harness broken at hinge
Rear wiper fuse blown

causes_en: Park switch in wiper motor failed

causes_en: Wiper motor worn
Wiper linkage binding or seized

Damaged SRS power wiring

causes_en: Door actuator motor failed or stripped

causes_en: Wiper motor brushes worn

causes_en: Bulb burned out

Vacuum pump weak

P0001.en: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit/Open
P0001.desc: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0001 is set when the control module detects that the control circuit of this valve is open, i.e. no plausible current flows when the valve is driven. Rail pressure can then no longer be controlled as intended. Whether the valve is open or closed without current depends on the design, so the same fault can cause excess pressure in one system and no pressure in another.

causes_en: Regulator sticking or worn due to dirt, debris or water in the fuel
High resistance at connector or wiring causing wrong current
Low-pressure supply problem: clogged filter or air in the fuel
Rail pressure sensor reading wrong values
P0002.en: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0002.desc: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. With P0002 the circuit is electrically intact, but command and effect do not match: the measured current does not fit the duty cycle, or rail pressure does not follow the regulator position plausibly. The cause is often mechanical, for example a sticking valve, rather than the wiring.

causes_en: Harness chafed through, short to ground

Water or corrosion in the connector
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
P0003.en: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Low
P0003.desc: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0003 means the control module measures a voltage or current below the expected range on the control circuit, typically because of a short to ground. On some output stages an open circuit is also reported as low. A short on the switched ground side can keep the valve permanently energised.

causes_en: Short to battery voltage in the harness

causes_en: Wire or connector interrupted or corroded

P0005.en: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P0005.desc: The fuel shutoff valve is a solenoid valve that opens or blocks the fuel supply. On diesel engines it is usually closed without current, so that the engine stops reliably when switched off. The engine control module energises it to let fuel flow and monitors its control circuit continuously. P0005 is set when this control circuit is open. A normally closed valve then cannot open, so the engine does not start or cuts out while driving. Which vehicles use this valve and code varies by manufacturer.

causes_en: Short to ground in the harness

Corroded connector
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

causes_en: Primary or timing chain stretched

P0008.desc: The engine control module learns how far each camshaft of bank 1 is offset from the crankshaft and compares this with a reference. P0008 is set when both camshafts of this bank are shifted in the same direction beyond a threshold. That points to the drive shared by the bank: a stretched primary timing chain, a worn tensioner, an idler gear or a crankshaft reluctor wheel that has slipped. A single faulty camshaft phaser does not set this code, because it affects only one camshaft.

P000A.en: A Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 1
P000A.desc: This monitor does not judge the end position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments. The adjustment speed depends directly on oil flow, so worn or wrong oil and a partly clogged screen are the usual causes. Drivability is often hardly affected; the fault is an early warning before the camshaft misses its target position altogether. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.

P000E.en: Fuel Volume Regulator Control Exceeded Learning Limit
P000E.desc: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. To compensate for tolerances and wear, the control module learns a long-term correction of the regulator control. P000E is set when this correction leaves its calibrated range. The regulator is electrically fine, but the system needs an unusually large correction all the time, which points to wear or contamination of regulator or pump, a weak low-pressure supply, or a missing calibration after a pump replacement.

P000F.en: Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Activated
P000F.desc: On common-rail diesel and some gasoline direct-injection systems a spring-loaded pressure relief valve protects the rail and injectors: if pressure rises too far, it opens and returns fuel to the tank, often holding a reduced pressure for limp-home operation. The control module recognises the opening from the rail pressure signal and stores P000F. The code reports an event, not a defect of the relief valve itself; the actual cause usually lies in pressure control, for example a regulator that delivers too much fuel.

causes_en: Solenoid coil of the oil control valve open or shorted

Supply voltage missing, e.g. blown fuse
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
P0010.desc: The engine control module drives the oil control valve (a pulse-width modulated solenoid) of the variable valve timing on the intake camshaft on bank 1. It checks the electrical state of this output and sets the code when the circuit is open, or when the measured state does not match the command, for example because of a short. Camshaft adjustment is then disabled and the phaser stays in its locked rest position: the engine keeps running, but with less torque and higher consumption. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.

P0011.en: "A" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance (Bank 1)
P0011.desc: The engine control module compares the commanded position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 with the actual position it calculates from the camshaft and crankshaft sensors. This code is set when the camshaft sits further advanced than commanded for longer than a calibrated time, or, depending on the manufacturer, when the target is missed in either direction ("system performance"). Typical cause is a phaser that does not return to its rest position, for example because the oil control valve sticks open or its screen is clogged. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.

Usually the phaser does not move far enough out of its rest position, because oil pressure is too low to release the locking pin, the oil control valve does not open, or the oil screen is blocked. A stretched timing chain also shifts the camshaft towards retarded. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.

P0016.en: Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation (Bank 1 Sensor A)
P0016.desc: The engine control module checks whether the signal of the intake camshaft on bank 1 (sensor A) arrives at the expected crankshaft position, usually while the camshaft phaser is in its rest position. P0016 is set when the deviation stays outside a calibrated window. The camshaft is then out of step with the crankshaft: a timing belt or chain has jumped a tooth, the chain is stretched, the phaser is stuck at an end stop, or a reluctor wheel has slipped. On engines with a single camshaft, sensor A is simply the only camshaft sensor.

P001A.en: A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P001A.desc: A camshaft profile actuator switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between two or more fixed cam profiles with different valve lift and duration, for example by shifting a cam piece axially or by locking rocker arms or tappets with oil pressure. Unlike a camshaft phaser it does not shift the timing continuously. The second letter "A" in the title numbers the actuator on this camshaft. This code is set when the control circuit of the actuator is open: no current flows when it is driven, because of a broken wire, an unplugged connector or an open coil. The engine usually stays on one profile, typically the base profile with low lift. Some manufacturers report these faults with their own codes instead.

P0026.en: Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P0026.desc: A solenoid valve routes engine oil to a valve control element on the intake side of bank 1. Depending on the manufacturer this is a valve lift changeover or a camshaft phaser. P0030.desc: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) only delivers a usable signal once its ceramic element is hot. A heating element inside the sensor gets it there quickly after a cold start. Typically the heater receives battery voltage via a fuse or relay, and the engine control module switches the ground side with a pulsed signal while comparing the commanded state with the measured voltage or current. P0033.en: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit
P0033.desc: The turbocharger bypass valve A is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve: it connects the pressure side of the compressor with the intake side upstream of the turbocharger. It opens when the throttle closes quickly at high boost, so the compressor does not surge and the compressor wheel keeps its speed for the next acceleration. P003A.en: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P003A.desc: The electric boost actuator A positions the variable turbine vanes or the wastegate and reports its position through a sensor. In a learning run, for example with the engine warm at idle or after switching off, the control module drives the actuator to its mechanical end stops and stores the sensor values as reference. P003A is set when a learned end position or the total travel lies outside the permitted limits. Typical reasons are worn or sticking vanes or linkage, a faulty actuator, a broken actuator lever, or a replacement actuator that has not been learned in. A usually denotes the first turbocharger in the exhaust flow.

P003C.en: A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P003C.desc: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed.

P0040.en: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0040.desc: On engines with two exhaust banks, the control module checks whether the upstream oxygen sensors are assigned to the right bank. It changes the mixture on one bank only, actively or as part of normal bank-wise control, and watches which sensor responds. If the sensor that should sit on the other bank reacts, the signals are swapped. This logic is documented for the manufacturer-specific predecessor codes; the usual cause is connectors plugged in crosswise after a repair. If the swap remains, each bank is controlled by the other bank's signal, so fuel trims drift towards their limits.

P0045.desc: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. The letters A and B denote two separate actuators, for example on the low- and high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system, not the cylinder banks. This code is set when the control circuit is open: with the driver switched off no load can be measured, or the measured state does not match the command. Real overspeed arises when too much exhaust energy reaches the turbine, for example because the wastegate or the turbine vanes stick closed, or because the turbocharger has to compensate for a charge-air leak or high altitude. Since a damaged turbocharger can fail completely, the cause should be found before driving on. Turbocharger B has its own code.

P004A.desc: "Boost control B" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. B is the second actuator, for example on the high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system or on the second turbocharger; it does not denote cylinder bank 2. P0050.desc: The heated oxygen sensor on bank 2 is the upstream sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter), used for mixture control. Its heating element brings it quickly to operating temperature. Typically the heater receives battery voltage via a fuse, and the engine control module switches the ground side with a pulsed signal while checking that the circuit state matches the command. P0050 is the general circuit fault: the measured state of the heater circuit does not fit the command, most often because the circuit is interrupted. Which physical fault sets the general, low or high code is defined by each manufacturer. Without heating, closed-loop mixture control starts late and cold-start emissions rise. Bank 2 codes occur only on engines with two exhaust banks (V or boxer engines).

P005A.en: B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P005A.desc: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed.

P0065.desc: Air-assisted injectors have an air sleeve around the nozzle tip: air flowing past at high speed breaks the fuel spray into finer droplets, which improves combustion and cold starts and lowers hydrocarbon emissions. On port-injected engines this air is taken upstream of the throttle and dosed by a pulse-width modulated bypass solenoid; because it bypasses the throttle, it is part of the idle air. The system is rare and mainly found on older engines. P0065 means the control is electrically in order, but the effect is implausible. One documented method compares the idle speed controller correction with the air assistance switched on and off during stable idle; if the difference is too large, the code is set.

P0068.desc: The engine control module compares the air quantity measured by the manifold pressure and/or mass air flow sensor with the quantity the throttle position leads it to expect. P0068 is set when they do not match, typically because more air arrives than the nearly closed throttle allows, i.e. an air leak behind the throttle, or because the throttle body is dirty or a sensor reads wrong. On engines with electronic throttle this check protects throttle control, so the engine often goes into reduced power. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

causes_en: Manifold pressure sensor drifting
MAP sensor hose blocked, kinked or leaking
Barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) faulty
5 V reference or connector faulty
P0069.en: Manifold Absolute Pressure - Barometric Pressure Correlation
P0069.desc: With the ignition on and the engine stopped, the intake manifold is at ambient pressure, so the manifold pressure sensor and the barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) must read almost the same. P0069 is set when they differ by more than a threshold. Some systems also compare the barometric reading with a value estimated from manifold pressure at wide-open throttle while driving. Altitude and weather shift both values equally and do not cause the code. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

causes_en: EGR valve dirty or sticking open
Air leak or crankcase ventilation hose leaking
Mass air flow sensor dirty or manifold pressure sensor faulty
Air filter or intake restricted
P006A.en: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 1
P006A.desc: The engine control module compares the air quantity measured by the mass air flow sensor with the quantity it calculates from manifold pressure, engine speed and temperature. P006A is set when the two deviate too far. A typical cause is an exhaust gas recirculation valve that does not close: recirculated exhaust raises manifold pressure without passing the air flow sensor. Air leaks, a leaking crankcase ventilation hose or a dirty sensor have the same effect. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

causes_en: Exhaust pressure sensor faulty or its hose sooted or blocked
Manifold pressure sensor faulty
EGR or turbocharger fault distorting pressures
P006B.desc: On engines with an exhaust pressure sensor, mostly turbocharged diesels, the control module checks whether manifold pressure and exhaust back pressure fit each other, for example with the engine stopped, when both should be at ambient pressure. P006B is set when they do not. No manufacturer description of this code was found; the explanation follows the general rule for plausibility checks of input sensors. Suspects are the exhaust pressure sensor or its sooted hose, and the manifold pressure sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

causes_en: Leak or disconnected hose in the charge-air path
Boost or inlet pressure sensor faulty
Manifold pressure sensor faulty
Throttle body fault
P006C.desc: On turbocharged or supercharged engines the control module compares manifold pressure with the pressure measured upstream of the throttle, for example at idle or with the throttle wide open, where the two must lie close together. P006C is set when the difference exceeds a threshold. Manufacturers interpret "inlet pressure" differently: some mean boost pressure upstream of the throttle, others the pressure at the compressor inlet. Typical causes are a leak in the charge-air path or a faulty pressure sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

causes_en: Inlet pressure sensor faulty

Wiring, connector or 5 V reference faulty
Clogged air filter lowering pressure ahead of the compressor
P006D.en: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 1
P006D.desc: Without boost, for example with the engine stopped or at low load, the pressure sensor ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger must read about the same as the barometric pressure sensor. P006D is set when the difference is too large; some manufacturers compare against an estimated barometric value instead and run the check once per ignition cycle. Typical causes are a faulty inlet pressure sensor, a faulty barometric sensor (often inside the control module) or a wiring or reference-voltage fault. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

P006E.en: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P006E.desc: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure, for example a wastegate solenoid, the control valve of variable turbine vanes or an electric actuator. Some engines supply it through two driver stages in the control module: a high side that switches the supply voltage and a low side that switches ground. The low side is covered by P0045 to P0048; this code concerns the high side. P006E is set when the switched supply voltage is too low, typically because the supply wire is shorted to ground or interrupted. Without supply the actuator stays in its rest position, which on most engines means low boost and reduced power.

causes_en: Low-pressure supply too weak: lift pump, clogged filter, low tank level or waxing
High-pressure pump worn

P0087.desc: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. P0087 is set when the actual pressure stays below the target by more than a threshold for some time. It is a system code: it does not say which component is at fault. Typical causes are a weak low-pressure supply, a worn high-pressure pump, a sticking control valve, a leak or a drifting pressure sensor; the engine usually goes into reduced power.

causes_en: Pressure control or metering valve sticking

P0088.desc: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. P0088 is set when the actual pressure stays above the target by more than a threshold for some time. On many gasoline systems the pump can only raise pressure, which is then reduced only by injecting. Typical causes are a sticking pressure control or metering valve, a drifting pressure sensor or, on diesels with a pressure control valve, a blocked return. Real overpressure can cause harsh combustion noise and smoke.

P0089.desc: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. The fuel pressure regulator A is the actuator the manufacturer designates for this: depending on the system a pressure control valve that releases fuel from the rail, or the control valve on the high-pressure pump. Some manufacturers report the pump valve under the "fuel volume regulator" codes instead. P0089 is a function check: pressure may still be plausible, but the regulator works at its limit, needs too much correction, or pressure does not follow its control signal. Typical causes are a sticking or worn regulator, a weak pump or a faulty pressure sensor.

The engine control module compares this supply pressure with its target. P008A is set when the supply pressure stays too low. Besides a weak tank pump or its control unit, a clogged filter or a faulty sensor, simply running the tank empty can set this code.

P0093 means the pump is already delivering at its limit and rail pressure still stays well below target. The leak can be external (line, rail) or internal (injector return, relief valve). An external leak is a fire hazard: stop the engine and inspect it.

P0094 is typically detected when rail pressure drops too fast during overrun with injection cut off, or when more pump delivery than expected is needed at idle. Possible leaks are injectors with too much leak-off, fittings or relief valves; internal leakage can dilute the engine oil with fuel, so a rising oil level is a warning sign.

P00AF.en: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Module Performance
P00AF.desc: Boost control A here is an electronic actuator with its own electronics (a "smart" actuator), usually on the variable turbine geometry, with its own position sensor and controlled over a data bus or a pulsed signal. It checks itself and reports internal faults to the engine control module; documented examples are pattern errors, overcurrent and checksum errors. The control module cannot narrow down a fault inside the actuator further. P00AF is set when actuator A reports such an internal fault. Manufacturer bulletins recommend checking the vane mechanism for free movement and, if it moves freely, replacing only the actuator rather than the whole turbocharger.

Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. After a long standstill (eight hours in a documented case) engine and radiator should be at the same temperature. P00B6 is set at the next start when the engine and radiator coolant temperature sensors differ by more than a threshold that may depend on intake air temperature. A detected engine block heater cancels the test. From this alone the control module cannot tell which sensor is wrong.

P00B7.desc: When the engine is hot, the thermostat should be open and coolant should flow through the radiator. P00B7 is set when the engine coolant temperature is very high (above about 117 to 119 °C in documented cases) while the radiator side stays much colder, so too little coolant flows through the radiator. The usual cause is a thermostat stuck closed; low coolant, air in the system, a pump that delivers too little or a blocked radiator have the same effect. If the temperature keeps rising, stop driving to avoid engine damage.

P00B8.en: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 2
P00B8.desc: On engines with two intake paths, the control module compares the manifold pressure of bank 2 with the measured or calculated air quantity of that bank. P00B8 is set when the two do not fit together; the code does not say which value is wrong. As with its bank 1 counterpart, typical causes are an air leak, an exhaust gas recirculation valve that does not close, or a dirty or drifting sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

P00B9.en: Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low. Low Ambient Temperature
P00B9.desc: This code reports too low a pressure in the low-pressure fuel supply between the lift pump and the high-pressure pump under the additional condition of low ambient temperature. It separates cold-related supply problems from the general case. A typical mechanism, documented for diesel engines, is wax separating from insufficiently winterised fuel at sub-zero temperatures and clogging the filter or tank strainer. No manufacturer description naming this exact code, its thresholds or the vehicles using it was found.

P00BA.en: Low Fuel Pressure - Forced Limited Power
P00BA.desc: "Forced limited power" is a term for a protective strategy in which the engine control module deliberately limits engine power. Regulations require the check engine light to come on within seconds when such an emissions-relevant limp-home mode is active. These codes report the reason for the limitation; usually further codes point to the actual cause. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. P00BA: power has been limited because fuel pressure is too low, which protects the engine and the pump against running lean or losing rail pressure.

P00BB: power has been limited because the injectors do not deliver enough fuel, for example due to coking or wear; low rail pressure or missing injector coding after a replacement have a similar effect.

P00BC.en: Mass or Volume Air Flow A Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too Low
P00BC.desc: The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more. Regulations allow manufacturers to use one code for both directions or separate codes, as here. P00BC concerns air flow meter A. Typical causes are air entering behind the meter, a charge-air leak, a dirty meter or a restricted intake. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

P00C0.en: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit
P00C0.desc: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. P00C5.desc: The control module has detected that turbocharger B runs above its permitted maximum speed. P00C6.en: Fuel Rail Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking
P00C6.desc: Direct-injection engines release injection only once the rail has reached a minimum pressure. P00C6 is set when this pressure is not reached quickly enough while cranking, or, in another documented variant, when it drops below the minimum again right after the high-pressure start. Cranking then takes longer or the engine does not start. The check runs once per start; some manufacturers only enable it above a minimum tank level.

Rail pressure can then not be controlled, causing starting problems, stalling or reduced power.

P00CE.en: Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
P00CE.desc: After a long standstill (six hours in a documented case) all intake air temperature sensors, for example intake air, charge air cooler and manifold temperature, should read about the same. The control module compares them in pairs: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own plausibility code. This code is set when no pair agrees, so no single sensor can be identified as faulty. A detected engine preheater suspends the test. Since it runs only after a long standstill, the code may take a night to return after being cleared. Some vehicles also disable start-stop while this code is stored.

P00D1.en: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
P00D1.desc: This code concerns the heated oxygen sensor upstream of the catalytic converter (sensor 1) on bank 1. Unlike the heater circuit codes, which report an open or short circuit, this code means the heater is driven but does not bring the oxygen sensor to the expected temperature. One documented method, used where no current-measuring shunt is fitted, measures the internal impedance of the sensor element: a hot element has a low impedance. If the impedance stays above a limit that depends on the calculated element temperature and the voltage at the sensor connector, the heating is judged insufficient. The test runs once per trip. Typical causes are an aged heating element or added resistance from corrosion in the heater circuit. For this sensor position no manufacturer description of the test was found; the code appears in a manufacturer's code list, and the explanation follows the documented counterpart for sensor 2.

P00D5.en: HO2S Sensor Correlation Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 1 Sensor 2
P00D5.desc: During fuel cut-off on overrun the exhaust gas is pure air, so the oxygen sensors before and behind the catalytic converter must both report the same lean value. A documented method averages and normalises the signals of both sensors during fuel cut-off and sets the code when they differ by more than a limit; it runs once per drive cycle and needs several overrun phases. The code points to one of the sensors having drifted, not to the catalytic converter. The manufacturer documenting it uses wide-band sensors in both positions.

P00D7.en: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Temperature Too High
P00D7.desc: Bypass valve A is the electric compressor recirculation valve, mounted close to the hot compressor and turbine housing. This code reports that its temperature is too high. How the temperature is detected is not described in published manufacturer documents; a documented principle for comparable turbocharger solenoids estimates the coil temperature from current, supply voltage and duty cycle and protects the coil by limiting or switching it off. With the valve switched off, the compressor may surge when lifting off the throttle. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

P00DE.en: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P00DE.desc: With indirect charge air cooling, a water-to-air charge air cooler cools the charge air; it sits in a separate low-temperature coolant circuit with an electric pump and its own radiator. P00E3.en: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Stuck Open
P00E3.desc: Some engines, mainly hybrids and fuel-saving designs, have an exhaust heat exchanger behind the catalytic converter that transfers exhaust heat into the coolant for faster warm-up of engine and cabin. A bypass valve sends the exhaust either through the heat exchanger or around it. Documented diagnostics compare the coolant temperature rise at the heat exchanger with the commanded mode: if it behaves like bypass while recovery is commanded, or the other way round, the valve is considered stuck. P00E3 reports the valve stuck open. How "open" and "closed" map to bypass and recovery is not publicly documented, so both possible effects should be considered: slow warm-up and weak heating, or excessive coolant heat. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

P00E7.desc: After a long standstill (six hours in a documented case) all intake air temperature sensors, for example intake air, charge air cooler and manifold temperature, should read about the same. The control module compares them in pairs: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own plausibility code. This code is set when no pair agrees, so no single sensor can be identified as faulty. A detected engine preheater suspends the test. Since it runs only after a long standstill, the code may take a night to return after being cleared. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; bank 2 codes are intended for engines with two separate intake paths.

P00F2.desc: The humidity sensor measures the relative humidity of the intake air; on documented vehicles it is built into the mass air flow sensor or a combined sensor. The engine control module uses the value, for example, to correct torque and in emission models. One documented design is capacitive and reports humidity as a pulsed signal with a duty cycle that the control module converts back. P00F2 reports an open or general circuit fault of the humidity sensor. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found.

P00F7.en: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 2
P00F7.desc: This is the bank 2 counterpart of the comparison between barometric pressure and the pressure ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger. At low air flow the inlet pressure sensor reads close to ambient pressure, minus the small loss across the air filter, so it must match the barometric reading. The code is set when the difference is too large; a clogged air filter or a leaking intake hose on bank 2 can cause it as well as a drifting sensor. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

P00F8.en: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P00F8.desc: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly at the compressor outlet. It is a separate code family from the boost pressure sensor, which usually measures the pressure just ahead of the throttle; engines use it where the pressure behind the compressor is needed in addition, for example to judge the pressure loss across the charge air cooler or to protect against compressor surge. One manufacturer documents it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. P00F8 is the general circuit fault of this sensor. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

P00FB.en: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P00FB.desc: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FB means the signal voltage is above its valid range: typically a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, an open ground, or a failed sensor. It does not mean the boost really is too high – that would be P0234. The circuit is monitored continuously from key-on; comparable GM pressure sensors fail above 86–97 % of the reference for about 4 s. The engine then works with a substitute value and may limit boost. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found.

causes_en: Connector loose, not latched, or terminals corroded or spread
Harness chafed or broken near the turbocharger (heat, vibration)
Sensor with internal dropouts

P00FC.en: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
P00FC.desc: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FC covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal that are each too brief for the low or high code, or changes faster than real pressure can move. Comparable intermittent monitors count range violations per drive cycle – Ford's MAP check, for example, sets after 25 events. The FCA case for the sibling code P00F9 was a sensor not fully seated with an unlatched connector, exactly the kind of fault that produces erratic signals; heat and vibration near the turbocharger add to it. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found.

Loose or corroded positive or ground connections at either battery
150 A fuse or fuse array in the power distribution centre open or poorly contacting
Battery separation relay stuck
Main battery faulty
P00FD.en: Battery B State of Charge Performance
P00FD.desc: Battery B' here is not a hybrid high-voltage battery (those have codes from P0B27) but, in the only documented use by FCA/Stellantis, the 12 V auxiliary battery of the start-stop system. When the engine restarts automatically, a relay separates main and auxiliary battery so that the auxiliary one keeps the control units stable while the main battery cranks. The engine module sets P00FD if the auxiliary battery is disconnected on the first start, drops below about 8 V during an auto-start, or repeatedly falls below 10.3 V (counter reaches ten). Start-stop is then disabled; often it follows a jump start or many short trips. Whether the MIL comes on is not stated in the sources.

causes_en: Kinked, pinched or misrouted vapour line between tank and canister
Charcoal canister broken down, grains blocking lines or valves
Rollover or fill-limit valve at the tank stuck closed (e.g. after overfilling)
Purge valve or leak detection module faulty
Tank pressure sensor reading wrong
P00FE.en: EVAP System Tank Vapor Line Restricted/Blocked
P00FE.desc: The evaporative emission system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister and later purges it into the engine. P00FE means the vapour path between tank and canister is restricted or blocked. That matters because a blocked line can hide the tank side from the leak test and disturb tank venting and refuelling. Ford, where P00FE replaces its own code P144A, checks this once per drive cycle during the cruise leak test, while purging with the vent valve closed, and confirms suspicious pressure responses with an intrusive test. VW used the same code on the 2013–2019 Golf, where the diagnosis covers the purge valve and the leak detection module. Typical causes are kinked or pinched lines and charcoal grains from a broken canister.

Software or calibration fault in the body control module
Communication fault on the data bus
Engine control module faulty
P00FF.en: Body Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P00FF.desc: P00FF is an information code in the engine control module: the body control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks over the data bus for the check engine light. The engine module stores P00FF so that a generic OBD scanner can see why the MIL is on; the actual fault is stored in the body control module as B or U codes and must be read there. GM documents two cases – a 2020 Cadillac CT5 with climate flap actuator codes and 2025 full-size SUVs with U1962 – both cured by reprogramming the body control module, not by replacing parts. The mechanism matches other 'module requested MIL' codes such as P069E. P00FF itself causes no limp mode.

causes_en: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open
Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics)
Supply fuse or relay failed
Control module input faulty
P0100.en: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit
P0100.desc: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0100 means the control module gets no usable signal at all. Ford uses it for a broken sensing element on digital sensors (period longer than 1.3 ms, i.e. below about 0.78 kHz, for half a second); on GM's 3.0 V6 in the Saab 9-4X it is set at 0 Hz. Many systems with voltage sensors skip P0100 and report low or high directly. The engine then runs on air mass calculated from manifold pressure, throttle angle and speed; Ford also disables start-stop.

causes_en: Air leak between sensor and engine (cracked or loose intake duct, boost leak)
Contaminated sensing element (oil from oiled sport filter, dust)
Leaking or disconnected crankcase ventilation
Clogged or wrongly fitted air filter, modified intake
Aged sensor or poor contact in the wiring
P0101.en: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0101.desc: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0101 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the engine's state. GM petrol engines model the expected air flow from manifold pressure, throttle, speed and boost and blame the MAF if it is off by more than 20 g/s; GM diesels check the measured-to-estimated ratio (0.8–1.2) with EGR closed; Bosch ME9 compares it with the throttle angle. Common causes are air leaks after the sensor, a soiled element (oiled sport filters) or a disconnected crankcase vent; GM also documents a bad crimp in the fuse box. Ford uses P0068 instead. Two trips are needed.

causes_en: Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector corroded or loose
Sensor electronics failed
Missing supply voltage (fuse, relay) or poor ground
Large leak or disconnected duct between sensor and throttle
P0102.en: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Low
P0102.desc: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0102 means the signal is below its electrical lower limit – a frequency that is too low or a voltage that is too low. Documented limits: GM petrol 450 Hz or less, GM diesel below 276 Hz, Ford digital below 1.5 kHz for 5 s, Ford analogue below 0.244 V. 'Low' describes the signal: typically an open or grounded signal wire, missing supply voltage or failed electronics. Saab notes that a large leak between sensor and throttle can also cause it. GM and Saab need two trips; the engine runs on a calculated substitute value.
