P014F.en: O2 Sensor Slow Response - Lean to Rich Bank 2 Sensor 1
P014F.desc: The upstream oxygen sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) is the main control sensor for the air-fuel mixture. 'Slow response' means the signal transition itself is too sluggish – it takes too long to pass between two voltage levels. This code covers the lean-to-rich direction, tested when fuel returns or the control module briefly enriches the mixture. Bank 2 only exists on V and boxer engines. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB and on the published principle of testing an upstream sensor by periodic mixture modulation, where a sensor time constant above a load-dependent limit counts as a fault. CARB requires separate detection of slow and delayed faults in each direction (phased in from 2009 for downstream and 2011 for upstream sensors).

causes_en: Wiring or connector of the bank 2 upstream sensor damaged, corroded or wet
Oxygen sensor faulty internally
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or mixture fault (plausibility versions)
Control module or sensor interface chip faulty
P0150.desc: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0150 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0130. Ford used it up to 2010 as the collective code for wiring faults of the bank 2 wide-band sensor reported by the interface chip and has used specific codes since 2011 (P0151, P0152, P2240/P2247/P2254). Other makers fill it as for bank 1 – an interface voltage check, a collective code or a plausibility test. No bank 2-specific manufacturer thresholds were found. If P0130 and P0150 appear together, look for a shared cause such as supply, ground or the control module. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes_en: Signal wire (or a wide-band sensor wire) shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on exhaust or gearbox
Sensor faulty or poisoned (permanently lean signal)
Large exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or misfires
Connector wet or corroded
P0151.en: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0151.desc: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0151 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0131. On switching sensors the signal stays below about 40–50 mV in closed loop with a stoichiometric target (GM LT4: 285 of 350 samples; GM 3.0/3.6 V6 within 50 s); on wide-band sensors the interface chip reports a sensor wire shorted to ground. Two trips. A genuinely lean bank 2 shows up as P0174 rather than this code. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to the heater supply or battery voltage (melted or chafed harness)
Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short)
Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire (GM reads its bias voltage)
Sensor contaminated by silicone, coolant or oil
P0152.en: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0152.desc: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0152 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0132. Switching sensors: GM above 1050 mV (100 of 125 samples, after warm-up), Ford above 1.1 V for 10 s – a reading the sensor cannot produce itself, so heater or battery voltage on the signal wire is the usual cause; GM also reads an open wire as high. Wide-band sensors: a sensor wire shorted to voltage. P0152 together with P0158 points to a shared short in the bank 2 harness. Two trips. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes_en: Aged, sooted or poisoned upstream sensor (oil, silicone, coolant, additives)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (manifold gasket, crack)
Sensor heater weak or intermittent (sensor too cold)
Mixture fault: air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor
Wiring resistance or aftermarket sensor with different characteristics
P0153.en: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0153.desc: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0153 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0133: the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes. GM measures passively the average response time in both directions across 300/400–600 mV over 60 s and also fails too few transitions; Ford modulates the mixture itself and evaluates amplitude, signal line length or response times. The test runs once per drive at warm part load, two trips. The previous obdex title of this code wrongly repeated P0152's 'High Voltage'.

causes_en: Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire, connector loose or corroded
Sensor faulty (cell high-resistance, worn out)
Sensor heater faulty – sensor does not get hot enough
Control module bias or measuring circuit faulty
P0154.en: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0154.desc: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0154 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0134: the sensor delivers no moving signal and the control module only sees its own bias voltage. On GM's 3.0/3.6 V6 the code is set when the signal stays at 350–550 mV after heater warm-up, within about 15 s, in closed loop after 150 s of running; two trips. Ford's Bosch wide-band systems have used P2240 instead since 2011. A failed heater (P0155) can also lead to this code. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes_en: Heater element of the sensor burnt out (sensor must be replaced)
Fuse or relay of the heater supply faulty
Heater wiring or connector open, corroded or shorted
Heater driver in the control module faulty
P0155.en: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0155.desc: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 2 (sensor 1) has its own electric heater. P0155 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0135: the heater current is outside its window or the driver voltage does not follow the command. GM fails it outside 0.3–3.1 A (8 s or 8 of 10 samples, two trips); Ford outside roughly 0.22–0.465 A minimum to 3 A, with related codes for heater temperature control (P0050) and resistance (P0059). Closed loop on bank 2 then starts late after a cold start, and the sensor checks are suspended. P0135 together with P0155 points to a shared supply or fuse.

causes_en: Downstream sensor aged or poisoned (stays in the middle band)
Signal or ground wire open or high-resistance, connector corroded
Sensor heater failed (sensor stays cold)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
P0156.desc: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0156 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0136. Ford sets it as 'no activity' when the downstream sensor on bank 2 never swings outside a narrow band around 0.45 V in its functional check, if needed after forced mixture changes, once per drive cycle. Exhaust systems with a Y-pipe have only one downstream sensor, which counts as bank 1. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground or melted against the exhaust
Sensor faulty (cracked element, thermal shock from water)
Signal circuit open (counts as low on Ford)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (lean reading)
P0157.en: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0157.desc: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0157 means the signal stays below the lower limit, the bank 2 counterpart of P0137. GM sets it below 50 mV (two trips), on its 3.0 V6 within 50 s in closed loop; Ford uses its pull-up resistance check and counts both open circuit and short to ground as P0157. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short)
Signal circuit open or high-resistance (GM bias logic)
P0158.en: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0158.desc: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0158 means the signal stays above the upper limit, the bank 2 counterpart of P0138. A zirconia sensor can hardly produce more than about 1 V, so readings above 1.05–1.15 V point to an outside voltage such as the heater supply on the signal wire; GM also sees an open circuit here because of its bias voltage. Ford: above 1.1 V for 10 s; GM: above 1050 mV. From 2020 Ford also uses a 1.9 V limit depending on the feedback circuit. Monitored continuously, two trips. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

P0159.en: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0159.desc: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0159 means the downstream sensor on bank 2 reacts too slowly to mixture changes, typically measured around fuel cut-off. Thresholds are documented only for the bank 1 counterpart P0139 (Subaru: 0.51 s rich to lean, 2 s lean to rich); Jaguar Land Rover lists P0159 for its mid-cat sensor after water-induced thermal shock. Newer GM and Ford systems report direction-specific codes P013C/P013D and P014A/P014B instead. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

P015A.en: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1
P015A.desc: The upstream oxygen sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) is the main control sensor for the air-fuel mixture. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late, or does not reach the target level at all, after the mixture has changed. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, usually tested during deceleration fuel cut-off. GM uses this on switching (narrow-band) sensors: while the fuel cut-off for the downstream tests is running, it measures how long the upstream sensor takes to start dropping from above 680 mV and fails a filtered delay above about 0.58 s after one trip. Conditions include warm engine, 40–78 mph and a hot converter. CARB requires separate detection of slow and delayed faults in each direction (phased in from 2009 for downstream and 2011 for upstream sensors).

causes_en: Learning conditions (overrun phases, temperatures) met too rarely
Control module software
Injectors outside tolerance or unstable fuel pressure
Injector wiring or sensors faulty
Engine control module faulty
P015E.en: Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Fuel Timing Control
P015E.desc: Diesel fuel systems correct injection timing and quantity in closed loop, often with learning routines that run during suitable overrun phases. CARB requires a fault when such feedback control does not start within a manufacturer-defined time. P015E is the code of this kind for injection timing control: the closed-loop correction does not become active in time, or does not learn. It belongs to a family of similar codes – Ford's 2023 diesels, for example, set the sister code P016D when rail pressure adaptation has learned nothing after 300 s. No manufacturer document describing P015E itself, or its threshold, was found; the description rests on CARB and the sister code. Frequent causes are learning conditions that occur too rarely, software, or injectors outside tolerance.

causes_en: Crankshaft wheel adaptation not learned or speed signal disturbed
Injector deviating strongly or injector circuit fault
Control module software
P015F.en: Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Cylinder Balance Control
P015F.desc: Cylinder balance control evens out the contribution of individual cylinders – on diesels by adjusting each injector's quantity based on crankshaft speed fluctuations. P015F, by its title, is set when this closed-loop control does not become active within the expected time after starting, for example because the crankshaft wheel has not been learned or the conditions are missing. No manufacturer using P015F was found: Ford's 2023 diesels run cylinder balancing (maximum correction 3.5–15 mg per stroke) but report problems as P0263–P0284. The description therefore rests on CARB's requirement for feedback controls and that comparable function; causes are derived, not documented.

causes_en: Signal or ground wire open or high-resistance, connector corroded
Sensor dead, poisoned or damaged by thermal shock
Heater failed or fuse blown by a heater short
Signal wire shorted to voltage
P0160.en: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0160.desc: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor used for converter monitoring and downstream mixture trim; it exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0160 means the sensor shows no change in voltage although it is heated and the engine is in closed loop; the control module only sees its own bias voltage, so the circuit is open or high-resistance or the sensor is dead. On GM's 3.0/3.6 V6 the code sets within 15 s after more than 150 s of running; newer GM systems apply 1900 mV and treat above 1700 mV as open; two trips. Ford does not use P0160 and reports 'no activity' as P0156. A failed heater (P0161) can also cause it. The previous obdex title mixed in 'Slow Response', which is P0159. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Heater element of the sensor burnt out
Heater wiring, connector or fuse open or corroded
Short in the heater circuit (current too high)
Driver in the engine module faulty
P0161.en: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0161.desc: The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 2 (sensor 2) has an electric heater so that it reaches working temperature quickly. P0161 concerns this heater circuit and its performance. GM measures the current through its low-side driver and fails it outside 0.3–2.9 A on the supercharged V8 (8 of 10 samples, two trips). Ford checks the driver voltage continuously and the current once per drive cycle once the sensor is estimated above about 120 °C; the lower limit is 0.22–0.55 A depending on sensor type, the upper 3 A. Without heat the sensor becomes active late or not at all, so P0159/P0160 can follow; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Sensor faulty or damaged by thermal shock
Wiring or connector under the car damaged
Engine module software (Jaguar Land Rover)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
P0162.desc: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0162 is the general circuit code of this sensor, the counterpart of P0142. Jaguar Land Rover assigns the code to that sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes; no thresholds are published for sensor 3, so the logic follows the sensor 2 checks. The previous obdex titles from P0162 to P0165 were shifted by one position; P0162 had carried the heater title of P0161. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed or melted)
Sensor faulty
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (apparently lean)
Engine module software (Jaguar Land Rover)
P0163.en: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0163.desc: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0163 means the signal stays close to 0 V – typically the signal wire is shorted to ground; on some modules an open circuit is also reported this way, and an exhaust leak ahead of the sensor can make it read lean. For the bank 2 sensor 2 counterpart GM uses below 50 mV within 50 s, Ford a pull-up resistance check (short below 10 Ω, open above 1 MΩ). Jaguar Land Rover assigns the code to that sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes; no thresholds are published for sensor 3, so the logic follows the sensor 2 checks. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to voltage or to the heater wire
Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short)
Sensor ground open (GM logic)
Engine module software (Jaguar Land Rover)
P0164.en: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0164.desc: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0164 means the signal is above about 1.05–1.15 V. A switching sensor can produce at most about 1 V, so anything higher is electrical: a short to voltage or to the heater wire, or – on GM's bias logic – an open ground. Ford's over-voltage test (above 1.1 V for 10 s) explicitly covers downstream sensors 2 and 3. Jaguar Land Rover assigns the code to that sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes; no thresholds are published for sensor 3, so the logic follows the sensor 2 checks. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Sensor aged or contaminated
Sensor heater weak
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Wiring or connector high-resistance
P0165.en: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0165.desc: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0165 means sensor 3 reacts too slowly to mixture changes, typically measured around fuel cut-off as for the downstream sensor 2 (Subaru limits for P0139: 0.51 s rich to lean, 2 s lean to rich). No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0162–P0164 and P0167 for this sensor. The description rests on CARB's response requirement for downstream sensors and the sensor 2 logic. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Signal or ground wire open, connector corroded
Sensor dead
Heater failed (sensor stays cold)
Engine control module
P0166.en: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0166.desc: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0166 means sensor 3 shows no voltage change or stays in the control module's bias band – an open or high-resistance circuit, or a cold or dead sensor. For downstream sensor 2 GM sets the equivalent code when the voltage does not change after heater warm-up (within 15 s) or sits at 401–548 mV. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Jaguar Land Rover does not list it and Ford uses only heater codes for sensor 3. A failed heater (P0167) can cause it. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Heater element burnt out
Heater wiring, connector or fuse
Short circuit (current above 3 A)
Engine module driver or software (Jaguar Land Rover)
P0167.en: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0167.desc: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0167 concerns its heater. Ford checks the driver voltage continuously and the heater current once per drive cycle when the sensor is estimated above about 120 °C and has heated for 30 s; below 0.22–0.55 A (depending on sensor type) or above 3 A is a fault, and the heater resistance has its own code (P0061). Jaguar Land Rover lists P0167 for its post-cat sensor of the second bank. A cold sensor can lead to P0165/P0166. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes_en: Fuel cooler (air or water cooler in the return) dirty or faulty, coolant circuit disturbed
Very little fuel in the tank at high load or heat
Excessive return flow from worn high-pressure pump or injectors, or faulty overflow valve
Fuel temperature sensor drifting and reading too high
Engine overheating or overload (trailer, gradient)
P0168.desc: P0168 is not a sensor fault but an operating condition, almost only on diesels: the fuel temperature sensor reports fuel hotter than a protective limit. The fuel heats up through the return flow from the high-pressure pump and injectors, especially with little fuel in the tank, at idle after full load, in hot weather or with a failed fuel cooler; one manufacturer patent names about 80 °C as the upper limit to protect seals, against a normal range of roughly 5–60 °C. On Saab's Bosch EDC16 diesels the code means an engine protection function is active and injection quantity is reduced. No manufacturer threshold was found, and GM's and Ford's diesel summaries do not use P0168. Whether the warning light comes on depends on the manufacturer.

causes_en: Wrong fuel (E85 in a non-flex-fuel vehicle, ethanol content outside calibration)
Water or contamination in the fuel
Fuel composition sensor drifting (value in range but wrong)
Control module software
P0169.desc: According to its title, P0169 means the control module has detected a fuel composition outside what is expected – wrong fuel or an impermissible ethanol or water content – while the composition sensor itself works. None of the manufacturer OBD documents checked (GM, Ford) uses the code: GM reports water or conductive fuel via the ethanol sensor frequency as P2269, and Ford has had no composition sensor since 2000. Claims that diesel makers use it for misfuelling or water could not be verified. The description therefore rests on CARB, which lists the fuel composition sensor as a monitored component, and on component information. Unrecognised fuel usually also shows up as mixture adaptation codes.

causes_en: Oxygen sensor heater not working (fuse, fuse holder, wiring, heater element)
Oxygen sensor sluggish or aged
Control module software (false setting)
Engine not warming up (thermostat open, coolant sensor)
P016A.en: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control
P016A.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. Closed loop needs a heated, working oxygen sensor and plausible engine data. P016A means the mixture control did not switch to closed loop within the calibrated time after starting; the engine then runs on map values with higher emissions but no actual limp mode. CARB requires this check, and since 2019 also after every automatic restart in start-stop systems. Bentley and other VW group petrol engines set it together with oxygen sensor heater codes when the heater fuse holder was damaged; Ram's 3.0 EcoDiesel listed it in bulletins fixed with new software and sensors. Time limits are not public.

causes_en: Fuel pressure too high / high-pressure pump or regulator fault (direct injection)
Leaking injectors
Purge valve open
Oxygen sensor or air flow/pressure sensor offset, control module software
P016B.en: Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Rich
P016B.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P016B means the mixture control as a whole has reached its lower limit: it already removes as much fuel as allowed and the mixture is still rich. In substance it matches P0172, but without a bank reference – for manufacturers whose strategy evaluates the control loop as a whole. CARB requires a fault once the adaptation has used up its range. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Hyundai documents the lean counterpart P016C. Typical causes are those of a rich mixture: excessive fuel pressure, leaking injectors or an open purge valve.

causes_en: Air leak (intake, crankcase ventilation)
Fuel pressure or delivery too low
Wrongly learned adaptation / control module software
Air flow or pressure sensor reading low, injectors clogged
P016C.en: Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Lean
P016C.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P016C means the mixture control as a whole has reached its upper limit: it already adds as much fuel as allowed and still cannot reach lambda 1. In substance it matches P0171, without a bank reference. Hyundai documents it on the 2021 Elantra 2.0: if the fuel adaptation was learned wrongly after starts below −10 °C, the engine could stall when stopping or at idle and set P016C; new engine software changed the learning logic. Otherwise the usual lean causes apply: air leaks, low fuel delivery or an air flow sensor reading low.

causes_en: Rail pressure sensor drifting (wrong slope)
Volume or pressure control valve sticking or worn
Unstable low-pressure supply (filter, lift pump, air in system)
Fuel leak or high injector return flow
Control module software
P016D.en: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control
P016D.desc: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016D means the pressure control has not settled into closed loop, or has not learned, in the time allowed. Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 and 3.0 litre) set it when, within the learning conditions – target rail pressure 600–1300 bar, fuel at most 40 °C – no new adaptation factor has been learned after 300 s; the check only runs while the rail pressure sensor and its supply are fault-free. Ford reports adaptation at its limit separately as P228E/P228F. Use on petrol engines was not found. Often there are no noticeable symptoms.

causes_en: Rail pressure sensor or its contacts/wiring (corrosion) giving a falsely high signal
Pressure or volume control valve sticking (lets too much through)
Return line from control valve or rail blocked or kinked
Control module software or calibration
P016E.en: Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too High
P016E.desc: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016E means the controller is already at its limit in the 'reduce pressure' direction and the measured pressure is still above target. That can be real overpressure – a control valve that lets too much through or a blocked return – or a falsely high reading. Volvo and Mack document P016E on their 11 and 13 litre truck diesels together with P0194, caused by corroded contacts at the rail pressure sensor; the fix is a new sensor and internal harness. No public thresholds exist; Ford reports the comparable condition as P228F. Use on passenger-car diesels or petrol engines was not documented.

causes_en: Weak low-pressure supply: lift/tank pump, pump control module, clogged filter
Connector or ground problems (corrosion, water) at pump module, low-pressure sensor or ground point
Pressure relief valve open or its control circuit interrupted
Worn high-pressure pump or internal leak
Engine control module software
P016F.en: Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too Low
P016F.desc: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016F means the controller is at its limit in the 'more pressure' direction and the actual pressure still stays below target. Which circuit is meant depends on the manufacturer: Volvo and Mack use it for rail pressure, for example as a follow-up when their electronic pressure relief valve stays open (P009B); on FCA's 3.0 EcoDiesel it concerns the regulated low-pressure supply via the fuel pump control module and appears with P025C and P01C6, partly fixed by new engine software. No public thresholds exist. Weak supply pumps, clogged filters and corroded connectors or grounds are typical causes.

causes_en: Air flow sensor dirty or drifting
Air leak or crankcase ventilation leaking
Injection quantity error (diesel: injector drift, rail pressure sensor; petrol: injectors, fuel pressure)
Oxygen or NOx sensor offset
P0170.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0170 is the older, direction-neutral code for 'mixture adaptation of bank 1 out of range'; whether lean or rich has to be read from the trim values. Users are Mercedes-Benz petrol engines, which often set P0170/P0173 instead of P0171–P0175 – a Mercedes-Benz magazine for independent workshops reports that cleaning or replacing the air flow sensor most often cures it – and Ford's 6.7 litre diesel, where it flags a fuel quantity error above 15 % in either direction from its fuel mass observer. GM and Ford petrol engines do not use it. Two trips.

causes_en: Air leak after the air flow sensor (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line)
Crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick)
Air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air)
Fuel pressure or delivery too low (weak pump, clogged filter, regulator, tank nearly empty)
Injectors clogged, or exhaust leak ahead of the oxygen sensor
P0171.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0171 means long-term trim on bank 1 is at its upper limit: the module already adds the maximum fuel and the mixture still stays lean. GM sets it at a long-term factor of about 1.30–1.36 (+30–36 %, engine-specific), Ford above +25 % with short-term trim above +1 %; it needs two trips and is suspended during heavy purge flow or intrusive tests. GM bulletins repeatedly trace it to leaking crankcase ventilation hoses or pipes on V6 and V8 engines; Ford found leaking direct injectors. P0171 together with P0174 points to a shared cause. Diagnosis hint: trims very high only at idle and normal under load point to an air leak; trims rising with load point to fuel shortage or an air flow sensor reading low. The oxygen sensor only reports what is in the exhaust and is rarely the cause.

causes_en: Purge valve stuck open or charcoal canister saturated
Leaking or dripping injectors (also direct injection)
Fuel pressure too high (faulty regulator, blocked return, regulator vacuum hose)
Fuel in the engine oil (short trips, leaking injectors), vapour via crankcase ventilation
Clogged air filter or intake, air flow sensor reading high; flex-fuel: wrongly learned ethanol content
P0172.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0172 means long-term trim on bank 1 is at its lower limit: the module already removes the maximum fuel and the mixture still stays rich. GM separates purge influence carefully: before the first purge it evaluates passively (factor 0.70 or below, i.e. −30 %), afterwards it closes the purge valve briefly for an active test, so a full charcoal canister is not counted as a fault. Ford only evaluates with purge off, at −25 %. Two trips. Bulletins name an open purge valve, leaking direct injectors and, on flex-fuel vehicles, a wrongly learned ethanol content. A permanently rich mixture can overheat the converter and dilutes the oil.

causes_en: Air flow sensor dirty or faulty
Air leak on bank 2 or at the crankcase ventilation
Fuel pressure or bank 2 injectors
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 oxygen sensor
P0173.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0173 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0170: a direction-neutral trim fault, so whether bank 2 runs lean or rich has to be read from the trim values. It is mainly used by Mercedes-Benz V6 and V8 petrol engines instead of P0174/P0175; their workshop magazine names the air flow sensor as the most frequent fix. P0170 and P0173 together point to a common cause. No manufacturer threshold was found; the description rests on CARB's fuel system monitoring requirement and that publication. Two trips.

causes_en: Air leak after the air flow sensor on bank 2 (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line)
Crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick)
Air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air)
Fuel pressure or delivery too low (weak pump, clogged filter, regulator, tank nearly empty)
Injectors clogged, or exhaust leak ahead of the oxygen sensor
P0174.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0174 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0171 and only exists on V and boxer engines with separate mixture control per bank. The limits match: GM a long-term factor of about 1.30 (engine-specific), Ford above +25 % with short-term trim above +1 %; an older Saab V6 flagged more than 25 % deviation for 20 s. Two trips, no limp mode. P0174 alone points to a leak, injector or exhaust leak on bank 2; together with P0171 to a shared cause such as the air flow sensor, fuel pressure or crankcase ventilation – exactly what several GM bulletins describe. Diagnosis hint: trims very high only at idle and normal under load point to an air leak; trims rising with load point to fuel shortage or an air flow sensor reading low. The oxygen sensor only reports what is in the exhaust and is rarely the cause.

causes_en: Purge valve stuck open or charcoal canister saturated
Leaking or dripping injectors on bank 2 (also direct injection)
Fuel pressure too high (faulty regulator, blocked return, regulator vacuum hose)
Fuel in the engine oil (short trips, leaking injectors), vapour via crankcase ventilation
P0175.desc: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0175 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0172: long-term trim at its lower limit, mixture still rich. GM evaluates it like bank 1 with a passive test before the first purge and an active test with the purge valve closed; Ford at −25 % with purge off. Two trips, no limp mode. P0175 alone points to a bank-specific cause such as a leaking injector on bank 2; together with P0172 to fuel pressure, purge, ethanol learning on flex-fuel vehicles or fuel in the oil. GM and Ford bulletins document wrongly learned ethanol content and a purge valve stuck open as causes.

causes_en: Flex-fuel sensor electrically failed (corrosion from road salt)
Connector or wire corroded, open or shorted
Supply (relay, fuse) missing
Engine control module
P0176.desc: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0176 is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. GM's current documents use P0178/P0179 instead, so P0176 is mainly to be expected on older flex-fuel vehicles or other makes. GM issued a special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models (10 years/150,000 miles) because road salt could make the sensor fail electrically, turning on the MIL and disabling remote start. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information.

causes_en: Sensor drifting or dirty inside
Water or contamination in the fuel
Loose contact in the connector
Control module or software
P0177.desc: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0177 means the signal lies within the valid frequency range but is implausible – it jumps, changes without a refuelling event or does not match the mixture adaptation. Such sensors measure permittivity, conductivity and temperature and compare them with tables of known blends. GM's documents only list low, high and P2269, so no manufacturer threshold for P0177 was found; the description rests on CARB's rationality requirement and component information.

causes_en: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
Sensor without supply (relay, fuse, ground)
Sensor electrically failed (corrosion)
Engine control module
P0178.desc: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0178 means the frequency is too low. GM sets it below 45 Hz with 50 of 63 samples failing at 100 ms intervals (about 6 s), monitored continuously with the powertrain relay above 11 V; two trips. 'Low' refers to the frequency, not to the ethanol content: an open wire, missing supply or short to ground gives 0 Hz. The control module then uses a learned or substitute ethanol value. GM's road-salt special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models concerns exactly this kind of electrical failure.

causes_en: Sensor electronics faulty
Interference or short on the signal wire
Water or conductive fuel near the P2269 limit
Engine control module
P0179.desc: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0179 means the frequency is above the physically possible range for E100 plus tolerance. GM sets it between 155 and 185 Hz (50 of 63 samples, two trips); above 185 Hz it sets P2269 instead, because such a high value indicates water or conductive fuel rather than a sensor fault. Typical causes of P0179 are failed sensor electronics or interference on the signal wire. With a falsely high ethanol value the mixture tends to run rich.

causes_en: Wiring or connector open or corroded
Sensor faulty (moisture in the housing)
Engine control module
P017A.en: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P017A.desc: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017A is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found: VW uses P017B/P017C/P017E for its sensor, and Ford's summaries list its own codes. Ford's published summaries still use its own codes P1289/P1290 for this sensor (fault below 0.244 V or above 4.96 V for 5 s). The description rests on CARB and component information. On a sensor fault the control module typically uses a modelled temperature and runs the radiator fan.

causes_en: Sensor damaged by moisture (O-ring)
Genuine temperature problem (air in cooling system, thermostat)
Contact resistance at the connector
Software or calibration
P017B.en: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P017B.desc: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017B means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – for example it does not fit other temperature sensors after a long standstill or does not rise as expected. Audi documents it on 2019–2021 V8 TFSI models and Bentley on V8 models from 2018 onwards, together with a cooling system fault code and a red coolant warning: a damaged O-ring at the sensor tip lets water into the housing and damages the sensing element, often intermittently; the fix is a new sender. GM lists P017B only as an exclusion condition in its diesel software. Thresholds are not public.

causes_en: Water or coolant inside the sensor (O-ring damaged)
Signal wire chafed against ground
Sensor shorted internally
Engine control module
P017C.en: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P017C.desc: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017C means the signal voltage is too low – a short to ground of the signal wire or a short inside the sensor; the control module would read an implausibly hot cylinder head. 'Low' refers to the signal, not the temperature. Audi and Bentley document it as a short to ground, most often caused by water inside sender G407 after O-ring damage. Ford flags the same condition on its own code below 0.244 V for 5 s. A substitute value is used; an overheating warning with a cold engine is a typical sign.

causes_en: Sensor faulty (series fault on Ford 5.0 litre 2019)
Connector unplugged or corroded, wire open
Signal wire shorted to voltage
Engine control module
P017D.en: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P017D.desc: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017D means the signal voltage is too high – the sensor or wire is open or shorted to voltage, and the control module would read an implausibly cold head. Ford's published summaries flag this under its own code P1289 above 4.96 V for 5 s, but a 2019 bulletin for the F-150 and Mustang 5.0 litre names P1289 and/or P017D and replaces the sensor – so at least that calibration also sets the generic code. GM lists P017D only as an exclusion condition in its diesel software. The engine uses substitute values; the radiator fan typically runs constantly.

causes_en: Moisture inside the sensor (O-ring)
Loose contact at connector or pin
Wire broken by engine movement or heat
Sensor faulty internally
P017E.en: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P017E.desc: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017E covers intermittent interruptions or an erratic signal. The VW group explicitly uses it for 'open circuit or loose contact', not only for jumps: on Audi and Bentley V8 engines moisture inside sender G407 after O-ring damage makes it fail intermittently, and an improved part has been introduced. Loose contacts and wires broken by heat or engine movement are other causes. The detection logic is not public.

causes_en: Leak detection pump filter dirty or blocked
Moisture or ice in filter or hose
Hose between filter and pump kinked or blocked
Pump module faulty (wrong reference)
P017F.en: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Module Air Filter Restricted
P017F.desc: Leak detection pump modules in the evaporative emission system (for example Bosch's DM-TL, used by VW, BMW, Porsche, Volvo, Mini, Land Rover and Kia/Hyundai) draw fresh air through their own filter, often mounted separately via a hose; at rest the charcoal canister is also vented through it. P017F means this filter is restricted – by dust, mud or water when fitted near a wheel arch. The reference measurement of the pump and the venting are then distorted, and the tank can pull a vacuum. A GM patent describes detection via the pressure difference across the filter during purge (above about 8 inH2O for 10–20 s). No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's requirement to monitor evaporative system components and these component sources.

causes_en: Wire or connector open or corroded
Sensor faulty
Control module reference or ground
P0180.desc: Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. P0180 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. None of the manufacturers checked (GM, Ford, Saab/Bosch, Nissan) uses it – they report P0181–P0184 instead. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information. With a sensor fault the control module uses a substitute temperature (Saab EDC16: 50 °C).

causes_en: Sensor drifting (characteristic shifted)
Comparison sensor wrong (charge air, coolant, intake air)
Block heater or unusual temperatures (cold fuel during self-test)
Wiring or connector (e.g. routing at the pump unit)
Control module software
P0181.en: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0181.desc: Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. P0181 is the plausibility check: after a long standstill fuel temperature must be close to another temperature sensor. Ford's 2023 diesels compare it after 6 h with the charge air cooler outlet temperature (limit 40 °C, or 20 °C without a block heater); GM diesels compare it after 8 h with a reference sensor (20 °C, two trips). Bulletins show other causes: Ford may set P0181 during a running self-test with fuel below 10 °C and warns against replacing parts without a confirmed fault; Nissan Rogues set it because of misrouted wires at the pump unit; Ford's 2018 6.7 diesel needed new software.

P018A.desc: Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). GM checks actively whether the sensor responds: if the pump duty sits at its limit for 5 s or the pressure error varies too little, the module changes pump output and fails the sensor if pressure moves 30 kPa or less – a 'frozen' sensor; two trips. P018F.en: Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Frequent Activation
P018F.desc: Common-rail diesels have a pressure relief valve in the rail – usually a spring-loaded valve, on some truck engines electronically controlled. It opens on overpressure and then holds a low limp-home pressure; every opening wears the seat, and after many openings it may no longer close tightly. P018F means the valve has opened too often: the control module recognises openings from the rail pressure trace (overshoot, then a steep drop to the limp-home level) and counts them. The code therefore usually points to an underlying problem – the pressure control repeatedly lets overpressure build up. No manufacturer document describing P018F was found; the function and counting logic come from patents on large engines (example: opening at about 1950 bar, then about 800 bar).

P0190.en: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P0190.desc: The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines – a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference. P0190 is the general circuit code used when a manufacturer does not split low and high; GM and Ford use P0192/P0193 instead. Bosch EDC16 diesels (Saab/Opel 1.9) report P0190 with a fault type byte, and a Saab bulletin traces it to corrosion in the sensor connector, sometimes with no restart for up to 15 minutes. On a sensor fault the engine runs on a calculated pressure in limp mode – on Saab's 3.0 V6 diesel with at most 40 MPa rail pressure and 20 % pedal.

P0191.en: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0191.desc: The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines; it is either a three-wire sensor (5 V reference, ground, signal rising with pressure, about 0.5 V at 0 bar) or a digital SENT sensor with two measuring channels. The engine module uses it as the feedback signal for rail pressure control. P0191 means the signal is electrically valid but not believable – stuck, offset or drifting. Manufacturers check it differently: Ford's 2023 diesels and GM's diesels test the offset with the system depressurised (Ford before starting after 10 min and 12 s after switch-off, window about 0.25–0.38 V; GM 6.5–14 % of supply); GM petrol direct injection compares the two SENT channels (limit 1.0 MPa); Saab's V6 diesel flags a large target deviation while the signal barely moves. GM treats it as a one-trip fault. Ford petrol direct injection uses P0087/P0088 instead. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power.

P0195.en: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0195.desc: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0195 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. With analogue sensors most manufacturers use P0197/P0198 instead. The documented use is Ford's 2023 diesels with a digital SENT oil temperature sensor: P0195 is set when the sensor reports a status or data fault for 5 s, while a complete loss of communication is U0667. The module then uses a substitute value (Saab: 100 °C), and functions relying on oil temperature are restricted.

P019A.en: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 3
P019A.desc: Sensor 3 on bank 1 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick; it exists on Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (on both banks) and on Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late after a mixture change – unlike 'slow response' (P0145/P0165), where the transition itself is too flat. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, tested during forced fuel cut-off. For sensor 2, GM checks whether the signal falls below 450 mV before a calibrated air mass has passed; behind two converters their oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0142ff/P0162ff for sensor 3 – so the description rests on CARB's response requirement and the sensor 2 logic. There is no limp mode; the converter monitor cannot complete.

P019E.en: Alternative Fuel Tank A Pressure Sensor Circuit
P019E.desc: These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. CNG is stored at up to about 250 bar (3600 psi); a regulator reduces it to a few bar for the gas rail and injectors. The tank pressure sensor A sits at or in the regulator; together with the tank temperature it gives the gas level, and it decides whether gas operation is possible. P019E is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. Ford's earlier bi-fuel CNG system showed the gauge as empty on a tank pressure sensor fault. Typical reaction: gas operation is blocked and a bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found; GM's bulletins only state that faults are reported like on petrol models. The description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design.

P01A3.en: Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit
P01A3.desc: These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. CNG is stored at up to about 250 bar (3600 psi); a regulator reduces it to a few bar for the gas rail and injectors. The gas rail pressure sensor measures the regulated low pressure at the rail – on GM's Impala controlled by the engine module to 68–130 psi (about 4.7–9 bar) – so that injection time can be matched to the actual gas pressure and density. P01A3 is the general circuit fault of this sensor. Without a valid rail pressure the module cannot dose gas correctly; Ford's earlier bi-fuel system started on gas only above about 5.2 bar and otherwise stayed on petrol. Typical reaction: gas operation is blocked and a bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found; GM's bulletins only state that faults are reported like on petrol models. The description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design.

P01A8.en: Alternative Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low
P01A8.desc: These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. Typical reasons are a nearly empty tank close to the regulator's minimum inlet pressure, a shut-off valve that does not open fully, clogged high- or low-pressure filters, or a regulator that sticks or ices up when its coolant heating fails. Typical reaction: gas operation is blocked and a bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol. P01A9.en: Alternative Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too High

P01AA.en: Alternative Fuel Tank Temperature Sensor Circuit
P01AA.desc: These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. The tank temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor: with CNG there is no float, so the gas level is calculated from tank pressure and tank temperature (GM: full at about 3600 psi at 21 °C, empty at about 400–500 psi). On GM's 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel the sensor is built into the tank and cannot be replaced separately. P01AA is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design.

P01AF.en: Alternative Fuel Tank A Level Sensor Circuit
P01AF.desc: These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. Tank level sensor A only exists where there is a real sender – typically LPG tanks with a float whose position is transmitted magnetically through the tank wall (Roush propane systems: 0.1–4.9 V). With CNG the 'level' is a calculated value. The documented systems report level faults under the petrol fuel level codes (Roush propane P0460–P0463, GM CNG van P0463), so no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found. P01AF is the general circuit fault of this sender.

P01B4.en: Alternative Fuel Rail Temperature Sensor Circuit
P01B4.desc: These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. The gas rail temperature sensor, often combined with the rail pressure sensor, measures the gas temperature at the injectors: gas cools strongly when it expands in the regulator, and the injected mass depends on density, i.e. on rail pressure and temperature, so the module corrects injection time with it. A Ford patent describes plausibility checks against engine bay temperature at idle and an expected cold rail at full load with a full tank. Roush propane systems report rail temperature faults as P0181–P0183; no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found. P01B4 is the general circuit fault of this sensor.

P01B9.en: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P01B9.desc: The engine oil temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. Sensor B is a second oil temperature sensor whose position is defined by the manufacturer. P01B9 is the general circuit fault of sensor B, the counterpart of P0195. No manufacturer document using the B-sensor codes was found, so it is unclear who fits a sensor B; the description follows sensor A and CARB's circuit monitoring requirement.

P01BE.en: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Bank 2
P01BE.desc: The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. Many V engines connect both rails and use only one sensor (P0190–P0194); the only documented user of the bank 2 codes is GM's 5.5 litre LT6 (Corvette Z06 2023–2024) with a digital sensor per rail. P01BE is the general circuit fault of the bank 2 sensor, the counterpart of P0190. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the logic follows the bank 1 sensor and CARB's circuit monitoring requirement. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power.

P01C8.en: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low Bank 2
P01C8.desc: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. P01C8 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0087: the actual pressure stays below target over time. Typical causes are a weak high-pressure pump on bank 2, a faulty volume control valve, low supply pressure or a leak. No manufacturer using exactly this code was found; the logic follows P0087 and CARB's requirement for pressure control. Not every two-rail engine uses them: GM's LT6 reports bank 2 pressure problems under other codes.

P01C9.en: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too High Bank 2
P01C9.desc: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. P01C9 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0088: the actual pressure is above target. P01CA.en: Fuel Rail Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking Bank 2
P01CA.desc: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. For bank 1 GM checks once per start that pressure exceeds about 3 MPa and does not fall below 2 MPa, with two trips. No manufacturer using exactly this code was found; GM's two-rail LT6 reports the same situation with the bank-neutral P00C6.

P01CB.en: Cylinder 1 Injection Timing Performance - Over Retarded
P01CB.desc: Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor. From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 1 needs clearly more energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too late – GM sets it above 80 µs of extra time, after two trips. Documented users are GM's 6.6 litre Duramax (LML, L5P) and FCA's 3.0 litre EcoDiesel; Ford reports the same function under P2B11ff. Bulletins often point away from the injector: GM fixed false settings on 2020–2021 L5P trucks with new software and warns that vibration, for example from off-road tyres, disturbs the evaluation; FCA lists wrong injector correction codes, boost leaks and loose injector clamps.

From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 5 needs clearly less energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too early or delivers too much – GM sets it below −90 µs, after two trips. Bulletins often point away from the injector: GM fixed false settings on 2020–2021 L5P trucks with new software and warns that vibration, for example from off-road tyres, disturbs the evaluation; FCA lists wrong injector correction codes, boost leaks and loose injector clamps.

P01E3.desc: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold. CARB requires such additional sensors to be monitored from model year 2019 onwards. P01E8.en: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open
P01E8.desc: Engine coolant heater A is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports an open control circuit – the module detects missing continuity, typically with the driver switched off. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports that the heater circuit is electrically intact but the heater does not work as commanded – for example a sticking relay or a weak element. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

causes_en: Thermostat stuck open or not sealing
Heated map thermostat, thermal management valve or switchable water pump faulty
Radiator fan running constantly (relay stuck)
Coolant sensor drifting cold
Low coolant or air in the system
P01F0.en: Coolant Temperature Relapsed Below Diagnostic Monitoring Temperature
P01F0.desc: Since model years 2019–2021 CARB requires petrol engines to detect a thermostat fault not only during warm-up but also when the coolant, after reaching operating temperature, drops back below the temperature needed for other diagnostics. P01F0 is this check. GM sets it when coolant falls below 64 °C with a conventional thermostat or 70.5 °C with an electrically heated one (2019 Corvette: 65/78.5 °C) after having been above it, with at least 0.8 km driven, ambient above −7 °C, enough heat input and no long overrun downhill; two trips. GM also uses it on the 6.6 litre Duramax diesel as a 'stuck open thermostat' check. Ford does not use the code in the documents checked. Usual cause is a thermostat stuck open.

causes_en: Sensor 4 aged or poisoned
Wiring or connector open, high-resistance or corroded
Sensor heater failed
Control module
P01F1.desc: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F1 is the general circuit code of this sensor, the counterpart of P0136/P0142 for sensors 2 and 3. Typical causes are an aged sensor, open or high-resistance wiring and a failed heater.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor faulty
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
P01F2.en: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F2.desc: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F2 means the signal stays near 0 V – typically a signal wire shorted to ground, a faulty sensor or an exhaust leak ahead of it; GM checks its other downstream sensors for a signal below about 40–60 mV.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Sensor faulty internally
Sensor ground open (bias logic)
P01F3.en: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F3.desc: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F3 means the signal is above about 1.05–1.1 V, which a switching sensor cannot produce – typically the heater supply or another voltage on the signal wire, or a heater-to-signal short inside the sensor.

causes_en: Sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Sensor heater weak
P01F4.en: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F4.desc: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F4 means the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes; CARB requires at least a rich-to-lean response test of downstream sensors during fuel cut-off. Behind several converters the oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide.

causes_en: Signal or ground wire open, connector corroded
Sensor aged or poisoned, produces no voltage
Sensor heater faulty, sensor does not reach operating temperature
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor
P01F5.en: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F5.desc: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F5 means that with a warm engine and heated sensor the signal does not switch between rich and lean but stays in the middle or at the bias voltage the module applies. For sensor 2, GM detects this when the signal stays above 1.7 V of a 1.9 V bias, a two-trip fault. Usual causes are an open signal or ground wire or a dead sensor.

causes_en: Sensor aged, characteristic shifted lean
Exhaust leak or false air upstream of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to ground or contact resistance
Misfires or mixture fault (excess oxygen)
P01F6.en: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F6.desc: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F6 means the sensor stays lean: the module deliberately enriches the mixture, and if the sensor does not reach the expected rich voltage before a set amount of air has passed, it counts as stuck lean. GM runs this test on sensor 2 once per trip as a two-trip fault. Usual causes are an aged sensor, an exhaust leak ahead of it or a signal wire shorted to ground.

causes_en: Sensor sooted, oil-fouled or aged
Signal wire shorted to voltage (e.g. heater supply)
Mixture genuinely rich (leaking injector, coolant or oil burning)
P01F7.en: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F7.desc: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F7 means the sensor stays rich: when the module leans the mixture or cuts fuel on overrun, the signal does not drop into the lean range. CARB names exactly this rich-to-lean transition during fuel cut-off as the minimum check for downstream sensors; GM tests sensor 2 this way as a two-trip fault. Usual causes are a sooted or oil-fouled sensor or a signal wire shorted to the heater supply.

causes_en: Short or partial short in heater element A
Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector
Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated
Heater running without coolant (low level, air pocket)
P01F8.en: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P01F8.desc: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater A through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. Such heaters warm the coolant around a cold start, shortening warm-up and providing cabin heat sooner; a GM patent describes how the module recognises a pre-heated engine so other temperature diagnostics do not misfire. No manufacturer using this code family was found in GM, Ford or FCA documents; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components. Siblings for heater A are P01E8–P01EB.

Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated
