causes_en: Connector or wiring of the bank 2 exhaust sensor open or corroded (signal, 5 V, ground)
Camshaft position sensor faulty
Oil contamination or leak at the sensor, sensor loose
Tone wheel on the phaser damaged or wrongly fitted after timing chain work
Engine module, or 5 V reference shorted by another sensor
P0390.en: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2
P0390.desc: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0390 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive from bank 2 while the crankshaft turns. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) sets it after 5.5 s without a cam pulse, 4 s of cranking or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s, after two trips; for GM it collects all circuit faults. GM's 3.6-litre V6 in the Saab 9-4X also counts 800 of 1,000 engine cycles without a pulse. Ford checks the crank-to-cam ratio from 200 rpm within 5 s, and the 2004 Northstar counts missing signal changes up to 16. The bank 2 exhaust phaser then locks in its base position; the engine keeps running on the crank and intake cam sensors. FCA advises saving the synchronisation data before replacing the sensor.

causes_en: Tone wheel on the bank 2 exhaust phaser damaged, loose or wrongly fitted
Interference or loose contact producing extra edges
Sensor loose, wrong O-ring or gap, chips on the magnet
Timing chain stretched or jumped
Sensor faulty
P0391.en: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2
P0391.desc: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0391 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal is present, but the number or position of its pulses does not fit the crankshaft. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) expects 4 to 6 pulses in the first 12 reference events and 398 to 402 per 100 engine cycles on the four-tooth wheel, after two trips; the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) checks pulses per crank revolution below 2,520 rpm. The 2004 Northstar requires each edge within a window of crank teeth, and GM's 2004 3.6-litre V6 (LY7) counts implausible signals over two drive cycles. The phaser then goes to its base position and the engine cranks longer. Mechanical causes – damaged tone wheel, jumped chain – matter more here than with P0390.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor faulty internally (output stuck low)
5 V reference missing (shorted by another sensor on the same circuit)
Engine module
P0392.en: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 2
P0392.desc: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0392 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal stays low without edges – typically a short to ground of the signal wire, a sensor output stuck low or a missing 5 V reference. Only manufacturers with separate low and high codes use it: on the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay low without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after more than 10 crank revolutions and below 2,520 rpm, after two trips; GM's 2004/2005 3.6-litre V6 (LY7, LP1) counts the fault over two drive cycles. Newer GM petrol engines (2015–2020) and Ford report the same fault as P0390. The consequence is as for P0390: cam timing on bank 2 in its base position, loss of power, longer cranking.

causes_en: Signal wire open or connector off
Sensor ground open
Signal wire shorted to positive
Sensor faulty
P0393.en: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 2
P0393.desc: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0393 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal stays high without edges. Because the engine module pulls the Hall sensor's signal line up, an open wire leads to 'high' just like a short to positive – GM's 2004 3.6-litre V6 (LY7) therefore calls the fault 'circuit continuity or high' and counts it over two drive cycles. On the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay high without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after two trips. Only manufacturers with separate low and high codes use it; newer GM petrol engines and Ford report the fault as P0390. The consequence is as for P0390: cam timing on bank 2 in its base position, loss of power, longer cranking.

causes_en: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector or harness
Interference (ignition wiring, add-on devices, ground problems)
Tone wheel or phaser damaged, or sensor loose
Sensor faulty, temperature-dependent
P0394.en: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent Bank 2
P0394.desc: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0394 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal now and then appears at a position where it is not expected relative to the crank reference – sporadic extra or missing edges. Ford checks this in its camshaft ignition system test from 200 rpm and decides within 5 s. FCA also uses the code and asks dealers to save the cam/crank synchronisation event data before replacing parts, a hint that the sensor itself is often not the culprit. GM does not use P0394 and reports such faults under P0391. Typical causes are a loose contact, interference or a damaged tone wheel.

causes_en: Connector at the pressure-sensing glow plug loose or corroded
Reference, signal or ground wire open or shorted
Sensor electronics in the glow plug faulty
Engine module (reference voltage or input)
P0395.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0395 is the general circuit code for this pressure sensor, meant for modules that do not separate open circuits and shorts into low and high. The only manufacturer we found using this code family – GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel, documented in Saab 9-5 workshop information – splits the faults into low and high (P0397, P0398) and does not use P0395; VW's US 2.0 TDI engines with pressure-sensing glow plugs report such faults with their own codes (P13CE ff). The description therefore follows CARB's requirement to monitor input sensors for circuit faults. The sensor has three wires (5 V reference, ground, signal); without it the module drops combustion control for that cylinder.

causes_en: Sensor in the glow plug drifting (deposits, ageing)
Glow plug leaking or wrongly torqued (pressure transmitted wrongly)
Contact resistance in connector or ground
Actual compression pressure differs (valve, rings)
P0396.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0396 means the sensor signal is electrically fine but does not fit the expected value. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows how such a check works: in overrun the measured peak pressure is compared with a compression pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the pressure values are also compared with limits and with crankshaft speed fluctuation. GM's European diesel in the Saab 9-5 uses the peak pressure in overrun anyway to find top dead centre. Typical causes are sensor drift from combustion deposits or a glow plug that leaks or is wrongly torqued. CARB requires a two-sided plausibility check of input sensors where feasible.

causes_en: 5 V reference wire open or shorted to ground
Signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor electronics of the glow plug faulty
Engine module supplies no reference
P0397.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0397 means the sensor signal stays below its lower limit. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) sets it when the signal is below the threshold for more than 2 s with the engine running, checked once per drive cycle, with the check engine light after two trips; the displayed maximum combustion pressure then reads 0 kPa instead of the normal 0–9,000 kPa. Saab names an open or grounded 5 V reference and a signal wire shorted to ground as causes; the glow plug should measure 3–12 Ω between reference and ground. Without the signal, combustion control for this cylinder is switched off, which is usually barely noticeable.

causes_en: Connector off or loose, signal wire open
Sensor ground wire open
Sensor in the glow plug faulty
Signal or reference wire shorted to positive
P0398.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0398 means the sensor signal stays above its upper limit. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) sets it when the signal is above the threshold for more than 2 s with the engine running, checked once per drive cycle, with the check engine light after two trips; the displayed maximum combustion pressure then reads 10,000 kPa instead of the normal 0–9,000 kPa. Saab names a 5 V reference shorted to positive, an open signal wire or one shorted to positive, and an open ground wire as causes – an unplugged connector is the most common. Without the signal, combustion control for this cylinder is switched off, which is usually barely noticeable.

causes_en: Loose contact at the glow plug connector
Chafing or broken wire in the engine harness
Sensor electronics of the glow plug unstable with temperature
Interference from ground problems
P0399.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0399 means the sensor signal is erratic or drops out for moments. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) calls it 'circuit erratic' and sets it when the signal is outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running; its fault table groups the erratic and pressure variation codes together as signal performance faults. The test plan checks a reference of 4.8–5.2 V and a ground below 5 Ω before the glow plug is replaced. Typical causes are a loose contact at the glow plug connector, a chafed engine harness or sensor electronics that become unstable with temperature. The code often comes and goes; combustion control for the cylinder is suspended while it is active.

causes_en: Compression loss (valve, piston rings, leaking glow plug seat)
Injector delivering too little or coked
Sensor drifting downwards (deposits)
Misfire or partial combustion
P039A.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039A means the pressure measured in the cylinder is lower than expected while the sensor itself is electrically fine. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; GM patents show how such an evaluation works: peak and minimum pressure are compared with limits and with a motoring pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is compared between cylinders. A low value can mean weak combustion or compression – leaking valve, worn rings, leaking glow plug seat, an injector delivering too little – or a sensor drifting downwards. The usual consequence is rough running and more smoke.

causes_en: Engine module software (Audi S3 2015, engine CYFB)
Injector delivering too much or dripping
Sensor drifting upwards (diesel pressure-sensing glow plug)
Knock or pre-ignition on a petrol engine
P039B.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039B means the pressure measured or calculated for the cylinder is higher than expected. It is documented by code at Audi, surprisingly on a petrol engine: on the 2015 S3 (2.0 TFSI, engine CYFB) the four 'pressure too high' codes came on with the EPC lamp, usually together with misfire codes P0300–P0304 and the manufacturer code for hiding a cylinder; the cause was a software fault that mis-detected misfire, and a software update fixed it. How Audi determines the pressure, the bulletin does not say. On diesels with pressure-sensing glow plugs GM patents describe a peak pressure above its limit – too much or too early injection, or a sensor drifting upwards. If the cylinder is shut off, power drops noticeably.

causes_en: Pressure-sensing glow plug faulty or coked (glow rod stuck)
Contact resistance in connector or ground
Actual compression loss or misfire in the cylinder
P039C.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) uses P039C as 'pressure variation too low', with three sub-checks, and sets it when the signal is outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running; its fault table counts it among the signal performance faults together with the erratic code. What exactly is measured, Saab does not explain; presumably it is the swing of the pressure signal within an engine cycle – too small a swing means the signal barely responds, for example because the glow rod is stuck by carbon and no longer transmits the pressure, or because pressure build-up is missing. Usually there are no noticeable symptoms.

causes_en: Sensor in the glow plug faulty (signal noise)
Loose contact or interference on the signal wire
Combustion anomaly (dripping injector, harsh combustion)
P039D.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) uses P039D as 'pressure variation too high' and sets it when the signal is outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running; its fault table counts it among the signal performance faults together with the erratic code. What exactly is measured, Saab does not explain; presumably it is the swing of the pressure signal within an engine cycle – too large a swing points to a noisy or overshooting signal or implausible pressure peaks, for example from faulty sensor electronics, interference on the signal wire or, less often, a combustion anomaly such as a dripping injector. Usually there are no noticeable symptoms.

causes_en: Injector coked, leaking or delivering the wrong quantity
Compression loss (valve, rings)
Partial combustion or misfire (fuel quality, EGR distribution)
Pressure sensor drifting
P039E.desc: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039E means the combustion quality in the cylinder, evaluated from the combustion pressure, is abnormal. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows the method: the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is turned into a measure of combustion energy, an inequality index against the neighbouring cylinders in firing order is formed, and a two-sided threshold detects partial combustion, misfire, injector and compression faults. CARB requires engines with a combustion or combustion quality sensor to detect misfire more sharply (5 % in 1,000 revolutions). Typical causes are a coked or leaking injector, compression loss or poor fuel; the engine runs roughly and smokes more.

P03E5.en: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1
P03E5.desc: On some engines the intake cam phaser (camshaft position actuator A) has its own position sensors, which tell the engine module where the phaser actually is; sensor C is the third of them, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. P03E5 is the general circuit code for this sensor: the module sees an open circuit or a signal outside its valid window on the supply, signal or ground line. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. GM's 2.7-litre engine monitors comparable position sensors on its sliding camshaft under other codes (P2C05 ff), with an open circuit above 200 kΩ and a short below 0.5 Ω in 4 of 5 samples – only as a comparison. The phaser is then usually held in its base position. CARB requires electronic parts of variable valve timing systems to be monitored as comprehensive components.

P03E9.en: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Exceeded Learning Limit
P03E9.desc: Engines with cam profile switching move the intake camshaft between lift profiles with actuators – for example pins that shift a sliding cam – and position sensors report which profile is engaged. The engine module learns reference values of position sensor A, such as its end-position levels or the expected pulse position relative to the crankshaft and camshaft sensors; a Ford patent describes correcting this position for the cam phase. P03E9 means the learned value lies outside the permitted adaptation limit, so profile detection is no longer reliable and the module usually stays in a safe profile. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code or its limits; GM's 2.7-litre sliding cam has no learning-limit code. CARB lists a pin that does not reach its position among the faults to be detected.

P03EC.en: A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P03EC.desc: With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. Actuator C is the third of these actuators – not a profile position. The only known user is GM's 2.7-litre turbo four (L3B, three-step sliding cam, from model year 2019). P03EC means the actuator's control circuit is open: GM checks the circuit with the driver on and sets the code at an impedance of 200 kΩ or more (4 of 5 samples, above 11 V, MIL on the first trip). The actuator can then not shift its cam piece, and lift switching and cylinder deactivation are blocked.

P03FA.desc: Ignition K is one of up to twelve control signal lines (A to L) from the engine module to an ignition coil with integrated output stage or to an ignition module – plausibly the 11th channel, but the code standard leaves the assignment to the manufacturer. The code concerns this logic-level signal, not the coil's primary circuit (coil K has its own codes, P0361 and P2330 ff). P03FA means the control line is open or high-resistance: with its driver switched off the module sees a voltage that indicates a missing load (GM uses more than 30 kΩ for comparable coil drivers). The coil fires wrongly or not at all; the misfire usually also sets P0300 ff, and many modules shut off injection to that cylinder to protect the catalyst. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it would only concern twelve-cylinder engines, whose makers publish no OBD summaries; GM and Ford tables stop at eight and ten cylinders.

causes_en: EGR passages or valve carboned up

Leak in the intake or EGR pipe

P0400.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0400 is the general flow fault of EGR system A, used where the module does not classify the error as too little (P0401) or too much (P0402). Ford petrol engines with a stepper-motor valve open and close the valve at steady part load and compare intake manifold pressure with and without EGR; too small a normalised difference (below 1.0) sets P0400, MIL after two trips. GM diesels use the code differently, for air-mass checks with excessive EGR rate. EGR is then usually switched off.

causes_en: EGR passages, valve or cooler carboned up
EGR valve faulty or stuck closed
Ford: DPFE sensor or its hoses blocked, cracked or swapped
Diesel: air mass meter drifting or air leak after the turbo
Vacuum control of the valve faulty
P0401.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0401 means too little exhaust is recirculated. Petrol engines open the valve briefly and expect a rise in manifold pressure (GM 2004 V6, MIL on the first trip); older Ford systems measure the pressure drop across an orifice (DPFE sensor). Diesels balance the air mass: if the meter sees more fresh air than the target EGR rate allows, too little exhaust flows (GM, Ford, Saab, usually MIL after two trips). Diesel causes are mostly a coked valve or cooler, petrol causes blocked passages.

causes_en: EGR valve stuck open, dirt under the seat
Ford: DPFE sensor drifting or hose wrong
Diesel: air leak between air mass meter and turbo, MAF drift
Valve control opens unintentionally
P0402.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0402 means too much exhaust is recirculated, or exhaust flows although the valve should be closed – CARB explicitly requires a leaking valve to be detected. Ford's DPFE check at idle with EGR off expects no pressure difference above the engine-off value; Ford diesels compare the measured EGR rate with the expected one, GM diesels the fresh-air deviation in the opposite direction. Petrol engines idle roughly or stall, diesels smoke and may lose power.

P0403.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0403 concerns the electrical drive of the EGR valve – solenoid, stepper motor, DC motor or vacuum regulator. The module checks the output and sets the code for an open circuit (GM: above 200 kΩ, MIL after two trips; Ford after 4 s, MIL after two trips). Newer systems report shorts separately as P0489 (low) and P0490 (high); Ford and older GM systems include them in P0403. EGR is then switched off for the rest of the trip.

P0404.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0404 is the function check of the valve drive: on valves with a position sensor the module compares commanded and actual position, and a persistent deviation means the valve sticks, is coked or its drive is too weak (GM diesel 2018 above 10 %, GM petrol 2004 above 15 %, both MIL after two trips). Ford calls it control stuck. Saab's V6 diesel deviates and uses P0404 for a short to positive. EGR control is then switched off and the valve de-energised.

P0405.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR sensor A is usually the valve position sensor with a 5 V supply; on Ford until about 2011 it was the DPFE differential pressure sensor. P0405 means its signal is below the lower limit – GM 2018 below 11 % of 5 V (MIL after two trips), Ford below 5 % of full scale for 4 s, Saab below 0.26 V. The cause is a short to ground or an open signal or 5 V wire. EGR position control is then switched off.

P040A.desc: EGR temperature sensor A measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P040A is its general circuit code. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – GM and Ford report this sensor as P040B to P040E – so the description follows CARB's requirement to check input circuits for continuity and range. A substitute value is used and the EGR cooler check is suspended.

P040B.en: EGR Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P040B.desc: EGR temperature sensor A measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P040B is its plausibility check: after a cold start the sensor must warm up once hot exhaust flows. Ford diesels set the code if it rises by less than 10 °C after load; GM diesels if it barely changes after at least 8 hours off and a defined EGR flow (MIL after two trips). A sooted sensor tip or a lack of EGR flow are typical causes.

P040E.en: EGR Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P040E.desc: EGR temperature sensor A measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. P040F.desc: The two EGR temperature sensors measure the gas temperature in the EGR path, before and after the cooler – which is A and which is B depends on the maker. P040F compares sensors A and B: after a long stop (GM: at least 8 hours) both must read about ambient temperature. If they differ by more than the calibrated limit at start-up (GM Duramax LML table, at least 20 °C, with exclusions for block heaters), the code is set, MIL after two trips. It does not say which sensor is wrong – compare both with intake air and coolant temperature. Ford diesels cover the same goal with P041B.

causes_en: Secondary air pump failed (water ingress, seized)
Combination or shut-off valve carboned up or stuck
Vacuum hose or electric changeover valve leaking or faulty
Pump relay or fuse faulty
Air ducts in the head carboned up or hose off
P0410.desc: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P0410 is the general function code for secondary air system A. Many Bosch-managed engines check it passively: with the pump running, the front oxygen sensor must read lean or the fuel control must react; Pierburg lists P0410 as no lean signal, i.e. no air detected. Saab's Motronic 900, by contrast, uses it for too much air. GM's systems with a pressure sensor use P0411 and P2440 ff instead. The check runs once per trip after a cold start; driving is unaffected.

causes_en: Pump weak or failed (water, filter debris)
Combination valve partly stuck or check valve faulty
Hoses blocked, leaking or off; ducts in the head carboned up
Pressure sensor port blocked or sensor drifting (pressure-sensor systems)
Pump relay or supply with contact resistance
P0411.en: AIR System A Incorrect Flow Detected
P0411.desc: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P0411 means the measured air flow does not match the expected value. Passive systems judge it from the oxygen sensor or fuel control (Saab 900: less than 12 points of correction within 12 s). GM measures actively with a pressure sensor between pump and valve and compares it with a model while pump and valve are on – from 2018 a deviation above 5.0 kPa or below −4.9 kPa sets the code, MIL after two trips. The test needs a cold engine after a long stop, so short warm trips do not complete it.

causes_en: Switching valve A faulty (coil open or shorted, water ingress)
Connector corroded or wire open or chafed
Valve supply missing (fuse, main relay)
Driver in the engine module
P0412.en: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit
P0412.desc: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0412 is the general electrical fault in the control circuit of valve A, detected by comparing the driver's feedback with its commanded state. GM has used it since about 2015 specifically for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips) and reports shorts as P041F and P044F; older GM systems and Toyota use it for any driver fault. The valve then stays shut, so secondary air is missing and P0411 or P2441 may follow.

causes_en: Wire to the valve open or connector loose or corroded
Valve coil burnt out
Fuse of the valve supply blown
Engine module
P0413.en: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit Open
P0413.desc: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0413 means the control circuit of valve A is open: with the driver switched off the module does not see the expected supply or pull-up level. The check runs continuously. Subaru's two-valve system assigns valve A to bank 1, and its bulletin advises checking the valve of the other bank as well. The valve stays shut and the bank gets no secondary air; flow codes such as P0411 may follow.

Wire chafed against ground or supply
Moisture or corrosion in the connector

P0414.en: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit Shorted
P0414.desc: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0414 means the control circuit of valve A is shorted. A short to ground keeps the valve energized and open; a short to supply or a shorted coil overloads the driver, which many modules then switch off for the rest of the trip. An open valve with the pump running can also set P2440, and exhaust can reach the pump if the check valve leaks. Subaru names P0414 in its bulletin for the two-valve system.

P0415.en: AIR System Switching Valve B Circuit

P0415 is the general electrical fault in the control circuit of valve B, the second valve on two-valve or two-bank systems such as V engines or Subaru's turbo boxer. It is detected like P0412 for valve A, by comparing the driver's feedback with its commanded state. No manufacturer document available to us describes P0415 specifically; Pierburg's fault table lists it with the same remedies as valve A.

P0416 means the control circuit of valve B is open – the module does not see the expected level with its driver switched off. On Subaru's two-valve system valve B serves bank 2; the bulletin advises checking the valve of the other bank too, because a shared supply can be the cause. P0417.en: AIR System Switching Valve B Circuit Shorted
P0417.desc: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0418.desc: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P041C.en: EGR Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P041C.desc: EGR temperature sensor B measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P041C means the signal is below its lower limit – very hot or shorted to ground; Ford puts below 0.10 V at about 961 °C. Thresholds: Ford diesel below 0.10 V for 3 s, Ford petrol below 0.32 V for 5 s, GM's Duramax LML below 0.46 V for 5 s, GM 2018 a resistance below 164 Ω; MIL after two trips. A substitute value is used and the EGR cooler check (P2457) is suspended.

P041D.en: EGR Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P041D.desc: EGR temperature sensor B measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P041D means the signal is above its upper limit – very cold or, far more often, an open circuit; Ford puts above 4.90 V at about −46 °C. Thresholds: Ford diesel above 4.90 V, Ford petrol above 4.94 V for 5 s, GM's Duramax LML above 4.84 V, GM 2018 a resistance above 859 Ω; MIL after two trips. A substitute value is used and the EGR cooler check is suspended.

P041E.en: EGR Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P041E.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR temperature sensor B is the second temperature sensor in the EGR path; on GM diesels it sits before the cooler, on Ford diesels after it. P041E means its signal jumps. GM's diesels of 2016–18, the only documented users, set it when the measured resistance changes by more than 25 Ω between two samples 100 ms apart – faster than any real temperature change, so a loose contact or cracked sensor is the cause (40 of 50 samples, MIL after two trips). Dependent checks such as EGR cooler efficiency are then suspended.

P041F.en: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit Low
P041F.desc: After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air into the exhaust; switching valve A is the electrically driven valve that opens this path. GM checks the valve circuit in three codes – P0412 open, P041F shorted to ground, P044F shorted to positive – while other makers use P0413/P0414 or P0412 for everything. P041F means the control circuit is shorted to ground: GM checks with the driver switched off and sets the code at 0.5 Ω or less to ground (20 of 25 samples of 250 ms, above 11 V, MIL after two trips). The valve is then energised and open although not commanded; P0411 or P2440 may follow.

P0420.en: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
P0420.desc: The engine module checks whether the catalyst of bank 1 still converts enough. On petrol engines it estimates the oxygen storage capacity by comparing the sensors before and after the catalyst – a good catalyst smooths the rear signal. GM uses a test on overrun (ratio below 0.35 sets the code on the first trip), Ford an index ratio above 0.75 or fuel integration after fuel cut-off. On diesels P0420 concerns the oxidation catalyst, checked by its heat release during filter regeneration (GM Duramax LML, Ford below 45 % of the expected heat). Ford names oil-borne poisoning as the most common cause.

P0421.desc: Catalyst 1 is the first catalyst in the flow direction of bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1) – the close-coupled or warm-up catalyst that lights off first after a cold start; the older wording was Warm Up Catalyst. P0421 means it no longer converts enough. Mitsubishi V6 engines with manifold catalysts and GM's 3.0/3.2-litre V6 of 2004/05 with Bosch control report it: the rear sensor amplitude is compared with a model, and a quality factor above 0.625 (2004) or 0.375 (2005) sets the code after two trips. GM's small diesels use P0421 for the close-coupled oxidation catalyst, tested by heat balance during filter regeneration.

P0423.en: Heated Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
P0423.desc: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of a support catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start (Emitec EMICAT, 12–48 V); it was tried on Californian petrol cars in the 1990s and is used today mainly on diesels, for example Audi's 3.0 TDI from 2014 and 48-volt diesel vans. P0423 means the heated catalyst of bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1) no longer converts enough; CARB requires it to be assessed like any other catalyst. The only manufacturer reference is two Ram software bulletins for the 6.7-litre Cummins HO (model years 2025/26), which list P0423 without saying which part is meant.

P0424.en: Heated Catalyst Temperature Below Threshold Bank 1
P0424.desc: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of a support catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start (Emitec EMICAT, 12–48 V); it was tried on Californian petrol cars in the 1990s and is used today mainly on diesels, for example Audi's 3.0 TDI from 2014 and 48-volt diesel vans. P0424 implements CARB's heated-catalyst rule for bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1): the catalyst must reach its intended temperature within a time set by the manufacturer after the start, measured by a temperature sensor or modelled from heating power. If it does not, the heater is too weak – supply voltage, contact resistance, an ageing element – or heat losses are too high. An open heater circuit is reported as P0429/P0439 instead. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code.

P042E.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P042E means the position-controlled EGR valve A is more open than commanded and cannot be closed. GM's diesels of 2016/17 set it when the valve stays too far open despite maximum closing duty (about 1–8 s); the 2018 tables check after switch-off whether it is below 5 % within 2 s – both with MIL on the first trip. Ford petrol engines compare the position with limits for 4 s, Ford diesels a deviation above 15 % for 25 s. Too much EGR causes rough idle, stalling and smoke; EGR control is switched off.

P042F.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P042F means EGR valve A does not follow the opening command: its actual position stays more closed than commanded although the actuator works with high opening duty. GM's diesels of 2016/17 set it after about 1–8 s with MIL on the first trip; a GM bulletin covers it on the 2017 Cruze diesel. Ford petrol engines use position limits for 4 s; Ford diesels report both directions under P042E. With too little EGR, NOx rises, petrol engines may knock and P0401 can follow.

P0430.en: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 2
P0430.desc: Like P0420, but for the catalyst of bank 2, so only on V and boxer engines with one catalyst per bank; Y-pipe systems with a shared catalyst report P0420 only. The module compares the oxygen sensors before and after the bank 2 catalyst – a good catalyst smooths the rear signal. GM checks on overrun and sets the code on the first trip if the ratio falls below 0.35; Ford evaluates an index ratio or fuel integration and usually needs several trips. The monitor only runs warm, in closed loop and without misfire, fuel or sensor faults.

P043E.en: EVAP System Leak Detection Reference Orifice Low Flow
P043E.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Systems with a leak detection pump (Bosch DM-TL at VW, Audi, BMW and Maserati, Denso's canister pump module at Toyota/Lexus) first measure a reference value with the pump working only through a built-in 0.5 mm (0.020 in) orifice; it is the yardstick for the small-leak test that CARB requires. P043E means the reference measurement shows too little flow – the vacuum (or with DM-TL the pressure and pump current) becomes stronger than expected, so the orifice or reference path is partly blocked, often by dirt or liquid after overfilling. GM and Ford do not use the code; Maserati fixed false triggering with software.

causes_en: Leak detection pump faulty (weak pump, leaking changeover valve, liquid damage)

P043F.en: EVAP System Leak Detection Reference Orifice High Flow
P043F.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Systems with a leak detection pump (Bosch DM-TL at VW, Audi, BMW and Maserati, Denso's canister pump module at Toyota/Lexus) first measure a reference value with the pump working only through a built-in 0.5 mm (0.020 in) orifice; it is the yardstick for the small-leak test that CARB requires. P043F means the reference measurement shows too much flow – the reference vacuum or pressure does not reach the expected value, because the reference path or changeover valve leaks, the pump is weak, or air enters through leaking valves in the test path. The leak test can then not be judged, since a weak yardstick would hide leaks. GM and Ford do not use the code.

causes_en: Fuel cap leaking, loose or wrong
Purge valve leaking or sticking
Leaking or cracked EVAP hoses, canister or vent valve
Engine module software
P0440.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0440 is the general code for a fault in this system without further narrowing down – leak, purge flow or component. Today most makers use the specific codes instead (P0441 ff, P0455–P0457, P0496); the GM and Ford tables of 2006–2023 do not contain P0440. It appears in VW code lists and in an FCA bulletin for the Alfa Romeo 2.0, fixed by software, where FCA calls it incorrect flow. What sets it is therefore manufacturer-specific; CARB requires purge flow and leaks to be monitored.

causes_en: Purge valve stuck open or not sealing
Purge valve stuck closed, purge line blocked, kinked or off
Leak detection pump with tolerance fault (VW)
Canister saturated or damaged, turbo purge check valve faulty
P0441.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0441 means the actual purge flow does not match the target – too little, or flow although the purge valve is closed. CARB requires a fault when no purge flow is detected. Strategies differ widely: Saab's Trionic T7/T8 sets it for flow with the valve closed (tank pressure falling faster than 27.5–40 Pa/s), VW and Audi check purge flow with the leak detection pump, Honda/Acura for a sticking purge valve. GM and Ford do not use P0441 – they report flow with the valve closed as P0496 or P1450 and missing flow as P0455.

causes_en: Fuel cap seal worn, wrong or not clicked in
Cracked or porous EVAP hoses or leaking connections
Purge or vent valve does not seal
Leak detection pump itself leaking (VW/Audi)
Filler neck corroded, tank or sender seal leaking
P0442.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0442 reports a small leak; what size that means depends on the maker. Ford detects 0.040 in (1 mm) with the engine running: the vent valve closes, engine vacuum pulls the tank down, the purge valve closes and a pressure rise above 2.5 inH2O in 15 s sets the code (0.020 in is P0456). GM uses the natural pressure change after switch-off for 0.020 in and averages several tests. Pump systems at VW and Audi compare against a reference leak. A worn or loose fuel cap is the most common cause.

mfr.Dodge: Medium EVAP Leak

causes_en: Purge valve connector corroded, loose or off
Purge valve coil open or shorted
Control wire broken or chafed, or supply missing (fuse, main relay)
Driver in the engine module
P0443.en: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit
P0443.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0443 is the electrical check of purge valve A, which the module switches to ground in pulses; it compares the driver's feedback voltage with the commanded state. GM uses it for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips) and reports shorts as P0458/P0459; Ford covers open and short in P0443 (5 s). Purging then stops, the canister is no longer regenerated, and the leak and purge monitors are suspended.

causes_en: Purge valve connector off or corroded
Valve coil open
Supply wire, fuse, main relay or control wire open
Control wire shorted to ground (Saab definition)
P0444.en: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit Open
P0444.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0444 belongs to the older scheme of circuit, open and shorted codes for purge valve A; Saab's Trionic T7 and VW use it, while GM reports an open circuit as P0443 and Ford covers everything in P0443. Saab checks with the output switched off: below 2 V the supply through the coil is missing or the line is grounded – Saab combines both under P0444, sets it after about 1 s and pauses the check until the next drive. Purging then stops.

causes_en: Purge valve coil shorted (shorted turns)
Control wire shorted to positive (chafed)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Driver in the engine module
P0445.en: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit Shorted
P0445.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0445 is the short-circuit code of the older scheme for purge valve A, used by Saab's Trionic T7 and VW; GM reports shorts as P0458/P0459, Ford covers them in P0443. Saab checks with the low-side output switched on: the voltage should then be near 0 V, and above 2 V means the line is shorted to positive or the coil is shorted, with the driver in current limiting. The code sets after about 1 s; the driver protects itself by switching off, so purging stops.

causes_en: Vent valve or filter blocked by dirt, dust or water (GM reading)
Vent valve electrically faulty, coil open or shorted (Ford reading)
Connector or wire to the vent valve corroded or open
Canister clogged with charcoal or liquid (overfilling)
Vent hose kinked or blocked by an insect nest
P0446.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The vent valve is normally open and closes for the leak test. By its wording P0446 is its control circuit, and Ford uses it that way for open and shorted circuits. GM, however, uses P0446 for vent system performance – a blocked vent path: while purging with the vent valve open, the tank must not build up vacuum; more than 2989 Pa for 5 s before 4 litres have been purged sets the code, MIL after two trips. GM reports vent circuit faults as P0449, P0498 and P0499. A blocked vent makes refuelling difficult.

causes_en: Vent valve connector corroded or off (underbody, splash water)
Vent valve coil open (resistance outside 10–100 Ω)
Wire to the module or supply from the main relay open
Engine module or its connector
P0447.en: EVAP System Vent Control Circuit Open
P0447.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0447 belongs to the older scheme for the vent valve circuit (P0446 circuit, P0447 open, P0448 shorted), used by Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X), VW and Nissan; GM reports an open vent circuit as P0449, Ford as P0446. On Subaru the valve is fed from the main relay and switched to ground by the module; if the voltage at the module output is missing or the coil is high-resistance (nominal 10–100 Ω), the code sets after two consecutive drives. The valve stays in its rest position and the leak test cannot run.

causes_en: Vent valve or vent path blocked by dust, dirt or water (Nissan reading)
Vent valve coil shorted (below 1 Ω)
Control wire shorted to positive
Module driver damaged
P0448.en: EVAP System Vent Control Circuit Shorted
P0448.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0448 is the short-circuit code of the older scheme for the vent valve. Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X) expects supply voltage above 10 V at the module output with the valve off; a short to positive or a coil below 1 Ω sets the code after two drives, and Subaru then also replaces the module, as its driver may be damaged. Nissan and Infiniti use P0448 differently, for a vent valve or vent path stuck closed by dust or water, with replacement of canister, valve and filler tube. GM and Ford do not use the code.

causes_en: Vent valve connector (usually at the canister or tank, underbody) corroded or loose
Vent valve coil open
Supply (fuse) or control wire open
Driver in the engine module
P0449.en: EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit/Open
P0449.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0449 belongs to the newer scheme for the vent valve circuit – P0449 open, P0498 low, P0499 high – used mainly by GM and also by VW. The normally open valve is fed from the battery and switched to ground; with the driver off, the output should show supply voltage. A floating 2.6–4.6 V, or an impedance of 200 kΩ or more, means an open circuit (GM: 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips). The leak test and the vent performance check P0446 are then suspended; purging continues.

causes_en: Connector or wire to sensor C open or corroded
Sensor faulty
5 V reference or ground disturbed (with other sensor codes)
Engine module
P044A.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. What EGR sensor C is depends on the maker: on Ford petrol engines from 2020 it is the DPFE sensor, which measures the pressure drop across an orifice in the EGR pipe (sensor A there is the valve position sensor); GM diesels assign it to the position sensor of a low-pressure EGR valve, but only within fault groups. P044A is the general circuit fault of this sensor. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – Ford splits it into P044C/P044D – so the description follows CARB's requirement to check input circuits for continuity and range. Without the sensor, EGR flow and cooler checks are suspended.

causes_en: Pressure hoses off, swapped or blocked (soot, condensate)
Sensor zero point drifted
Orifice or EGR pipe coked
Contact resistance in the connector
P044B.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. What EGR sensor C is depends on the maker: on Ford petrol engines from 2020 it is the DPFE sensor, which measures the pressure drop across an orifice in the EGR pipe (sensor A there is the valve position sensor); GM diesels assign it to the position sensor of a low-pressure EGR valve, but only within fault groups. P044B means its signal is electrically valid but implausible – for example a pressure difference with the valve closed, or no reaction when it opens. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; Ford checks the DPFE plausibility under its own codes P139A–P139C (hoses swapped, front or rear hose off or blocked). EGR flow diagnosis is then suspended.

P044C.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. What EGR sensor C is depends on the maker: on Ford petrol engines from 2020 it is the DPFE sensor, which measures the pressure drop across an orifice in the EGR pipe (sensor A there is the valve position sensor); GM diesels assign it to the position sensor of a low-pressure EGR valve, but only within fault groups. P044C means its signal is below the lower limit. Ford petrol engines from 2020 set it below 0.25 V for 5 s – a value the sensor cannot produce, since 0.5 V already means −11 kPa – so the signal is shorted to ground, the 5 V supply is open or the sensor is faulty. EGR flow, hose and cooler checks are then suspended; MIL after two trips.

causes_en: Sensor ground open
Signal shorted to 5 V or positive
Sensor faulty internally
Engine module
P044D.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P044D means its signal is above the upper limit. Ford petrol engines from 2020 set it above 4.65 V for 5 s, beyond the measuring range that ends at 4.5 V (about +18 kPa) – typically an open sensor ground, a signal shorted to 5 V or positive, or a faulty sensor. causes_en: Loose contact in the connector or broken wire
Condensate in the sensor or hose (DPFE)
Sensor unstable internally
Interference or ground problems
P044E.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. What EGR sensor C is depends on the maker: on Ford petrol engines from 2020 it is the DPFE sensor, which measures the pressure drop across an orifice in the EGR pipe (sensor A there is the valve position sensor); GM diesels assign it to the position sensor of a low-pressure EGR valve, but only within fault groups. P044E means short dropouts or jumps in its signal, too brief for P044C/P044D or with an impossible rate of change. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; Ford applies the same idea to sensor A as P046D, where a limit violation of only 0.4 s counts. EGR diagnosis is then suspended.

Control wire chafed against a supply wire
Water in the connector bridging to the supply
Driver in the engine module
P044F.en: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit High
P044F.desc: After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air into the exhaust; switching valve A is the electrically driven valve that opens this path. GM checks the valve circuit in three codes – P0412 open, P041F shorted to ground, P044F shorted to positive – while other makers use P0413/P0414 or P0412 for everything. P044F means the control circuit is shorted to positive or the coil is low-resistance: when the driver switches on, the line stays high. GM sets the code at 0.5 Ω or less to the supply (20 of 25 samples of 250 ms, above 11 V, MIL after two trips). The valve then does not open, secondary air is missing and P0411 may follow.

causes_en: Connector at the tank pressure sensor corroded or loose (underbody, splash water)
Tank pressure sensor faulty
Damaged 5 V, ground or signal wire
Engine module software
P0450.en: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit
P0450.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The tank pressure sensor measures small pressures around ambient for the leak tests. Its direction differs by maker – on GM vacuum raises the voltage, on Ford and Bosch pressure does – so low and high refer to the signal voltage only. P0450 is the general circuit fault of tank pressure sensor A; makers that separate the fault use P0452 or P0453. Only Audi (2022/23) is documented with the code, as an electrical fault of the tank ventilation pressure sensor; GM, Ford and Saab do not use it. The leak tests are then suspended.

causes_en: Tank pressure sensor offset shifted or sluggish
Vent line or canister blocked (pressure does not release)
Sensor hose or port leaking, kinked or blocked
Tank overfilled, fuel in the lines
P0451.en: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit Range/Performance
P0451.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The tank pressure sensor measures small pressures around ambient for the leak tests. Its direction differs by maker – on GM vacuum raises the voltage, on Ford and Bosch pressure does – so low and high refer to the signal voltage only. P0451 is its plausibility check. GM checks during the engine-off leak test that the signal settles to ambient pressure with the vent open and averages several tests; Ford checks the offset after at least 4–6 hours off (±0.5 kPa). Saab's Bosch ME9 watches start pressure, the drop during purging and excessive oscillation. On Subaru a leaking or blocked hose between sensor and tank is a frequent cause.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground or connector corroded
Tank pressure sensor faulty internally
5 V reference open or shorted (shared reference)
Engine module
P0452.en: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit Low
P0452.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The tank pressure sensor measures small pressures around ambient for the leak tests. Its direction differs by maker – on GM vacuum raises the voltage, on Ford and Bosch pressure does – so low and high refer to the signal voltage only. P0452 means its signal voltage is below the lower limit: GM below 0.15 V (640 of 800 samples, MIL after two trips), Ford below 0.1 V for 5 s, Saab below 0.1 V for more than 5 s. Common causes are a signal wire shorted to ground, an interrupted or shorted 5 V reference or a faulty sensor. Leak and purge tests are then suspended.

causes_en: Signal or ground wire open, connector off
Tank pressure sensor faulty
Signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Engine module
P0453.en: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit High
P0453.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The tank pressure sensor measures small pressures around ambient for the leak tests. Its direction differs by maker – on GM vacuum raises the voltage, on Ford and Bosch pressure does – so low and high refer to the signal voltage only. P0453 means its signal voltage is above the upper limit: GM above 4.85 V (640 of 800 samples, MIL after two trips), Ford and Saab 9-4X above 4.9 V for 5 s. Ford states explicitly that an open circuit sets P0453, because the module's pull-up then drives the signal high. Other causes are a short to 5 V or battery voltage. Leak tests are then suspended.

causes_en: Loose contact at the connector to the tank pressure sensor
Chafed harness at the tank
Sensor faulty internally (noisy signal)
Fuel sloshing in an overfilled tank or refuelling misdetected
P0454.en: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit Intermittent
P0454.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The tank pressure sensor measures small pressures around ambient for the leak tests. Its direction differs by maker – on GM vacuum raises the voltage, on Ford and Bosch pressure does – so low and high refer to the signal voltage only. P0454 means the signal jumps. Ford checks continuously for a jump above about 1 kPa between two samples 100 ms apart or a brief open or short. GM (and the Saab 9-4X) checks only during the engine-off leak test: a jump of about 112 Pa within 1 s that refuelling cannot explain, 2 of 3 tests, MIL on the first trip. Saab's ME9 does not use the code. The engine-off small-leak test is then discarded.

causes_en: Fuel cap missing, not clicked in or seal faulty (or capless flap)
Hose off or cracked (canister, filler neck, purge line)
Vent valve stuck open or purge valve stuck closed
Canister or filler neck cracked or corroded
P0455.en: EVAP System Leak Detected - Large Leak
P0455.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0455 means a large leak or that no vacuum builds up. Ford pulls the closed system down with engine vacuum and expects about −2 kPa within 30 s; after refuelling it sets P0457 instead. GM sets the code if 20 litres have been purged without reaching 2740 Pa tank vacuum (once per cold start, MIL after two trips). Saab's ME9 uses a pressure drop below 525 Pa. The code also covers blocked purging, for example a purge valve stuck closed.

mfr.Dodge: Large EVAP Leak

causes_en: Fuel cap seal worn or cap not clicked in
Purge or vent valve not sealing
Porous hoses or O-rings, hairline crack in canister or filler neck
Leak detection pump itself leaking (VW/Audi)
P0456.en: EVAP System Leak Detected (very small leak)
P0456.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0456 reports a very small leak of 0.020 in (0.5 mm), as CARB requires. Ford uses the engine-off natural vacuum test: after switch-off the closed system must build at least about 190 Pa pressure or 125 Pa vacuum, judged statistically. Saab's Bosch ME9 also tests with the engine off for up to 45 minutes; VW and Audi use a leak detection pump. GM reports this leak size as P0442 instead. The code often appears only after many trips and depends on the weather.

causes_en: Fuel cap not closed, not clicked in or forgotten
Fuel cap seal faulty or non-original cap
Filler neck sealing surface damaged or capless flap sticking
Vent valve stuck open
P0457.en: EVAP System Leak Detected (fuel cap loose/off)
P0457.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0457 is a large leak attributed to the fuel cap: Ford detects refuelling and treats a vacuum that is not reached afterwards (about −2 kPa in 30 s) as an open cap. CARB allows a separate check fuel cap lamp instead of the warning lamp, and the code is cleared once the cap is found tight again. Ford sets the lamp after two to three trips depending on calibration, Subaru after two. GM and Saab's ME9 do not use the code.

causes_en: Purge valve control wire chafed against ground
Purge valve coil shorted internally
Connector scorched or wet
Driver in the engine module
P0458.en: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit Low
P0458.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Purge valve A is switched to ground by the module and fed from the main relay. P0458 means its control wire is shorted to ground: GM detects it with the driver off, when the line sits at ground instead of supply (20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips); Saab's ME9 uses below 2.6 V at the output. The valve is then energised and open all the time, purging is uncontrolled – rough idle, rich mixture or hard starting after refuelling are possible.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or supply
Purge valve coil low-resistance (shorted turns)
Connector or harness damaged
Engine module
P0459.en: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit High
P0459.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Purge valve A is switched to ground by the module and fed from the main relay. P0459 means its control wire is shorted to positive, detected with the driver switched on, when the line should sit at ground (GM 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips; Saab ME9 above 4.6 V). The valve then cannot open, the canister is not purged and fills up; the driver protects itself and the leak tests are suspended.

causes_en: Connector at EGR valve B corroded or loose
Harness chafed or heat-damaged
Actuator motor in valve B open
Driver in the engine module
P045A.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR B is a second EGR valve next to valve A – on diesels with two EGR circuits the low-pressure valve, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor. GM's diesels of 2016–18 and FCA's 2.2-litre diesel in the Jeep Wrangler use it. P045A is the general electrical fault in the drive circuit of valve B, typically an open circuit (for valve A GM uses 200 kΩ or more). GM lists this code among those that switch off the low-pressure EGR position control, but publishes no thresholds for it; the description follows the comparable valve A checks and CARB, which requires output circuits to be monitored. Low-pressure EGR is then switched off.

causes_en: Valve B coked or stiff
Contact resistance in connector or wiring
Actuator motor worn internally
Engine module software or calibration
P045B.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR B is a second EGR valve next to valve A – on diesels with two EGR circuits the low-pressure valve, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor. GM's diesels of 2016–18 and FCA's 2.2-litre diesel in the Jeep Wrangler use it. P045B means the drive circuit of valve B is electrically valid, but the feedback – current, voltage or position response – does not match the command. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows the valve A counterpart P0404 and CARB, which requires output functions to be checked where feasible. Typical is a coked, stiff valve.

Actuator motor winding shorted
Water or corrosion in the connector
Driver in the engine module
P045C.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR B is a second EGR valve next to valve A – on diesels with two EGR circuits the low-pressure valve, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor. GM's diesels of 2016–18 and FCA's 2.2-litre diesel in the Jeep Wrangler use it. The driver is switched off for protection and the valve stays in its rest position. GM lists this code among those that switch off the low-pressure EGR position control, but publishes no thresholds for it; the description follows the comparable valve A checks and CARB, which requires output circuits to be monitored.

Actuator motor shorted internally (overcurrent)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Engine module
P045D.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR B is a second EGR valve next to valve A – on diesels with two EGR circuits the low-pressure valve, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor. causes_en: Soot or condensate deposits in the low-pressure valve
Valve position sensor fault as the trigger
Actuator gear or return spring faulty
Foreign matter or filter debris in the low-pressure circuit
P045E.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR B is a second EGR valve next to valve A – on diesels with two EGR circuits the low-pressure valve, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor. GM's diesels of 2016–18 and FCA's 2.2-litre diesel in the Jeep Wrangler use it. P045E means valve B does not close: its actual position stays above the target despite the close command. On FCA's 2.2-litre diesel in the Jeep Wrangler, deposits in the low-pressure valve cause it; the bulletin prescribes a cleaning routine of nine ignition cycles that moves the valve repeatedly. Another FCA bulletin shows P045E following a position sensor fault (P0407/P0408). Too much EGR causes misfire, lack of power and smoke.

causes_en: Low-pressure valve coked or stuck
Actuator motor or gear faulty
Icing or condensate in the low-pressure circuit
Position sensor reports a wrong position
P045F.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR B is a second EGR valve next to valve A – on diesels with two EGR circuits the low-pressure valve, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor. GM's diesels of 2016–18 and FCA's 2.2-litre diesel in the Jeep Wrangler use it. P045F means valve B does not open: its actual position stays below the target despite the open command. GM lists the code among those that switch off low-pressure EGR control; Ford's comparable valve A check (P042F) compares the position with a calculated lower limit. Too little EGR raises NOx while driving stays normal. Icing or condensate can block a low-pressure valve – FCA runs its cleaning routine only above 0 °C.

causes_en: Resistor track worn or float arm sticking
Wire or connector at the tank unit open or shorted (corrosion)
Instrument cluster or gateway sends a wrong value (if the level comes via the bus)

P0460.desc: The fuel level sensor is a float on a resistor track in the tank unit. P0465.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. A purge flow sensor – a heated thermistor in the purge line between purge valve and intake manifold, as described in a Ford patent – measures purge flow directly for the CARB purge monitor. Today indirect methods (fuel trim, tank vacuum) have largely replaced it; no manufacturer document available to us uses these codes. P0465 is the general circuit fault of the sensor (heater supply, signal or ground), which CARB requires to be checked continuously. The purge flow monitor can then not be evaluated.

P046A.desc: Some engines measure the catalyst temperature with sensors instead of only modelling it. P046A compares catalyst temperature sensors 1 and 2 of bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1): both are electrically valid, but their readings do not match – for example they differ after a long stop, or the difference does not fit the operating state. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; FCA's EcoDiesel has only one such sensor per bank, and most makers handle exhaust temperature sensors and their correlation under EGT codes such as P0544 ff or P24C2. The description follows CARB's plausibility requirement for input components.

P046C.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Which part EGR sensors A and B are depends on the maker: sensor A is usually the position sensor of EGR valve A; GM's Duramax diesels of 2017/18 use sensor B for the coolant temperature sensor at the inlet of the high-pressure EGR cooler, FCA for the position sensor of the low-pressure valve. P046C means the signal of sensor A is electrically valid but implausible. GM's diesels (6.6-litre Duramax LML and others from 2014) set it when the actual valve position deviates from the target by 5 % or more for 8 s, with offset learning completed and at least 11 V (MIL after two trips). Ford uses P0405/P0406/P046D for sensor A instead. EGR is then switched off or limited.

P0470.desc: The exhaust pressure sensor measures the pressure ahead of the turbine or in the manifold (Ford: turbine upstream pressure, Cummins: exhaust manifold pressure, older Ford diesels: EBP). The module uses it to calculate EGR flow, to control the variable turbine and engine braking, and to protect against overpressure. P0470 is the general circuit fault of sensor A. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel with a digital SENT sensor sets it when the sensor reports an error status or its raw data leave their limits for 5 s; a loss of communication is U0691 instead. Analogue sensors use it for an open or unspecified circuit fault where low and high are not separated.

P0471.en: Exhaust Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P0475.desc: The exhaust pressure control valve is a flap in the exhaust: on older Navistar/Ford diesels a warm-up flap that raises back pressure when cold, on Ram and others an exhaust brake, on VW's 2.0 TDI a flap that drives the low-pressure EGR, and on Audi and Bentley a sound flap. P0476.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Range/Performance
P0476.desc: The exhaust pressure control valve is a flap in the exhaust: on older Navistar/Ford diesels a warm-up flap that raises back pressure when cold, on Ram and others an exhaust brake, on VW's 2.0 TDI a flap that drives the low-pressure EGR, and on Audi and Bentley a sound flap. P0480.desc: The engine module switches the radiator fan either through a relay, whose coil it pulls to ground, or with a PWM signal to a fan control module. The circuit is an output that CARB requires to be checked continuously. P0480 concerns the control circuit of fan 1. GM sets it for an open circuit – 200 kΩ or more with the driver off, 50 of 63 samples, above 11 V, MIL after two trips – and reports a short to ground or positive as P0691/P0692; Saab models on GM technology set it after 5 s (relay) or 1 s (PWM). FCA bulletins also name it with the warning lamp. Ford's OBD summaries do not contain the code. If the fan stops, the engine can overheat in traffic and the air conditioning weakens at standstill.

P0481.desc: The engine module switches the radiator fan either through a relay, whose coil it pulls to ground, or with a PWM signal to a fan control module. The circuit is an output that CARB requires to be checked continuously. P0481 concerns the second fan control circuit – depending on the design a second fan or a second speed stage; on GM and Saab, relays 2 and 3 switch the fans in series or parallel for low and high speed. GM sets it for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 50 of 63 samples, MIL after two trips) and reports shorts as P0693/P0694. Ford's OBD summaries do not contain the code. One fan stage then fails or runs constantly; cooling usually remains partly available.

P0482.desc: The engine module switches cooling fan stages through relays, pulling each relay coil to ground. P0482 concerns the control circuit of the third stage or relay: with the driver off the line should sit at battery voltage through the coil, and the internal pull-up level means an open circuit (Saab ME9: more than 1 s, 10–18 V, engine running). On the GM-based Saab 9-5 of 2011 it is relay 3 (medium stage) of a two-fan network, with shorts reported as P0695/P0696. GM tables list P0482 only in fault groups; Ford's OBD summaries do not contain it. One fan stage then fails.
