P0483.desc: Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0483 checks the fan's function, not its circuit. With a speed sensor (GM viscous fans) commanded and actual speed are compared: GM's Duramax diesels of 2014–18 set it at more than ±500 rpm for at least 120 s, GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups of 2004–06 at more than 1000 rpm – MIL after two trips. Without a sensor Subaru (and the Saab 9-2X) judges indirectly: if coolant at 100 °C or more does not fall within 5 minutes at idle with the fan on, the code sets after two trips. Ford's OBD summaries do not contain it.

causes_en: Fan motor stiff (bearing damage) or blocked (foreign object, ice, bent blade)
Shorted turns or worn brushes in the fan motor
Short in the load circuit (pinched or chafed wire)
Fan control module faulty (wrong current measurement)
P0484.desc: P0484 monitors the current drawn in the fan's load circuit: if it exceeds a threshold – blocked or stiff motor, shorted turns, a short in the load circuit – the code sets. This is only possible where the fan runs on a current-measuring semiconductor driver or fan module; plain relay circuits do not measure load current. Supplier patents (Bosch and others) describe current limiting or switch-off after a few seconds of overcurrent, ignoring the inrush current. No manufacturer table available to us lists P0484, so thresholds and warning-lamp behaviour remain open; CARB requires output components to be monitored.

causes_en: Fan or fan module ground loose, corroded or broken
Fan fuse blown or fuse holder overheated or corroded
Relay power contact burnt – voltage drop under load
Connector at the fan scorched, water ingress
Fan control module faulty
P0485.desc: P0485 monitors the supply or ground path of the fan or its control module – not the control line. It is typical of fans with their own module (PWM or LIN), which can report undervoltage or a missing ground. The high currents involved, often 20–60 A, make contact resistance at ground and supply connections and fuse holders the main cause. No manufacturer table available to us lists P0485, so thresholds and warning-lamp behaviour remain open; CARB requires output components to be monitored. The fan then runs intermittently or not at all.

causes_en: Connector or harness to sensor B corroded or open (heat at the exhaust)
Sensor B faulty
5 V reference or ground disturbed
Engine module or software
P0486.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Which part EGR sensor B is depends on the maker: FCA uses it for the position sensor of the low-pressure EGR valve, GM's Duramax diesels for the coolant temperature sensor at the EGR cooler inlet. P0486 is its general circuit fault without a low or high assignment. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – makers report sensor B as P0407/P0408, P046E and P046F – so the description follows CARB's input component rules. EGR is then switched off or uses a substitute value.

causes_en: Connector at the flap corroded or loose, wire open
Flap actuator motor faulty (winding open)
Pneumatic version: vacuum converter faulty
Driver in the engine module
P0487.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. The EGR throttle is a regulating flap ahead of the intake manifold on diesels: by closing partly it lowers manifold pressure below exhaust back pressure so that enough exhaust is recirculated, and it also helps filter regeneration and shuts off air at engine stop. It is usually a DC motor with position sensor. GM and Ford report this flap under P02E0 ff; no manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P0487 means its drive circuit is open or has a general circuit fault, detected by the output stage. The flap then stays open, so the EGR rate cannot be raised enough and filter regeneration may be blocked.

causes_en: Flap coked by soot and oil mist (EGR plus crankcase ventilation)
Actuator gear or motor worn or broken
Position sensor in the flap faulty or implausible
Corrosion on flap or housing
P0488.en: EGR Throttle Control Circuit A Range/Performance
P0488.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. The EGR throttle is a regulating flap ahead of the intake manifold on diesels: by closing partly it lowers manifold pressure below exhaust back pressure so that enough exhaust is recirculated, and it also helps filter regeneration and shuts off air at engine stop. It is usually a DC motor with position sensor. GM and Ford report this flap under P02E0 ff; no manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P0488 is its function check: the actual position reported by the sensor deviates from the target for too long, or the position signal is implausible – typically a coked, stiff flap or a broken gear. The flap then goes to its rest position or the engine enters limp mode, and the EGR rate cannot be controlled.

causes_en: Harness chafed at the exhaust with short to ground
EGR valve winding shorted to its housing
Water or corrosion in the connector
Driver in the engine module
P0489.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0489 means the drive circuit of EGR valve A – solenoid, stepper or DC motor – is shorted to ground. GM's Duramax LML sets it at 0.5 Ω or less to ground for 3 s, GM's 2016 diesels after 96 of 120 samples, Ford diesels after 0.35 s, Saab's 2.0 TiD likewise – MIL after two trips. The valve is usually switched off; with low-side control a short to ground can keep it energised and open, causing rough idle or stalling.

causes_en: Flap or flap shaft corroded or coked (stiff)
Flap actuator (motor or gear) faulty or too weak
Linkage between actuator and flap broken or misadjusted
Position sensor reports wrongly
P048A.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Stuck Closed
P048A.desc: An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve A is the first such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P048A means valve A is commanded open but its position feedback stays closed. On VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI of 2009–13 water and road salt corrode the shaft of the low-pressure EGR flap so it sticks; the code appears with P047F, P0477, P048B/P048C and P0401. The bulletins advise removing the flap and checking it moves freely, otherwise replacing it; improved parts were introduced. A closed flap keeps back pressure high.

causes_en: Actuator with integrated position sensor faulty
Connector or wire at the underbody corroded, chafed or open
Engine module (sensor supply or input)
P048B.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Sensor/Switch Circuit
P048B.desc: An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve A is the first such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P048B is the general circuit fault or open circuit of valve A's position sensor or end switch. VW's 2.0 TDI of 2009–13 sets it with a corroded flap; on the 2015 engine it appears with P048E, P0475, P0477 and P0478 and the actuator with its integrated electronics is replaced; Bentley's V8 of 2023 reports it for bank 1 together with P048D. As the sensor sits in the actuator, a circuit fault often means actuator electronics.

causes_en: Flap or shaft corroded or coked (stiff)
End positions not relearned after replacement
Position sensor in the actuator drifting
Contact resistance in the connector
P048C.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance
P048C.desc: An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve A is the first such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P048C means valve A's position signal is electrically valid but does not match the commanded position or the learned end positions. It is documented only on VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI of 2009–13, together with P047F, P048A, P048B and P0401, caused by the corroded, sticking flap shaft. After replacing the actuator, the end positions must be relearned.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed at the underbody)
Position sensor or actuator faulty internally
5 V sensor supply open or shorted
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
P048D.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low
P048D.desc: An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve A is the first such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P048D means valve A's position signal is below its permitted voltage window – the signal wire is shorted to ground or the sensor's 5 V supply is missing. Bentley's Continental and Flying Spur V8 of 2023 report it for bank 1 together with P048B; the bulletin advises checking wiring and contacts, otherwise replacing the actuator and carrying out the basic setting.

causes_en: Actuator electronics (position sensor) faulty
Signal or ground wire open
Connector corroded
Signal shorted to positive
P048E.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High
P048E.desc: An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve A is the first such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P048E means valve A's position signal is above its window – an open signal pulled up, or a short to positive. VW's 2.0 TDI third generation of 2015 sets it together with P048B, P0475, P0477 and P0478: the flap is welded into the pipe, so with electronic faults only the actuator is replaced – an electrostatic-sensitive part that must be scrapped if dropped.

causes_en: Loose contact or corrosion at the actuator connector
Wire broken by vibration or heat
Position sensor worn
P048F.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P048F.desc: An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve A is the first such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P048F means valve A's position signal jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than physically possible. Bentley stores sporadic sensor faults under the low code with a sporadic status instead. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows the sibling codes P048B–P048E and CARB.

causes_en: Harness shorted to a supply wire (chafing)
EGR valve with shorted turns (low resistance, overcurrent)
Moisture in the connector
Driver in the engine module
P0490.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0490 means the drive circuit of EGR valve A is shorted to battery voltage, or its output stage sees overcurrent. GM's Duramax LML sets it at 0.5 Ω or less to the supply for 3 s, GM's 2017 diesels at an H-bridge current above 8 A (160 of 200 samples), Ford diesels after 0.35 s – MIL after two trips. The output stage switches off for protection and the valve falls into its spring position, closed; EGR is off.

causes_en: Secondary air passages in the cylinder head coked
Combination valve stuck or stiff
Vacuum supply or changeover valve leaking, valve closes too early
Secondary air pump weak or water in the pump
Hose between pump and valve leaking or off
P0491.desc: After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; CARB requires the air flow to be monitored per bank. P0491 means too little air reaches bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1). VW and Audi calculate the injected air mass per bank from the front oxygen sensor's reaction during the cold-start phase; an Audi bulletin names values of 0.4–0.7 on both banks as too little together, often from coked air passages in the cylinder head. On VW/Audi V engines each bank has its own combination valve with a shared pump. Ford assigns the code to the bank 1 secondary air monitor; GM uses P0411 instead.

causes_en: Secondary air passages in the cylinder head coked
Combination valve stuck or stiff
Vacuum supply or changeover valve leaking, valve closes too early
Secondary air pump weak or water in the pump
Hose between pump and valve leaking or off
P0492.desc: After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; CARB requires the air flow to be monitored per bank. P0492 means too little air reaches bank 2 (the side without cylinder 1). VW and Audi calculate the injected air mass per bank from the front oxygen sensor's reaction during the cold-start phase; an Audi bulletin names values of 0.4–0.7 on both banks as too little together, often from coked air passages in the cylinder head. On VW/Audi V engines each bank has its own combination valve with a shared pump. Ford assigns the code to the bank 2 secondary air monitor; GM uses P0411 instead.

causes_en: Viscous clutch seized – fan runs rigidly with the belt drive
Interference or faulty signal from the fan speed sensor
Clutch solenoid or its control stuck at fully engaged
Engine module or software
P0493.desc: Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0493 is documented only on GM petrol engines of 2004–06 with a viscous fan: the measured fan speed exceeds a limit that is hardly physically possible (about 6400 rpm), so it is effectively a plausibility check of the speed signal or a seized clutch at high engine speed. Two counts set it, with the warning lamp on the first trip – unlike P0495, which needs two trips. Ford, FCA and GM from 2014 were not found to use it.

causes_en: Fan motor or fan module faulty or worn (brushes, bearings, electronics)
Fan slowed or blocked (water, snow, ice, foreign object, distorted shroud)
Viscous clutch slipping or low on fluid, clutch valve faulty
High-resistance supply or ground, connector problems
Faulty speed signal (sensor or LIN feedback)
P0494.desc: Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0494 means fan 1 turns slower than commanded, judged from the speed reported by a LIN fan module or the clutch's speed sensor. GM's 2.0-litre turbo of 2020 uses a lower limit of about 59 % of the target at 750 rpm, rising to about 76 % at 2750 rpm and above. GM bulletins name an internal fan fault on the Equinox/Terrain 1.5 and water slowing the fan on the Hummer EV; Ford's 6.7-litre Super Duty uses it for the viscous fan and warns against replacing the clutch too quickly.

causes_en: Viscous clutch does not release (gummed, overfilled, seized)
Clutch solenoid or its control stuck open (short to positive, valve sticking)
Wrong speed signal (sensor, wiring, interference)
Electric fan: module runs uncontrolled at full speed or relay sticking
P0495.desc: Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0495 mainly concerns viscous fans: with the fan commanded off it turns faster than the permitted drag speed, so the clutch does not release. GM thresholds: Duramax 2016 above 1500 rpm, Duramax 2018 above a calculated drag speed, petrol SUVs of 2004–05 above 1600 rpm without command – all with the warning lamp after two trips; Ford's 6.7-litre Super Duty uses it the same way. On GM's 2020 2.0-litre turbo with a LIN electric fan it means a reported speed above 2900 rpm.

causes_en: Purge valve leaking or stuck open (charcoal dust in the seat)
Vent valve stuck closed or vent filter or line blocked
Vapour line kinked or blocked
Tank pressure sensor reading wrong
P0496.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0496 means vapour flows into the intake although the module is not purging – usually a purge valve that leaks or sticks open. GM and Saab seal the system after a cold start with the engine running; if tank vacuum exceeds 2491 Pa for 5 s, the code sets (fuel 10–90 %, MIL after two trips). Ford, which replaced its old code P1450 with P0496, also sets it for excessive vacuum during the leak test, for example with a vent valve stuck closed. Hard starting right after refuelling is typical.

causes_en: Purge valve stuck closed, does not open
Purge line off, kinked or blocked (check valve sticking)
Canister or vent filter blocked (e.g. after overfilling)
Vent valve stuck closed
P0497.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0497 is the counterpart of P0496: the module purges but sees too little or no purge flow, judged indirectly from fuel trim, idle control or tank vacuum – CARB requires missing purge flow to be detected. Code-specific use is documented only by Land Rover (5.0-litre V8) and in a GM fault group for systems with a sealed tank (Volt, ELR); standard GM and Ford systems use other codes, such as P0455. The canister is then not purged and saturates.

causes_en: Vent valve control wire chafed against ground (underbody, tank area)
Vent valve coil shorted internally
Corrosion or water in the connector
Driver in the engine module
P0498.en: EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit Low
P0498.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The vent valve is normally open and switched to ground by the module; P0449 (open), P0498 and P0499 form the newer code scheme for its circuit, used mainly by GM and Saab models with GM engines, while Ford uses P0446. P0498 means the control wire is shorted to ground: GM sees 0.5 Ω or less to ground with the driver off (20 of 25 samples), Saab below 2.6 V – MIL after two trips. The valve is then permanently energised and closed, so the tank is not vented and refuelling becomes difficult.

causes_en: Control wire touching battery positive or the valve supply (chafed harness)
Vent valve coil with shorted turns, driver switches off
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Driver in the engine module
P0499.en: EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit High
P0499.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The vent valve is normally open and switched to ground by the module (GM scheme P0449/P0498/P0499; Ford uses P0446). P0499 means the control wire is shorted to positive: with the driver on the output stays high – GM sees 0.5 Ω or less to the supply, Saab above 4.6 V; MIL after two trips. The valve then cannot close, the system cannot be sealed, and the leak tests are suspended because they would otherwise report a large leak.

causes_en: Low-pressure EGR valve sooted or sticking
Low-pressure EGR cooler or line blocked or leaking
Flap creating the pressure difference faulty
Sensors (air mass, pressure difference, position sensor B) implausible
P049A.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Circuit B is the second EGR path; on diesels with two circuits it is the low-pressure EGR, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor (GM diesels 2016–18, FCA's 2.2 and 3.0 diesels). P049A is the general flow fault of circuit B, used where the module does not separate too little from too much; CARB requires low and high flow to be detected, mostly by comparing air mass, manifold pressure or lambda with a model. No manufacturer document available to us uses P049A – GM has only position and actuator codes for its low-pressure EGR, FCA uses P049B. Low-pressure EGR is then switched off.

causes_en: Software or calibration (false trigger)
Low-pressure EGR valve sooted or stuck closed
Low-pressure EGR cooler or line blocked
Implausible sensors (air mass, pressure difference)
P049B.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Circuit B is the second EGR path; on diesels with two circuits it is the low-pressure EGR, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor (GM diesels 2016–18, FCA's 2.2 and 3.0 diesels). P049B means too little flow in circuit B: with the low-pressure valve open the module expects a change in fresh air mass or manifold pressure, or a modelled EGR volume, and the actual flow stays below the threshold. FCA documents it on the 3.0-litre EcoDiesel third generation in the 2020 Ram 1500, partly as a false trigger fixed by a software update; thresholds are not published.

causes_en: Low-pressure EGR valve stuck open or not sealing (soot)
Position sensor B implausible (valve seemingly closed)
Leak between exhaust side and intake
Air mass meter reading too low
P049C.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Circuit B is the second EGR path; on diesels with two circuits it is the low-pressure EGR, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor (GM diesels 2016–18, FCA's 2.2 and 3.0 diesels). P049C means too much flow in circuit B – fresh air mass drops further than modelled, or EGR flows with the low-pressure valve closed; CARB explicitly requires a leaking valve to be detected. No manufacturer document available to us uses P049C; the closest is FCA's P045E for a low-pressure valve stuck open. Smoke, lack of power and rough idle follow, and low-pressure EGR is switched off.

causes_en: Soot or deposits at the valve seat, valve does not close fully
Position sensor A faulty or characteristic shifted
New or cleaned valve not taught in, or wrong part
Position sensor circuit fault as the primary cause
P049D.en: EGR A Control Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P049D.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P049D checks the learned zero point – the fully closed position – of EGR valve A. The module learns the position sensor voltage with the valve closed, at GM during the after-run following ignition off; if the learned value lies outside a window (GM 2018: 83.5–93.5 % of 5 V, GM 2016: 16.4–25.1 %) or the values scatter too much (GM Duramax LML above 30 %), the code sets – MIL after two trips at GM, immediately after learning at Ford. Usually soot at the seat keeps the valve from closing, or a new valve was not taught in.

causes_en: Low-pressure EGR valve sooted, does not close fully
Position sensor of the low-pressure valve faulty or shifted
Valve replaced without teaching in
Harness or connector of the low-pressure valve
P049E.en: EGR B Control Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P049E.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Circuit B is the second EGR path; on diesels with two circuits it is the low-pressure EGR, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor (GM diesels 2016–18, FCA's 2.2 and 3.0 diesels). P049E is the counterpart of P049D for valve B: the learned zero point of its position sensor lies outside the permitted window. GM lists it only in a fault group of its low-pressure EGR (whose position sensor is sensor C there, P044C/P044D), and in the 2016 calibration it is explicitly disabled; thresholds are not published. The description therefore follows GM's P049D strategy by analogy. Low-pressure EGR position control is then switched off.

Wire or connector at the actuator damaged
Control wire open
Driver in the engine module
P049F.desc: An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve B is the second such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P04A0.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve B Range/Performance

P04A4.en: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve B Stuck Open

P04AB.en: EVAP System Purge Control Valve B Circuit/Open
P04AB.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Purge valve B is a second electric purge valve, usually for the high-load purge line of a turbo engine, which purges to the compressor inlet when there is boost in the manifold (Ford patent). Many makers solve this path with one purge valve and passive check valves instead – Ford tests it as P04F0 – and then have no valve B. CARB requires every purge path to be checked. P04AB means the control circuit of purge valve B is open; the high-load path then does not purge. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the comparable purge valve A checks (for GM P0443/P0458/P0459).

P04B0.desc: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Plug-in hybrids and range extenders with a sealed, pressurised tank have an electric valve in the vapour line between tank and canister. It is normally closed and opens before refuelling, so that the tank is depressurised – the filler flap is only released then – and refuelling vapour reaches the canister (Ford patent). No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford reports its tank isolation valve as P2418/P2450 – so the description follows CARB and the component patent.

P04B4.en: Refueling Vapor Control Valve Stuck Closed
P04B4.desc: Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. When the driver presses the fuel button, the system opens the valve, lets the pressure escape into the canister and only then unlocks the filler door. A switch reports whether the door is open or closed, so that the tank can be sealed again afterwards. P04B4 is the function check of the valve between tank and canister: after the open command the tank pressure must move towards canister or ambient pressure, and if the rate of change stays below a threshold the valve counts as stuck closed (Ford patent). The tank then cannot be depressurised, the door does not unlock or only after a long delay, and during refuelling vapour cannot reach the canister. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code.

P04B5.desc: Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. Stellantis re-enables the check only after more than 16 miles and names a missing plunger or magnet, the cap tether blocking it, or a short to ground of the status line.

P04BB.en: Fuel Fill Door Lock Control Circuit/Open
P04BB.desc: On plug-in hybrids with a sealed, pressurised tank, pressing the fuel button (open request) starts a refuelling mode: the module opens the tank valve, releases the pressure into the charcoal canister and only then unlocks the filler door via an electric actuator (Ford patent). P04CE.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. The code standard allows up to four EGR temperature sensors, A to D – for example before and after the cooler, or in the high- and low-pressure circuits; which is which depends on the maker. Sensor C is the third of them, usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. P04CE is its general circuit fault, without separating low and high. FCA lists sensor C codes for its part 68142905A (Ram 2014 6.4 and 3.0 litre, Jeep and Dodge 3.6 Pentastar 2016) together with P040B, P0401 and P2457. Thresholds are not published. Without a valid temperature the EGR flow model is wrong, so the module uses a substitute value or switches EGR off.

P04CF.en: EGR Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P04CF.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Comparable checks on sensors A and B compare it after a long stop with coolant and intake air, or look for a temperature change during EGR operation (Ford diesels, GM diesels above 10 °C). No manufacturer document available to us uses P04CF; FCA lists P040B as the range code for its sensor C part.

P04D3.desc: The exhaust brake input is the driver's request for the exhaust or engine brake – a button or stalk on diesel pick-ups and trucks. On GM's 6.6-litre L5P, for example, the button must be pressed again after every start. GM uses the exhaust brake status as an enable condition for other emission monitors, which is why CARB requires the input to be checked. P04D8.en: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop EGR Control
P04D8.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Where EGR is closed-loop controlled – on flow, valve position or pressure difference – CARB requires the control to start within a time set by the maker after starting; otherwise a fault is due, and P04D8 is that code. Typical prerequisites are coolant or cooler temperature, valid sensors and an operating range; Ford diesels, for example, run their EGR monitors only with EGR in closed loop. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04D8 – many monitor the inputs individually instead, as CARB permits.

Software or driving profile with long low-load operation
P04D9.en: Closed Loop EGR Control At Limit - Flow Too Low
P04D9.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04D9 means the EGR control has used up its authority and still gets too little flow – CARB requires this to be detected. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel sets it when the desired minus the measured EGR rate stays above 50 points for 20 s. Volvo cars from 2022 also set it after long low-load driving and fix it with a software update and an activation drive; a Mack/Volvo truck bulletin traces it to wrong EGR temperature readings from worn connector contacts.

causes_en: EGR valve not closing (soot at the seat, stuck open)
Air mass meter reading too little fresh air (EGR rate calculated too high)
Position or EGR temperature sensor giving a wrong value
Intake or exhaust throttle wrong (pressure difference too large)
P04DA.en: Closed Loop EGR Control At Limit - Flow Too High
P04DA.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DA is the counterpart of P04D9: the control cannot lower the flow far enough even at the end of its range. CARB requires this for petrol engines from model years 2019–21 and for diesels. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel sets it when the desired minus the measured EGR rate stays below −60 points for 20 s with EGR in closed loop. Too much exhaust in the cylinder causes soot, rough running and, on petrol engines, misfire up to stalling at idle.

Hose cracked or porous, or nipple broken

P04DB.desc: The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04DB means a disconnection: without the pressure drop the clean-air side is off, without the pulses the crankcase side. GM's LSY uses the product of normalised offset and noise (below 0.63 kPa², MIL after two trips); Ford's EcoBoost checks the dirty side at cranking and the clean side above 5 lb/min of air. Engines without such a sensor may report a disconnection through mixture or load codes, as CARB allows. FCA bulletins cover it on the Alfa Romeo 2.0 turbo and the Ram 3.0 EcoDiesel.

P04DC.en: Fuel Fill Door Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance
P04DC.desc: Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. When the driver presses the fuel button, the system opens the valve, lets the pressure escape into the canister and only then unlocks the filler door. A switch reports whether the door is open or closed, so that the tank can be sealed again afterwards. P04DC means the door switch signal is electrically valid but implausible. A GM patent detects refuelling from a rising fuel level at standstill with low tank pressure; if the switch reported open for less than about 20 s, or closed for too long, it is faulty. A Ford patent sets a fault if the fuel level rose and the car drove off without the switch ever reporting open – the valve then stays open and the driver is warned. If the door state is unknown, the system leaves the tank open to the canister as a precaution and suspends the leak tests. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules and patents for the door switch.

P04DD.en: Cold Start EGR A Flow Insufficient Detected
P04DD.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DD monitors EGR A while a cold-start emission reduction strategy is active and commands EGR: if the flow does not react as intended, too little exhaust is recirculated in the warm-up phase. CARB requires separate codes for such cold-start faults, which is why P04DD exists alongside P0401. The only manufacturer reference is a FCA bulletin for a six-cylinder diesel with high- and low-pressure EGR, naming it as a consequence of a failed position sensor (P0407/P0408) – repair that first.

P04DE.en: Cold Start EGR A Flow Excessive Detected
P04DE.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DE is the counterpart of P04DD: during an active cold-start strategy the flow of EGR A is too high – the strategy calls for little or limited EGR, but the valve lets more through. CARB requires separate codes for cold-start faults. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04DE; FCA uses the neighbouring code P04DD, so its use there is plausible but not documented. Too much exhaust in a cold engine causes rough running, smoke and in extreme cases stalling.

P04DF.en: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Performance/Stuck Open
P04DF.desc: Purge valve A is the main EVAP purge valve between charcoal canister and intake manifold (on turbo engines the low-load path); its electrical circuit faults are P0443, P0458 and P0459. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows GM's comparable check P0496, Subaru's valve B counterpart P04AE and CARB's purge flow requirement. P04DF means valve A does not react as commanded or lets vapour through when closed: with the system sealed and the valve not driven, vacuum must not reach the tank. Intake vacuum then draws vapour all the time – rich mixture and hard starting after refuelling are typical.

P04E0.en: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Stuck Closed
P04E0.desc: Purge valve A is the main EVAP purge valve between charcoal canister and intake manifold (on turbo engines the low-load path); its electrical circuit faults are P0443, P0458 and P0459. P04E0 means valve A does not open although it is driven: no vacuum builds up in the tank and the mixture does not react while purging – CARB requires missing purge flow to be detected. Sensor D is the fourth of up to four EGR temperature sensors, conceivable on engines with high- and low-pressure EGR and a sensor before and after each cooler; it is usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D; the description follows CARB and Ford's checks on sensor B as a comparison. P04E6 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – for example it differs from other temperatures after a long stop, does not react when EGR opens, or freezes. Ford compares sensor B with intake and charge air after at least 6 hours off and flags more than 25 °C.

causes_en: Signal line chafed against ground or the engine
Sensor shorted internally
Water or corrosion in the connector
Module input faulty
P04E7.en: EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P04E7.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Sensor D is the fourth of up to four EGR temperature sensors, conceivable on engines with high- and low-pressure EGR and a sensor before and after each cooler; it is usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D; the description follows CARB and Ford's checks on sensor B as a comparison. P04E7 means the signal is below its lower limit – a signal line shorted to ground or, theoretically, an extremely high temperature. For sensor B Ford uses below 0.19 V. A substitute value is used and EGR may be reduced.

causes_en: Connector off or loose, or pin corroded
Sensor open internally (heat damage)
Sensor ground line open
Signal line shorted to positive

A substitute value is used.

causes_en: Loose contact in connector or harness (vibration, heat)
Sensor with an internal hairline crack
Chafed harness
Module or ground connection
P04E9.en: EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P04E9.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Sensor D is the fourth of up to four EGR temperature sensors, conceivable on engines with high- and low-pressure EGR and a sensor before and after each cooler; it is usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D; the description follows CARB and Ford's checks on sensor B as a comparison. P04E9 means the signal briefly leaves its valid range or changes impossibly fast – typically a loose contact. Ford detects such sporadic faults on other sensors with short limit violations of about 0.4 s.

causes_en: Fuel cap or seal leaking or not closed properly (tether trapped)
Filler neck or tank vent line leaking
Sender or pump flange seal leaking
Tank valve or tank pressure sensor faulty
P04EA.en: EVAP System Small Leak Detected - Fuel Tank Side
P04EA.desc: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EA reports a small leak (0.040 in) in the tank section – tank, filler neck, cap and lines up to the tank valve. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB and the Ford patent.

causes_en: Crack or leaking connection at the canister or vent lines
Vent valve or leak check module not sealing
Purge valve leaking
Rodent bite or chafing on lines under the car
P04EB.en: EVAP System Small Leak Detected - Fresh Air Side
P04EB.desc: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EB reports a small leak (0.040 in) in the canister and vent section – canister, vent valve or leak check module, dust filter and lines up to the purge valve – typically checked with the leak check pump with the engine off. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB and the Ford patent.

causes_en: Fuel cap not closed properly or tether trapped
Cap or filler neck sealing surface poor
Recirculation or vent line loose at the quick connector
Tank pressure sensor or valve faulty
P04EC.en: EVAP System Large Leak Detected - Fuel Tank Side
P04EC.desc: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EC reports a large leak in the tank section: it cannot be brought to test pressure or loses it at once – cap missing or open, line off. Stellantis documents it on the Jeep Wrangler 4xe plug-in hybrid only, whose conventional models report P0455; several bulletins name a cap not closed properly or a trapped tether, with a forced leak test via the scan tool.

causes_en: Line at the canister or leak check module off or broken
Vent valve or leak check module not closing
Canister housing cracked
Purge valve stuck open

No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB and the Ford patent.

Purge valve not sealing (Ford hybrids) – plus software
Leaking quick connector or vent line at the tank
Hairline crack in tank lines or flange seal

causes_en: Purge valve not sealing
Vent valve or leak check module leaking
Hairline crack or leaking connections at the canister
Module software (misjudgement)
P04EF.en: EVAP System Very Small Leak Detected - Fresh Air Side

P04EF reports a very small leak (0.020 in) in the canister and vent section; the leak check module compares the vacuum against a 0.020 in reference and the section does not reach it. On Ford's C-Max, Fusion and MKZ hybrids and Energi a leaking purge valve is the typical trigger, fixed per bulletin with the valve and software.

causes_en: Check valve in the purge line leaking, stuck open, fitted wrongly or missing
High-load purge line to the turbo or venturi off, cracked or blocked
Purge line pressure sensor wrongly connected or faulty (VW group)
Purge valve or venturi faulty
P04F0.en: EVAP System High Load Purge Line A Performance
P04F0.desc: Turbocharged engines also purge the charcoal canister under boost, through a high-load line to the compressor inlet via a venturi; check valves keep boost out of the EVAP system, and CARB requires this path to be monitored. P04F0 checks it: Ford (2020–23, replacing P144C) runs the test once per trip under boost with the vent closed and purge open, and sets the code if tank pressure rises faster than 0.5 or 1 inH2O/s or the vacuum rate is out of range, within 5–10 s. VW, Audi and Bentley monitor the line with their own pressure sensor.

causes_en: Purge line to the intake manifold off, kinked or blocked
Check valve in the low-load path sticking
Purge valve not opening fully
Tank pressure sensor misreading
P04F1.desc: P04F1 is the function check of a purge line that is not the high-load path A – by the wording of another code list the low-pressure path to the intake manifold, counterpart of P04F0. The purge valve opens and the tank pressure or mixture reaction is missing or wrong: the line is blocked or off, or a check valve sticks. CARB requires every purge path to be checked; a FCA patent describes such a stepwise test. No manufacturer document available to us names this code.

causes_en: 48 V or high-voltage supply weak (battery, charge, cold, DC-DC converter)
Fuse, relay or power switch faulty
Contact resistance or corrosion at high-current connector or ground
Module or voltage measurement faulty
P04F2.desc: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04F2 concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code monitors the supply voltage of the heater: if it lies outside its window when heating is requested, the heater cannot deliver its power and is limited or switched off, so the catalyst lights off later. A Subaru patent detects faults in the supply path when the heater is commanded. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.

causes_en: EGR valve stiff from coking (motor working against resistance)
High thermal load (full load, poor valve cooling, low coolant)
Valve motor or H-bridge driver faulty (overcurrent)
Module software
P04FA.en: EGR A Control Temperature Too High
P04FA.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04FA is a protective check of the electrically driven EGR valve A (DC motor on an H-bridge with position sensor): the module detects overtemperature or thermal overload of the actuator, modelled from current, actuating work and position behaviour, and limits or switches off EGR. Ford petrol engines from 2020 run it continuously with 4 s to fault above 8.25 V and 400 rpm. Pierburg documents heat damage to VW's 12 V electric EGR valves. EGR then closes, NOx rises.

causes_en: Pressure sensor drifting (zero point error)
Sensor port or line blocked by oil or ice (value frozen)
Contact resistance in supply, ground or signal
Residual crankcase pressure after switch-off (blocked ventilation)
P04FB.en: Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Range/Performance
P04FB.desc: The crankcase ventilation hose connection sensor is a pressure sensor in the PCV line that measures pressure relative to atmosphere; it is the basis for detecting a disconnected hose (P04DB). P04FB is its plausibility check: GM's 2.0-litre LSY checks the zero point with the engine stopped (at least 10 s, coolant 70 °C or more) – a reading outside ±0.63 kPa or a frozen value sets the code in 128 of 160 samples, MIL after two trips. The disconnection check P04DB is then not possible.

causes_en: Module software (FCA false trigger)
PCV valve or oil separator blocked or sticking
Ventilation or fresh-air hose leaking or loose, oil filler cap leaking
Increased blow-by (piston rings)
P04FC.desc: The crankcase ventilation routes blow-by gas into the intake, and CARB requires it to be monitored. P04FC is a general function check: pressure or flow in the system deviates from the model. FCA uses it on the 2.0-litre turbo in the Wrangler and Cherokee (2018–19) and the 3.6 Pentastar in the Challenger (2020), with known false triggers fixed by engine module software; the strategy is not published, a FCA patent evaluates a pressure sensor in the fresh-air line.

causes_en: Engine or actuator software (false trigger)
Electronics in the EGR actuator faulty (heat, moisture)
Actuator supply or ground unstable
Valve stiff, causing a control fault in the actuator
P04FD.en: EGR Actuator A Control Processor Performance
P04FD.desc: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Some EGR actuators have their own electronics (smart actuators), with position control inside the actuator and communication with the engine module by bus or PWM. P04FD means the actuator reports an internal processor or electronics fault, or its self-test failed. CARB does not require such internal faults to be reported, so the code is a voluntary detail. Volvo and Mack trucks with turbocompound document it with false triggers fixed by engine software. The actuator then goes to its default position and EGR is off.

causes_en: Heating disc aged (resistance increased, cracks, electrode damage)
Supply drops under load (cold or weak 48 V battery, contact resistance)
Catalyst or exhaust temperature sensor implausible
Software or calibration
P04FE.desc: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04FE concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code is the function check: the circuit is electrically sound but the effect does not fit – for example the energy delivered in a time window after switch-on stays below target, which a Toyota patent evaluates as a ratio, or the catalyst temperature does not rise as modelled. Ageing of the disc raises its resistance. The pure temperature result code is P0424/P0434. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.

causes_en: ABS/ESP module or wheel speed sensor faulty (signal source)
Output speed sensor or vehicle speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris on the magnet)
Wire or connector open or shorted, corrosion
CAN communication fault (message missing)
Wrong tyre or axle data programmed
P0500.desc: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0500 is the general code for this signal. Ford checks plausibility: the car must be moving (high load, positive torque), yet the signal stays below 1–5 mph for 5 s; Ford diesels flag a missing CAN message after 0.5 s. GM's Saturn ION of 2004 used high load with below 3 mph for 6.2 s (MIL after two trips); GM's 2018 tables use P0502/P0503 instead. Cruise control is then disabled and substitute values are used.

causes_en: Wheel speed sensor or tone ring damaged or dirty (ABS source)
Wrong tyre size, axle ratio or coding
Sensor with weak signal or damaged tone wheel
Interference from damaged shielding or ground
P0501.en: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0501.desc: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0501 means the signal is present but does not fit the driving state or lies outside the physically possible range. Saab's Trionic T5 sets it above 270 km/h; other makers typically compare it with engine speed times gear ratio, wheel speeds or the transmission output speed. GM's 2018 tables and Ford do not use P0501 (GM: P0503, Ford: P0500). Cruise control is then disabled.

causes_en: Speed or output speed sensor faulty
Wire open or shorted to ground, connector corroded
ABS module sends no speed signal
Tone wheel damaged or sensor dirty
P0502.en: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
P0502.desc: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. Despite its wording, all makers found check plausibility: the car is clearly moving (load, torque, overrun), yet the signal stays at zero. GM's 2018 tables use the transmission output speed: below 12 rpm (petrol) or 60 rpm (diesel) for 4.5 s, MIL on the first trip. Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X) sets it below 1 km/h on overrun for over 4 s with the MIL at once; Saab's T5 after 4 s without signal above 1800 rpm. Electrical faults give the same picture.

causes_en: Loose contact, chafed wire, corroded connector
Interference from damaged shielding or the ignition
Sensor with weakened magnet or damaged tone wheel
ABS/ESP fault (signal source)
P0503.en: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic/High
P0503.desc: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0503 combines three fault patterns: sporadic signal loss, jumping values and a value that is too high. GM detects a sudden signal drop quickly (0.3 s, 5 counts, MIL on the first trip); Subaru sets it at 240 km/h or more for a cumulative 4 s, Saab's diesel above 220 km/h. In limp mode Subaru sets the speed to zero, disables fuel cut-off on overrun and raises the fan.

causes_en: Brake light switch faulty (burnt or corroded contact)
Switch misadjusted or retaining clip or stop pad worn
Wire, connector or brake light fuse faulty
Moisture in fuse or junction boxes
P0504.desc: The brake pedal switch has two contacts – A usually for the brake lights, B for cruise control and brake information – working in opposite sense, so the module expects opposite states on every brake application. P0504 means they disagree. The signal is used for cruise control cut-off, brake override with electronic throttle, the shift interlock and start-stop. Ford sets it only after more than 25 (petrol) or 40 (diesel) disagreeing brake applications, with the wrench lamp instead of the warning lamp; a NHTSA investigation covers Hyundai brake light switches.

causes_en: Throttle body or idle valve dirty or gummed
False air (hoses, intake gasket, crankcase ventilation)
Idle valve faulty mechanically or electrically
Learned values not reset after cleaning
P0505.desc: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0505 is the general fault of the idle control, used where the maker does not separate too low from too high or the control is at its limit. With an idle valve it is typically sticking or gummed (Saab T5: idle outside 700–1200 rpm); on electronic throttles a Ford investigation shows P0505 from deposits in the throttle body. Ford's 2020–23 engines disable start-stop with P0505–P0507. Warning lamp behaviour depends on the maker.
