Unlike circuit codes such as P0122/P0123 or P2135, which judge a present but faulty signal, this says the input was not found for the configuration. No manufacturer document or patent available to us describes this check; the explanation is derived from the J2012 wording. CARB requires input components to be checked for circuit continuity and plausibility, and modules with several variants to detect a wrong one. Possible causes are an unplugged throttle body or open wiring, or software meant for a different vehicle. Without a throttle signal an electronic throttle runs in limp mode.

causes_en: Coolant temperature sensor not connected, connector or wire open
Wrong module software or variant
Faulty sensor
Internal module fault
P063F.en: Auto Configuration Engine Coolant Temperature Input Not Present
P063F.desc: Some modules configure themselves at start-up by detecting which inputs are present. P063F means the module expects a coolant temperature input but does not detect it during this self-configuration. It differs from the circuit codes P0117/P0118 (signal low/high) and the plausibility codes P0116, P0125 and P0128, which judge a present signal. No manufacturer document or patent available to us describes this check; the explanation is derived from the J2012 wording. CARB requires the coolant temperature sensor to be monitored for circuit, range and warm-up. Possible causes are an unplugged NTC sensor, an open wire or software for a different vehicle. Expect a substitute temperature, a constantly running fan, a dead temperature gauge and poorer cold starts.

causes_en: Heater relay or switching module faulty
Control wire or connector open or corroded
Heater grid burnt out or shorted to ground
Heater main cable or fuse loose or faulty
Glow plug or engine module faulty
P0640.desc: Some diesels (for example GM's 6.6 L Duramax LML and the Cummins in Ram trucks) warm the intake air with a heater grid switched by a relay or semiconductor switch. P0640 reports a fault in its control circuit. GM's LML glow plug module expects a digital feedback from the heater while it is commanded on; if it is missing for 2 s (75 % of 4 s), the code sets and the lamp follows after two trips. Current, voltage and temperature faults run under GM's own codes P154A–P154D. CARB requires intake air heaters to be checked for response, current and voltage drop. The result is poor cold starts, white smoke and rough running after a cold start; a relay stuck on drains the battery – Ram recalled 2021 trucks because a shorted heater relay could overheat. Ford's 2023 diesel does not use P0640.

causes_en: Short to ground or voltage at one of the supplied sensors or its wire
A sensor signal wire shorted to voltage
Harness damage (chafing, rodent bite, water in connector)
Module internal (reference regulator)
P0641.desc: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time. P0641 is the general code for circuit A. GM puts everything into this one code: reference outside 4.875–5.125 V or jumping (filtered against unfiltered value), 19 of 39 counts or 0.19 s in a row, lamp in the first trip; circuits 2–4 are P0651, P0697 and P06A3, and GM does not use P0642/P0643. GM Europe's 2.0 L diesel flags it outside 4.5–5.5 V for 0.5 s with reduced engine power (two trips), the 2.0 L petrol after 1 s or 10 s cumulative (first trip). Because throttle and pedal sensors may be affected, limp mode is common.

causes_en: 5 V wire or sensor shorted to ground
Internal short in a supplied sensor (e.g. pressure sensor)
Chafed harness or water ingress
Module reference regulator faulty
P0642.en: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit Low
P0642.desc: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time. P0642 means the voltage of reference circuit A is too low – typically the 5 V wire or a connected sensor is shorted to ground. Ford checks continuously from ignition on and sets it below 4.75 V after 5 s; GM Europe's 2.0 L petrol after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, lamp in the first trip. GM North America reports it as P0641. All sensors on the circuit then read near 0 V, with matching 'low' codes. High is P0643, range/performance P06A6.

causes_en: 5 V wire shorted to battery voltage
Signal wire of a supplied sensor shorted to voltage
Sensor faulty internally
Module faulty
P0643.en: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit High
P0643.desc: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time. P0643 means the voltage of reference circuit A is too high – the 5 V wire is shorted to battery voltage or to a higher potential, for example a sensor signal wire shorted to voltage. Ford sets it above 5.25 V after 5 s; GM Europe's 2.0 L petrol after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, lamp in the first trip; GM North America reports it as P0641. Sensors then read too high, and battery voltage on the reference can damage them. Low is P0642.

causes_en: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Display or instrument cluster faulty or without supply (fuse, ground)
Low system voltage during cranking
Output driver in the module faulty
P0644.desc: P0644 concerns a dedicated serial line on which the engine module sends values or warnings to a driver display or information display – not the general vehicle CAN bus. The module reports missing or invalid communication on that line (open, short, display not answering); CARB requires digital outputs to be checked for communication faults. GM Europe's 2010 Saab, for example, passes engine data such as fuel level over CAN to the body module and on to the instrument unit and information display – where such data runs on the bus, a failure is reported as a U code (e.g. U0155) instead. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. Displays then show missing, frozen or jumping information; the engine runs normally.

causes_en: A/C clutch relay faulty (coil open)
Control wire or connector open, terminals spread
Relay or clutch supply fuse blown (e.g. shorted clutch coil)
Output driver in the module faulty
P0645.desc: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0645 is the general circuit fault of the relay coil control, usually an open circuit. GM Europe's 2011 Saab 9-5 sets P0645/P0646 for an open or short to ground and P0647 for a short to voltage, with the engine running and A/C requested; Ford's commercial trucks report it without the check engine light. Older Saab diesels (Bosch EDC16/PSG16) use a different assignment (P0645 short to voltage, 0.6 s). GM found a no-start with P0645 on the 2002–04 Alero/Grand Am 3.4 L because a shorted compressor clutch coil blew a fuse shared with the engine control; Ford traced warm air with P0645 on the 2020–23 Explorer to spread terminals at the body module. The compressor then does not engage or runs constantly.

causes_en: Control wire between relay and module shorted to ground (chafing)
Relay faulty internally (coil, ground)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Output driver in the module faulty
P0646.en: A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit Low
P0646.desc: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0646 means the voltage at the control output is too low while the driver is off – the control wire is shorted to ground, so the relay can pull in permanently and the compressor keeps running, which can ice up the evaporator. Saab's EDC16 diesels set it after more than 0.6 s with the engine running; GM Europe's 2011 Saab 9-5 also includes an open circuit here. Ford's OBD summaries list P0646/P0647 in a 5 V reference section for Bosch modules – an unusual assignment not covered here. The code is not emission relevant and does not light the check engine lamp at most makers.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to a supply wire (chafing)
Relay with internal short (coil bypassed, very low resistance)
Wrong relay fitted
Output driver in the module faulty
P0647.en: A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit High
P0647.desc: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0647 means the voltage at the control output stays too high while the driver switches on (it should pull to ground) – the control wire is shorted to voltage; the driver shuts off for protection and the relay does not pull in, so there is no cooling. GM Europe's 2011 Saab 9-5 uses P0647 only for a short to voltage (check: less than 0.3 V on the control wire with ignition on and the module unplugged); Saab's EDC16 diesels use it for an open circuit instead (0.6 s). Not emission relevant; usually stored without the check engine light.

causes_en: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Instrument cluster (board, connector) faulty
Output driver in the module faulty
P0648.desc: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0648 concerns the immobiliser or security lamp where the engine module drives it directly by wire – on GM and Saab systems this lamp shows the immobiliser learn mode and faults. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. The lamp then does not show the immobiliser status, or shows it permanently; the immobiliser itself keeps working, because start authorisation is separate (key faults are P0513/P0633). The immobiliser is not an emission component, so no check engine light is expected.

causes_en: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Instrument cluster faulty
Output driver in the module faulty
P0649.desc: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0649 concerns the cruise control ('speed control') indicator where the engine module drives it by wire. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. CARB names cruise control as an example of a function outside the test cycles, and GM rates its cruise control diagnostics as emission neutral without the check engine light. The indicator then does not work or stays on; whether cruise control is also disabled depends on the maker. Cruise control inputs and switches have their own codes (P0564–P0581).

causes_en: Pump control module faulty internally (output stage, electronics)
Output stage overheating from a stiff or worn pump or poor module cooling
Supply or ground fault or corrosion at the module (often on frame or tank)
Disturbed monitor line, so a wrong duty cycle is read
P064A.desc: Demand-controlled fuel systems drive the pump through a separate pump control module; the engine module sets the target and reads its status back. P064A means this module reports an internal fault. Ford petrol engines encode the status as a duty cycle on a monitor line – 30 % (±4 %) means internal driver fault, 20 % invalid data (P025B), no signal U0109 – and set the code after 2–5 s; Ford's 2023 diesel checks the period of the monitor signal (0–1.2 s, 0.5 s). GM's pump module sets P064A when its output stage exceeds 150 °C (3 of 15 samples), with the lamp after two trips; Ford petrol stores it without the lamp. Pump output may be reduced or switched off, so low fuel pressure, stalling or a no-start can follow. A stiff, worn pump drawing high current can overheat the module.

causes_en: Engine or PTO module software or calibration (implausible torque or speed request)
PTO equipment installed or programmed incorrectly by the upfitter
Harness, connector or supply of the PTO module or switches
PTO control module faulty
P064B.desc: A power take-off (PTO) drives equipment on trucks and pick-ups – tipper, crane, hydraulic pump or winch – from the engine or transmission. A PTO control module, or the PTO function in the engine module, manages switching, working speed and release conditions; P064B reports a fault of this module or an implausible PTO request. The only manufacturer document found is a Chrysler case for Ram chassis cabs: with the PTO engaged the engine speed hunts and does not rise above about 1100 rpm, P064B sets together with the torque monitoring code P061B and the PTO switches off; the cause was software, so check upfitter installation and programming before replacing parts. CARB defines PTO units and allows monitors to pause while one is active. Thresholds and lamp status are not published; driving is usually normal.

causes_en: Glow plug module faulty internally (switches, memory)
Insufficient supply or ground (battery, corrosion, main fuse)
Short in a glow plug or wire overloading a driver
Moisture or corrosion in the connector of the engine-mounted module
P064C.desc: On diesels a glow plug control module switches the glow plugs (at Ford also the DEF heaters) with semiconductor switches, diagnoses itself and reports to the engine module. P064C means this module reports an internal fault. GM's 2017–18 Duramax checks for a switch that is commanded on but delivers less than 3.2 A and 0 V at the plug (3.5 s), ROM, RAM and EEPROM checksums, the charge pump of the high-side drivers and reverse polarity; the LML (2011–16) used under 6.6 A for 75 % of 4 s; lamp after two trips. Ford's 2023 diesels flag drivers that do not switch or overheat, a RAM checksum error, supply below 6.5 or above 16.5 V and module temperature above 125 °C, within about 1 s. The glow system then fails partly or completely: hard cold starts, white smoke and higher cold-start emissions.

causes_en: Engine module (lambda chip) faulty
Wiring or sensor fault pushing the chip into an invalid state (short to battery voltage, water in connector)
Faulty wide-band sensor (e.g. heater-to-signal short)
Voltage dips or software
P064D.en: Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1
P064D.desc: Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064D means this chip for bank 1 sensor 1 does not work correctly or its messages are invalid. Ford validates the SPI communication continuously and sets P064D/P064E after 10 s at 11–18 V with the sensor heater working; an internal chip fault adds Ford's P1646/P1647. GM (wide-band engines such as the 3.0 L twin turbo, 2018–2025) evaluates two error counters from the chip and sets the code at 128 of 160 samples (about 4 s), more than 20 s after start-up, with the lamp after two trips. Fuel control then runs open loop and oxygen sensor monitors are disabled – fuel consumption and emissions rise. Faults in the sensor or wiring can also push the chip into an invalid state.

causes_en: Engine module (lambda chip bank 2) faulty
Wiring or connector fault of the bank 2 sensor 1
Bank 2 wide-band sensor faulty
Voltage dips or software
P064E.en: Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 2
P064E.desc: Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064E is the bank 2 counterpart of P064D and only occurs on V and boxer engines with two sensors before the catalysts. Ford sets it when the SPI communication with the bank 2 chip fails (10 s; an internal chip fault adds Ford's P1647); GM uses the same error counters as for bank 1 (128 of 160 samples, lamp after two trips). Fuel control on bank 2 then runs open loop, with higher consumption and emissions. Check the bank 2 sensor 1 wiring and sensor first; if they are fine, the engine module is the likely cause.

causes_en: Unapproved or tuned software (chip tuning, programmer)
Faulty or interrupted reflash, outdated software
Used or replaced module without learning the security keys, wrong configuration
Module faulty internally (key storage)
P064F.desc: P064F means the module has found that its software or calibration is not the version released by the manufacturer, or fails an authenticity check (signature, checksum, security keys). CARB requires manufacturers to protect calibrations against changes without special tools and to report calibration IDs and checksums. GM's 2025 engine modules set it when the embedded message authentication table for secured bus messages is invalid, with the lamp in the first trip; chassis modules also check missing key storage or wrong key-slot configuration. Chrysler fixed P064F on the 2017 Ram 3500–5500 chassis cab 6.7 L Cummins by reprogramming – so it is not only about tuning. Typical triggers are tuning software, an interrupted or wrong reflash, a module from another vehicle, or a module replaced without learning its security keys. Programming released software usually clears it.

causes_en: Wire or connector between engine module and instrument cluster open or corroded
MIL bulb burnt out or LED/instrument cluster faulty
MIL supply in the cluster missing (fuse, ignition feed)
Short in the circuit (at GM reported as P263A/P263B)
Output driver in the module faulty
P0650.desc: The engine module switches the check engine light (MIL) through a low-side driver – or sends the command over CAN – and monitors the circuit: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V. CARB requires the MIL to light for a bulb check at ignition on with the engine off (at least 15 s since model year 2005). GM's 2018–2025 modules use P0650 only for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, above 11 V, 50 ms) and P263A/P263B for shorts to ground and voltage – stored without lighting the MIL, since a broken MIL cannot report itself; older GM diesels combine all faults in P0650. GM Europe's Saab 9-5 V6 checks only once the MIL has been commanded on and off. The engine runs normally, but emission faults go unseen and inspections fail if the lamp does not light at the bulb check.

causes_en: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor (camshaft, pedal, pressure)
Chafing or water in harness or connector
A sensor signal wire shorted to voltage
Module internal voltage regulator
P0651.desc: The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V. P0651 is the general code for circuit B. GM puts all faults into it: reference outside 4.875–5.125 V or jumping, 19 of 39 counts or 0.19 s in a row, with the lamp in the first trip (2018; GM's 2006 V6 used 10 s and two trips). GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo feeds all four camshaft sensors and pedal sensor 1 from it and also uses P0652/P0653 (1 s or 10 s cumulative). Ford reports reference B only as range/performance P06A7. Expect limp mode if the pedal sensor is affected, and starting problems or stalling if camshaft sensors are.

causes_en: 5 V reference wire shorted to ground (chafing)
Sensor on the reference circuit shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in a connector
Module
P0652.en: Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit Low
P0652.desc: The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V. P0652 means reference B is too low – usually the 5 V line or a connected sensor is shorted to ground. GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY (2004–05) sets it below 4.7 V for 2 s; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, each with the lamp in the first trip. Newer GM engines report it under the collective code P0651, and Ford does not use P0652. All sensors on the circuit then read low, with matching codes, limp mode and possibly starting problems.

causes_en: Reference or sensor signal wire shorted to a 12 V line
Faulty sensor feeding in external voltage
Module voltage regulator
P0653.en: Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit High
P0653.desc: The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V. P0653 means reference B is too high – often a signal wire of a connected sensor has chafed onto a 12 V line, less often the reference wire itself. GM's Duramax LB7/LLY (2004–05) sets it above 5.2 V for 2 s; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, each with the lamp in the first trip. Newer GM engines report it as P0651, Ford does not use it. Sensor readings then become implausibly high and limp mode follows.

causes_en: Wire between module and tachometer or receiver open, connector corroded
Output wire shorted
Instrument cluster or receiving module faulty (input stage)
Output driver in the module faulty
P0654.desc: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0654 concerns the engine speed output: the module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer and other modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle. P0654 reports an open circuit or other fault on this output. Saab's EDC16 diesels use P0654 differently (a sensor supply group). No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. The tachometer then reads zero or jumps; devices using the signal may fail, while the engine itself runs normally because the crankshaft input is intact.

causes_en: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Lamp supply missing (fuse)
Output driver in the module faulty
P0655.en: Engine Hot Lamp Output Control Circuit
P0655.desc: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0655 concerns the engine hot or coolant warning lamp that the engine module switches by wire from the coolant temperature signal. CARB links overtemperature protection strategies to this lamp: a protective reaction that only starts after the hot lamp lights needs no MIL. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. If the circuit fails, the driver may not be warned of overheating – check it promptly even though the check engine light usually stays off. Actual overheating is P0217; the coolant sensor circuit is P0117/P0118.

causes_en: Wire or connector between module and instrument cluster open or shorted
Instrument cluster (fuel gauge input) faulty
Output driver in the module faulty
Fuel level sender fault as root cause
P0656.desc: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. Where the engine module reads the fuel level sender itself – it needs the level for the evaporative leak test – it passes the level on to the fuel gauge. GM Europe's 2010 Saab 9-5 reads two senders (0.5–3.5 V), calculates the level in percent and sends it over CAN via the body module to the instrument cluster; there a failure would be a U code. P0656 reports a fault on a hard-wired level output. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. The gauge then reads empty, full or jumps and the low fuel warning is wrong; engine and evaporative test are not affected. Sender input faults are P0460–P0464.

causes_en: Open or connector fault at the transmission pass-through connector or wire to the valve body
Damaged harness
Internal high-side switch in the engine or transmission module
Internal transmission harness
P0657.desc: Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0657 is the open-circuit code; it is documented at Ford: the high-side switch of the 5R110W and 6R80 automatics feeds all shift solenoids, and the 2023 diesels split them into two supplies (P0657 and P2669), checked continuously. On a fault the solenoids are de-energised and the transmission falls back to a mechanical limp gear with maximum line pressure – harsh shifts and a single forward gear. Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the lamp depending on the variant. GM does not use P0657 and reports opens together with ground faults under P0658.

causes_en: Actuator supply wire shorted to ground
Actuator (solenoid) shorted internally
Transmission harness or connector (also open, in transmission modules)
Module internal (main cause on the Saab diesel)
P0658.en: Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit Low
P0658.desc: Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0658 means the supply output is too low with the driver on – a short to ground (0.5 Ω or less). GM's engine module checks its shared high-side driver in 20 of 25 samples; the lamp rating changed from none (2016) via two trips (2017–18) to the first trip (2025). GM's transmission modules include an open circuit here, set it in the first trip and block the solenoid diagnostics, so the gearbox goes into limp mode. On GM Europe's 2.0 CDTI it means the internal 5 V supply is too low – no MIL, and if it recurs, the engine module is replaced.

causes_en: Actuator supply wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Harness chafed against a 12 V line
Module (driver shorted; internal on the Saab diesel)
External voltage fed back through a faulty actuator
P0659.en: Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit High
P0659.desc: Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0659 means a short to voltage on the supply output, checked with the driver off – the output should then be dead (GM: 0.5 Ω or less to the supply, 20 of 25 samples; lamp after two trips in 2017–18, none in 2016). The driver can then no longer switch the actuators off; GM's transmission modules block their solenoid diagnostics while P0658/P0659 are active, and limp mode follows. On GM Europe's 2.0 CDTI it means the internal 5 V supply is too high, without MIL – the engine module is replaced.

causes_en: Electrical fault in another module (lighting, wipers, blower) disabling smart charging
Loose or corroded B+ or high-current connection
Engine module software
Alternator or regulator faulty
P065A.desc: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065A is the function check of the whole charging strategy. Chrysler (Stellantis) explains it as a non-MIL code: the engine module switches off demand-controlled charging and falls back to normal charging because of electrical faults in other modules – returned alternators replaced for P065A were found to be fine. Other Stellantis cases trace it, together with P2503/P2504, to loose B+ or high-current connections, and the Ram 1500 3.0 EcoDiesel Gen 3 received a software update. The result is a constant charging voltage instead of smart charging, possibly with a battery lamp; there is no power limitation. Check codes in other modules and the main battery connections before replacing the alternator.

causes_en: LIN or control wire between alternator and module (connector, corrosion, open)
Weak battery, jump start or external charging
Alternator regulator faulty
Ground or B+ connections
P065B.desc: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065B is the plausibility check of the control channel to the alternator regulator (LIN or a dedicated smart-charge line): command and feedback do not match, or the signal is out of range (too low or too high). A manufacturer table published via NHTSA for a gateway with LIN alternator shows the battery lamp and disabled stop-start, notes that jump starting or charging can set it briefly, and says to check P065C (belt) first; Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the lamp depending on the variant. The regulator then falls back to a default target voltage. Circuit faults are P0620; L and F lines are P0621/P0622.

causes_en: Drive belt slipping (tension, wear, oil)
Weak belt tensioner
Alternator overrunning pulley faulty
Alternator bearing or rotor stiff
P065C.desc: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065C points to the alternator's mechanical drive: the alternator does not deliver as commanded or its feedback does not match engine speed, typically because the belt slips. The only manufacturer document found – a table for a gateway with LIN alternator published via NHTSA – shows the battery lamp and disabled stop-start and names checking and adjusting the drive belt tension as the fix, to be checked before P065B. Thresholds are not published. Belt wear or oil contamination, a weak tensioner, a faulty overrunning pulley or a stiff alternator bearing are the obvious mechanical causes. Hybrid starter-generators use other codes.

causes_en: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Lamp supply missing (fuse)
Driver in the engine or SCR module faulty
P065D.en: Reductant System Malfunction Lamp Control Circuit
P065D.desc: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. On SCR diesels a separate lamp or symbol warns of low DEF/AdBlue level, poor quality or system faults and announces speed or start restrictions (inducement). P065D reports a fault in the control circuit of this lamp. CARB requires inputs and outputs of the inducement strategy to be monitored on diesels from model years 2019–2021, and US federal rules define the inducement stages; Detroit Diesel, for example, shows the symbol below 1/8 tank and flashes it with a speed limit when empty. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. Without the lamp the driver may run into an inducement stage without warning; the code itself is not known to trigger one.

causes_en: Valve shaft or linkage stiff or sooted (oil mist from crankcase ventilation or EGR)
Plastic lever or ball joint between actuator and shaft broken or detached
Actuator motor or solenoid faulty (weak, gears)
Manifold leak or, on vacuum-operated actuators, a leak in the vacuum line
P065E.en: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Performance Bank 1
P065E.desc: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P065E is the function check for bank 1 (or the only valve): the valve does not follow its command. It can be detected with a position sensor or, as a GM patent describes, without one from the intake pressure pulsation in steady running – a closed, tuned manifold pulses more. No manufacturer table available to us uses P065E itself: GM reports the same fault on this valve as P2070/P2071 (end position not reached within 5 s, 320 of 400 samples, two trips), and Ford's valve has no feedback at all. A valve stuck in one position leaves a torque gap in part of the rev range; sooted shafts and broken linkages are typical causes.

causes_en: Bank 2 valve or shaft sooted or stiff
Linkage between actuator and valve broken or unhooked
Bank 2 actuator faulty internally
Manifold or vacuum leak
P065F.en: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Performance Bank 2
P065F.desc: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P065F is the function check of the bank 2 valve: it does not follow its command, detected via a position sensor or the intake pressure pulsation (GM patent). Bank 2 codes require a V-engine manifold with two separately switched valves; many V engines use a single central valve between the plenums, and no manufacturer document available to us uses this code, so the description follows bank 1. A stuck valve causes a torque gap in one rev band and can make the banks fill unevenly. Bank 2 circuit faults are P0663–P0665.

causes_en: Actuator connector loose, corroded or spread
Actuator coil or motor open internally
Broken or chafed wire (control or supply)
Supply (fuse, main relay) to the actuator missing
Output driver in the engine module faulty
P0660.en: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P0660.desc: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P0660 means the control circuit of the bank 1 (or only) valve is open. GM evaluates the line voltage with the driver off: too low means the supply through the coil is missing (200 kΩ or more). GM's engines with this valve (low-side driver) check with ignition voltage of at least 11 V and the engine above 400 rpm and set the code after 40 of 50 samples (about 0.6 s), with the check engine light after two trips. Ford uses P0660 (older: P1549) as the electrical check of its actuator, which has no position feedback and stays closed and unpowered below about 2600 rpm – without the check engine light (5 s). The valve then stays in its rest position and power at high revs suffers.

causes_en: Low-side control wire shorted to ground by chafing on engine or manifold
Actuator shorted internally to housing or ground
Open circuit (connector, coil) – included under P0661 at GM
Output driver in the engine module faulty
P0661.en: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P0661.desc: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P0661 means the bank 1 control circuit voltage is too low with the driver off – a short to ground (0.5 Ω or less), which bypasses the driver and keeps the valve energised; GM also includes an open circuit (200 kΩ or more) here, so P0660 may set alongside. GM's engines with this valve (low-side driver) check with ignition voltage of at least 11 V and the engine above 400 rpm and set the code after 40 of 50 samples (about 0.6 s), with the check engine light after two trips. Ford does not use P0661.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to battery or supply voltage (harness)
Actuator winding shorted (very low resistance, overcurrent)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector between supply and control pin
Output driver in the engine module faulty
P0662.en: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit High Bank 1
P0662.desc: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P0662 means a short to voltage in the bank 1 control circuit: with the driver on, the low-side line should be pulled to ground, but the voltage stays high (0.5 Ω or less to positive); the driver protects itself and the valve is not actuated. GM's engines with this valve (low-side driver) check with ignition voltage of at least 11 V and the engine above 400 rpm and set the code after 40 of 50 samples (about 0.6 s), with the check engine light after two trips. Ford does not use P0662. The valve stays in its rest position, with a power loss around the switch-over speed.

causes_en: Module faulty internally (temperature sensor or measuring circuit)
Moisture or corrosion in the module or valve body
Supply or ground problems of the module
P0666.en: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0666.desc: Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P0666 is the general circuit fault of this sensor A. No manufacturer table available to us uses P0666 itself – GM splits the circuit faults into low (P0668) and high (P0669), plausibility is P0667. Expect a warning lamp and, in a transmission module, changed shift quality because a substitute temperature is used.

causes_en: Transmission module or valve body (internal sensor) faulty
Transmission fluid temperature sensor reads wrong (comparison partner)
Unusual conditions (long standing in extreme cold or heat, fluid level or condition)
P0667.en: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P0667.desc: Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P0667 is the plausibility check: GM compares the module (substrate) temperature with the transmission fluid temperature and the temperature measured at power-up. The Saab 9-4X sets it when, within 5 of 6 minutes, fluid and substrate differ by more than 20–50 °C and power-up and substrate by more than 8–10 °C (two trips); GM's 2019 table uses 3000 of 3750 samples. The module then uses the power-up temperature instead. Check the fluid temperature sensor (P0711) first – it is the comparison partner.

causes_en: Module faulty internally (sensor or measuring circuit shorted)
Moisture or fluid in the electronics of the valve body
Module supply problem
P0668.en: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0668.desc: Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P0668 means the sensor signal is at the low voltage end: GM converts it into a temperature and treats −249 °C or less – a physically impossible value – for 60 s as a fault, with the lamp after two trips and the power-up temperature as substitute. 'Low' refers to the voltage; depending on the sensor type that need not mean a low temperature.

P0669.en: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0669.desc: Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P0669 means the sensor signal is at the high voltage end (internal open or short to voltage): GM treats a converted value of 249 °C or more for 60 s as a fault, with the lamp after two trips and the power-up temperature as substitute. Unlike P0634, which reports a plausibly high real temperature (GM: 142 °C), P0669 reports a physically impossible value.

causes_en: Glow plug cylinder 1 shorted internally (element against body)
Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground (block, bracket)
Wrong plug type (resistance or voltage rating)
Driver in the glow or engine module faulty, or software (GM 3.0 L 2020)
P066A.en: Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
P066A.desc: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P066A means the circuit to the cylinder 1 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag a circuit impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples at 100 ms) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off, so plug 1 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow. A plug shorted internally is the usual cause; a wrong plug type is another.

causes_en: Cylinder 1 plug wire touching battery positive (chafing in the harness)
Moisture or corrosion in the module or plug connector (leakage between pins)
Driver in the glow or engine module shorted (permanently on)
Glow module software (GM 3.0 L 2020)
P066B.en: Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit High
P066B.desc: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P066B means the circuit to the cylinder 1 glow plug is shorted to battery voltage, so the driver cannot switch it off. GM's engine-module drivers detect an impedance to the supply below 0.5 Ω (0.14 Ω for low-resistance plugs) in 10 of 20 samples, with the lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke sees 0 A through its measuring path while the plug is commanded on (about 1 s). A permanently powered low-voltage plug can overheat and burn through, after which an open-circuit code follows, and the battery may drain.

Output driver in the engine module faulty
P0670.en: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit/Open
P0670.desc: In today's J2012 meaning P0670 is the electrical check of the activation line from the engine module to glow plug control module 1 for an open circuit; a short to ground is P0383, a short to voltage P0384, and serial communication between the modules P0683/P0684. On Bosch systems (Saab 2.2 TiD and EDC16) the engine module switches this line, detects an open load with the output off and a short to voltage with it on, and also compares the glow module's diagnostic feedback, which must switch inversely – Saab reports all line faults under P0670. GM's LB7/LLY Duramax (2004–05) used P0670 in an older meaning for glow module performance (50 of 100 samples, two trips). No current GM or Ford table uses it. If the line fails, no plug heats: hard or no cold start in frost, smoke and rough running.

causes_en: Glow plug cylinder 1 burnt out (element open)
Plug connector loose or corroded, terminal nut loose, wire broken
Glow module supply or ground (several cylinder codes at once)
Glow module or driver faulty, or software (GM 3.0 L 2020)
P0671.desc: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P0671 means the load circuit of the cylinder 1 glow plug is open while glowing. Thresholds: GM engine-module drivers 200 kΩ or more (two trips), GM's L5P glow module less than 4.0 A at over 6 V, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke less than 1 A for about 1 s. Older GM systems (LB7/LLY, LML) report open and short under this one code. Chrysler advises checking the main B+ feed and ground of the glow module first when several cylinder codes appear together.

Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground
Wrong plug type (resistance or voltage rating)
Driver in the glow or engine module faulty, or software (GM bulletins)
P067A.en: Cylinder 4 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
P067A.desc: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P067A means the circuit to the cylinder 4 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag an impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off and plug 4 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow.

causes_en: Cylinder 4 plug wire touching battery positive (chafing in the harness)
Moisture or corrosion in the module or plug connector
Driver in the glow or engine module shorted (permanently on)
Glow module software (GM bulletins)
P067B.en: Cylinder 4 Glow Plug Control Circuit High
P067B.desc: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P067B means the circuit to the cylinder 4 glow plug is shorted to battery voltage, so the driver cannot switch it off. GM's engine-module drivers detect an impedance to the supply below 0.5 Ω (0.14 Ω for low-resistance plugs) in 10 of 20 samples, lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke sees 0 A in its measuring path while the plug is commanded on. A permanently powered plug can overheat and burn through.

causes_en: Glow plug cylinder 10 burnt out (element open)
Plug connector loose or corroded, terminal nut loose, wire broken
Glow module supply or ground (several cylinder codes at once)
Glow module or driver faulty, or software (GM bulletins)
P0680.desc: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single faulty plug to be detected and named. P0680 means the load circuit of the cylinder 10 glow plug is open while glowing. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – the only diesel with more than eight cylinders sold under OBD II in the US, VW's Touareg V10 TDI (2006–07), is documented only with a general glow plug tip naming no codes. The description therefore follows cylinders 1–8 (GM 200 kΩ, Ford below 1 A). A weak battery strains the glow system on such engines.

causes_en: Communication or feedback wire between glow and engine module open, chafed or connector corroded
Glow module without supply or ground (fuse, main cable) – does not answer
Glow module faulty internally
Glow or engine module software or programming
P0683.en: Glow Plug Control Module 1 to PCM Communication Circuit
P0683.desc: Glow plug module 1 reports to the engine module over a feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the activation line) or the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106, Saab as P0380/P1380, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0683/P0684 themselves. P0683 means communication or feedback from the glow module to the engine module is missing or the line is open or shorted. The engine module then no longer receives plug status reports, so the individual plug monitoring fails; depending on design the glow module keeps glowing on its own timing or not at all. The activation line in the other direction is P0670/P0383/P0384.

causes_en: Contact resistance or corrosion at connectors or pins of the communication line (signal distorted)
Supply or ground problem at the glow module (voltage dip at high glow currents)
Glow module faulty, or software/configuration not matching the engine module
Engine module input stage faulty
P0684.en: Glow Plug Control Module 1 to PCM Communication Circuit Range/Performance
P0684.desc: Glow plug module 1 reports to the engine module over a feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the activation line) or the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106, Saab as P0380/P1380, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0683/P0684 themselves. P0684 means communication exists but is implausible: wrong level or duty cycle, implausible content or a feedback that does not match the activation state – as in the Saab logic, where the feedback must be the inverse of the command. The engine module can then no longer rely on the glow system status; individual plug faults may go unreported. Contact resistance at the pins and voltage dips at the glow module during high glow currents are typical causes.

causes_en: Open or corroded control wire between relay coil and module or connector
Relay coil open or relay badly seated
Relay coil supply missing (fuse, battery positive)
Weak battery or voltage dip
Module driver faulty
P0685.desc: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0685 means the relay control circuit is open: GM measures with the driver off and flags 200 kΩ or more to ground. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo compares commanded and actual state for 2 s, Ford's 2023 diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s. A real open keeps the relay from pulling in – no start; on Saab's V6 there is then no communication with the engine module and the MIL flashes. GM notes P0686 may set alongside.

causes_en: Control wire between relay and module chafed to ground
Relay shorted internally or water in the relay carrier
Module driver shorted internally
P0686.en: ECM/PCM Power Relay Control Circuit Low
P0686.desc: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0686 means the control line is shorted to ground: with the driver off it should carry battery voltage through the coil, but it sits at ground (0.5 Ω or less). The relay then stays energised and the module can no longer switch it off – after-run and shutdown are disturbed and the battery can drain. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. The former obdex title (the wording of P0685) was a shifted entry; P0686 is the 'low' code.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to positive (harness, external voltage)
Relay coil shorted (very low resistance)
Module driver faulty
P0687.en: ECM/PCM Power Relay Control Circuit High
P0687.desc: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0687 means the control line is shorted to voltage: when the driver switches on and should pull it to ground, it stays high (0.5 Ω or less to positive) or the driver goes into overcurrent protection, so the relay does not pull in – no supply to the loads, no start or stalling. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. The former obdex title (a sense-circuit wording) was a shifted entry; P0687 is the 'high' code of the control circuit. A high voltage on the sense line is P0690.

causes_en: Terminal in the sense or ASD circuit connector bent, pushed back or spread
Blown fuse in the monitored load circuit (e.g. shorted ignition coil)
Relay contact does not close
Module input faulty
P0688.desc: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0688 means the expected switched voltage does not arrive on the sense line – the line is open, a fuse in the monitored path has blown or the contact does not close. Chrysler (Stellantis) calls the relay 'auto shutdown (ASD) relay'; a service case for intermittent no-starts with P0688 points first to spread or pushed-back terminals in the ASD circuit connector. GM does not use P0688 and reports an open sense line as P0689. The former obdex title (a duplicate of P0690) was a shifted entry.

causes_en: Relay contact burnt or not closing, relay faulty
Fuse in the relay load or sense path blown
High resistance or corrosion in relay carrier, connector or wire
Weak battery
P0689.en: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Low
P0689.desc: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0689 means the sense voltage is too low although the relay is commanded on – the contact does not close or has high resistance, the sense line is open or grounded, or a fuse in the load circuit has blown. GM sets it at 5 V or less with more than 9 V supply in 5 of 6 samples at 1 s, lamp after two trips; GM Europe's V6 below 6 V for 1 s and the 2.0 L turbo below 5 V, both without the lamp. GM includes an open sense line here. Starting problems or stalling follow, and on Saab the throttle control, which uses this voltage, may go into limp mode.

causes_en: Engine module software (false report)
Battery disconnected during or right after switch-off, or severe voltage dip
Open, high resistance or short to ground in the relay coil or contact supply
Relay faulty (drops out with vibration or heat)
P068A.en: ECM/PCM Power Relay De-Energized Performance Too Early
P068A.desc: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P068A means the relay dropped out before the module released it. Ford explains it as the non-volatile memory write after ignition off not being completed before the module lost power; the 2023 diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel checks with the engine running for an unexpected loss of relay voltage (no MIL). VW (2017–18 Jetta 1.4 T) and Stellantis (2026 Dodge Charger 3.0 twin turbo) fixed false reports by software updates. Real triggers include disconnecting the battery right after switch-off and loose contacts in the relay supply; learned values may be lost.

causes_en: Relay contact sticking or welded
Relay control wire shorted to ground (coil stays energised)

P068B.en: ECM/PCM Power Relay De-Energized Performance Too Late
P068B.desc: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P068B is the counterpart of P068A: after ignition off and the module's switch-off command the relay voltage remains – the relay drops out late or not at all. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel runs this check from ignition off until the module shuts down and names a control line shorted to ground (coil stays energised), an output line shorted to voltage or a sticking contact as causes, without lighting the MIL. Modules and loads then stay powered and the battery drains. GM reports the same electrical faults as P0686/P0690 instead. A Ford diesel table lists 'P068B' for a memory error, which is evidently a typo for P06B8.

causes_en: Relay contact sticking or welded

P0690.en: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit High
P0690.desc: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0690 means the sense voltage is too high: voltage is present although the relay has been off for 2 s – a welded or sticking contact, or external voltage fed in through a short – or, on some systems, overvoltage above 18 V with the relay on. GM sets it at 4 V or more with the relay off, in 50 of 63 samples at 100 ms, lamp after two trips; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo above 2 V with the relay off or above 18 V with it on, for 2 s, and advises fixing other short-to-voltage codes first. Modules, fans or pumps may keep running after switch-off and the battery drains overnight.

causes_en: Control wire to fan relay or module shorted to ground (chafing)
Water or corrosion in fan or relay connector
Fan relay faulty (coil shorted or low-resistance)
Engine module driver faulty
P0691.desc: The engine module switches the radiator fan relays (or the input of a PWM fan module) through output drivers and checks each control circuit electrically. GM sets a short to ground or voltage at 0.5 Ω or less after 50 of 63 samples, with the lamp after two trips; GM Europe's 2011 Saab 9-5 covers P0691–P0696 with relay assignments, the Saab 9-4X's PWM fan module reacts within 1 s. P0691 means the fan 1 control circuit is shorted to ground. GM fixed a related problem with bulletin 16-NA-123, Ford with SSM 47999 for the 6.7 L diesel. The former title 'Cooling Fan 1' was shortened to the J2012 wording, as for P0480.

causes_en: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor
Chafing or water in harness or connector
A connected sensor faulty internally
Module internal voltage regulator
P0697.desc: The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down, so all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. Which sensors hang on circuit C depends on the maker – pedal sensor 2 is common to all: GM 2016–2025 feeds only pedal sensor 2 from it, the Saab 9-4X also the MAP sensor, the Saab 9-5 2.0 L turbo also throttle, crankshaft and A/C pressure sensors, and Bentley's 2026 Bentayga V8 lists its own set. P0697 is the general code for circuit C. GM puts all faults into it: reference outside 4.875–5.125 V or jumping, 19 of 39 counts or 0.19 s, lamp in the first trip; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo also uses P0698/P0699.

GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY sets it below 4.7 V for 2 s, GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, each with the lamp in the first trip; newer GM engines report it as P0697.

P069A means the circuit to the cylinder 9 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag an impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off and plug 9 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code for cylinders 9 and above; the description follows cylinders 1–8.

causes_en: Fault in the fuel pump circuit (pump, wiring, ground) stored in the pump module
Fuel pressure sensor or its wiring or 5 V reference
Pump module faulty internally or overheated (corrosion, moisture)

P069E.en: Fuel Pump Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P069E.desc: P069E is not a component fault but a notice in the engine module: the separate fuel pump control module has detected and stored an emission-related fault of its own and requests the check engine light – over serial data or, on older systems, a request line. GM uses it (2014–2019 tables) and lists P069E itself as 'type A, no MIL': the lamp is lit because of the fault in the pump module, not because of P069E. The actual cause must therefore be read from the fuel pump module's own memory – typically pump circuit, fuel pressure sensor, module overheating or supply. On GM diesels (2014) this module also controls the active grille shutters. Clear the code only after repairing the module's fault.

causes_en: Open or short in the lamp wire between engine module and cluster
Lamp/LED or its driver in the instrument cluster faulty
Connector at cluster or module corroded or loose
Engine module driver faulty
P069F.en: Throttle Actuator Control Lamp Control Circuit
P069F.desc: P069F concerns the hard-wired control circuit of the electronic throttle warning lamp (called 'reduced power', wrench or EPC lamp depending on the maker), which lights when the throttle control detects a fault and limits power. The module monitors this output electrically for open circuit and shorts; it cannot see whether the lamp lights. No manufacturer document available to us uses P069F – Ford, for example, switches its wrench lamp via the instrument cluster over the bus, not on its own wire. CARB requires output circuits to be monitored. Without a working lamp the driver is not warned when the engine enters throttle limp mode. The MIL circuit is P0650.

causes_en: Compressor control valve faulty (coil open)
Connector at the compressor corroded or loose, wire open
Low or incorrect refrigerant charge misleading the diagnosis
Engine module driver faulty
P06A0.desc: Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their swash-plate stroke via an electric control valve: a PWM current sets the crankcase pressure and thus the output. Where the engine module drives this valve (Ford's 'EVDC' compressors 2013–2019), it monitors the circuit; where the climate control module drives it (Hyundai, VW/Audi, GM), faults appear in that module instead. CARB requires monitoring only where the A/C affects engine control. P06A0 is the general circuit fault of the compressor control valve. Ford's service messages for its EVDC compressors (2013–2019) describe it with weak or no cooling, typically from a valve with an open coil or a corroded connector at the compressor; low refrigerant can also mislead the diagnosis. The compressor then runs at minimum stroke or does not cool. Not emission relevant in most cases.

Engine module driver faulty
P06A1.en: Variable A/C Compressor Control Circuit Low
P06A1.desc: Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their swash-plate stroke via an electric control valve: a PWM current sets the crankcase pressure and thus the output. P06A1 means the control valve circuit is too low – a short to ground, or the driver sees ground potential with the output off; shorted coil turns are another cause. No manufacturer document available to us names P06A1 itself; the description follows P06A0 and the Ford EVDC system. The compressor then delivers no controlled output.

causes_en: Valve control wire shorted to voltage
Valve coil open (seen as 'high' with low-side drivers)

Engine module driver faulty

P06A2.desc: Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their swash-plate stroke via an electric control valve: a PWM current sets the crankcase pressure and thus the output. causes_en: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor

P06A3.desc: The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down, so all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. On GM engines (2016–2025) circuit D feeds pedal sensor 1 and both throttle position sensors, on the Saab 9-4X the throttle and pedal sensor 1 – a fault therefore usually means electronic throttle limp mode. P06A3 is the general code for circuit D. GM's petrol engines (2016–2025) and 2018 diesels use it as the only code for this circuit (4.875–5.125 V, lamp in the first trip); the 2014 6.6 L LML used 4.6 V or less for 1 s with two trips. Saab's 9-3 (2012) also reports it.

causes_en: Transmission fluid too hot (cooler, lines, level)

P06AA.en: Control Module Internal Temperature B Too High
P06AA.desc: Control modules can carry a second internal temperature sensor (B). In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics, sensor A measures the circuit board (substrate) temperature, sensor B the 'power-up temperature' used as a reference and substitute; both sit inside the transmission module in the valve body, so repairs mean module or valve body. P06AA would report an overtemperature measured by sensor B – the counterpart of P0634 for sensor A (GM: 142 °C, Saab 9-4X: 146 °C with a limp mode in reverse and 5th gear). No manufacturer document available to us uses P06AA itself; GM reports overtemperature via sensor A. Check transmission fluid temperature, cooler and charging voltage first.

causes_en: Transmission module or valve body (internal sensor) faulty
Moisture or fluid in the module electronics
Module supply or software
P06AB.en: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P06AB.desc: Control modules can carry a second internal temperature sensor (B). In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics, sensor A measures the circuit board (substrate) temperature, sensor B the 'power-up temperature' used as a reference and substitute; both sit inside the transmission module in the valve body, so repairs mean module or valve body. P06AD.en: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P06AD.desc: Control modules can carry a second internal temperature sensor (B). In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics, sensor A measures the circuit board (substrate) temperature, sensor B the 'power-up temperature' used as a reference and substitute; both sit inside the transmission module in the valve body, so repairs mean module or valve body. Unlike most temperature sensors, low here corresponds to an implausibly cold reading. The module then uses a substitute value.

causes_en: Software fault in engine, transmission or hybrid module
Processor fault in one of the modules
CAN communication disturbance between the modules
Supply interruption or poor ground of a module
P06AF.en: Torque Management System Forced Engine Shutdown
P06AF.desc: GM uses P06AF for a cross-check between two control modules: the monitored module (engine or transmission module, each with main and secondary processor) sends a fixed answer sequence over CAN only if both its processors work together correctly; the monitoring module (engine, transmission or hybrid control module) sets P06AF if the pattern is wrong or missing. In all GM tables from 2016 to 2025 it is type A – lamp in the first trip – and the torque management may shut the engine down for safety. Typical causes are processor or software faults in one of the modules, communication problems or supply interruptions. Look for further processor codes (P0606, P060A, P060B) and software bulletins. No other manufacturer document available to us uses P06AF.

causes_en: Blown fuse or open feed to the module
Internal supply circuit of the motor control module faulty
Connector or wiring fault
Short in a supplied component (resolver, gate driver)
P06B0.desc: Despite the similar name, 'sensor power supply' is not the 5 V sensor reference (P0641 ff). It is documented in GM hybrid drive motor control modules: a 15 V supply that excites the motor position sensor (resolver) and powers the gate drivers of the inverter transistors, kept separate from the 5 V reference and the 12 V supply. In GM's 2008 Two-Mode hybrid, A and B are the two motor control modules. P06B0 is the general or open-circuit code of supply A. Only Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander bulletin lists this code (as a main code with low/high sub-codes), without thresholds or sensor assignment. Low and high are P06B1/P06B2; GM documents those with thresholds. Check fuses and feeds of the motor control module first.

causes_en: Blown supply fuse (e.g. 175 A or 7.5 A at GM eAssist)
Supplied component or wire shorted to ground
Internal supply circuit of the motor control module faulty
Low 12 V system voltage

An NHTSA review of the 2013 GM eAssist found P06B1 after blown 175 A and 7.5 A fuses – the cause is often on the supply side. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander lists it as a sub-code.

causes_en: Engine module software (GM bulletin)
Internal knock processor or test circuit faulty
Knock sensor wiring with high resistance or intermittent contact
Knock sensor faulty
P06B6.en: Internal Control Module Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Processor 1 Performance
P06B6.desc: To detect an open knock sensor circuit, GM's engine modules feed a 20 kHz test signal into the sensor circuit and check whether it returns. P06B6 checks the internal test circuit or knock signal processor for sensor 1: it sets when the returned 20 kHz component lies between the open-circuit thresholds, so the module cannot decide 'connected' or 'open'. GM rates it type B (two trips), type A in some 2025 modules; Saab retards ignition timing as a reaction. GM bulletin 22-NA-229 calls for reprogramming only, not part replacement. Ford uses P06B6 for lost communication with its knock chip (more than 200 cylinder events). Knock sensor circuit codes are P0325–P0328.

Knock sensor faulty
P06B7.en: Internal Control Module Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Processor 2 Performance
P06B7.desc: To detect an open knock sensor circuit, GM's engine modules feed a 20 kHz test signal into the sensor circuit and check whether it returns. P06B7 checks the internal test circuit or knock signal processor for sensor 2: it sets when the returned 20 kHz component lies between the open-circuit thresholds. GM rates it mostly type B (two trips); Saab retards ignition timing as a reaction, and GM bulletin 22-NA-229 calls for reprogramming only. Ford does not use P06B7. Knock sensor 2 circuit codes are P0330–P0333.

causes_en: Interrupted shutdown (battery disconnected, voltage dip, main relay too early)
Engine module software
Weak battery or poor ground
Memory defect in the module
P06B8.en: Internal Control Module Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) Error
P06B8.desc: Non-volatile RAM keeps its content without power; among other things it stores the permanent fault codes CARB requires, which cannot be cleared with a scan tool. Ford sets P06B8 when the checksum of this permanent-code memory is wrong; a common companion is P068A (main relay dropped out too early, memory write incomplete). Ford's commercial and propane variants list it with or without the check engine light depending on the vehicle; Ford's 2023 diesel table misprints it as 'P068B'. GM and Saab do not use P06B8. Typical causes are interrupted shutdowns (battery disconnected, voltage dips), software faults and, rarely, a memory defect. After a software check, clearing and an ignition cycle with normal shutdown often resolve it.

causes_en: Glow plug cylinder 1 aged or high-resistance

Engine or glow module software (Ram 6.7 L from 2025)
P06B9.desc: The glow module calculates each plug's resistance from voltage and current while glowing. 'Range/performance' means the circuit is electrically intact but the resistance or current lies outside the specified window – typically an aged, high-resistance or wrong plug or contact resistance at the connector. CARB requires a single plug outside specification to be detected from model year 2010. Ford's 2023 6.7 L/3.0 L Power Stroke runs this check during heating after the open and short checks and flags a circuit above 2 Ω after about 3 s. GM does not use this code family. Ram's 6.7 L Cummins (from model year 2025, with glow plugs instead of the grid heater) set these codes falsely; the fix was reprogramming the engine module. On the 2014–15 Ram ProMaster 3.0 L diesel, plugs without an inner O-ring caused it; all plugs were replaced.

causes_en: Wrong glow plug type fitted in cylinder 1 (steel/ceramic, voltage rating)
Plug resistance drifted (ageing, damage)
Glow module software or check during cranking (false report)
Contact resistance at the plug connector
P06C5.desc: A glow plug has no identification; the control unit recognises its type only from its electrical behaviour – cold resistance at switch-on and how resistance rises during heating (R = U/I). A Beru patent describes how steel and ceramic plugs are told apart this way so the right heating profile is used and a wrong or mixed type is reported. A low-voltage plug on an 11 V control burns out, an 11 V plug on a low-voltage control glows too weakly. GM uses 'incorrect' for any resistance outside the window: the 2025 diesels check 0.22–2.00 Ω (15 of 25 samples, two trips), the L5P glow module a ramp-dependent window. P06C5 reports this for cylinder 1. VW's 2.0 TDI (Jetta, Golf, Passat 2011–13) checks the type 2 s after ignition on – starting during that time caused false codes from the voltage dip, fixed with new glow module software.

causes_en: Coil driver chip or internal communication in the engine module faulty
Engine module software
Supply or ground problem at the module
Shorted coil overloading the driver
P06D1.en: Internal Control Module Ignition Coil Control Performance
P06D1.desc: On ignition systems where the coils are driven through a separate driver chip inside the engine module, P06D1 reports that this internal coil control does not work correctly. Ford checks the communication with the coil driver chip continuously and sets the code within 1 s at 200–3200 rpm, positive torque and 11–16 V. GM Europe's V6 (Saab 9-5 2.8 T) reports it as an internal engine module fault with the lamp after two trips. Misfires or rough running can follow if coils are no longer fired correctly. Primary circuit faults of individual coils are P0351–P0360, driver shorts P2300 ff. Check supply and ground, look for software updates; otherwise the module is the likely cause.

causes_en: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor
Chafing or water in harness or connector
A connected sensor faulty internally
Module internal voltage regulator or components
P06D2.desc: The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down and all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. P06D2 is the general code for circuit E. GM uses it as the collective code for its fifth 5 V reference: petrol engines 2015–2019 flag a reference outside 4.875–5.125 V in 19 of 39 samples with the lamp in the first trip, the 6.6 L Duramax LML/LGH 4.6 V or less for 0.1 s with two trips; GM includes it in its 'engine power limited' group. Which sensors are on circuit E is not listed. GM's hybrid control module uses P06D2 for a separate 12 V reference.

causes_en: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor

A connected sensor faulty internally
Engine module internal fault (e.g. leaking capacitor, Ram 2023)
P06D3.en: Sensor Reference Voltage E Circuit Low
P06D3.desc: The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down and all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. P06D3 means reference E is too low – typically a short to ground. Ram's 2023 6.7 L Cummins set P06D3 together with P0642/P0652 because of a leaking capacitor in the engine module; the fix was replacing the module. GM reports circuit E under the collective code P06D2.
