causes_en: Connector at the control valve loose or corroded (often at the pump in the oil pan)
Valve coil open or valve broken
Supply (main relay) or control wire broken
Engine module software
P06DA.desc: A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. P06DA means the control circuit of this valve is open: it can no longer be powered, so the pump stays at high pressure. GM measures the voltage with the driver off and flags more than 200 kΩ after two trips; some GM modules set P06DB instead. GM checks the low-side driver at 11 V or more relay voltage over 40 of 50 samples (100 ms); Ford's smart driver reports output faults after 5 s with the battery at 11 V or more. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander uses the same code. The engine is not at risk, the pump just can no longer be regulated.

causes_en: Control wire chafing against ground (engine block, oil pan)
Control valve shorted internally
Oil or moisture in the connector
Engine module driver stage
P06DB.en: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Low
P06DB.desc: A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. P06DB means the control wire behind the valve is shorted to ground. With a low-side driver the valve is then powered all the time, so the pump stays at the low stage even at high load and speed. That endangers the engine, so GM flags a short below 0.5 Ω after just one trip, unlike open circuit and short to positive. GM checks the low-side driver at 11 V or more relay voltage over 40 of 50 samples (100 ms); Ford's smart driver reports output faults after 5 s with the battery at 11 V or more. A short to positive is P06DC, a pump stuck at low pressure without a circuit fault P06DE.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to positive
Valve coil shorted (looks like a short to positive at the driver)
Engine module
P06DC.en: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit High
P06DC.desc: A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. P06DC means the control wire is shorted to positive: the low-side driver can no longer pull it to ground, so the valve stays unpowered and the pump at high pressure – the safe state. GM checks this with the driver on and flags a short below 0.5 Ω after two trips. GM checks the low-side driver at 11 V or more relay voltage over 40 of 50 samples (100 ms); Ford's smart driver reports output faults after 5 s with the battery at 11 V or more. Apart from slightly higher consumption there are usually no symptoms. An open circuit is P06DA, a short to ground P06DB.

causes_en: Control valve stuck or broken, screen clogged
Oil level too low, wrong viscosity or sludge
Mechanical pump or drive damage (tensioner, drive gear, pump face)
Valve not seated correctly (retaining clip)
Oil pressure sensor inaccurate
P06DD.en: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P06DD.desc: A switchable oil pump changes its output via a solenoid valve; unpowered it delivers high pressure. To test it, the module switches the pump between stages (GM up to 15 times, with oil at 50–110 °C and 1350–2500 rpm, expecting more than 100 kPa difference) and watches the oil pressure sensor; Ford checks each switch-over of a two-stage pump within 1 s, or a variable pump over 10 s, from 30 s after start. P06DD means the pressure does not react and stays above the threshold – the pump acts as if the valve were stuck off, at high pressure; GM sets it after two trips. Yet GM bulletins for V8 and 2.5 L engines list P06DD with low oil pressure, too: broken valve tips, unseated valves, a loose pump drive gear or worn tensioners also stop the pressure from changing. Check oil level and pressure before replacing parts.

causes_en: Control valve stuck in the powered position
Low oil level, diluted or sludged oil, aeration
Pump wear or internal leakage
Engine module software (FCA 3.6 L)
Oil pressure sensor
P06DE.en: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Stuck On
P06DE.desc: A switchable oil pump changes its output via a solenoid valve; powered it runs at the low stage. To test it, the module switches the pump between stages (GM up to 15 times, with oil at 50–110 °C and 1350–2500 rpm, expecting more than 100 kPa difference) and watches the oil pressure sensor; Ford checks each switch-over of a two-stage pump within 1 s, or a variable pump over 10 s, from 30 s after start. P06DE is the counterpart of P06DD: the commanded high stage is not reached and the pressure stays below the threshold, as if the valve were stuck on. Too little oil pressure at high load endangers the engine, so GM sets it after just one trip; a Ford patent raises idle speed in this case. A short to ground on the control wire (P06DB) has the same effect electrically. An FCA bulletin for the 3.6 L V6 fixes false codes by software.

causes_en: Glow plug control module faulty internally (memory, controller)
Failed or interrupted programming of the module
Voltage dip or spike at power-up (weak battery, poor ground)
Moisture or corrosion in module or connector
P06DF.en: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Memory Checksum Error
P06DF.desc: A diesel glow plug control module has its own microcontroller. On power-up it forms a checksum over its memory and compares it with the stored value; P06DF means they differ, so the module's program or data cannot be trusted. Ford's 2023 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke list P06DF among the glow module checks, run at power-up and flagged on a RAM checksum mismatch after about 1 s. GM's L5P performs the same check on ROM (4.5 s, two trips) but reports it as P064C. CARB treats the module as a 'smart device' whose internal faults need not be pinpointed, so this is extra diagnosis by the manufacturer. The usual remedy is reprogramming or replacing the module; until then preheating may be missing.

causes_en: Cylinder 11 glow plug shorted internally
Plug wire chafed through to ground
Burnt connector or terminal nut, tracking through oil or moisture
Driver stage in the glow module defective
P06E0.en: Cylinder 11 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
P06E0.desc: Diesel glow systems switch each plug through its own power semiconductor and switch off a faulty channel; CARB requires single-plug detection from model year 2010. P06E0 means the circuit to the cylinder 11 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. For cylinders 1–8, GM's engine-module drivers flag below 0.11 Ω to ground after two trips, and Ford's 2023 Power Stroke more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s while heating. The channel is switched off and the plug stays cold; the other plugs keep working. An internally shorted plug or a chafed wire is the usual cause. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it needs at least 11 cylinders, and the only US OBD II diesel above eight, VW's Touareg V10 TDI, has ten; the description follows cylinders 1–8.

causes_en: Plug wire shorted to supply in the harness
Driver stage in the glow module shorted (permanently on)
Moisture or corrosion bridging to a supply pin
Glow module software
P06E1.en: Cylinder 11 Glow Plug Control Circuit High
P06E1.desc: Diesel glow systems switch each plug through its own power semiconductor and switch off a faulty channel; CARB requires single-plug detection from model year 2010. P06E1 means the circuit to the cylinder 11 glow plug is shorted to positive: voltage is present although the driver is off, or no current flows when it is on. For cylinders 1–8, GM's engine-module drivers flag a short to positive below 0.5 Ω after two trips, and Ford's 2023 Power Stroke 0 A while commanded for about 1 s. The plug may glow permanently and fail early; the other plugs keep working. Wiring shorted to supply or a failed driver are the usual causes. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it needs at least 11 cylinders, and the only US OBD II diesel above eight, VW's Touareg V10 TDI, has ten; the description follows cylinders 1–8.

causes_en: Module software (false setting, permanent code does not clear)
Wake-up line or connector open or shorted
Weak 12 V battery, voltage dips at wake-up
Engine or hybrid control module faulty
P06E4.desc: Control modules are woken by a dedicated wake-up line or a network wake-up – at ignition on, when a charging cable is plugged in, or on a timer for engine-off diagnostics and battery management. P06E4 means this wake-up signal is implausible: the module wakes too late or not at all, stays awake, or the line state does not match the network status. In practice the code appears mainly on hybrids: FCA fixes it on the Pacifica plug-in hybrid and the Wrangler 4xe with module software, where it remained as a permanent code that blocked emission inspections; GM's hybrid integration module lists it as a fault bundle. No manufacturer publishes thresholds or timing.

causes_en: Glow plug control module faulty internally (drivers do not switch)
Poor supply or ground of the module (main feed, fuse, ground)
Module overheating (mounting location, short at a plug)
Module software
P06E5.desc: P06E5 means glow plug control module 1 does not respond correctly to the glow command: its outputs do not switch or its internal drivers report faults or overheating. Ford's 2023 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke list P06E5 among the glow module checks, run continuously, with a fault after about 1 s when internal drivers for glow plugs, DEF heaters or relays fail to switch or overheat for more than 1 s – Ford does not assign each threshold to a single code. GM files the same check under P064C: on the L5P a plug commanded on but drawing under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s, on the LML a total current under 6.6 A; both after two trips. The plugs then heat partly or not at all, with hard cold starts and white smoke. There is no limp mode.

causes_en: Open circuit or connector problem in the supply circuit
Short in the supply wire or a supplied sensor
Supply regulator inside the module faulty
Vehicle under- or overvoltage
P06E6.desc: Sensor power supply' is a separate J2012 family next to the 5 V sensor reference (P0697 ff): an additional supply from the module for sensors or drivers – in GM hybrids a 15 V supply for resolvers and inverter gate drivers, there as supplies A and B. Supply C is a third such circuit. P06E6 is the general or open-circuit code of supply C: the module measures the output of its supply regulator and finds the voltage missing. Low and high are P06E7/P06E8. Only Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander lists P06E6 as a main code with sub-codes for low and high, called internal control module, without thresholds or the sensors fed. All sensors on the circuit then deliver invalid values, so several follow-up codes and limp mode are possible.

causes_en: Short to ground in the supply wire or a supplied sensor
Supply regulator inside the module faulty
Connector problem in the supply circuit
Vehicle undervoltage
P06E7.en: Sensor Power Supply C Circuit Low
P06E7.desc: Sensor power supply' is a separate J2012 family next to the 5 V sensor reference (P0697 ff): an additional supply from the module for sensors or drivers – in GM hybrids a 15 V supply for resolvers and inverter gate drivers, there as supplies A and B. Supply C is a third such circuit. P06E7 means the voltage of supply C is too low – a short to ground, an overload from a supplied sensor or a failed regulator; Mitsubishi marks it as a short-to-ground sub-code. Open circuit and high are P06E6/P06E8. Only Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander lists P06E6 as a main code with sub-codes for low and high, called internal control module, without thresholds or the sensors fed. All sensors on the circuit then deliver invalid values, so several follow-up codes and limp mode are possible.

causes_en: Short to positive in the supply wire or a supplied sensor
Supply regulator inside the module faulty
Vehicle overvoltage (alternator)
P06E8.en: Sensor Power Supply C Circuit High
P06E8.desc: Sensor power supply' is a separate J2012 family next to the 5 V sensor reference (P0697 ff): an additional supply from the module for sensors or drivers – in GM hybrids a 15 V supply for resolvers and inverter gate drivers, there as supplies A and B. Supply C is a third such circuit. P06E8 means the voltage of supply C is too high – external voltage, a short to positive or a regulator fault; Mitsubishi marks it as a short-to-battery sub-code. Open circuit and low are P06E6/P06E7. Only Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander lists P06E6 as a main code with sub-codes for low and high, called internal control module, without thresholds or the sensors fed. All sensors on the circuit then deliver invalid values, so several follow-up codes and limp mode are possible.

causes_en: Starter worn or solenoid contacts intermittently open
Weak battery, voltage drop on main cables or ground
Starter relay or its control
Engine module software
P06E9.desc: On cars with stop-start or keyless start the engine module operates the starter relay itself and watches the start: if cranking is commanded but the engine does not turn, turns too slowly or the start is aborted, it sets P06E9. CARB counts an engine start from 150 rpm below warm idle. Thresholds for speed and time are not published. Bulletins show both sides: VW traces P06E9 on the Tiguan to dirt inside the starter that opens its contacts intermittently, and on the Atlas has relays, battery and voltage drop checked; Audi's SQ5 and FCA's Jeep Compass need module software instead. Ford lists P06E9 among the starter faults that disable stop-start.

causes_en: Faulty electronics in the NOx sensor control unit
Moisture or corrosion in control unit or connector (underbody location)
Under- or overvoltage or dips in the sensor supply
Unsuitable replacement sensor or software
P06EA.en: NOx Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
P06EA.desc: A modern NOx sensor is a smart sensor: a ceramic sensing element with pump cells and heater plus its own control unit with a microcontroller, which regulates the pump currents, calculates NOx and oxygen and sends them to the engine module over CAN. P06EA means this control unit of sensor 1 (before the SCR catalyst) reports an internal fault – its self-tests of RAM and ROM or EEPROM checksums fail – so the electronics, not the sensing element, are at fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: Ford's 2023 diesels run exactly these checks continuously, with a fault after 5 s, but report them as P2200; GM uses the P2200 family and U029D/U029E. The NOx value is then invalid, so SCR dosing runs on a model or stops, a warning appears and, depending on market, a countdown to a start lock.

causes_en: Faulty electronics in the NOx sensor control unit
Moisture or corrosion in control unit or connector (underbody location)
Under- or overvoltage or dips in the sensor supply
Unsuitable replacement sensor or software
P06EB.en: NOx Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1 Sensor 2
P06EB.desc: A modern NOx sensor is a smart sensor: a ceramic sensing element with pump cells and heater plus its own control unit with a microcontroller, which regulates the pump currents, calculates NOx and oxygen and sends them to the engine module over CAN. P06EB means this control unit of sensor 2 (after the SCR catalyst) reports an internal fault – its self-tests of RAM and ROM or EEPROM checksums fail – so the electronics, not the sensing element, are at fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: Ford's 2023 diesels run exactly these checks continuously, with a fault after 5 s, but report them as P229E; GM uses the P2200 family and U029D/U029E. The NOx value is then invalid, so SCR dosing runs on a model or stops, a warning appears and, depending on market, a countdown to a start lock.

causes_en: Emission-related fault in the injector control module or its injectors/sensors (code stored there)
Supply, ground or relay problem of the module
Internal module fault (memory, processor)
Software level of engine or injector module
P06EC.en: Fuel Injector Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P06EC.desc: P06EC is a notice code like P0700: a separate fuel injector control module has stored an emission-related fault of its own and asks the engine module over CAN to switch on the check engine light. The actual fault is stored in that module and must be read there; simple OBD readers show only P06EC. GM uses it on the 2019 Corvette ZR1, whose LT5 engine adds port injection driven by its own module with its own crank and cam inputs; the code runs continuously from key on and is listed as type A without its own MIL – the lamp comes from the module's fault. Older separate injector modules (Ford 6.0 L Power Stroke, GM bi-fuel CNG trucks) report through P0611 or U codes instead. Any limp mode follows the module's fault.

causes_en: Speed output wire chafing against ground
Receiver (instrument, add-on device) shorted internally
Aftermarket tachometer or accessory wired wrongly
Engine module driver stage
P06ED.desc: The engine module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer, transmission or body-builder modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle. P06ED means this output is too low, typically shorted to ground, so it can no longer switch high. It is the counterpart of P0654 (open circuit) and P06EE (high). CARB requires output circuits to be checked; the signal is emission-relevant only if a receiving module uses it for emission functions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB, the component and P0654. The tachometer then reads zero or jumps, and modules using the signal lose it, while the engine runs normally.

causes_en: Output wire shorted to 12 V
Wrongly connected accessory (speed pick-up)
Receiving device faulty
Engine module
P06EE.desc: The engine module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer, transmission or body-builder modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle. P06EE means this output is too high, typically shorted to supply voltage, so it can no longer switch to ground; the driver may shut down for protection. It is the counterpart of P0654 (open circuit) and P06ED (low). CARB requires output circuits to be checked. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB, the component and P0654. The tachometer then reads nothing or full scale, and modules using the signal lose it, while the engine runs normally.

causes_en: Starter or starter-generator worn, contacts intermittently open
Engine module software
Weak stop-start battery (AGM/EFB) or battery sensor
Fuel pressure or ignition at restart
P06EF.desc: P06EF concerns the automatic restart after the system itself has stopped the engine – stop-start or hybrid. The restart, by starter, reinforced stop-start starter or belt starter-generator, takes too long or fails. CARB does not count such a commanded shutdown as a stall. No manufacturer publishes the time limit. VW's Tiguan bulletins list P06EF together with P06E9 and trace both to dirt inside the starter; FCA fixes it on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler with engine-module software and lights the check engine light. Stop-start is then disabled. Besides the starter, a weak stop-start battery or fuel and ignition problems at restart can be the cause.

causes_en: Reductant control module or pump unit faulty (sensor is on the board)
Water ingress or corrosion in the module (DEF crystals, underbody location)
Supply or ground problems at the module
Module software or calibration
P06F0.en: Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit
P06F0.desc: Some SCR diesels have a separate reductant control module that drives the DEF pump, heaters and dosing valve – Ford calls it the pump motor controller (fault above 130 °C under P20FF), GM's L5P an SCR power module. It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F0 is the general circuit fault of this internal sensor: the signal is missing, open or cannot be evaluated. Range, low and high are P06F1–P06F3; the DEF tank temperature sensor is a different part. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow.

causes_en: Reductant control module or pump unit faulty (sensor is on the board)
Water ingress or corrosion in the module (DEF crystals, underbody location)
Supply or ground problems at the module
Module software or calibration
P06F1.en: Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Range/Performance
P06F1.desc: Some SCR diesels have a separate reductant control module that drives the DEF pump, heaters and dosing valve – Ford calls it the pump motor controller (fault above 130 °C under P20FF), GM's L5P an SCR power module. It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F1 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – it jumps, freezes or differs from comparison temperatures such as ambient or tank temperature after a long stop. Circuit faults are P06F0, P06F2 and P06F3. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow.

Module software or calibration
P06F2.en: Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P06F2.desc: Some SCR diesels have a separate reductant control module that drives the DEF pump, heaters and dosing valve – Ford calls it the pump motor controller (fault above 130 °C under P20FF), GM's L5P an SCR power module. It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F2 means the signal is below its minimum; with the usual NTC voltage divider that is a short to ground, and the reading appears implausibly hot. The opposite fault is P06F3, an implausible reading P06F1. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow.

It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F3 means the signal is above its maximum; with the usual NTC voltage divider that is an open circuit or short to positive, and the reading appears implausibly cold. The opposite fault is P06F2, an implausible reading P06F1. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow.

causes_en: Wire or connector to the indicator open or shorted
Indicator or instrument cluster faulty
Engine module driver stage
P06F4.desc: When the engine module switches a lamp through its own wire, it checks the output driver electrically like other lamp outputs: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V – GM's MIL driver, for example, flags an open circuit at 200 kΩ or more. It cannot see whether the bulb lights, and on cars that send the lamp command over CAN such faults appear as U codes. P06F4 concerns the indicator showing that stop-start is active or disabled; the code reports a fault in its control circuit. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; the description follows CARB's output check and other lamp circuits. Only the display is affected – the stop-start function itself has its own codes (P06E9, P06EF).

causes_en: Glow plug control module 2 faulty internally
Poor supply or ground of module 2
Module software or configuration
P06F5.desc: SAE J2012 provides a complete code family for a second glow plug control module, mirroring module 1 code for code. P06F5 is the general or internal fault of module 2, the counterpart of P064C. For module 1, GM's L5P groups driver faults (under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s) and a ROM checksum error under P064C, after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke lists P064C among the module checks with detection in about 1 s. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P064C). The plugs fed by module 2 then heat poorly or not at all.

causes_en: Line from engine module to glow module 2 open, connector loose or corroded
Input of glow module 2 faulty or module not connected
Engine module output driver faulty
P06F6.en: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit/Open
P06F6.desc: P06F6 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is open or has a general circuit fault – the counterpart of P0670 for module 1. The engine module's output driver detects an open load while the driver is off. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0670). Shorts on the same line are P06F7 (to ground) and P06F8 (to positive); the feedback line back to the engine module is P06FC/P06FD. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.

causes_en: Command line to glow module 2 chafed through to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the connector bridging to ground
Input of glow module 2 or engine module driver faulty
P06F7.en: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit Low
P06F7.desc: P06F7 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is too low, typically shorted to ground – the counterpart of P0383 for module 1. The engine module's output driver detects the short by its current when switched on or by the line voltage when switched off. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0383). An open line is P06F6, a short to positive P06F8. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.

causes_en: Command line shorted to positive or supply
Corrosion in the connector bridging to a B+ pin
Engine module driver shorted
P06F8.en: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit High
P06F8.desc: P06F8 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is too high, typically shorted to positive – the counterpart of P0384 for module 1. Note that Ford's 2023 diesels use P0384 differently, for the supply voltage of the glow module (below 6.5 V or above 16.5 V); in J2012 that is P052F, and for module 2 P06F9. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0384). An open line is P06F6, a short to ground P06F7. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.

causes_en: Main feed to glow module 2 open or high-resistance (fuse, fusible link, B+ wire)
Weak battery or discharged auxiliary battery
Module ground corroded
Charging voltage too high
P06F9.en: Glow Plug Control Module 2 System Voltage
P06F9.desc: P06F9 means the supply voltage of glow plug control module 2 is out of range – the counterpart of P052F for module 1. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke flags below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or an open supply after about 1 s; GM's L5P checks the same under P163C (below 6.0 V with ignition above 9 V, or implausible against ignition voltage, 4 s). An FCA bulletin shows P052F together with the glow plug open codes, because without supply no current flows. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P052F). Check main feed, fuses and ground first.

causes_en: Glow module 2 faulty internally (drivers do not switch)
Poor supply or ground of module 2
Module overheating
Module software
P06FA.desc: P06FA means glow plug control module 2 does not respond correctly to the glow command – the counterpart of P06E5 for module 1. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke flags internal drivers that fail to switch or overheat for more than 1 s; GM's L5P files the same check under P064C (under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s, two trips). No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P06E5). Internal checksum errors are P06FB, overheating P263F. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.

causes_en: Glow module 2 faulty internally (memory)
Interrupted programming or faulty software
Voltage dip at power-up
P06FB.en: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Memory Checksum Error
P06FB.desc: P06FB means glow plug control module 2 has found a memory checksum error – the counterpart of P06DF for module 1. The module forms a checksum over its memory at power-up and compares it with the stored value. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks the RAM checksum at power-up (about 1 s); GM's L5P checks the ROM checksum (4.5 s, two trips) and reports it as P064C. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P06DF). The usual remedy is reprogramming or replacing the module. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.

causes_en: Feedback or bus line open or shorted, connector corroded
Glow module 2 without supply (does not transmit)
Glow module 2 or engine module interface faulty
P06FC.en: Glow Plug Control Module 2 to PCM Communication Circuit
P06FC.desc: P06FC means the feedback or communication from glow plug control module 2 to the engine module is missing, or the line is open or shorted – the counterpart of P0683 for module 1. Depending on design the module reports over a single feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the command line) or over the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106 rather than P0683. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0683). The engine module then loses the plug status reports; implausible messages are P06FD. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.

causes_en: Loose contact or contact resistance in the feedback or bus line
Ground offset between module and engine module from glow currents
Software mismatch between modules or module faulty
P06FD.en: Glow Plug Control Module 2 to PCM Communication Circuit Range/Performance
P06FD.desc: P06FD means signals or messages from glow plug control module 2 arrive at the engine module but are implausible – wrong duty cycle or pattern, feedback not matching the command, or single messages timing out. It is the counterpart of P0684 for module 1; Saab's Bosch-based diesels, for example, expect the feedback signal to be inverse to the command line. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0684). A missing signal or open line is P06FC, a lost bus link usually U0106. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.

causes_en: Intake throttle coked with soot and oil (EGR, crankcase ventilation)
Throttle motor or gear stiff, position sensor faulty
Ice or condensate in the intake in frost
Contact resistance in connector or wiring, low voltage
P06FE.en: Cold Start Diesel Intake Air Flow Control Performance
P06FE.desc: Diesel intake air flow control' is the diesel's electric intake throttle with position sensor (P02E0 ff). During cold start many diesels close it partly: the extra load raises exhaust temperature so the catalysts light off sooner. CARB requires such cold start elements to be monitored, with their own codes separate from normal operation. P06FE means the throttle does not reach its target position while the cold start strategy is active – it is not the intake air heater. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06FE: GM's 2025 diesels run this check under P2957 (deviation above 16 % or 10 %, two trips), Ford's 2023 diesels under P02E4 in cold start mode. Cold start emissions rise; driveability usually stays normal.

causes_en: Wire or connector to the lamp open or shorted
Lamp or instrument cluster faulty
Engine module
P06FF.desc: When the engine module switches a lamp through its own wire, it checks the output driver electrically like other lamp outputs: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V – GM's MIL driver, for example, flags an open circuit at 200 kΩ or more. It cannot see whether the bulb lights, and on cars that send the lamp command over CAN such faults appear as U codes. P06FF concerns an economy indicator such as an ECO lamp that the engine module switches directly; the code reports a fault in its control circuit. It should not be confused with a body electrics 'economy mode' that saves battery energy. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's output check and other lamp circuits. Driving is not affected.

causes_en: Actual fault stored in the transmission module (sensor, solenoid, ratio, speed sensor)
Wrong transmission fluid level or condition causing slip or ratio codes
Harness or connector at the transmission corroded or damaged
Low system voltage or weak battery
Transmission module or software faulty
P0700.desc: P0700 is a notice code: the separate transmission control module has stored an emission-related fault of its own and asks the engine module to switch on the check engine light. The actual fault – a sensor, solenoid, ratio or speed sensor code – is stored in the transmission module and must be read with a tool that can address it; simple OBD readers often show only P0700. GM's engine module reads the request message from 3 s after start; Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) light the MIL at once and clear it after three fault-free cycles. Ford's engine modules with integrated transmission control do not use P0700. Any limp mode comes from the transmission fault, not from P0700.

mfr.Audi: Defective Shift Solenoids, Defective Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor, Defective Valve Body, Dirty transmission fluid that restricts the hydraulic passages

causes_en: Transmission control faulty internally or software
Implausible input signals (speed or range sensor) without own circuit fault
Wrong fluid level or quality – hydraulics do not respond
Harness or connector with contact resistance
P0701.desc: P0701 means the transmission control system works outside its expected range or its function is implausible – without a circuit fault. What exactly is checked is up to the manufacturer; no GM, Ford, Saab or bulletin document available to us describes the strategy. The only manufacturer evidence is Ford's engine module list for 6.8 L E- and F-Series trucks, where P0701 is stored without the check engine light. Typically the control cannot plausibly achieve the requested gear, pressure or torque, and the transmission goes into limp mode. Individual components have their own codes (P0705 ff range sensor, P0715 ff speed sensors, P0750 ff solenoids).

causes_en: Transmission actuator supply interrupted (fuse, relay, ground)
Harness or connector at transmission or module damaged, corroded or oil-soaked
Transmission module output stage or supply switch faulty
Low or fluctuating system voltage
P0702.desc: P0702 reports an electrical fault in the transmission control system as a whole – typically the supply of the transmission actuators (solenoid supply, transmission relay, supply switch in the module) or a circuit fault not assigned to a single component. No manufacturer document available to us describes it in detail; Ford's engine module list for 6.8 L E- and F-Series trucks stores it without the check engine light. If the solenoid supply is lost, transmissions usually fall back to a hydraulic limp gear. Individual solenoids have their own codes (P0750 ff); actuator supply is P0657 ff.

causes_en: Brake light or double switch worn, corroded or misadjusted
Wiring or connector at the pedal damaged, fuse blown
CAN message from the body module disturbed (GM: software, bus fault)
Aftermarket LED lamps or trailer module distorting the circuit
P0703.desc: Brake switch A is usually the brake light switch, B a second, redundant contact or signal used to cancel cruise control, release the converter clutch, check 'brake before throttle' and for stop-start. Since about 2014 GM receives it as a CAN message from the body module and checks its integrity (rolling counter, protection value: 3 of 10 faulty in 2014, 9 of 17 in 2025) without the check engine light; cruise control is disabled. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) check the circuit electrically during stops and starts and light the MIL after two trips. An NHTSA investigation of Hyundai and Kia brake light switches lists P0703 with a brake light that stays on. Brake switch A codes are P0571–P0573, disagreement between A and B is P0504.

causes_en: Clutch switch faulty or misadjusted (does not switch or too late)
Connector or wiring at the pedal box damaged or corroded
Floor mat or pedal stop shifted, switch bracket broken
Driving style (pulling away or shifting without fully depressing the clutch)
P0704.desc: Only on cars with a clutch pedal: the clutch switch tells the engine module that the clutch is depressed, used to cancel cruise control, smooth load changes when shifting and for stop-start. The check is a plausibility test over driving events rather than a voltage check: Saab's Trionic T8 expects a change of state every time the car pulls away from 3 to 50 km/h (four misses in a row), the EDC16 diesel at gear changes (25 in a row, above 35 km/h and 1500 rpm), and Ford compares its two clutch switches continuously. None of them lights the check engine light; cruise control is disabled. Separate clutch pedal switch codes are P0830–P0835.

causes_en: Range sensor worn, dirty or with oil or water ingress
Sensor misadjusted or selector cable out of adjustment
Harness or connector at the transmission damaged, short to ground
Transmission or engine module input faulty
P0705.en: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit (PRNDL Input)
P0705.desc: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0705 is the circuit or pattern fault: the module receives a combination that matches no valid position. Ford flags an invalid pattern after 5 s (digital sensor) or 200 ms (4-bit sensor), checking continuously with the check engine light; Saab's 9-5 (9600) detects an impossible combination of its four contacts and goes into limp mode with the gearbox warning. The transmission no longer knows the range reliably – limp mode, start interlock or reversing light may be affected. Check the harness for shorts to ground before replacing the sensor.

causes_en: Range sensor or transmission module with integrated sensor faulty
Selector cable or sensor misadjusted (position between two ranges)
Contact resistance in sensor supply or ground
Moisture or oil in harness or connector
P0706.en: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0706.desc: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0706 means the signal is present but implausible. Ford uses it per transmission: for its PWM sensor when the frequency leaves 100–175 Hz (nominal 125 Hz), for the 6F digital sensor when it stays in the transition zone between two positions. Saab's 9-5 (9650), whose sensor sits in the transmission module, flags a sum of the two opposing channels more than 0.29 V away from 5 V, with the lamp in the first trip; adaptations are frozen, the gearbox holds 2nd gear in D and the engine may not restart after switch-off.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing at the transmission case)
Sensor faulty internally
Sensor supply missing (5 V reference, fuse)
Connector corroded or oil in the connector
P0707.en: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Low
P0707.desc: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0707 means the sensor A signal is too low – usually a short to ground or lost supply. GM's T87A transmission module flags a PWM duty cycle below 8.8 % for 0.5 s within 1.5 s, with the lamp in the first trip; Ford flags a duty cycle below 10 %, an analog sensor below 0.2 V for 5 s or a dual-analog channel below 0.127 V for 200 ms; Saab's 9-5 (9650) below 0.127 V for 100 ms twice. 'Low' refers to the signal, not to a gear.

causes_en: Sensor connector off or signal/ground wire open
Signal wire shorted to voltage
Sensor faulty internally
Poor sensor or transmission ground
P0708.en: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit High
P0708.desc: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0708 means the sensor A signal is too high – a short to voltage or, depending on the circuit, an open line pulled up. GM's T87A transmission module flags a PWM duty cycle above 91.2 % for 1.8 s within 2.25 s, lamp in the first trip; Ford flags a duty cycle above 90 %, an analog sensor above 4.8 V for 5 s, a dual-analog channel above 4.84 V for 200 ms, and explicitly an open circuit on its digital sensor (all switches open, e.g. unplugged); Saab's 9-5 (9650) above 4.87 V for 100 ms twice, with 2nd gear held and a restart interlock.

causes_en: Loose contact or corrosion in the range sensor connector
Worn sliding contacts in the selector switch
Harness chafing on transmission or bracket, breaking when moved
Misadjusted sensor or selector cable (position at the limit)
P0709.en: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0709.desc: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0709 means the sensor A signal jumps briefly to invalid values or drops out without being permanently low or high. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0709 – Ford catches short invalid states under P0705 and P0706 instead – so the description follows the sibling codes. Sliding contacts in older selector switches are a typical source; the transmission may briefly lose the range and go into limp mode.

causes_en: Fluid level sensor faulty
Wire or connector to the sensor (often through the sump or transmission connector) open or oil-soaked
Transmission module input faulty
P070A.desc: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump (capacitive or voltage-based) report the oil level to the transmission module; measurements are only valid under defined conditions – an Allison patent names fluid temperature, vehicle at rest, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070A is the general circuit fault of this sensor (open or fault in the signal circuit). Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. An actually low oil level is not a P070A fault. Range, low, high and intermittent are P070B–P070E; fluid temperature has its own codes (P0710 ff).

causes_en: Fluid level sensor drifting or dirty (wear debris, sludge)
Fluid level actually wrong (over- or underfilled) or wrong fluid
Contact resistance in connector or wire
Faulty tilt or temperature compensation (fluid temperature sensor fault)
P070B.en: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P070B.desc: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump (capacitive or voltage-based) report the oil level to the transmission module; measurements are only valid under defined conditions – an Allison patent names fluid temperature, vehicle at rest, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070B means the signal is present but implausible – it does not change, does not fit temperature or operating state, or lies outside the physically possible range. Such checks only make sense within the valid measuring window. A truly wrong oil level (overfilled, underfilled) or the wrong fluid can also appear as an implausible signal. The circuit fault is P070A.

causes_en: Signal wire to the level sensor shorted to ground (chafing, transmission connector)
Level sensor faulty internally
Transmission connector soaked in oil or corroded
Module input faulty
P070C.en: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Low
P070C.desc: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070C means the sensor signal is below its lower limit – typically the signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor shorted internally. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. An actually low oil level is P070F.

causes_en: Wire or connector to the level sensor open
Sensor faulty (open)
Signal wire shorted to positive
Control module faulty
P070D.en: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit High
P070D.desc: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070D means the sensor signal is above its upper limit – typically an open signal or ground wire, pulled up inside the module, or a short to positive. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. The opposite fault is P070C.

causes_en: Loose contact in transmission connector or harness
Sensor with internal contact fault
Contaminated or foaming fluid at the sensor
P070E.en: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P070E.desc: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070E means the level signal drops out briefly or jumps unrealistically – usually a loose contact or a wire breaking under movement. Sloshing and tilt also make readings vary, which is why valid measurements need the vehicle at rest. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display.

causes_en: Leak (pan gasket, shaft seals, cooler lines)
Underfilled after fluid change or repair
Level sensor reading wrong (drift)
P070F.desc: P070F is not a circuit fault but a condition: a working fluid level sensor reports a level below the target band. In the Allison patent the module compares the measured height in millimetres with a tilt-dependent band and reports at least a quart too little or too much – only with the vehicle at rest, fluid above about 30–40 °C and low input speed. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. Take it seriously: real fluid loss leads to slipping, overheating (P0218) and ratio errors. Leaks at the pan gasket, seals or cooler lines and wrong filling after service are the usual causes.

causes_en: Fluid temperature sensor faulty (often part of the internal harness or valve body)
Transmission connector leaking or corroded, oil in the connector
Wire open or shorted
Transmission or engine module faulty
P0710.en: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0710.desc: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0710 is the general circuit code used when a manufacturer does not separate low and high. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag 0.1 V or less or 4.7 V or more, light the MIL after two consecutive trips and use 80 °C as substitute. Ford's 2023 diesels use P0710 alongside P0712/P0713 for open and short circuits, without MIL, after 5–12 s, substituting coolant temperature. GM uses only the split codes. With the substitute value the shift quality suffers: harsh shifts and a late converter clutch.

causes_en: Fluid temperature sensor drifting or stuck
High contact resistance in connector or harness (oil, corrosion)
Very cold weather or short trips (fluid does not reach warm-up threshold)
Outdated module software
Fluid cooler thermostat faulty
P0711.en: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0711.desc: P0711 means the fluid temperature signal is electrically valid but implausible. Manufacturers check three things: the fluid does not warm up as expected (GM 2025 still below 15 °C after the calibrated warm-up time, Saab's AF40 below 20 °C after 10 minutes of driving), the value is stuck (Ford: within ±2 °F for about 2.5 minutes below 70 or above 225 °F), or it jumps unrealistically. GM's 6T70 compares it with the module's internal temperature. The MIL rating varies: GM's newer modules after two trips, Saab AF40 none, Ford none; a 2013 Ram 6.7 bulletin moved P0711–P0714 from one to two trips. A substitute value then limits adaption and converter clutch control.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground (internal harness, chafing)
Sensor shorted internally
Transmission actually severely overheated
Control module faulty
P0712.en: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0712.desc: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0712 means the signal is too low – the sensor reads extremely hot, or the signal wire is shorted to ground. GM's 2025 transmission modules flag below 13.5 Ω for 5 of 6 s after two trips; the 2018 LT4 engine module below 17.88 Ω (over 150 °C) without MIL; the 2007 Allison 1000 150 °C or more for 2.5 s; Saab's AF40 over 200 °C; Ford below 0.05 V for 5–12 s without MIL. The module substitutes a value (coolant temperature, 80 °C or a hot mode) and may shift with hot-fluid strategy. Real overheating with a good sensor is P0218.

causes_en: Transmission connector loose or corroded, wire open
Sensor open internally
Signal wire shorted to positive
Control module faulty
P0713.en: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0713.desc: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0713 means the signal is too high – the sensor reads extremely cold, or the circuit is open or shorted to positive. GM's 2025 modules flag above 284 kΩ for 5 of 6 s after two trips; the 2007 Allison 1000 −45 °C or below for 2.5 s; Saab's AF40 below −43 °C; Ford above 4.6 V for 5–12 s without MIL. Many require prior running time or a warm engine so a genuine −40 °C cold start does not count (Allison: coolant above 20 °C; Saab: over 10 minutes of driving). The transmission then stays in its cold strategy: open converter clutch, late upshifts.

causes_en: Loose contact in transmission connector (oil, corrosion, spread pins)
Internal harness chafing from movement or vibration
Sensor with internal contact fault
Module software (false warning)
P0714.en: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0714.desc: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0714 means the signal drops out or jumps briefly – not long enough for P0712 or P0713. Ford's 2012 6R80 transmission names P0714 among its fluid temperature checks for open, short and in-range faults. Ram 6.7 bulletins of 2013 changed P0711–P0714 from a one-trip to a two-trip MIL to avoid needless warnings. GM files such jumps under P0711 instead. No source publishes thresholds for P0714 itself. A loose contact in the transmission connector or a chafing internal harness is the usual cause.

causes_en: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted)
Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector)
Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel
Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty
P0715.en: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit
P0715.desc: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0715 is the general circuit code. Ford uses it for 'no signal' too: the vehicle is moving under power (engine above converter stall speed, output speed plausible) but the sensor reports under 200 rpm for 5–30 s; Ford's DPS6 dual-clutch sets it for a hardware-detected fault of input shaft sensor 1. Subaru-based systems flag an open or shorted circuit, Saab's Aisin box no input signal while the output sensor works, substituting output speed. GM does not use P0715. Limp mode, harsh shifts and a disabled converter clutch follow.

causes_en: Loose contact or chafing in the sensor circuit
Sensor faulty, wrong air gap or metal debris
Reluctor wheel or clutch drum damaged
Sensor wires swapped after repair or interference
P0716.en: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0716.desc: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0716 means a signal is present but implausible: too high, or dropping suddenly without recovering. GM's 2025 modules count drops of more than 650 rpm between 25 ms samples and fail after more than three; the 6T70 in the Saab 9-4X flags a 1350 rpm drop for 1 s; the 2007 Allison 1000 also detects noise and swapped sensor wires; all after one trip. Ford's 6R80 flags turbine speed above 7700 rpm. The 6T70 then runs only reverse and fifth gear, with maximum line pressure and no converter clutch.

causes_en: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted)
Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector)
Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel
Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty
P0717.en: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit No Signal
P0717.desc: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0717 means there is practically no input speed signal although the vehicle is driving under power. GM's 2025 modules flag under 200 rpm for more than 4 s with torque applied, the 6T70 under 50 rpm for 5 s, the Allison 1000 under 61 rpm with output above 500 rpm; Ford under 200 rpm for 5–30 s; all after one trip. GM calls it 'circuit low voltage', but means missing frequency. On GM's 10-speed both input and output sensors share a supply – P0717 together with P0722 points to that supply rather than two sensors.

causes_en: Loose contact, corroded connector or chafing
Electrical interference (shielding, ground, added consumers)
Metal debris on the sensor or loose mounting
Sensor faulty internally (temperature-dependent)
P0718.en: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0718.desc: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0718 means the signal is present but jumps or drops out briefly. Ford's petrol modules from 2012 to 2023 count 200 turbine speed spikes above 400 rpm with at most 1.5 s between them in a forward gear. GM's Honda-built five-speed of 2006 flags jumps of more than 3 mph per 10 ms three times in 500 ms, after two trips; GM's own transmissions file such jumps under P0716 instead. Loose contacts and electrical interference are the usual causes; shifts become erratic and limp mode may follow at times.

causes_en: Brake light switch faulty or misadjusted
Wire to the module open (GM) or shorted to ground (Saab T8)
Connector at the pedal box corroded
Brake light circuit fuse blown
P0719.desc: Brake switch B is the brake signal to the transmission module or a second brake switch channel, used to release the converter clutch, adapt shift strategy on grades and cancel cruise control. Low and high describe the signal voltage, and what that means depends on polarity: GM's converter clutch brake switch is closed at rest (12 V), while Saab's Trionic 8 sees 12 V when braking. Detection is always a plausibility check against driving: the brake reads applied during accelerations or never applied during decelerations. P0719 means the signal stays low. For GM that reads as brake applied: 2006 transmission modules flag it after eight accelerations without the brake releasing, without MIL. Saab's Trionic 8 flags the brake light signal not changing during four decelerations from 40 to 3 km/h and disables cruise control. The opposite is P0724.

causes_en: Mode switch A faulty (selector lever or console)
Wiring or connector in the console damaged (spilled drinks, chafing)
Resistor coding drifted (analog buttons)
Control module faulty
P071A.desc: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071A is the general circuit fault of mode switch A: its state is invalid or implausible. The transmission then usually stays on its normal schedule. Low and high are P071B/P071C, switch B has P071D–P071F; the range sensor (PRNDL) is P0705 ff.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground
Button stuck pressed (switching to ground)
Moisture or dirt in the button
Control module faulty
P071B.en: Transmission Mode Switch A Circuit Low
P071B.desc: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071B means the signal of mode switch A is below its lower limit: with analog, resistor-coded buttons a short to ground, with digital buttons switching to ground a button stuck pressed. The opposite is P071C.

causes_en: Wire or connector to the button open
Button open internally
Signal wire shorted to positive
P071C.en: Transmission Mode Switch A Circuit High
P071C.desc: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071C means the signal of mode switch A is above its upper limit – typically an open circuit pulled up inside the module, or a short to positive. The mode then cannot be selected. The opposite is P071B.

causes_en: Mode switch B faulty (selector lever or console)
Wiring or connector in the console damaged (spilled drinks, chafing)
Resistor coding drifted (analog buttons)
Control module faulty
P071D.desc: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071D is the general circuit fault of a second mode switch B, for example a separate winter and sport or tow/haul button. The second mode is then unavailable. Low and high are P071E/P071F; switch A has P071A–P071C.

causes_en: Signal wire shorted to ground
Button stuck pressed (switching to ground)
Moisture or dirt in the button
Control module faulty
P071E.en: Transmission Mode Switch B Circuit Low
P071E.desc: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071E means the signal of mode switch B is below its lower limit – a short to ground or a button stuck against ground. Mode B may then be unavailable or permanently active. The opposite is P071F.

causes_en: Wire or connector to the button open
Button open internally
Signal wire shorted to positive
P071F.en: Transmission Mode Switch B Circuit High
P071F.desc: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071F means the signal of mode switch B is above its upper limit – an open circuit or short to positive. Mode B then cannot be selected. The opposite is P071E.

causes_en: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted)
Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector)
Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel
Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty
P0720.desc: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0720 is the general circuit code. Ford also uses it for 'no signal': while engine and turbine speed show the vehicle moving, the sensor reports under 100–200 rpm for 5–30 s; ZF's 6HP26 in Ford vehicles flags an open or short after 0.6 s. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag an impossible 255 km/h or 0 km/h while driving and light the MIL after two trips, substituting the other sensor. GM does not use P0720 but P0722. Speedometer and cruise control may fail, often with a vehicle speed code as well.

causes_en: Output speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris)
Contact problems or interference in the sensor circuit
Wrong tyre size or axle ratio, faulty wheel speed sensor
Reluctor wheel damaged or sensor mounted wrongly
P0721.en: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0721.desc: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0721 means the output speed is present but implausible: too high (Ford 6R80 above 7450 rpm), not matching wheel or input speed in the engaged gear (ZF 6HP26 more than 200 or 250 rpm apart, Ford's F21 more than 15 % for 10 s), or jumping (Allison 1000: 500 rpm within 0.15 s). On GM's 10-speed with a direction-sensing sensor, P0721 means the reported direction of rotation does not fit – since 2025 after two trips, earlier after one. Wrong tyre sizes or a faulty wheel speed sensor can also falsify the comparison.

P0722.en: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit No Signal
P0722.desc: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0722 means the output speed signal is missing while the vehicle is driving. GM's 2025 modules flag under 60 rpm for 3.5–5 s with more than 50 Nm torque and check wheel speeds as well; a 2006 GM table flags no output pulse during 6000 input pulses; Ford under 100–200 rpm for 5–30 s; Saab's Aisin box from 4 km/h. GM rates it after one trip. The transmission goes into limp mode, and speedometer and cruise control may stop working. On GM's 10-speed, P0717 and P0722 together point to the shared sensor supply.

causes_en: Loose contact, corroded connector or chafing
Electrical interference (shielding, ground, added consumers)
Metal debris on the sensor or loose mounting
Sensor faulty internally (temperature-dependent)
P0723.en: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P0723.desc: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0723 means the output speed drops or jumps briefly. GM's 2006 tables flag road speed falling below 61 rpm while driving; the 2019–2025 modules count sudden drops (for example 700 rpm) and fail after more than five, after one trip. In Ford vehicles the ZF 6HP26 flags a drop of more than 1000 rpm with the converter clutch locked, the CFT30 more than 6000 rpm per second. The speedometer needle twitches, shifts become erratic and limp mode may follow at times. Loose contacts are the usual cause.

causes_en: Brake light switch sticking or misadjusted
Signal wire shorted to positive (Saab T8) or switch permanently closed (GM)
Retrofitted trailer or LED lights feeding back
Module input faulty
P0724.desc: Brake switch B is the brake signal to the transmission module or a second brake switch channel, used to release the converter clutch, adapt shift strategy on grades and cancel cruise control. Low and high describe the signal voltage, and what that means depends on polarity: GM's converter clutch brake switch is closed at rest (12 V), while Saab's Trionic 8 sees 12 V when braking. Detection is always a plausibility check against driving: the brake reads applied during accelerations or never applied during decelerations. P0724 means the signal stays high. For GM that reads as brake never applied: 2006 transmission modules flag it after eight decelerations without a brake signal of at least 2 s, without MIL. Saab's Trionic 8 flags a brake light signal that reads on while accelerating from 3 to 40 km/h, four times, and disables cruise control. The opposite is P0719.

causes_en: Crankshaft or camshaft sensor fault in the engine module (speed invalid there)
CAN fault between engine and transmission module (wiring, termination, connector)
Engine module software or fault
Transmission module faulty
P0725.desc: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0725 is the general fault of this input; with CAN it means the engine module marks its speed value as invalid. Saab's Aisin transmissions and a 2006 GM table set it after about 4 s, the GM table with immediate MIL. A Saab bulletin notes that behind P0725 there is always a crankshaft or camshaft sensor code in the engine module (P0016, P0335–P0339) – so read the engine module first. Limp mode follows; a completely missing CAN message is U0100.

Interference (shielding, ground)
Wrong bus value from the engine module (crankshaft sensor problem)
Transmission module
P0726.desc: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0726 means the engine speed value is present but implausible. The Allison 1000, which reads its own sensor, flags a jump of 600 rpm within 0.15 s or noise of ±650 rpm, with the engine above 600 rpm and a gear engaged, after two trips. Saab's 9-3 of 2000, which receives the value over the bus, flags more than 7200 rpm for at least 10 s. The converter clutch is then locked out and shifts may be harsh. No signal at all is P0727.

P0727.en: Engine Speed Input Circuit No Signal
P0727.desc: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0727 means the engine speed signal is missing although the transmission is turning. The Allison 1000 flags under 61 rpm for 4 s with turbine speed of 400 rpm or more, after two trips; Saab's 9-3 of 2000 input speed above 2000 rpm for more than 5 s without engine speed; a 2006 GM table the CAN engine speed failing to answer. The module then works without converter slip information, usually locks out the converter clutch and may enter limp mode.

P0728.desc: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0728 means the engine speed signal at the transmission module drops out briefly. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: GM's Allison 1000 detects jumps and noise of this input under P0726/P0727, and Saab's bus-based systems use those codes, too. By analogy with P0718/P0723 dropouts are counted. A loose contact in the signal or CAN circuit or an intermittent crankshaft sensor fault in the engine module is the likely cause; shifts may be harsh at times.

causes_en: Fluid level too low or fluid worn or contaminated
Clutch for sixth gear worn (linings, piston seal)
Sticking shift or pressure valve, leaking valve body gasket, blocked passages
GM manual transmissions only: gear position sensor faulty or not learned
P0729.desc: The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0729 concerns sixth gear. Saab's Aisin six-speed also checks whether the actual ratio matches fourth or fifth – the sixth gear clutch is not holding and the box drops into another gear. Ford stores it only if the fault does not fit a particular solenoid (otherwise P0751 ff). On GM manual transmissions (LT4) it checks the gear position sensor instead.

causes_en: Shift fork or synchronizer for this gear sticking

Transmission module
On planetary automatics: clutch or brake not releasing (sticking valve)
P072A.desc: Ford's DPS6 dry dual-clutch transmission moves its gears with two electrically driven shift drums whose position is read by Hall sensors: drum A shifts 1st, 3rd and 5th, drum B reverse, 2nd, 4th and 6th. Ford's 2012 summary lists 'stuck in gear' codes for each drum: the module commands the drum out of a gear, but the gear stays engaged. It gives no thresholds or MIL rating. P072A means the transmission stays in neutral although a gear is commanded – no drive. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the DPS6 reports drum position faults under its own codes. On dual-clutch or automated manuals a drum or fork would fail to engage a gear, on planetary automatics clutch pressure would be missing. The opposite is P073D.

Ford's 2012 summary lists 'stuck in gear' codes for each drum: the module commands the drum out of a gear, but the gear stays engaged. It gives no thresholds or MIL rating. Shift solenoid or pressure control valve sticking or faulty
Clutch or brake wear, or worn variator belt, chain or pulleys
Faulty speed sensor signal
P0730.desc: P0730 reports a wrong transmission ratio without assigning it to a gear. Two uses are documented. Older Aisin-type automatics (a 2006 GM table, Saab's 9-5 of 2002) set it when fourth or fifth gear shows the ratio of third – a shift solenoid (Saab: S3) is not switching; GM lights the MIL at once, Saab enters limp mode. GM's continuously variable transmissions of 2023 and 2025 use it when the pulleys do not reach the commanded variator ratio – the belt or chain slips or clamping pressure is too low – after one trip. Ford and newer GM step automatics use gear-specific or clutch valve codes instead. Check fluid level and condition first.

P0731.desc: The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0731 concerns first gear. A 2006 GM table uses a tighter 4 % limit here and caps output speed at 1260 rpm; Saab's 2002 9-5 flags 3 % with the brake released. With a one-way clutch in first, slip shows as slipping when pulling away. On GM manual transmissions it checks the gear position sensor instead.

Reverse clutch or low/reverse brake worn
Valve body, shift valve or gasket
Oil pump or pump cover
P0736.desc: The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0736 concerns reverse. The check needs reversing under load, so short manoeuvres are often not enough; a 2006 GM table sets it after 2 s of slip above 100 rpm without the diagnostic gear step used for forward gears. Slipping or delayed engagement of reverse, especially uphill, is typical; a worn reverse clutch or low/reverse brake is the usual cause.

causes_en: Wire to the receiver open or shorted
Receiver (e.g. instrument cluster) shorted internally
Connector corroded
