For an analogue sensor, low would mean a voltage below its valid range. CARB requires such out-of-range checks on transmission inputs. P0995 is the high counterpart.

causes_en: Open signal wire or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to voltage
Switch stuck open inside the valve body module
P0995.en: Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit High
P0995.desc: The signal of pressure sensor or switch F stays high: with a normally closed switch the contacts stay open, which looks like permanent pressure, or the wire is open or shorted to voltage. No manufacturer documents this use publicly. Hyundai/Genesis bulletins 17-AT-001-G and 21-AT-016HG list P0995 in their subject lines, but their tables pair it with Auto Shift Manual Mode Circuit (SBC), and 21-AT-016HG prints the DTC as P095500; this is a misprint for P0955 and does not count as a use of P0995. GM's matching switch E code P0990 is a Special No Trip without MIL; Saab's 9-4X text treats an open and a short to voltage alike as high. CARB requires such checks on transmission inputs. P0994 is the low side.

causes_en: Loose or corroded connector contact
Debris or delaminated film making the switch chatter
Chafed harness shorting or opening under vibration
P0996.en: Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit Intermittent
P0996.desc: The signal of pressure sensor or switch F drops out or flickers for short moments without staying low or high. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and no transmission with a sixth pressure switch was found: GM's six-speeds end at switch 5 (E), Mitsubishi's 2019 six-speed uses letters B, D and E. Because such switches are thin film-and-piston units inside the valve body module, as Sonnax shows, debris or a delaminated film can make the contact chatter, and connector or harness faults do the same electrically. CARB requires transmission inputs to be checked for circuit faults; an intermittent code is the slot for faults too short to set P0994 or P0995. Expect occasional rough shifts, often without a warning light.

causes_en: Solenoid coil resistance out of specification
High-resistance connector or harness contact
Weak driver stage in the transmission control module
P0997.en: Shift Solenoid F Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0997.desc: The drive circuit of shift solenoid F works electrically but its measured current or voltage does not fit the command. No manufacturer was found to document this code. The users of the F block, Nissan's RE0F11A CVT and a 2019 Mitsubishi six-speed, list only P0998 and P0999. FCA's nine-speed bulletin 21-019-17 (2015 Chrysler 200 and Jeep Cherokee) shows how the slot is used for solenoids 2 to 5, with P0975, P0978, P0981 and P0984 for control circuit performance, but stops before a sixth solenoid. Genesis reports an electrical fault of its solenoid F under P2709 instead. CARB requires transmission outputs to be checked for proper function. P097F is the open circuit, P0998/P0999 low and high.

causes_en: Solenoid or valve body (control valve) internal fault
Control wire shorted to ground in harness or connector
Transmission control module driver fault
P0998.en: Shift Solenoid F Control Circuit Low
P0998.desc: Low-voltage fault, typically a short to ground, in the control circuit of shift solenoid F. Two makers document it. Nissan lists P0998 as shift solenoid F in bulletin NTB15-037 for the 2012–2017 Versa, Versa Note and Sentra with the RE0F11A CVT, whose two-speed auxiliary gearbox uses a low brake, a high clutch and a reverse brake; if the shop manual check points to the transaxle, the bulletin has only the control valve replaced. Mitsubishi's 2019 service manual for a six-speed automatic names P0998/P0999 the low clutch shift solenoid valve system and counts it among faults that can cause gear ratio errors. CARB requires transmission outputs to be checked for circuit faults. P0999 is high, P097F open.

causes_en: Open solenoid coil inside the valve body
Open control wire or short to voltage
Connector pin pushed out or corroded
P0999.en: Shift Solenoid F Control Circuit High
P0999.desc: High-voltage fault in the control circuit of shift solenoid F, from a short to voltage or, where the driver uses a pull-up, an open coil or wire. Nissan's bulletin NTB15-037 for the 2012–2017 Versa, Versa Note and Sentra with the RE0F11A CVT names P0999 together with P0998 as shift solenoid F and calls for replacing the control valve rather than the whole CVT when diagnosis confirms the fault. Mitsubishi's 2019 six-speed assigns P0998/P0999 to the low clutch shift solenoid; for its sister valve G it detects an open circuit as a high reading. Other makers handle F elsewhere: Genesis under P2709, Ford's summaries stop at solenoid E. CARB requires output circuit checks. P0998 is the low side.

causes_en: Solenoid coil resistance out of specification
High-resistance connector or harness contact
Weak driver stage in the transmission control module
P099A.en: Shift Solenoid G Control Circuit Range/Performance
P099A.desc: The drive circuit of shift solenoid G is electrically intact, but current or voltage feedback does not fit the command. No manufacturer was found to document this code. The two documented users of the G control circuit codes report only the hard faults: Mitsubishi's 2019 six-speed (low-reverse brake shift solenoid) uses P099B for a short and P099C for an open, and Nissan's RE0F11A CVT lists P099B/P099C. Hyundai and Genesis report their on/off solenoid G under P075A and P075D. The slot would follow the pattern FCA uses for solenoids 2 to 5 (P0975 to P0984, control circuit performance). CARB requires transmission outputs to be checked for function. Low and high are P099B/P099C, open P09A0.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to ground in harness or connector
Shorted solenoid inside the valve body
Transmission control module driver fault
P099B.en: Shift Solenoid G Control Circuit Low
P099B.desc: Low-voltage fault, usually a short to ground, in the control circuit of shift solenoid G. Mitsubishi's 2019 service manual for a six-speed automatic uses it for the low-reverse brake shift solenoid: with transmission relay voltage at 2 V or more and the solenoid commanded on, the module sets P099B if the actual voltage stays below 3.7 V for 0.5 s. The check runs continuously; the solenoid is normally energised only in reverse and first-gear coasting. Nissan lists P099B as shift solenoid G in bulletin NTB15-037 for the 2012–2017 Versa, Versa Note and Sentra with the RE0F11A CVT and replaces the control valve when diagnosis confirms it. P099C is the high side, P09A0 the generic open.

causes_en: Open control wire or connector between module and valve body
Open solenoid coil inside the valve body
Control wire shorted to voltage
P099C.en: Shift Solenoid G Control Circuit High
P099C.desc: High-voltage fault in the control circuit of shift solenoid G. Mitsubishi's 2019 six-speed uses P099C for an open circuit of the low-reverse brake shift solenoid: with the solenoid commanded off and transmission relay voltage of 2 V or more, a reading of 3.7 V or more for 0.5 s sets the code. So on this design an open shows up as high, not under P09A0. The drive cycle needs only 10 s with the ignition on. Causes named are the harness, connectors, the TCM and the solenoid in the valve body. Nissan lists P099C as shift solenoid G for the 2012–2017 Versa, Versa Note and Sentra with the RE0F11A CVT, with control valve replacement as the fix. P099B is the low side, P099A performance.

causes_en: Solenoid coil resistance out of specification
High-resistance connector or harness contact
Weak driver stage in the transmission control module
P099D.en: Shift Solenoid H Control Circuit Range/Performance
P099D.desc: Electrical feedback from the drive circuit of shift solenoid H does not fit the command, although no hard short or open is seen. No manufacturer was found to document this code. Solenoid H means an eighth shift solenoid. The only documented H user, the 2017–2018 Genesis G80 and G90, reports its on/off solenoid for the shift-by-wire park function under P076A and P076D, outside this block. Ford's OBD summaries describe shift solenoid checks only up to E, with separate open, short to ground and short to power codes and 0.5 to 5 s electrical monitoring. CARB requires transmission outputs to be checked for proper function. Low and high are P099E/P099F, the open circuit is P09A1.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to ground
Shorted solenoid coil
Transmission control module driver fault
P099E.en: Shift Solenoid H Control Circuit Low
P099E.desc: Low-voltage fault, typically a short to ground, in the control circuit of shift solenoid H. No manufacturer was found to document this code. A solenoid H exists only on transmissions with eight or more shift solenoids; Genesis' 2017–2018 G80/G90, the one documented H user, reports its park-function on/off solenoid under P076A and P076D. The closest documented logic is from lower letters: Mitsubishi detects a short on its solenoid G when the voltage stays below 3.7 V for 0.5 s while commanded on, and Ford's summaries store separate short-to-ground codes for solenoids A to E, checked continuously. CARB requires such circuit checks on transmission outputs. P099F is the high side, P09A1 the open circuit.

causes_en: Open control wire or connector
Control wire shorted to voltage
Open solenoid coil
P099F.en: Shift Solenoid H Control Circuit High
P099F.desc: High-voltage fault in the control circuit of shift solenoid H, from a short to voltage or, on pull-up driver designs, an open coil or wire. No manufacturer was found to document this code. Genesis' 2017–2018 G80/G90 shift-by-wire, the only documented H user, files its park-function on/off solenoid under P076A and P076D, and bulletin 21-AT-016HG fixes it by replacing valve and electronic module. For the high-side logic, Mitsubishi's six-speed is the nearest model: on solenoid G it treats 3.7 V or more for 0.5 s while commanded off as an open circuit. Ford's summaries give short to power its own code for each of solenoids A to E. CARB requires output circuit checks. P099E is the low side.

causes_en: Broken control wire or unplugged connector
Open solenoid coil
Pin backed out of the connector housing
P09A0.desc: Open circuit or general circuit fault in the drive of shift solenoid G. It is a late addition to J2012: older code lists still show P09A0 to P09FF as reserved. No manufacturer was found to document it. The known users of the G block send opens elsewhere: Mitsubishi's 2019 six-speed reports an open low-reverse brake shift solenoid as P099C, Nissan's RE0F11A CVT lists only P099B/P099C, and Hyundai/Genesis use P075A and P075D for their on/off solenoid G. Ford shows the usual split for solenoids A to E, with the open in the base code (P0750 and so on) and separate ground and power shorts. CARB requires every transmission output to be checked for circuit continuity. P099A to P099C are performance, low and high.

causes_en: Broken control wire or unplugged connector
Open solenoid coil
Pin backed out of the connector housing
P09A1.desc: Open circuit or general circuit fault in the drive of shift solenoid H, the eighth shift solenoid. Like P09A0 it is a late J2012 addition that older code lists still show as reserved. No manufacturer was found to document it. Genesis' 2017–2018 G80/G90, the only documented H user, reports its park-function on/off solenoid under P076A and P076D, and bulletin 21-AT-016HG has valve and electronic module replaced for those. Ford's summaries show what an open check looks like for solenoids A to E: a separate open code, run continuously with 0.5 to 5 s of electrical monitoring. CARB requires every transmission output to be checked for circuit continuity. P099D to P099F cover performance, low and high of solenoid H.

causes_en: Loose, corroded or wet connector at the select sensor or actuator unit
Chafed or broken signal wire of circuit B near the gearbox
Faulty select sensor, often integrated in the shift and select actuator
Faulty input stage for circuit B in the transmission control module
P09A2.desc: General electrical fault on the second gate select position signal (circuit B) of an automated manual gearbox. The published designs from Isuzu (one select potentiometer) and Aisin AI (one select stroke sensor) show only a single sensor, so it is not documented whether B is a redundant second track of that sensor or a separate sensor. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P09A4 and P09A5 are the more specific low and high faults of circuit B, P09A3 its plausibility fault; unlike circuit A (P0908) there is no intermittent variant. P0904 and P09A6 cover circuits A and C. Expect shifting to be restricted.

causes_en: Worn or drifting select sensor, signal B no longer agrees with the reference
Gate positions not relearned after actuator, clutch or module replacement
Contact resistance at connector pins distorting signal B
Sluggish or worn select mechanism so the measured gate lags the commanded one
P09A3.en: Gate Select Position Circuit B Range/Performance
P09A3.desc: Plausibility fault of gate select circuit B: the signal is electrically valid but does not match what the module expects. That could be the reading of circuit A, the learned gate positions, or the target gate the module has commanded, as in the Aisin AI select control that compares actual and target gate. Which comparison applies depends on whether B is a redundant track or a separate sensor, and no manufacturer publishes that or uses this code in citable material. CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P09A2, P09A4 and P09A5 are electrical faults of B, P0905 and P09A7 the same check on circuits A and C. A fallback mode with limited shifting is likely.

causes_en: Signal wire of circuit B chafed through and shorted to ground
Sensor reference supply interrupted or shorted
Internal short or broken wiper in the select sensor
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module
P09A4.en: Gate Select Position Circuit B Low
P09A4.desc: Set when the gate select signal on circuit B stays below its lowest valid value for longer than a calibrated time. Likely causes are a signal line shorted to ground, a lost sensor supply or an internal sensor short; with potentiometer sensors like the select position sensor in an Isuzu patent, an open signal wire often reads low too. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, nor whether B is a second track or another sensor. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P09A5 is the opposite fault, P09A2 the general circuit fault, P0906 and P09A8 the low faults of circuits A and C. If A and B are both low, look for a shared supply or ground.

causes_en: Signal wire of circuit B shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground or corroded ground pin
Internal fault of the select sensor
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module
P09A5.en: Gate Select Position Circuit B High
P09A5.desc: Indicates that the gate select signal on circuit B has stayed above its highest valid value for longer than allowed. Typical reasons are a short of the signal wire to the sensor supply or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or a defective sensor. No manufacturer publishes how it uses this code or what circuit B physically is. An Aisin AI patent shows the consequence of losing select feedback: warning, request to stop, then a limp-home in first gear. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P09A4 is the low counterpart, P09A2 the general fault, P0907 and P09A9 the high faults of circuits A and C. A gearbox that can no longer confirm its gate restricts shifting.

causes_en: Loose, corroded or wet connector at the select sensor or actuator unit
Damaged signal wire of circuit C in the gearbox harness
Faulty sensor supplying signal C
Faulty input stage for circuit C in the transmission control module
P09A6.desc: Electrical fault on a third gate select position signal (circuit C) that fits none of the more specific C codes. Public AMT designs show far fewer channels: Aisin AI and Isuzu use one select sensor, and a Mannesmann Sachs patent combines motor encoders with an extra neutral position sensor. What a third channel is in practice remains open. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P09A7 to P09A9 are the plausibility, low and high faults of C; as with circuit B there is no intermittent variant. P0904 and P09A2 cover circuits A and B. Gear changes may be limited.

causes_en: Drifting or worn sensor so signal C disagrees with the other channels
Select positions not relearned after repair work on the actuator or gearbox
Loose sensor mounting or magnet shifting the measured position
Contact resistance in the connector of circuit C
P09A7.en: Gate Select Position Circuit C Range/Performance
P09A7.desc: Rationality fault on gate select circuit C: the value is electrically valid, yet it disagrees with the other select channels, the learned gate positions or the commanded movement. A Mannesmann Sachs patent shows why several select signals can exist: when one sensor fails, the remaining ones still allow controlled positioning before an emergency mode based on stored drive times takes over. No manufacturer documents this code or the role of circuit C publicly. CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P09A6, P09A8 and P09A9 are electrical faults of C, P0905 and P09A3 the same check on A and B. The driver usually notices slower or restricted shifting.

causes_en: Signal wire of circuit C shorted to ground
Sensor supply for circuit C missing or pulled down
Internal short in the sensor delivering signal C
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module
P09A8.en: Gate Select Position Circuit C Low
P09A8.desc: The module stores this code when the gate select signal on circuit C remains below its valid range for a calibrated time. Common triggers are a signal wire shorted to ground, a missing sensor supply or an internal sensor fault; depending on the sensor type, a broken signal wire can read low as well. No manufacturer documents this code publicly or explains what circuit C measures. Patents from Isuzu and Aisin AI show the select sensor as the feedback the module needs to line up the right gate. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P09A9 is the high counterpart, P09A6 the general C fault, P0906 and P09A4 the low faults of A and B.

causes_en: Signal wire of circuit C shorted to supply or battery voltage
Open or corroded sensor ground
Internal fault of the sensor delivering signal C
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module
P09A9.en: Gate Select Position Circuit C High
P09A9.desc: Logged when the gate select signal on circuit C sits above its highest plausible value for longer than a calibrated time. Usual suspects are a short to the sensor supply or battery voltage, an interrupted sensor ground, or a sensor with an internal fault. No manufacturer publicly documents this code, and the physical meaning of circuit C is not published either. An Aisin AI patent describes the fallback once select feedback is lost: warning, stop request and a limp-home in first gear. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P09A8 is the low counterpart, P09A6 the general C fault, P0907 and P09A5 the high faults of A and B. Shifting is usually curtailed.

causes_en: Corroded or loose connector at the sensor in the inverter coolant loop
Temperature sensor element failed
Damaged signal or reference wire between sensor and hybrid control module
Fault in the input stage of the hybrid or inverter control module
P0A00.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0A00.desc: General circuit fault on temperature sensor A in the separate coolant loop that cools the inverter and other drive electronics of a hybrid or electric vehicle. The module flags it when the sensor signal cannot be used at all, without a more specific low, high or plausibility verdict; those cases have their own codes P0A01 to P0A04. No manufacturer documents P0A00 publicly. GM's Two-Mode hybrid trucks monitor the same sensor only through P0A01 to P0A03, and CARB requires every input of the inverter thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. Without a valid reading the control unit usually limits electric drive power to protect the electronics.

causes_en: Sensor characteristic drifted, reading offset against the other temperature sensors
Added resistance at a corroded connector shifting the reading
Low coolant or air pocket at the sensor in the electronics loop
Fault actually in the engine coolant or intake air sensor used for comparison
P0A01.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0A01.desc: The sensor delivers a value inside its electrical range, but it does not fit the other temperatures in the vehicle. GM uses this code on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado and Sierra as a cold-start test: after the vehicle has stood for more than 28,800 s (8 h), the power electronics coolant temperature at power-up may differ from engine coolant temperature by no more than 30 °C, provided engine coolant and intake air agree within 15.75 °C. A failure is a Type B code with MIL after two trips. Nissan describes a similar comparison between inverter coolant and power element temperatures. Hard electrical faults are P0A02 and P0A03.

causes_en: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in the thermistor
Moisture or coolant in the connector bridging signal to ground
P0A02.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0A02.desc: The signal voltage of the coolant temperature sensor in the electronics loop sits below its valid window. Because the sensor is an NTC thermistor, a low voltage means an implausibly hot reading, typically a short to ground. GM uses P0A02 on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado and Sierra: the converted temperature reaches the 162.1 °C limit in 30 of 50 samples taken every 100 ms, after more than 10 s of propulsion active and with no intake air sensor fault (P0112, P0113) present. It is a Type B code with MIL after two trips. The opposite fault is P0A03. Expect a warning light and possibly reduced electric power.

causes_en: Connector unplugged, loose or with a pushed-back terminal
Broken signal or ground wire of the sensor
Thermistor element open internally
Signal wire shorted to a voltage supply
P0A03.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0A03.desc: The sensor signal voltage is above its valid window, which for an NTC thermistor reads as an impossibly cold coolant temperature. Typical reasons are an open circuit in the sensor or its wiring, or a short to a voltage source. GM monitors this on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado and Sierra with a limit of -59.1 °C, counted as 30 failures in 50 samples at 100 ms intervals once propulsion has been active for over 10 s and the intake air sensor codes P0112 and P0113 are clear; Type B, MIL after two trips. P0A02 covers the reverse case. Because the system cannot see real heat any more, it often reduces electric power as a precaution.

causes_en: Loose or fretting terminal at the sensor or module connector
Partly broken wire that opens under vibration or heat
Sensor with an internal intermittent contact
P0A04.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0A04.desc: The temperature signal from the drive electronics coolant loop jumps or drops out for short moments, then returns to normal. Coolant temperature changes slowly, so a sudden step that the physics cannot explain points to a loose contact rather than a real temperature change. No manufacturer documents P0A04 publicly. GM's Two-Mode hybrids check the same sensor only for steady faults (P0A01 to P0A03), and a Nissan patent shows how an inverter coolant sensor is compared with the power element temperature to catch implausible readings. CARB requires such inverter cooling inputs to be monitored. The driver may see a warning light that comes and goes, with occasional power reduction.

causes_en: Pump connector loose or corroded, often from road splash at the low-mounted pump
Broken control wire between module and pump
Failed electronics or open winding inside the pump
Blown pump fuse or missing supply, so the control input sees no load
P0A05.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit/Open
P0A05.desc: The electric pump that circulates coolant through the inverter, converter and drive motor loop is driven by a control line from the hybrid module. P0A05 means that line shows an open circuit or a fault the driver cannot classify further. No manufacturer documents P0A05 publicly. GM's Chevrolet Volt tables cover the same pump under P0CE9, set when the control line is open or shorted in 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms, Type B with MIL after two trips. CARB requires inverter cooling outputs to be checked, and Toyota patents describe how pump faults are told apart from other cooling faults. Low and high faults are P0A06 and P0A07; pump B is P0B38. Without circulation the electronics heat up quickly and power is cut.

causes_en: Control wire chafed against the body and shorted to ground
Internal short at the pump's control input
Water or coolant in the pump connector
P0A06.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low
P0A06.desc: The control line of pump A in the drive electronics coolant loop sits at a voltage below what the module expects for the commanded state, usually because the line or the pump input is shorted to ground. Depending on the driver design, the pump then runs uncontrolled or not at all. No manufacturer documents P0A06 publicly; GM's Volt reports a short of the comparable pump control line under P0CE9 (16 of 20 samples at 250 ms, Type B). CARB requires circuit checks of inverter cooling outputs, and Toyota patents show why a failed pump must be separated from radiator or fan faults. P0A05 is the open case, P0A07 the short to voltage. A failing pump soon leads to power reduction.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition supply wire
Pump control electronics failed, pulling the input high
Output driver in the control module damaged
P0A07.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High
P0A07.desc: The module measures a voltage on the pump A control line that is higher than the commanded state allows, typically because the line touches a supply wire or the pump input has failed internally. The pump in the inverter and motor cooling loop may then be stuck on or never receive a valid command. No manufacturer documents P0A07 publicly. GM's Volt flags a short to voltage on its equivalent pump line as P0CE9, with 16 failures in 20 samples at 250 ms and a two-trip MIL. CARB requires inverter cooling outputs to be monitored for such circuit faults; Toyota patents describe pump speed and coolant flow checks for the same loop. P0A05 and P0A06 cover open and short to ground.

causes_en: Internal fault in the DC/DC converter reported by its self-diagnosis
Damaged or corroded status line or connector between converter and hybrid control module
Converter overheating due to a fault in the inverter/converter coolant loop
Faulty input stage in the hybrid control module
P0A08.desc: General fault on the status line through which the DC/DC converter reports its condition to the hybrid control module. The converter replaces the alternator: it steps the traction battery voltage down to charge the 12 V battery. When its self-diagnosis detects an internal problem it signals this back, and the controller reacts. P0A08 is the broad verdict for an unusable or implausible status signal; a signal stuck low or high has its own codes P0A09 and P0A10. No manufacturer documents P0A08 publicly in an official source. Toyota's Prius c recall shows the consequence of a dead converter: warning lights, then a draining 12 V battery that can shut the hybrid system down. Drivers should not keep driving for long.

mfr.Audi: Inverter/converter assembly failure, Powertrain Control Module (PCM) failure, Wiring issue

causes_en: Blown high-voltage fuse feeding the converter, e.g. after an on-board charger failure (Mitsubishi i-MiEV)
DC/DC converter internal fault pulling the status output low
Status line shorted to ground or chafed harness
Faulty input stage in the hybrid/EV control module
P0A09.desc: The status signal that the DC/DC converter sends to the hybrid control module stays below its expected range, typically from a short to ground, an open line read as low, or a converter that pulls its status output down because of an internal fault. Mitsubishi uses P0A09 on the 2012-2013 i-MiEV for a DC-DC converter fault; its bulletins tie it to a failed on-board charger that blows the high-voltage fuse feeding the converter, after which the 12 V battery and drive battery stop charging. That usage predates the current split into P0A08, P0A09 and P0A10. Siblings: P0A08 covers the general circuit fault, P0A10 a signal stuck high. Expect warning lights and a 12 V battery that slowly runs flat.

causes_en: HV connector or service disconnect not fully seated after repair
Spread, bent or corroded interlock pins or damaged connector seals
Interlock wiring chafed or cut
Battery pack control module software fault (Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid 2024-2025)
P0A0A.en: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A
P0A0A.desc: The high-voltage interlock loop (HVIL) is a low-voltage signal loop routed through every HV connector, the service disconnect and component covers. If it opens, the control module opens the main contactors so no one can touch live parts. P0A0A is the general circuit fault on loop A. Stellantis sets P0A0A-00 on the Jeep Wrangler and Grand Cherokee 4xe when an HV connector is torqued but not fully seated after repair, and on the 2024-2025 Pacifica Hybrid it was traced to battery pack control module software; there the car will not start on either power source. Mercedes logs P0A0A00 in the DC converter of model line 243. CARB counts the HVIL as a safety-only system, so MIL behaviour varies. Low, high, performance and intermittent faults use P0A0B to P0A0E.

causes_en: Oxidised interlock pins in low-voltage connectors raising loop resistance
Improperly connected HV connector or bent interlock pins on an HV component
Twisted or chafed interlock harness rubbing on the body
Faulty interlock driver or receiver in a control module
P0A0B.en: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Performance
P0A0B.desc: The interlock loop A responds electrically, but its behaviour does not match what the module expects – for example a loop resistance outside the window, a signal that does not follow the commanded test pattern, or two modules on the same loop disagreeing. Mercedes-Benz logs P0A0B00 in the battery management system, the DC converter and the on-board charger of model line 243 when the vehicle will not start; its listed causes include oxidised interlock pins in the low-voltage connectors, twisted or chafed harnesses and bent pins on HV components. Patent literature explains why voltage-based loops are prone to false alarms from contact resistance and interference. Unlike P0A0C/P0A0D this is not a clear short. Expect the HV system to stay off.

causes_en: HV connector, cover or service disconnect open, interrupting the loop
Interlock wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed at a module or the body
Corroded or pushed-back interlock pins
Faulty interlock source or sense stage in the battery or hybrid module
P0A0C.en: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Low
P0A0C.desc: The voltage sensed on interlock loop A is too low while the module drives the loop – typically an opened loop or a short to ground. GM documents it codegenau: in its 2016 HPC2 table P0A0C sets when the sensed interlock voltage stays below 30 % of the 5 V test signal in 2 of 2 samples (12.5 ms each) with the 12 V supply above 10.2 V; it is Type A, so the MIL lights after one trip. The 2011 Volt tables used a 10 % threshold. Mercedes-Benz model line 243 stores P0A0C00 in the DC converter and on-board charger as a short to ground in the interlock circuit. The opposite fault is P0A0D. Since the loop guards against live HV parts, the system drops the contactors and the car will not drive on electric power.

causes_en: Service/safety plug not fully inserted or with poor contact (Hyundai Sonata Hybrid)
Interlock wire shorted to a 12 V or reference voltage
Damaged interlock harness or connector after body or battery work
Faulty interlock stage in the battery or hybrid control module
P0A0D.en: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A High
P0A0D.desc: The voltage sensed on interlock loop A is higher than expected – most often a short to a voltage source, or the loop not being pulled down when the module expects it. GM checks both states: in the 2016 HPC2 table P0A0D sets when the sensed voltage exceeds 24 % of 5 V with the source switched off (5 of 8 samples) or 44 % with it switched on (4 of 6 samples), Type A with MIL after one trip. Hyundai's Sonata Hybrid 2011-2015 bulletins send P0A0D straight to the HEV safety plug, alongside high-voltage path and relay codes, with check engine light and no ready mode. Mercedes model line 243 stores P0A0D00 in the battery management as a short to positive. P0A0C is the low-side counterpart; both leave the HV system switched off.

causes_en: Loose or spread interlock contacts in an HV or low-voltage connector
Harness section with a broken strand that opens under vibration
Moisture entering through a damaged connector seal
Electrical interference on the interlock line or a weak module input
P0A0E.en: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Intermittent
P0A0E.desc: The interlock loop A signal drops out or jumps for short moments and then recovers, so the module sees an unstable loop rather than a lasting open or short. Typical are connectors with loose or spread contacts, harness sections that move with the body or drivetrain, and moisture in seals. No manufacturer documents P0A0E publicly; the GM tables only list P0A0C and P0A0D for the same loop. Reference designs and patents on interlock monitoring describe the loop as a current or voltage path through each HV connector and point out that contact resistance and interference can cause brief false trips. CARB treats the HVIL as a safety-only system. For the driver this means sudden HV shutdowns or no-starts that come and go; static faults use P0A0A to P0A0D.

causes_en: Vacuum leak, e.g. separated purge VSV/PCV hose at the throttle body (Toyota Prius)
Shorted sensor harness pulling down the engine ECU 5 V reference (Kia Niro)
Fuel delivery or ignition fault preventing combustion
Failed automatic restart of a mild hybrid with a cold engine (Audi A6/A7 2019)
P0A0F.desc: The control module commanded an engine start – by the hybrid system or an automatic start/stop restart – but the combustion engine did not reach a self-sustaining run within the allowed attempts. The code describes the result, not the cause. Toyota sets P0A0F with MIL on the 2010-2013 Prius and Prius v when a separated purge VSV/PCV hose leans out the mixture, often with P3190, P3191 and P0171. Kia traced P0A0F on the 2017-2018 Niro hybrid to an A/C pressure sensor harness chafed by an idler pulley, which disturbs the engine ECU 5 V reference. Audi sets P0A0F00 on 2019 A6/A7 3.0 mild hybrids after the second failed automatic restart, with a drive system warning. Look at fuel, air, ignition and engine sensor faults first.

mfr.Audi: Hybrid transaxle assembly failure, Internal engine failure, Power management control module failure

causes_en: Status line shorted to 12 V or another supply
Open ground or signal return at the converter connector
DC/DC converter internal fault driving the status output high
Faulty input stage in the hybrid control module
P0A10.desc: The status signal from the DC/DC converter to the hybrid control module sits above its valid range, typically because the line is shorted to a voltage source, its ground or pull-down path is open, or the converter drives the output high after an internal failure. The converter supplies the 12 V system from the traction battery, and its self-diagnosis reports problems over this status path. No manufacturer documents P0A10 publicly in an official source; older lists that call it a hybrid battery voltage sense circuit are wrong for today's J2012. Siblings: P0A08 is the general status fault, P0A09 the low signal. A converter that stops working shows up as warning lights and a falling 12 V voltage until the hybrid system shuts down.

causes_en: Broken enable wire or unplugged connector between control module and converter
Corroded or pushed-out terminal at the converter enable pin
Faulty enable output driver in the control module
Faulty enable input inside the DC/DC converter
P0A11.desc: General or open-circuit fault on the enable line with which the hybrid or battery control module tells the DC/DC converter that it may deliver power to the 12 V system. In typical designs a high enable level permits converter output, and a CAN message carries the same permission in parallel, so the two can be cross-checked. If the line is open, the converter cannot be switched on reliably and the 12 V battery is no longer charged. No manufacturer documents P0A11 publicly in an official source; Honda's hybrid recall shows what follows when the converter shuts down: charging warning, discharged 12 V battery, possible loss of drive. Low and high faults on the same line are P0A12 and P0A13; status line faults are P0A08 to P0A10.

causes_en: Enable wire shorted to ground
Weak or failed enable output driver in the control module
Converter enable input internally shorted
P0A12.desc: The enable line to the DC/DC converter reads low when the control module is commanding it on. Because a low enable level usually means converter output is not permitted, the converter stays off and the 12 V system loses its charging source. Typical causes are a short to ground on the enable wire, a weak output driver in the module, or an input stage in the converter that loads the line. Older lists name this code DC/DC converter communication; today's J2012 wording is enable circuit low. No manufacturer documents P0A12 publicly in an official source, so the description rests on CARB and on patent descriptions of hard-wired enable lines. P0A11 covers an open line, P0A13 a line stuck high. Drivers see a charging warning and a draining 12 V battery.

causes_en: Enable wire shorted to 12 V or another supply
Enable output driver in the control module stuck on
Open pull-down or ground reference at the converter input
P0A13.desc: The enable line to the DC/DC converter reads high when the control module expects it low, for example while the converter should be switched off. The usual reasons are a short to battery voltage on the enable wire, a stuck output driver, or a missing pull-down. Since a high enable level normally permits converter output, the converter may keep running when it should not – during shutdown, a fault or high-voltage disconnection – which the module treats as a safety and battery-drain risk. No manufacturer documents P0A13 publicly in an official source; the explanation relies on CARB and on patents describing hard-wired DC/DC enable lines cross-checked against a CAN request. P0A11 is the open line, P0A12 the low fault; status-side faults are P0A08 to P0A10.

causes_en: Mount actuator connector loose, corroded or unplugged after engine work
Open coil in the mount actuator or switching solenoid
Wire broken where the harness flexes with engine movement
Fault in the engine or mount control unit output
P0A14.desc: Some vehicles use switchable or active engine mounts that the powertrain or a mount control unit changes between soft and firm, or drives with an actuator against vibration. P0A14 reports an open or undefined fault in the control circuit of mount A. Ford lists it in its 2020 to 2023 gasoline OBD summary as the active mount circuit check: the low-side driver reports the fault and it matures after about 5 seconds; mount B uses P0AB6 to P0AB8. Honda's active control engine mounts, for example on the 2008 Pilot V6, use P0A14 for the front mount actuator and P0AB6 for the rear. P0A15 and P0A16 cover low and high faults. The car stays drivable, but vibration may increase.

causes_en: Control wire chafed on the engine or subframe and shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the mount actuator or solenoid, often after fluid leakage
Moisture in the mount connector
P0A15.en: Engine Mount A Control Circuit Low
P0A15.desc: The control circuit of switchable or active engine mount A shows a voltage or current below the expected level, which usually points to a short to ground on the line or inside the actuator. Ford uses P0A15 in its 2020 to 2023 gasoline OBD summary for the active mounts: the low-level driver reports the fault and the PCM matures it after about 5 seconds; the partner mount B has P0AB7. Honda's active control engine mount system on the 2008 Pilot V6 assigns P0A15 to the front mount actuator and P0AB7 to the rear. Ford engineers describe these mounts as switched between a damping and a stiffening mode, so a stuck mount is felt as vibration. The open circuit is P0A14, the high fault P0A16.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition supply
Mount actuator or solenoid failed with an open low side
Driver stage in the engine or mount control unit damaged
P0A16.en: Engine Mount A Control Circuit High
P0A16.desc: The module sees a higher voltage on the control circuit of engine mount A than it should for the commanded state, usually a short to a supply line or a failed actuator input. The mount can then no longer be switched or driven as intended. Ford lists P0A16 in its 2020 to 2023 gasoline OBD summary under the active mount circuit check, matured after about 5 seconds once the driver reports the fault; mount B uses P0AB8. On Honda's active control engine mounts, such as the 2008 Pilot V6, P0A16 belongs to the front mount actuator and P0AB8 to the rear one. A Ford patent shows the mounts are toggled between soft and firm, so a fault means either harsh idle or more movement. See P0A14 and P0A15.

causes_en: Loose or corroded sensor connector at the drive unit
Damaged sensor wiring between drive unit and control module
Torque sensor or its excitation electronics failed, often only replaceable with the drive unit
Input stage of the hybrid or motor control module faulty
P0A17.desc: Some electric drive units measure the torque on the motor or generator shaft directly, for example with a magnetostrictive sensor inside a hollow motor shaft as described in Honda patents for hybrid drive systems. The control unit uses that value to check the torque it commands. P0A17 is the general circuit fault of this sensor, set when the signal is missing or cannot be evaluated at all. No manufacturer documents P0A17 publicly. CARB requires a monitoring plan for drive motor faults that affect propulsion or emission strategies, which covers such feedback sensors. Plausibility is P0A18, low and high P0A19 and P0A20, intermittent P0A21. Expect reduced electric power and a hybrid warning.

causes_en: Sensor offset or gain drifted, reading off against the torque model
Electrical interference on the signal from damaged shielding or ground
Missing or outdated calibration after module or drive unit replacement
Mechanical fault in the drive unit that changes the real torque
P0A18.desc: The motor torque sensor delivers an electrically valid signal, but the torque it reports does not match what the control unit expects from the commanded motor current, speed and operating state. Typical checks compare measured and estimated torque or look for an offset when no torque is applied. Honda patents show such a sensor mounted inside the hollow output shaft of a traction motor, where electromagnetic noise is a known accuracy issue. No manufacturer documents P0A18 publicly. CARB requires approved monitoring of drive motor faults that impair propulsion. P0A17 is the plain circuit fault; P0A19 and P0A20 are out of range low and high. The drive system usually limits electric torque.

causes_en: Sensor signal or supply line shorted to ground
Sensor reference or excitation supply missing
Corroded or loose connector at the drive unit
Torque sensor electronics failed, often replaced with the drive unit
P0A19.desc: The control unit watches the voltage of a torque sensor that measures load directly on the traction motor shaft, such as the magnetostrictive sensor in a hollow motor shaft shown in a Honda patent. P0A19 sets when the signal stays below its valid window for a calibrated time, typical of a short to ground, a broken supply or an open signal line pulled low. No manufacturer documents P0A19 publicly; CARB only requires an approved drive motor monitoring plan. P0A20 is the opposite fault, P0A18 a plausible voltage with wrong torque, P0A21 dropouts. The driver usually sees a hybrid warning and reduced electric drive power.

causes_en: Internal failure of the inverter or generator control electronics
Control software fault, fixed by an update where the maker provides one
Supply, ground or bus connection to the module faulty
P0A1A.desc: P0A1A reports a fault of the electronics that control the generator, either inside a hybrid inverter or in a belt starter-generator. Toyota lists P0A1A for the 2010-2015 Prius and 2012-2017 Prius V together with P0A94, P324E and P3004 as a malfunction inside the inverter assembly with converter; the repair can mean replacing the MG ECU, IPM transistors or the whole inverter. Audi stores P0A1A00 in the engine control unit of 2025 models with a Valeo 48 V starter-generator, paired with a 48 V system fault, and blames starter-generator software. CARB requires monitoring of the generator system. Effects range from a MIL to lost charging or no hybrid drive.

causes_en: Control software fault, several makers resolve it by reprogramming
Internal processor or memory fault in the inverter control board
Weak 12 V supply during start-up or shutdown
P0A1B.en: Drive Motor A Control Module Performance
P0A1B.desc: P0A1B flags a self-test failure of the processor that controls drive motor A, usually inside the inverter. In GM hybrid tables (2016) it sets when the processor fails an inhibit path test at power-down, three or more times, proving it could not take the system to a safe state; in 2011 tables internal SPI, RAM or cache faults in 28 of 32 samples count. Both are Type A, MIL on the first trip. Land Rover sets P0A1B in the inverter of 2024-25 PHEVs at start-up, VW lists P0A1B00 for the ID.4 front drive. Toyota uses subtype P0A1B-1F on the 2023-24 Corolla Hybrid. Drive motor B is P0A1C. Expect a red loss-of-drive warning.

causes_en: Internal processor or memory fault on the motor B control board
Calibration or software fault in the inverter
Unstable 12 V supply or ground to the inverter electronics
P0A1C.en: Drive Motor B Control Module Performance
P0A1C.desc: P0A1C is the counterpart of P0A1B for the second electric machine, drive motor B, and reports that its control processor is no longer trustworthy. GM hybrid tables use it for the motor control processor B: in 2016 calibrations the code sets when an inhibit path test at power-down fails three or more times, in 2011 calibrations internal processor integrity faults such as SPI, RAM or cache errors are counted. Both are Type A with MIL on the first trip. The code concerns the control electronics, not a phase current sensor; those faults use their own codes. Expect a hybrid warning and loss of the affected motor function.

causes_en: Internal fault of the hybrid control module
Code stored by a scan tool communication error, not by a real defect
Supply, ground or network fault at the module
P0A1D.desc: The hybrid powertrain control module coordinates engine, motors and battery. P0A1D says this module has reported an internal failure or is no longer working reliably. In GM hybrid tables (2013) the engine control module stores P0A1D when a message from motor control processor A signals a hybrid controller status failure in 3 of 4 counts, as a Type B code with MIL after two trips. GM 2016 tables list P0A1D among codes that limit engine power. Subaru warns for the 2014-16 Crosstrek Hybrid that generic OBD readouts may store P0A1D from a scan tool communication error; replace the module only if the code returns. P0E43 covers module B.

causes_en: Loose wiring connection at the starter-generator
Starter-generator software fault, fixed by update
Starter-generator with integrated electronics failed
P0A1E.desc: Mild and full hybrids often start the engine and recharge the battery with a belt-driven starter-generator that has its own control electronics. P0A1E means that controller has reported a fault or works incorrectly. Audi stores P0A1E00 in the starter-generator control module of the 2020-2022 Q3 mild hybrid and cures it with a software update. Ford logs P0A1E in the engine control module of 2021-2023 F-150 PowerBoost and 2020-2026 Explorer and 2020-2023 Aviator hybrids; its bulletins name a loose connection at the belt integrated starter-generator or its software. Drivers notice a wrench or MIL lamp, no start-stop and no electric-only driving.

causes_en: Module software fault, fixed by a new calibration
Internal hardware fault of the battery control module
Unstable 12 V supply causing module resets
P0A1F.en: Battery Energy Control Module A Performance
P0A1F.desc: The battery energy control module supervises cell voltages, current and temperatures of the high-voltage pack. P0A1F reports that this module failed its own integrity checks. In GM hybrid tables (2011) a single reset of the module by its software watchdog is enough, and the code sets in one trip. GM told dealers for the 2011-2012 Chevrolet Volt not to replace the module for P0A1F but to install a new calibration. FCA lists subtype P0A1F-09, internal component failure, on the 2018 Jeep Wrangler with eTorque and also fixes it by reflashing the battery pack control module. Lost communication with the module is U0111. Expect a MIL and limited hybrid function.

causes_en: Signal line shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground return
Sensor electronics output stuck high
P0A20.desc: This code covers the upper electrical limit of a torque sensor fitted to the traction motor shaft, for example the magnetostrictive design inside a hollow output shaft described in a Honda patent. The control unit sets P0A20 when the sensor voltage remains above the valid range for a calibrated time, which points to a short to the supply voltage, an open ground return or a sensor output stuck high. No manufacturer documents P0A20 publicly; CARB requires an approved drive motor monitor. Siblings: P0A19 low, P0A18 implausible torque, P0A21 intermittent, P0A17 general circuit. Expect a hybrid warning and limited electric torque.

causes_en: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Chafed sensor wiring that shorts briefly under vibration
Damaged shield letting inverter noise into the signal
P0A21.desc: Here the torque sensor on the traction motor shaft delivers a signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing permanently. Such shaft sensors, as in the Honda patent with a sensor inside a hollow motor shaft, sit in an area with strong electromagnetic fields and vibration, so loose terminals, chafed wires and interference are the usual suspects. P0A21 sets when the control unit counts too many implausible signal changes. No manufacturer documents P0A21 publicly; CARB demands an approved drive motor monitor. Steady faults would show as P0A19 or P0A20. The warning may come and go.

causes_en: Sensor connector at the generator unplugged, loose or corroded
Open circuit in the sensor harness
Generator torque sensor or its electronics failed
P0A22.desc: In series or power-split hybrids a separate electric machine runs as generator, driven by the combustion engine. A Honda patent claims a torque sensor inside the hollow shaft of either the traction motor or this generator. P0A22 is the general circuit fault of the generator torque sensor: the control unit receives no usable signal at all, without a more specific low, high or intermittent pattern. No manufacturer documents P0A22 publicly; CARB requires an approved monitoring plan for the generator system. Related: P0A23 plausibility, P0A24 low, P0A25 high, P0A26 intermittent. Charging and engine-driven power generation may be limited.

causes_en: Sensor zero point or gain drifted
Electromagnetic interference from the generator or inverter
Contact resistance in the connector skewing the signal
P0A23.desc: The generator torque sensor sends an electrically valid voltage, but the torque it reports does not fit the generator current, speed and engine load the control unit knows. Typical checks compare the measured value with a torque model or look for an offset while the generator is idle. Such a sensor can sit in the hollow generator shaft, as a Honda patent claims, where magnetic noise and ageing shift the reading. No manufacturer documents P0A23 publicly; CARB requires approved monitoring of generator faults. Pure wiring faults appear as P0A22, P0A24 or P0A25. The system tends to cap generator torque.

causes_en: Signal line shorted to ground
Sensor supply voltage missing
Sensor electronics failed with output stuck low
P0A24.desc: P0A24 is stored when the voltage from the generator torque sensor stays under its lower diagnostic limit for a calibrated time. Electrically this means the line is pulled toward ground, the sensor supply is missing or the signal wire is broken. The sensor measures torque on the shaft of the engine-driven generator; a Honda patent describes such a sensor inside a hollow generator or motor shaft. No manufacturer documents P0A24 publicly; CARB requires an approved generator monitoring plan. The upper limit is P0A25, implausible but valid readings are P0A23, short dropouts P0A26. Electric generation may be cut back.

causes_en: Signal line shorted to supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground
Sensor output stuck high
P0A25.desc: With P0A25 the control unit sees the generator torque sensor signal above its permitted upper limit for longer than the calibrated debounce time. The common electrical explanations are a short from the signal line to the supply or battery voltage, an interrupted sensor ground, or a sensor output stuck at its maximum. The sensor belongs to the engine-driven generator of a hybrid; a Honda patent shows torque sensing inside a hollow generator or motor shaft. No manufacturer documents P0A25 publicly; CARB only demands an approved generator monitor. Opposite fault: P0A24; plausibility: P0A23; intermittent: P0A26. Generator torque is usually limited.

causes_en: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Chafed wiring near the generator housing
Shield or ground damage letting inverter noise in
P0A26.desc: P0A26 points to short interruptions or jumps in the generator torque sensor signal rather than a constant fault. The control unit counts implausible signal changes or brief out-of-range events and sets the code once a calibrated limit is exceeded. Because the sensor works next to the generator, as in the Honda patent with a sensor in a hollow generator or motor shaft, heat cycles, vibration and inverter noise favour loose contacts and chafed wires. No manufacturer documents P0A26 publicly; CARB requires an approved generator monitor. Permanent faults show as P0A24 or P0A25. Symptoms often appear only on rough roads.

causes_en: Contactor or its driver does not release when power-off is commanded
Internal fault in the inverter/power unit that controls the contactors (Honda Civic Hybrid)
Damaged wiring or loose terminal on the hardwired power-off line
Crash or emergency shutdown signal stored or still active
P0A27.desc: P0A27 covers the circuit that tells the high-voltage battery to drop off the bus, i.e. the command path that opens the main contactors at key-off, after a fault or after a crash signal. Patents describe such a path as a dedicated hardware line in addition to CAN, so the contactors open within milliseconds. The code sets when commanded and actual state disagree. Honda lists P0A27 as High Voltage Contactor Stays Activated on the 2012-15 Civic Hybrid, where it is one of the codes that call for replacing the motor power inverter. P0A28 and P0A29 are the low and high voltage faults of the same line. The driver may see a hybrid warning and the car may refuse to start or power down.

causes_en: Power-off signal line shorted to ground
Poor terminal fit or corrosion at the battery or control module connector
Missing supply or blown fuse feeding the power-off circuit
Faulty driver stage in the battery or hybrid control module
P0A28.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Power Off Circuit Low
P0A28.desc: The control unit watches the voltage on the line that commands the high-voltage battery to disconnect. P0A28 sets when that signal stays below its valid window for a calibrated time, typical of a short to ground or a lost supply on the line. No manufacturer documents P0A28 publicly; GM only lists it as a search keyword in a general pin-fit bulletin. Patents show the power-off path as a hardwired line next to CAN that opens the contactors within milliseconds; CARB requires hybrid components that can affect emissions to be monitored. P0A29 is the opposite fault, P0A27 a mismatch between command and contactor state. Expect a hybrid warning and, depending on strategy, no ready mode.

causes_en: Open power-off line or unplugged connector
Power-off line shorted to battery voltage
Spread or corroded terminals at the connectors
Faulty input or driver stage in the control module
P0A29.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Power Off Circuit High
P0A29.desc: P0A29 is stored when the voltage on the hybrid battery power-off line sits above its plausible range for longer than allowed, which points to an open line pulled up internally or a short to a supply voltage. No manufacturer explains P0A29 publicly; GM merely names it as a keyword in a generic bulletin on terminal fit. The circuit itself is the hardwired disconnect path that patents describe beside the CAN crash message, and CARB 1968.2 requires monitoring of hybrid components relevant to emissions. Related: P0A28 for a signal too low, P0A27 when the contactors do not follow the command. A stuck-high line can keep the system from powering up or from shutting down correctly.

causes_en: Broken or shorted sensor wire between motor and inverter
Loose or corroded connector at the drive unit
Thermistor failed inside the motor or transaxle
Faulty sensor input in the inverter/motor control module
P0A2A.en: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0A2A.desc: A thermistor in the stator of traction motor A reports winding temperature so the inverter can cut torque before the insulation overheats. P0A2A is the general circuit fault; the failure type sits in the extension byte. McLaren uses P0A2A1C on the Artura when a short or broken wire drives the sensor voltage out of range and P0A2A29 for an invalid signal. GM instead splits the electrical faults into P0A2C and P0A2D. Siblings: P0A2B plausibility, P0A2C low signal (hot), P0A2D high signal (cold or open), P0A2E dropouts, P0A2F real overheating; P2DAC is the same fault on a second sensor B. Hyundai shows the sensor sits inside the transaxle. Expect a hybrid warning and reduced electric power.

causes_en: Thermistor drifted out of its resistance curve
Added resistance from a worn or corroded connector (Audi A7 e quattro)
Fault in a reference temperature such as inverter or fluid temperature
Motor cooling problem that makes a real temperature look implausible
P0A2B.en: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0A2B.desc: This is the rationality check: after a long soak, motor A's temperature should match other temperatures in the drive. GM compares it with the average inverter module temperature on its 2013 two-mode trucks and sets P0A2B, Type B, if they differ by more than 28 °C after at least 360 minutes off; the 2011 table uses 20 °C against coolant and transmission fluid, the 2013 MGU mild hybrid 25 °C. Hyundai's Sonata Hybrid bulletin lists the code with resistance specs for the NTC; Audi pairs it on the A7 e quattro with P0A2E and a worn connector. McLaren also files over-temperature under P0A2B98. P0A2C/P0A2D are hard electrical faults, P0A2F real heat. Expect reduced electric power.

causes_en: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Thermistor internally shorted (often only with transaxle or motor)
Chafed extension harness between drive unit and inverter
Faulty sensor input in the inverter/motor control module
P0A2C.en: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0A2C.desc: The motor A sensor is an NTC thermistor, so its signal voltage falls as the winding heats; Hyundai's Sonata Hybrid bulletin gives about 11 to 13 kOhm at 20 °C for 2014-15 units. P0A2C means the voltage is too low, which the module reads as an impossibly hot motor: GM sets it on 2013 two-mode trucks above 230 °C (near 0 V), Type B, two trips; the 2011 table uses 184 °C, the 2013 MGU mild hybrid 236 °C. The usual cause is a signal wire shorted to ground or a shorted sensor. P0A2D is the opposite fault, P0A2F a real over-temperature that only counts while the sensor is in range. Hyundai reports a stuck 417 °F reading as a circuit fault. The driver sees a warning and derated electric drive.

causes_en: Open signal or ground wire of the motor temperature sensor
Connector unplugged or terminal pushed out, often after drive unit work
Thermistor open inside the motor or transaxle
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
P0A2D.en: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0A2D.desc: With an NTC thermistor, a high signal voltage stands for a cold motor, and a voltage close to the 5 V pull-up means the circuit is open. GM sets P0A2D on its 2013 two-mode trucks when the reading falls below -40 °C, Type B over two trips; if the fault is already present at start-up it waits until the motor has warmed up under load for at least 1.5 minutes. The 2011 table uses -41 °C, the 2013 MGU mild hybrid -48 °C with torque above 10 Nm. Typical causes are a broken signal or ground wire, an unplugged connector or an open sensor. Hyundai checks the sensor resistance at the transaxle connector. P0A2C is the low-voltage counterpart. Motor protection is lost, so electric power is limited.

causes_en: Worn contacts in a coupling connector of the sensor line (Audi A7 e quattro)
Resistance jumps in the sensor crimp at high temperature (Bentley hybrids)
Chafed or loosely routed sensor wire with intermittent contact
P0A2E.en: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0A2E.desc: P0A2E flags short jumps or dropouts in the motor A temperature signal that are too brief or too erratic for the low/high checks. Bentley documents it for the Bentayga PHEV and Flying Spur Hybrid 2020-23: the resistance in the sensor crimp changes suddenly at high temperature, and only the sensor has to be replaced, although the engine and gearbox come out to reach it. Audi lists it on the 2021-22 A7 e quattro together with P0A4000 and/or P0A2B00, caused by contact wear in a coupling connector, fixed with new gold-plated pins. Siblings: P0A2C/P0A2D for a steady out-of-range signal, P2DB0 for sensor B. The car shows a MIL or HV warning and may limit electric drive.

causes_en: Motor cooling failure such as a weak pump, low fluid or blocked cooler
Sustained high load such as towing or long climbs in electric mode
Temperature sensor reading too high while still within range
P0A2F.desc: Unlike its siblings, P0A2F reports a real thermal problem: the sensor works, but motor A stays too hot. GM sets it on 2013 two-mode trucks when the temperature exceeds 200 °C and does not fall below the 135 °C reset level, Type B, provided no circuit or plausibility fault is active. The 2011 table uses 159 °C; on the 2013 MGU mild hybrid the limit is 165 °C, and torque is already cut linearly from 100 % to zero between 155 and 165 °C. Hyundai lists the code in its Sonata Hybrid sensor bulletin, so a skewed sensor can mimic it. McLaren handles over-temperature under P0A2B98 and points to the dielectric cooling circuit. Expect a warning and sharply reduced electric power.

causes_en: Loose, corroded or damaged connector between motor B and its control module
Chafed or broken sensor wiring at the drive unit
Thermistor in the motor winding failed (often only replaceable with the motor)
Faulty sensor input in the motor control module
P0A30.en: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit
P0A30.desc: P0A30 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor in the second traction motor (motor B). It is meant for faults the control unit can see on the sensor line but cannot classify as too low, too high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0A30 publicly; GM two-mode hybrids and Mitsubishi (rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV) use the specific codes P0A31 to P0A33 for the same sensor instead. CARB 1968.2 requires hybrid components whose failure can affect emissions to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid winding temperature the motor cannot be protected against overheating, so the system usually cuts electric drive power and lights a hybrid warning.

causes_en: Motor B thermistor reading drifted out of tolerance
Corroded terminals adding resistance in the sensor circuit
Comparison sensor (inverter, coolant or fluid temperature) is wrong
Uneven cooling of the drive unit, e.g. low fluid level
P0A31.en: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0A31.desc: P0A31 checks whether the motor B temperature reading makes sense, typically after a long rest when all parts should be close to the same temperature. GM compares it with other temperatures: the 2011 tables flag a gap above 20 °C to the average of power-electronics coolant and transmission fluid after 6 h without propulsion (Type A); the 2013 two-mode trucks allow 28 °C against the inverter module after 360 min key-off (Type B, two trips). Mitsubishi (2023 Outlander PHEV rear motor) compares two coil sensors after 5,400 s soak and sets it at 13 °C difference. P0A32 and P0A33 cover hard circuit faults; P0A35 is only judged while this test passes. Expect a hybrid warning and limited electric drive.

causes_en: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Thermistor shorted inside the motor
Chafed harness between drive unit and motor control module
Faulty sensor input in the motor control module
P0A32.en: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P0A32.desc: P0A32 means the motor B temperature signal sits below its valid voltage range. GM uses an NTC thermistor, so a voltage near 0 V reads as an impossibly hot winding: the 2011 hybrid tables set it above 184 °C (Type A, one trip), the 2013 two-mode trucks above 230 °C (Type B, two trips). Mitsubishi sets it on the rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the sensor voltage is 0.065 V or less for 0.5 s. A signal wire shorted to ground or a shorted thermistor is the typical cause. P0A33 is the opposite fault, P0A31 the plausibility check, and P0A35 a real over-temperature that GM only evaluates while no out-of-range fault is active. The system derates electric drive and warns the driver.

causes_en: Open sensor circuit or unplugged connector
Spread or corroded terminals at the motor or module connector
Thermistor open inside the motor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
P0A33.en: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P0A33.desc: P0A33 is stored when the motor B temperature signal stays above its valid voltage range. With GM's NTC thermistor a voltage near 5 V reads as an impossibly cold motor: GM sets it below -41 °C in the 2011 tables (Type A) and below -40 °C on the 2013 two-mode trucks (Type B, two trips). Mitsubishi flags the rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the voltage reaches 4.761 V or more for 0.5 s. That pattern points to an open sensor circuit, an unplugged connector or a short to a voltage source. P0A32 is the low-side fault, P0A31 the rationality check, P0A35 the over-temperature code. Because winding temperature is unknown, the system limits electric drive power and shows a warning.

causes_en: Loose or fretting terminal in the sensor connector
Wire insulation chafed through at a moving harness section
Cracked joint at the thermistor leads inside the motor
P0A34.en: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P0A34.desc: P0A34 covers a motor B temperature signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing permanently. A winding temperature cannot change by tens of degrees within milliseconds, so such steps point to a loose contact, a chafed wire or a cracked solder joint. No manufacturer documents P0A34 publicly; GM and Mitsubishi only list the permanent faults P0A32 and P0A33 for this sensor, with debounce times of a few hundred milliseconds to seconds that a brief dropout may not meet. CARB 1968.2 requires circuit monitoring of emission-relevant hybrid components. The fault often comes and goes with vibration or heat, and the hybrid system may limit electric drive while it is active.

causes_en: Electric coolant pump of the drive cooling circuit failed or weak
Low coolant or transmission fluid in the motor cooling path
Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked
Extended high load such as towing or long climbs
P0A35.desc: Unlike the sensor codes, P0A35 reports that motor B is actually too hot according to a working sensor. GM's 2011 hybrid tables set it above 149 °C (Type A, one trip); the 2013 two-mode trucks use 200 °C, clear it only below 135 °C and run it only while P0A31 is not active (Type B). Mitsubishi sets it on the rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the coil reaches 177 °C for one second and names the motor assembly, electric water pump, EV cooling circuit and radiator fan as suspects. Sustained heavy load, towing or a cooling fault are the usual triggers. P0A2F is the same check for motor A, P0A3D for the motor B inverter. The system cuts motor B torque until it has cooled down.

causes_en: Loose or corroded connector between generator and its control unit
Damaged sensor wiring near the transaxle
Generator coil thermistor failed (usually replaced with the generator)
Faulty input in the generator control unit
P0A36.desc: P0A36 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor in the hybrid generator, the machine that is mainly driven by the engine to produce electricity. It covers faults the module detects on the sensor line without classing them as low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0A36 publicly; Mitsubishi (2023 Outlander PHEV) monitors its generator coil sensor with the specific codes P0A37 to P0A39 instead. CARB 1968.2 requires circuit monitoring for hybrid components that can affect emissions. With the generator temperature unknown, the system cannot protect the windings, so it usually restricts generator output and series operation and shows a hybrid warning.

causes_en: Generator coil sensor reading out of tolerance
Corroded connector or damaged harness in the sensor circuit
Fault in the power drive unit that evaluates the sensor
Comparison sensor (motor coil or oil temperature) reads wrong
P0A37.desc: P0A37 tests whether the generator temperature reading is believable. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: once per drive cycle, after at least 5,400 s of soak and with the inverter switched off, the generator W-phase coil temperature is compared with the front motor coil and with the oil temperature. A gap of 26 °C to the motor or 22 °C to the oil, held for 0.8 s, sets the code. Suspects are the power drive unit, the coil sensor inside the generator and the wiring. P0A38 and P0A39 are hard voltage faults of the same sensor, P0A3B the real over-temperature. Mitsubishi is the only manufacturer found that documents P0A37 publicly. The driver sees a warning and generator use may be limited.

causes_en: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Generator coil sensor shorted internally
Damaged connector or harness between generator and power drive unit
Faulty sensor input in the power drive unit
P0A38.desc: P0A38 means the generator temperature signal has fallen below the range a healthy sensor can produce. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the voltage of the generator W-phase coil sensor is 0.1 V or less for at least 0.5 s while the generator control unit has at least 8 V supply. Such a low voltage usually comes from a signal wire shorted to ground or a shorted sensor; Mitsubishi lists the power drive unit, the generator coil sensor and damaged wiring or connectors as suspects. P0A39 is the matching high fault, P0A37 the plausibility check and P0A3B a genuine over-temperature. Mitsubishi is the only manufacturer found that documents P0A38. Expect a hybrid warning and restricted generator use.

causes_en: Open sensor circuit or unplugged generator connector
Spread or corroded terminals at the generator or power drive unit
Generator coil sensor open internally
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
P0A39.desc: P0A39 is the high-side counterpart of P0A38: the generator temperature signal stays above the range a working sensor can deliver. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the generator W-phase coil sensor voltage reaches 4.93 V or more for at least 0.5 s. A voltage that close to the reference typically means the sensor circuit is open, a connector is unplugged or a terminal has lost contact, less often a short to a supply. Mitsubishi points to the power drive unit, the coil sensor in the generator and the harness. P0A37 handles implausible but in-range readings, P0A3B a real overheat. No other manufacturer documents P0A39 publicly. The system cannot protect the generator and limits its use.

causes_en: Loose or fretting terminal in the generator sensor connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Harness chafed against the transaxle housing
P0A3A.desc: P0A3A flags a generator temperature signal that is interrupted or jumps only briefly. Since the thermal mass of a generator winding rules out sudden steps, such behaviour indicates a contact or wiring problem rather than a real temperature change. No manufacturer documents P0A3A publicly; Mitsubishi (2023 Outlander PHEV) only lists the permanent faults P0A38 and P0A39 for its generator coil sensor, each needing at least 0.5 s outside the valid voltage before it sets, so short dropouts would not trigger them. CARB 1968.2 calls for circuit monitoring of emission-relevant hybrid parts. Symptoms come and go, often with heat, vibration or moisture, and generator use may be restricted while the fault is present.

causes_en: Fault in the oil cooling circuit of the generator (low oil, leak, pump)
Radiator fan not working
Internal generator fault such as damaged winding insulation
Power drive unit commanding excessive generator current
P0A3B.desc: P0A3B reports that the hybrid generator itself has become too hot, with the temperature sensor working correctly. Mitsubishi documents it as generator coil temperature high on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the monitor runs continuously and sets the code when the W-phase coil temperature criterion of 199 °C is met for one second. Mitsubishi's checks cover higher-priority codes, the radiator fan, and the EV oil cooling circuit that cools the generator; if those are fine, the generator is replaced. P0A37 to P0A39 are the sensor faults that must be ruled out first, P0A3E the over-temperature of the generator inverter. No other manufacturer documents P0A3B publicly. The system restricts generator output, which can cut charging and series-mode power.

causes_en: PCU or inverter radiator damaged or leaking (Honda Accord/Civic Hybrid)
Internal inverter defect such as a cracked solder joint (Honda Civic Hybrid 2012-15)
Low coolant or failed electric pump in the inverter cooling circuit
Radiator fan not running
P0A3C.en: Drive Motor A Inverter Over Temperature
P0A3C.desc: P0A3C reports overheating of the inverter that powers drive motor A, usually measured at its IGBT power switches. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the front motor control unit reads 166 °C or more at the U-phase upper IGBT for 0.12 s; other switch positions have their own P30xx codes. Honda calls it motor control module overheating and lists it among the codes caused by a cracked solder joint in the 2012-15 Civic Hybrid motor power inverter, covered by a warranty extension. On the 2023-25 Accord Hybrid and 2025-26 Civic Hybrid, Honda links it to a PCU radiator damaged by road debris. P0A78 is the general inverter performance code, P0C11 to P0C13 are phase-specific. Power is cut to protect the inverter.

causes_en: Electric water pump of the EV cooling circuit failed
Low coolant or air in the EV cooling circuit
Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked
Internal fault in the rear motor and inverter assembly
P0A3D.en: Drive Motor B Inverter Over Temperature
P0A3D.desc: P0A3D is the over-temperature code for the inverter feeding drive motor B. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV this is the rear motor control unit, and Mitsubishi sets the code when its IGBT temperature is 156 °C or higher for one second. Mitsubishi's hints list the rear motor assembly, the electric water pump driven by the PHEV-ECU, the EV coolant circuit and the radiator fan, so cooling problems come before electronics. No other manufacturer documents P0A3D publicly; CARB 1968.2 requires monitoring of hybrid components that affect emissions. P0A35 is the over-temperature of motor B itself, P0C14 to P0C16 phase-specific inverter codes and P0A79 the general inverter performance code. Rear drive power is reduced until the inverter cools down.

causes_en: PCU radiator punctured or leaking after road debris (Honda Accord/Civic Hybrid)
Low coolant or failed electric pump in the inverter cooling circuit
Radiator fan not running
Internal fault in the power drive unit
P0A3E.desc: P0A3E reports that the inverter controlling the hybrid generator is too hot. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the generator control unit reads 156 °C or more at the U-phase IGBT for 0.12 s; the other switches report via P30AD to P30B1. Its hints are the power drive unit, the EV water cooling circuit and the radiator fan. Honda lists P0A3E among the PCU overheating codes on the 2023-25 Accord Hybrid and 2025-26 Civic Hybrid, where road debris can puncture the PCU radiator because the original guard is too weak. P0A3B is the generator's own over-temperature, P0A3C and P0A3D cover the motor inverters. Output is restricted, so charging and power drop and further warnings may follow.

causes_en: Spread or poorly seated terminal at the resolver connector (documented on the Chevrolet Bolt)
Open or shorted excitation, sine or cosine wire between motor and inverter
Low 12 V auxiliary battery voltage disturbing the motor control module (Subaru, fixed by reprogramming)
Resolver coil failed inside the motor
Faulty resolver excitation or input stage in the inverter/motor control module
P0A3F.en: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit
P0A3F.desc: The rotor position of a traction motor is read by a resolver: one excitation coil and two pickup coils that return sine and cosine signals. P0A3F is the basic circuit code for motor A and mostly means the signal is gone.
