P0AE7.desc: P0AE7 is stored when the control line of precharge contactor A carries too much voltage for its commanded state, typically a short to the 12 V supply. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the high-side driver output reads between 5.27 and 19.7 V while the contactor is commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips. GM's 2013 eAssist controller looks for a short to power on its low-side driver in the on state, 3 of 5 samples at 50 ms, Type B. A coil energized by a short may keep the precharge path closed when it should be open, so P0AE2 can follow. CARB requires circuit monitoring of such hybrid outputs. The negative and positive main contactor counterparts are P0AE0 and P0ADC.

causes_en: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor D and sensing board
Temperature sensor D failed
Fault in the battery controller input stage
P0AE8.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit
P0AE8.desc: Battery temperature sensor D is a further thermistor inside the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the matching codes as temperature sensor 4 of nine. P0AE8 is the general circuit code for it, used when the controller finds an electrical fault without classifying it as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables report the more specific siblings P0AE9 to P0AEC instead. CARB requires temperature inputs of hybrid batteries to be monitored for circuit faults. With one value missing, the controller has a gap in its temperature picture and usually limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits on a module or sensing board inside the pack, so checks require high-voltage safety procedures.

causes_en: Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342)
Temperature sensor D drifting out of tolerance
Genuine local temperature difference in one battery module
Increased contact resistance in the sensor circuit
P0AE9.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P0AE9.desc: P0AE9 is the plausibility check for battery temperature sensor D, GM's sensor 4: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors. In GM's 2016 and 2019 tables it fails when the value is more than 25 °C away from the average of the others in 50 of 67 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use more than 15 °C in 90 of 100; the eAssist table 13OBDG05C allows 8.55 °C after a long module off time; GM's 2018 table uses 20 °C for 5 s within 6.7 s. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 counts P0AE9 among sensor codes that set falsely in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming. Otherwise a drifting sensor or a real hot spot in one module is the likely cause.

causes_en: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Temperature sensor D internally shorted
Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342)
Moisture or damage on the battery sensing board
P0AEA.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P0AEA.desc: P0AEA means the voltage of battery temperature sensor D is below its valid range. GM uses NTC thermistors with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an extremely hot cell, usually from a short to ground. Thresholds vary: above 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples in the 2016 and 2019 tables; above 95 °C in 30 of 40 on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids; below 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 in the eAssist table 13OBDG05C; above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s in a 2018 controller. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists P0AEA among codes that can set falsely and calls for a software update first. A genuinely hot pack would trip lower limits earlier, so treat it as electrical.

causes_en: Open circuit or unplugged connector at sensor D
Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342)
Temperature sensor D open internally
P0AEB.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P0AEB.desc: P0AEB reports that battery temperature sensor D delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensors this reads as extreme cold, pointing to an open wire, a backed-out pin at the sensing board or a cracked thermistor. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids below -45 °C in 30 of 40, the eAssist table 13OBDG05C above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10, and a 2018 controller below -40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; all Type B, two trips. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links such codes to a Battery Too Cold message above -25 °C ambient and prescribes reprogramming. A pack the controller believes frozen gets strict charge and power limits.

causes_en: Loose terminal or connector not fully latched at sensor D
Partly broken or chafed sensor wire
Fault on the battery sensing board
P0AEC.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AEC.desc: P0AEC flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor D: the reading jumps faster than the heavy battery mass could ever warm or cool. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables. The controller sums the absolute changes of the sensor value across a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips. GM applies the same logic to sensors A to C. The older two-mode and eAssist tables list no erratic code for sensor D. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a partly broken wire or a connector not fully latched after pack service. If several sensors jump at once, suspect the sensing board rather than the individual thermistor.

causes_en: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
P0AED.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0AED.desc: The inverter of an electric drive motor carries thermistors near its power switches so the controller can derate before the IGBTs overheat. In GM's hybrid tables, inverter temperature sensor A is the phase U sensor of the inverter for motor A. P0AED is the general circuit code for it, used for an electrical fault that is not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the specific siblings P0AEE, P0AEF and P0AF0 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components and their sensors for circuit faults. Without a valid inverter temperature the controller has to assume the worst and usually limits motor torque. The sensor is built into the power inverter module, so repair often means replacing that unit.

causes_en: Controller software error (Audi Q5/A7 e quattro bulletin)
Inverter temperature sensor A drifting out of tolerance
Failing power inverter module (e.g. Honda MPI solder joints)
Uneven inverter cooling after soak
P0AEE.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0AEE.desc: P0AEE checks whether inverter temperature sensor A reads sensibly. GM's 2016 to 2019 tables compare it after a cold soak with an average temperature of the vehicle; more than 20 °C apart sets Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt compares it with the other power electronics sensors (20 °C, Type A), the 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off (15 °C), eAssist with module and MGU temperatures (20 °C). GM bulletin PIC6303A notes that on Volt, Malibu and LaCrosse with 5ET50 the code alone triggers no remedy; the inverter is only replaced with P0AC4. Audi fixes P0AEE00 on Q5 and A7 e quattro by software, and Honda lists it among inverter faults of the 2012-15 Civic Hybrid with extended warranty.

causes_en: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
P0AEF.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0AEF.desc: P0AEF means the signal of inverter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. GM describes it as an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an impossibly hot inverter, usually a short to ground or an internal sensor fault. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; above 159 °C, Type A, one trip, in another 2019 table; above 150 °C on eAssist; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks. Stellantis lists P0AEF-11 for the 2026 Jeep Compass PHEV outside the US among codes behind an Electric Traction System Fault and a no-start, repaired by replacing the inverter.

causes_en: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Motor control unit software (Kia Sorento Hybrid 2025)
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter
P0AF0.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0AF0.desc: P0AF0 reports a signal from inverter temperature sensor A above its valid range, which for an NTC sensor reads as an extremely cold inverter: open wire, lost ground or a broken sensor. GM's 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables set it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only after at least 90 s of inverter warm-up at 20 Nm or more, so a really cold car does not trigger it; Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C (Type A), eAssist below -70 °C and the two-mode trucks below -40 °C (Type B). Kia's 2025 Sorento Hybrid bulletin lists P0AF0 with P0A3C and P1B77 after intermittent motor operation during engine clutch learning and fixes it with a motor control unit update.

causes_en: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Electrical interference on the sensor signal
P0AF1.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AF1.desc: P0AF1 is meant for an inverter temperature sensor A signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of failing permanently. Inverter heat sinks are liquid-cooled and change temperature smoothly, so sudden steps point to a contact problem or an internal fault in the sensing circuit. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables cover sensor A only with the plausibility, low and high codes P0AEE, P0AEF and P0AF0. GM's method for erratic battery sensors, such as P0AEC, sums signal changes over 10-sample windows and fails after 4 of 5 bad windows, which shows how such a check usually works. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for this kind of fault. Freeze-frame data help, since the fault often comes and goes.

causes_en: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
P0AF2.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0AF2.desc: Inverter temperature sensor B is, in GM's hybrid tables, the phase U thermistor of the second inverter, the one that drives motor B in two-motor systems. P0AF2 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's tables report the specific siblings P0AF3, P0AF4 and P0AF5 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components and their sensor circuits. Without a valid temperature the controller cannot protect the power switches of inverter B and usually limits that motor's torque. Whether a vehicle uses sensor B at all depends on its layout, so read the full code list and check the inverter connectors.

causes_en: Inverter temperature sensor B drifting out of tolerance
Failing power inverter module
Uneven inverter coolant flow after soak
P0AF3.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0AF3.desc: P0AF3 is the plausibility test for inverter temperature sensor B, the phase U sensor of GM's motor B inverter. In the 2016 to 2019 tables the sensor is compared after a cold soak with a calculated average vehicle temperature; a difference above 20 °C sets the code, Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt compares it with the other power electronics sensors at 20 °C, Type A, and the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off at 15 °C, Type B. GM bulletin PIC6303A lists P0AF3 with P0AEE and the other inverter thermistor codes on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal with the 5ET50 drive: alone they cause no noticeable effect, and the inverter is replaced only if P0AC4 set at the same time.

causes_en: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
P0AF4.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0AF4.desc: P0AF4 reports a signal of inverter temperature sensor B below the valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up, so a low voltage reads as an inverter far hotter than possible, usually from a short to ground or an internal sensor fault in the motor B inverter. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; above 159 °C, Type A, one trip, in another 2019 table; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks. A genuine overheat is reported separately as an over-temperature code such as P0A3D or P0C14. Because the sensor sits inside the inverter, the fix is usually the inverter assembly.

causes_en: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
Lost sensor ground
P0AF5.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0AF5.desc: P0AF5 means inverter temperature sensor B delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor that equals an implausibly cold inverter, so an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked thermistor is likely. In GM's 2016 to 2019 tables the code sets below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only once the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more, which rules out a genuinely cold start; Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C with Type A, one trip; the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks use below -40 °C, Type B. Until the value is valid, the controller protects inverter B with substitute values and may reduce motor B power. Check connectors at the inverter before condemning the unit.

causes_en: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Electrical interference on the sensor signal
P0AF6.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AF6.desc: P0AF6 targets an inverter temperature sensor B signal that jumps or drops out briefly. Since the heat sink of the motor B inverter is liquid-cooled and warms or cools gradually, abrupt changes in the reading indicate a contact problem or an intermittent fault in the sensing circuit rather than real temperature. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables only list P0AF3, P0AF4 and P0AF5 for sensor B. For erratic battery temperature sensors such as P0AEC, GM sums the signal changes over 10-sample windows and fails after 4 of 5 bad windows, a likely model for this check. CARB requires sensor inputs of hybrid systems to be checked for erratic behaviour. Watch live data while gently moving the inverter harness.

causes_en: Restricted cooling, weak coolant pump or failed cooling fan
Sustained high 12 V load or weak 12 V battery
Internal fault of the DC/DC converter
P0AF7.en: 14 Volt Power Module Internal Temperature Too High
P0AF7.desc: The 14 V power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery in hybrids and EVs. P0AF7 reports that its internal temperature has exceeded the protection limit, a real overheat rather than a sensor circuit fault. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's 2013 eAssist table shows how the same module is watched: its Accessory Power Module has two temperature sensors with their own circuit codes, and the separate code P0C32 compares sensor 1 with a thermal model and fails if they differ by more than 15 °C. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components. Common causes are a blocked cooling path, a weak coolant pump or fan, or a constantly high 12 V load. The module then derates its output, so the 12 V battery may run down.

causes_en: Loose or arcing high-voltage battery cable connection
Pack or bus voltage sensing circuit inaccurate
Low 12 V supply or loose 12 V power fuse affecting the measuring modules
High resistance in a pack fuse or main contactor
P0AF8.desc: P0AF8 compares the battery pack voltage reported by the battery controller with an independent measurement on the high-voltage bus. GM calls it system voltage correlation: with the contactors closed, the 2019 tables fail it when the pack reading differs from the inverter bus voltage by more than 13.95 V, or from the charger bus voltage by more than 14.95 V, 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms, Type A. The 2011 Volt table uses 12 V and Type A, the 2013 eAssist table 5.77 V against the motor controller, Type B. GM's Saturn Vue Hybrid PIP4005A links P0AF8 with P0AFB to a loose negative battery cable, and Volt PIC6089B mentions it with low 12 V system faults. P0AFA and P0AFB judge the voltage level itself.

causes_en: Loose high-voltage terminal or busbar connection
Degraded cell group collapsing under load
Main contactor with intermittent contact
P0AF9.desc: P0AF9 is meant for a traction battery voltage that fluctuates more than load changes can explain, for example through a loose terminal, an intermittent contactor or a cell group that collapses under load. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, covers system voltage with P0AF8 (correlation), P0AFA and P0AFB (low and high), and reports uneven cell groups as P0BBE pack voltage variation, which bulletin 19-NA-117 ties to degraded cells in the Volt and ELR. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs to be monitored for circuit and rationality faults. Typical effects are intermittent power limits and warnings; check high-voltage connections and cell voltages under load.

causes_en: Degraded or self-discharging cell groups
Pack drained by repeated failed engine starts or long standing
Open high-voltage fuse or manual disconnect
Loose or high-resistance ground on 48 V systems
P0AFA.desc: P0AFA protects the traction battery from deep discharge: the pack voltage, or in some versions any cell voltage, has fallen below a temperature-dependent limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it after 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack or 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch it so that only a technician command can clear it. GM bulletins name causes: degraded cell groups in 2011-15 Volt and ELR (19-NA-117), a blown fuse in the Bolt EV manual disconnect lever (18-NA-225), cell contamination in the 2015 Spark EV (17-NA-131) and repeated cranking that empties the Malibu Hybrid pack (PIC6229). A Ram eTorque parts notice names it for the 48 V power pack. Expect a no-start.

causes_en: Loose or arcing battery cable causing voltage spikes
Control unit software allows overvoltage (Mercedes 48 V bulletins)
Cell imbalance so that one cell overcharges
Faulty voltage sensing reporting too high a value
P0AFB.desc: P0AFB guards against overcharging: the pack voltage, or a single cell, exceeds a temperature-dependent upper limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables use 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack and 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch the code until a technician clears it by command; the 2011 Volt table also uses Type A. On the 2007-09 Saturn Vue Hybrid, GM's PIP4005A finds P0AFB together with P0AF8 caused by a loose negative battery cable. Mercedes-Benz uses P0AFB00 on 48 V starter-alternator systems for an on-board voltage that is too high, with software fixes for M256 engines, S-Class and GLE/GLS. Toyota's Prius Prime tech tip uses P0AFB11 with a current sensor text.

causes_en: Radio interference from an aftermarket antenna near the battery (Toyota Camry Hybrid)
Battery voltage sensor module internally defective
Supply or communication wiring of the sensor module faulty
P0AFC.desc: Some hybrid packs carry a separate sensor module that measures block voltages and passes them to the battery controller; Toyota calls it the battery voltage sensor or battery smart unit. P0AFC reports a fault of this module itself, such as a failed self-check or disturbed data transfer. Toyota documents it for the 2012-2015 Camry Hybrid in tech tip T-TT-0359-15 (repair manual entry P0AFC-123): an aftermarket antenna in the trunk, for example for CB radio, can set the code, and relocating it is the first step before following the regular diagnosis. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs to be monitored. Without valid block voltages the hybrid system usually shuts down or limits power.

causes_en: Vehicle parked unplugged in extreme cold
Battery heater or coolant heater not working
Temperature sensor reading too cold (sensor or software)
P0AFD.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Temperature Too Low
P0AFD.desc: P0AFD indicates that the traction battery is colder than its permitted operating range. At very low temperatures cell resistance rises and charging risks lithium plating, so the controller restricts or blocks charging and discharging. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. As a related case, GM's bulletin 18-NA-342 describes a Chevrolet Volt showing Battery Too Cold, Plug in to Warm above -25 °C because of faulty temperature sensor readings, fixed by reprogramming. CARB requires hybrid battery temperature inputs and their plausibility to be monitored. Distinguish a genuinely cold pack, which warms up on the charger or through the battery heater, from a sensor or heater fault; sensor circuit faults have their own codes.

causes_en: Pack deeply discharged or weak under load
High-resistance connection between battery and converter
Converter input voltage measured too low
P0AFE.en: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Too Low for Voltage Step Up Conversion
P0AFE.desc: Many hybrids raise the battery voltage with a step-up (boost) converter before it reaches the inverters; Toyota's second-generation Hybrid Synergy Drive, for example, boosts a pack of around 200 V to 500 V or more. The converter needs a minimum input voltage to reach its target without excessive current. P0AFE is set when the battery-side voltage is below that minimum, so the converter cannot boost properly. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires hybrid components such as converters to be monitored for functional faults. A deeply discharged or weak pack, a high-resistance connection or a voltage measurement fault are the obvious suspects. Expect reduced electric assist; a low pack voltage is reported separately as P0AFA.

causes_en: High-voltage or 48 V bus voltage too low (discharged pack, open contactor)
High-resistance input connection or fuse of the DC/DC converter
DC/DC converter internal measuring fault
P0AFF.en: System Voltage Too Low for Voltage Step Down Conversion
P0AFF.desc: A step-down (buck) DC/DC converter, often called the accessory power module, supplies the 12 V system from the high-voltage or 48 V bus. To regulate its output it needs an input voltage above a minimum. P0AFF is set when the input system voltage is too low for this conversion, so the converter cannot hold its 12 V output. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM monitors the related function in its 2013 eAssist table: P0CA2 flags a step-down failure of the 14 V power module after a shoot-through fault in its switching device, one trip, Type A. CARB requires such hybrid components to be monitored. Expect a charging system warning and a slowly draining 12 V battery.

causes_en: Loose, corroded or unlatched phase U connection at the pump motor
Current sensing in the pump inverter faulty (shunt or phase sensor)
Power stage of phase U in the pump control module faulty
Winding fault in phase U of the pump motor
P0B00.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current
P0B00.desc: P0B00 is the general fault for phase U of the three-phase motor that drives the electric auxiliary transmission fluid pump, the pump that keeps line pressure while the engine is stopped. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM, which runs such pumps on the Volt, ELR, Spark EV and CT6, monitors phase U instead with the low-side code P0B01 and catches overcurrent on any phase with P0C28. A Hitachi patent for an idle-stop sub-oil pump shows that the inverter often derives every phase current from one DC-bus shunt, so a U fault may come from the shared sensor rather than the phase itself. Expect a warning lamp, a stopped pump and, depending on design, no engine auto-stop or a no-start. P0B01/P0B02 are the low and high variants, P0B03 and P0B06 phases V and W.

causes_en: Pump motor connector not fully seated or latched (Chevrolet Spark EV)
Open circuit in the phase U lead or terminal of the pump motor cable
Phase U switch in the pump inverter not conducting
Open winding of phase U in the pump motor
P0B01.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current Low
P0B01.desc: P0B01 means the pump inverter sees almost no current in phase U of the auxiliary fluid pump motor, typically an open phase. GM documents the check for the Volt motor control processor (2016) and its hybrid tables of 2018 and 2019: with the drive state in Run, the inverter in normal PWM above 50 V and a squared current command above 5 A2 (2016) or 14.97 A2 (2018), the peak current on the U axis is compared while the rotor is within 30 degrees of it; below 1 A for 0.4 s of a 0.6 s window, the code sets as Type A, MIL on the first trip. On the 2014-15 Chevrolet Spark EV, GM bulletin PI1433 links P0B01, P0B04 or P0B07, Service Vehicle Soon and reduced propulsion to an unlatched pump connector. P0B04/P0B07 are phases V and W, P0B02 the high side.

causes_en: Phase U lead shorted to another phase or to ground
Pump binding mechanically, raising motor current
Current sensing in the pump inverter reads too high
Shorted turns in phase U of the pump motor
P0B02.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current High
P0B02.desc: P0B02 reports excessive current in phase U of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump motor, an overcurrent condition that the pump inverter must cut off to protect its switches. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM handles the same case differently: on the Volt and later hybrids it sets P0C28 when the absolute current of any phase exceeds 35 A for a few milliseconds, Type A. A phase-specific high code therefore points to a shorted U lead, a shorted winding, a jammed pump or a U current sensor reading too high. The Hitachi idle-stop pump patent shows phase currents being reconstructed from one bus shunt, which makes a sensing error a real candidate. The pump usually stops; auto-stop or electric driving is blocked. P0B01 is the low side, P0B05 and P0B08 the same fault on V and W.

causes_en: Poor contact in the phase V lead or pump connector
Current sensing in the pump inverter faulty
Phase V power stage in the pump control module faulty
Winding fault in phase V of the pump motor
P0B03.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current
P0B03.desc: P0B03 covers a general current fault in phase V of the brushless motor of the electric auxiliary transmission fluid pump. No manufacturer publicly describes a monitor for it. GM's 2013 eAssist (BAS Plus) tables name P0B03 only once, as a code that must be inactive before another speed check runs, without a description of its own. In GM's Volt and CT6 tables phase V is watched by the low-side code P0B04, and any overcurrent goes to P0C28. A GM, BMW and Daimler patent on a hybrid transmission pump explains why the pump matters: it must hold transmission pressure when the engine is stopped, otherwise gear engagement can be lost. The general code is a catch-all for implausible V current that fits neither low nor high. P0B04/P0B05 are the low and high variants, P0B00 and P0B06 phases U and W.

causes_en: Pump motor connector not fully seated or latched (Chevrolet Spark EV)
Open circuit in the phase V lead or terminal
Phase V switch in the pump inverter not conducting
Open winding of phase V in the pump motor
P0B04.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current Low
P0B04.desc: P0B04 indicates that phase V of the auxiliary fluid pump motor carries too little current, usually because the phase is open somewhere between inverter and winding. GM tests it on the Volt (2016) and in the 2018 and 2019 hybrid tables like its U and W siblings: in Run, with normal PWM, more than 50 V on the inverter and a minimum squared current command, the V current is sampled while the rotor sits within 30 degrees of the V axis. Under 1 A for 0.4 s out of 0.6 s (0.08 s windows in 2019) sets a Type A fault. GM bulletin PI1433 for the 2014-15 Spark EV names P0B04 with Service Vehicle Soon and reduced propulsion and points to the pump connector not being latched. P0B01 and P0B07 are phases U and W, P0B05 the high side, P0B03 the general V code.

causes_en: Phase V lead shorted to another phase or to ground
Pump seized or contaminated, motor draws excess current
Pump restart logic in the inverter software causing overcurrent
Shorted turns in phase V of the pump motor
P0B05.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current High
P0B05.desc: P0B05 flags overcurrent in phase V of the electric auxiliary transmission fluid pump motor. No manufacturer publicly documents this specific code. GM monitors the same physical fault without naming the phase: P0C28 trips when any of U, V or W exceeds 35 A for about 10 ms within a 62 ms window, and a 2018 Cadillac CT6 plug-in service update shows how a faulty pump restart routine alone can push the current over that limit. Likely triggers for a V-specific high code are a short in the V lead, shorted turns, a seized or contaminated pump, or a restart against a stalled rotor. The Hitachi patent on sub-oil pump drives shows the phase currents come from a shared sensor. Auto-stop is usually blocked. P0B04 is the low side, P0B02 and P0B08 phases U and W.

causes_en: Poor contact in the phase W lead or pump connector
Current sensing in the pump inverter faulty
Phase W power stage in the pump control module faulty
Winding fault in phase W of the pump motor
P0B06.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current
P0B06.desc: P0B06 is the general current fault for phase W of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump motor. No manufacturer publishes a monitor description for this exact code. GM covers phase W in its Volt, ELR and CT6 calibrations with the low-side code P0B07 and treats overcurrent on any phase as P0C28. CARB requires hybrid and transmission components whose failure affects emissions or other monitors to be checked for circuit faults and rationality, which is why manufacturers can use the general code for implausible readings. The Hitachi sub-oil pump patent describes a sinusoidal drive whose W current is calculated from a single bus shunt, so wiring, sensing and the power stage are all suspects. The pump stops and auto-stop is blocked. P0B07/P0B08 are the low and high variants, P0B00 and P0B03 phases U and V.

causes_en: Pump motor connector not fully seated or latched (Chevrolet Spark EV)
Open circuit in the phase W lead or terminal
Outdated inverter software (Cadillac CT6 plug-in, service update 18199)
Open winding of phase W in the pump motor
P0B07.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current Low
P0B07.desc: P0B07 means phase W of the auxiliary fluid pump motor carries less current than commanded, the typical sign of an open W path. GM uses it on the Volt and later hybrids: below 1 A peak W-axis current for 0.4 s of 0.6 s, with the inverter in normal PWM above 50 V, sets a Type A fault. A GM service update for the 2017-18 Cadillac CT6 plug-in shows the code had been calibrated off; a W phase loss then shut the car down or prevented starting with no code and no MIL, until reprogramming of the drive motor power inverter module enabled P0B07 as Type A. On the 2014-15 Spark EV, bulletin PI1433 ties P0B01, P0B04 or P0B07 to an unlatched pump connector. P0B01 and P0B04 are phases U and V, P0B08 the high side, P0B06 the general W code.

causes_en: Phase W lead shorted to another phase or to ground
Pump binding mechanically, raising motor current
Current sensing in the pump inverter reads too high
Shorted turns in phase W of the pump motor
P0B08.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current High
P0B08.desc: P0B08 is set when the current in phase W of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump motor rises above the permitted limit. No manufacturer documents this exact code in public sources. In GM's 2016 Volt calibration the equivalent protection is P0C28, which fails on any phase above 35 A or on a d-axis current below a temperature-dependent limit, both within milliseconds to protect the IGBTs. A W-specific high code points to a short in the W lead or winding, a binding pump or a sensing error; the Hitachi patent shows the W value may be calculated rather than measured directly. CARB requires such output drivers to be monitored for circuit faults. The pump shuts down, so start-stop and electric driving are restricted. P0B07 is the low side, P0B02 and P0B05 phases U and V.

causes_en: Blown fuse or open relay in the pump supply
Open supply wire or loose terminal at the pump connector
Poor ground connection of the pump motor
Voltage sensing input in the controller faulty
P0B09.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
P0B09.desc: P0B09 concerns the power feed of auxiliary pump A's motor: the controller sees no valid supply voltage, usually because the circuit is open. GM documents it for its 2012-13 eAssist mild hybrids (BAS Plus): the hardware input reports an out-of-range voltage flag on the auxiliary pump circuit, enabled with ignition voltage above 9 V; failing for at least 0.375 s within a 1.2 s sample sets P0B09 as Type B, MIL after two trips. A related GM check, P2797, verifies during auto-stops that the pump draws power and that turbine speed does not flare on restart. A Hitachi patent on a battery-fed sub-oil pump shows the controller inhibits engine auto-stop when pump current behaves abnormally. Typical results: no auto-stop and a lamp. P0B0A/P0B0B are the low and high variants.

causes_en: Corroded terminal or high resistance in the pump feed or ground
Weak 12 V battery or poor charging
DC/DC converter or alternator output too low (hybrid)
Voltage sensing input in the controller faulty
P0B0A.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P0B0A.desc: P0B0A means the supply voltage measured at the motor of auxiliary pump A is lower than expected while the pump should be running. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's eAssist tables only cover the open-circuit case as P0B09. A Mikuni patent shows why the controller measures this voltage at all: it combines motor current, supply voltage and speed to judge the hydraulic load, so a sagging supply also falsifies pump diagnosis. Causes are high resistance in the feed or ground, a weak 12 V battery, a failing DC/DC converter or a voltage drop when the pump starts. CARB requires circuit checks on such outputs. The pump runs slowly or not at all and start-stop is usually inhibited. P0B09 covers an open circuit, P0B0B a supply that is too high, P0562 low system voltage in general.

causes_en: CVT fluid entering the pump motor via a leaking relief valve O-ring (Subaru XV Crosstrek Hybrid)
Supply circuit shorted to a higher voltage source
Oil pump inverter or its voltage sensing faulty
P0B0B.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit High
P0B0B.desc: P0B0B reports a supply voltage at the motor of auxiliary pump A that is above the expected range. Subaru documents it on the 2014-15 XV Crosstrek Hybrid (bulletin 16-94-15R), together with P172A: a leaking O-ring at the electric oil pump relief valve can let CVT fluid into the pump motor. The check removes the three U, V and W cables at the oil pump inverter and reads AC voltage across them with the engine held at 1800 rpm in Park; 0.5 V or more means the drive motor and case assembly with the damaged seal must be replaced, less means the cause lies elsewhere. Subaru adds that P0C79, drive motor inverter voltage too high, appears only together with these codes and does not mean the inverter is faulty. P0B09 and P0B0A are the open and low variants.

causes_en: Internal leak at the parking pawl locking piston (Jeep Avenger/Compass hybrid DCT)
Worn seal or valve leaking inside the hydraulic circuit
External leak and low transmission fluid level
Internal wear of the auxiliary pump
P0B0C.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Hydraulic Leakage
P0B0C.desc: P0B0C says the circuit fed by auxiliary pump A loses pressure through a leak, so the pump cannot hold the demanded pressure. Stellantis documents it as P0B0C 7A for the 2023-26 Jeep Avenger and 2026 Compass with hybrid dual-clutch transmission outside the US (TSB 21-061-26): an internal leak at the parking pawl locking piston causes jerking and power loss and may stop the engine from restarting after a stop; with P07E4 or P07E6 present and more than 5 km on the clock, the piston or the transmission is replaced. How a controller can see a leak shows a Nidec patent: after a speed change the pump current keeps falling instead of recovering, and the pump is stopped. P0B0B and P0B09 cover the supply, P2797 a pump that does not deliver.

causes_en: Electric pump with integrated control electronics failed (Jeep 4xe 8P75PH)
Processor or memory fault inside the pump control module
Supply voltage dips or poor ground at the module
P0B0D.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Control Module
P0B0D.desc: P0B0D is an internal fault of the module that drives the auxiliary pump motor. GM documents it for the auxiliary transmission pump controller (ATPC) in its 2011 and 2014 hybrid tables and for the 2016 Cadillac ELR: it checks processor integrity, such as SPI hardware faults or a wrong seed and key between processors, with more than 9.5 V supply; 28 failures out of 32 samples in a 6.25 ms loop, detected within about 200 ms, set a Type A fault. Stellantis lists P0B0D-00 on the 2021-25 Jeep Wrangler 4xe and 2022-25 Grand Cherokee 4xe with the 8P75PH plug-in transmission (TSB 21-038-25, revised 21-041-26): MIL and limp mode, sometimes with U0287; the fix is a new in-pan electric pump. U0287 is lost communication with the pump module, P0C23 to P0C25 its circuit.

causes_en: Signal or ground wire of channel B damaged or connector loose
Current sensor or junction block with integrated sensor defective
Sensor supply voltage faulty
Battery ECU input defective
P0B0E.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit
P0B0E.desc: Many packs measure current with two channels or two sensors so the controller can cross-check them; sensor B is the second channel next to sensor A (P0ABF to P0AC3). P0B0E is its general circuit code. Toyota uses it as the base of internal codes on the 2020-25 RAV4 Hybrid: the sensor sends a voltage rising with current on channel IB0 (sensor A) and an inverse one on IB1 (sensor B). P0B0E11 (IB1 too low) and P0B0E15 (IB1 too high or open) are reported to a generic scan tool as P0B10 and P0B11, one trip, MIL on. GM monitors its fine-range channel B with P0B10, P0B11 and the A/B correlation P0B13. CARB requires circuit monitoring. State of charge then becomes uncertain.

causes_en: Current sensor B offset drift or ageing
Ground offset or high resistance in the sensor wiring
Sensor displaced on the busbar or magnetic interference
P0B0F.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0B0F.desc: P0B0F flags a current sensor B signal that is electrically in range but implausible, for example an offset at zero current or a value that does not match the other measurement. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM handles comparable faults differently: on its dual-range sensor, the 2019 table P0B13 compares sensors A and B and fails when they differ by more than 10 A while both read between -20 and 20 A, 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms, Type A; offset errors of sensor A are P0AC0. CARB requires rationality checks for hybrid battery inputs. A drifting current reading corrupts the state-of-charge calculation, so the controller tends to narrow the usable battery window.

causes_en: Sensor B signal line shorted to ground
5 V supply of the current sensor missing
Current sensor or junction block with integrated sensor defective
P0B10.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Low
P0B10.desc: P0B10 means the output of current sensor B lies below its valid range. GM uses a dual-range Hall sensor whose channel B covers small currents with high resolution: the 2019 battery energy control module table sets P0B10 when this fine current reads below -24 A (ADC count under 82) for 1.6 s within a 2 s window, Type A, one trip; the 2011 Volt table uses -23 A for 175 ms within 250 ms, one trip. Toyota reports P0B10 for the 2020-25 RAV4 Hybrid when the inverse channel IB1 voltage is excessively low (internal code P0B0E11), one trip, MIL on immediately. A short to ground or a lost sensor supply is typical. The high-side code is P0B11.

causes_en: Open signal or ground wire of sensor B
Signal line shorted to the sensor supply or 12 V
Current sensor or junction block with integrated sensor defective
P0B11.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit High
P0B11.desc: P0B11 is set when current sensor B delivers a signal above its valid range. In GM's dual-range design, channel B is the fine channel for small currents: the 2019 battery energy control module table fails it above +24 A (ADC count over 4013) for 1.6 s within a 2 s window, Type A, one trip, and the 2011 Volt table above +23 A for 175 ms within 250 ms, one trip. Toyota maps its internal code P0B0E15, excessively high or open IB1 channel voltage, to P0B11 on the 2020-25 RAV4 Hybrid, with one-trip logic and immediate MIL. An open ground, a signal shorted to the supply or a failed sensor are typical. The low-side code is P0B10, the sensor A equivalent P0AC2.

causes_en: Loose connector or poor terminal contact at the current sensor
Chafed signal or ground wire
Electrical noise on the sensor ground
P0B12.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B12.desc: P0B12 covers a current sensor B signal that jumps or drops out in a way real current cannot, typically from a loose connector, a chafed signal wire or noise on the sensor ground. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM monitors its sensor B channel with the range limits P0B10 and P0B11 and compares it with sensor A through P0B13, which fails above a 10 A difference in 400 of 500 samples, Type A; an erratic channel often shows up there first. CARB requires circuit and rationality monitoring for hybrid battery inputs. Because the fault comes and goes, the code may be the only trace, but during dropouts the controller can still cut battery power or light a warning.

causes_en: Battery controller software fault, fixed by update (Audi, GM)
Disturbance from an external charging station during charging
Offset drift of one of the two current channels
Internal communication fault between switching unit and current sensor
P0B13.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A/B Correlation
P0B13.desc: P0B13 compares the two pack current readings, sensor A and sensor B, and sets when they disagree. On the Chevrolet Volt GM pairs a coarse and a fine channel: the code fails when they differ by more than 10 A while both read between -20 and 20 A, for example 10 s within a 12.5 s window (2016) or 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms (2019), Type A, one trip. Bulletins show P0B13 on the GM Lyriq, Hummer EV and BrightDrop Zevo after suspect public chargers, and on the Audi Q5 PHEV and e-tron GT, where software of the battery controller caused it. Single-sensor faults use P0ABF to P0AC3 and P0B0E to P0B12. The driver sees a high-voltage warning and reduced power.

causes_en: Voltage sense lead or its fuse open inside the pack
Sense connector at the battery controller loose or corroded
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B14.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit
P0B14.desc: SAE J2012 reserves up to four pack voltage measurements, A to D; voltage sense B is the second one. P0B14 is its general circuit code: the battery controller sees an electrical fault on this input, typically an open or implausible raw signal. Which tap a manufacturer calls B is not standardised. No manufacturer documents P0B14 publicly. For the comparable channel A GM checks pack-side voltage against fixed limits and against the sum of cell voltages (P0ABB to P0ABD). CARB requires battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems to be monitored like any input component. Range, low, high and erratic faults have their own codes, P0B15 to P0B18. The system usually limits or blocks high-voltage operation.

causes_en: Drift or calibration error of measurement channel B
Faulty cell voltage acquisition distorts the reference sum
Increased contact resistance at sense terminals
Battery controller software needs an update
P0B15.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit Range/Performance
P0B15.desc: P0B15 marks pack voltage measurement B as electrically valid but implausible: the value lies within the sensor range yet does not match a reference, typically the sum of the cell voltages or another pack measurement. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM shows the principle on channel A: P0ABB fails when pack voltage and summed cell voltages differ by more than 12 V, 20 of 25 samples at 25 ms, Type A, one trip. CARB demands rationality checks for battery voltage sensors of the hybrid storage system. Hard circuit faults of channel B are P0B14, P0B16 and P0B17. Because state of charge and cell protection rely on this value, the controller restricts power or charging.

causes_en: Sense lead of channel B shorted to ground
Fuse or resistor in the sense path open
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B16.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit Low
P0B16.desc: P0B16 sets when pack voltage measurement B reports a value below its plausible minimum, usually an electrical cause such as a sense lead shorted to ground or an open input that pulls the reading down. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM uses the same logic on channel A: on its BECM P0ABC sets when the pack-side voltage drops below 24 V for 1.6 s within a 2 s window, Type A, one trip. CARB requires out-of-range monitoring of battery voltage sensors in hybrid storage systems. The opposite fault is P0B17, implausible but in-range values are P0B15. Without a trustworthy pack voltage the controller may refuse to close the contactors or limit operation.

causes_en: BMS measurement inaccuracy, fixed by software update (Mercedes eSprinter)
Sense lead of channel B shorted to a higher potential
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B17.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit High
P0B17.desc: P0B17 means pack voltage measurement B reads above its plausible maximum. Mercedes-Benz uses this exact code on the eSprinter 907: inaccurate BMS measurements can store P0B171C, voltage sensor B in the high-voltage battery module shorted to positive with the value out of range, together with P0ABD00 for sensor A. The result is an intermittent no-start or no Ready status, fixed by a BMS software update. GM checks channel A against 479 V on its BECM (P0ABD, Type A). CARB requires out-of-range monitoring of battery voltage sensors. The low counterpart is P0B16. A real overvoltage is not implied; the measurement itself is suspect.

causes_en: Loose or corroded sense connector
Sense lead chafed, intermittent contact
Battery controller software misinterprets transients
P0B18.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B18.desc: P0B18 reports that pack voltage measurement B jumps or drops out briefly instead of failing steadily. The controller detects implausibly fast changes or short signal losses that disappear again, so the fault often shows up as a history code. No manufacturer documents P0B18 publicly; GM, for example, monitors only channel A in its published tables (P0ABB to P0ABD). CARB requires battery voltage sensors of the hybrid storage system to be monitored for circuit faults. Steady faults of channel B use P0B14 to P0B17. Typical triggers are loose sense connectors or chafed leads that react to vibration and temperature, so symptoms come and go.

causes_en: Voltage sense lead C or its fuse open
Sense connector loose or corroded
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B19.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense C Circuit
P0B19.desc: Voltage sense C is the third of up to four pack voltage measurements defined in SAE J2012. P0B19 is its general circuit code and sets when the battery controller finds this input electrically unusable, for instance open or without a valid raw value. Which measuring point a manufacturer assigns to C is its own choice. No manufacturer documents P0B19 publicly. GM shows the principle for channel A, checking pack-side voltage against limits and against the summed cell voltages (P0ABB to P0ABD). CARB requires battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems to be monitored as input components. The detailed fault types of channel C are P0B1A to P0B1D. High-voltage operation is usually limited.

causes_en: Drift or calibration error of measurement channel C
Cell voltage acquisition faulty, reference sum wrong
Increased resistance at sense terminals
Battery controller software needs an update
P0B1A.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense C Circuit Range/Performance
P0B1A.desc: P0B1A flags pack voltage measurement C as in range but not believable. The controller compares it with a reference, usually the sum of the cell voltages or another pack voltage reading, and sets the code when the difference stays too large. No manufacturer documents P0B1A publicly. As an analogue, GM fails P0ABB on channel A once pack voltage and summed cell voltages differ by more than 12 V for 20 of 25 samples, Type A. CARB requires rationality monitoring for battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems. Electrical faults of channel C are P0B19, P0B1B and P0B1C. A distorted pack voltage undermines state of charge and cell protection, so power or charging is restricted.

causes_en: Sense lead of channel C shorted to ground
Fuse or resistor in the sense path open
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B1B.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense C Circuit Low
P0B1B.desc: P0B1B sets when pack voltage measurement C delivers a reading below its plausible lower limit. Typical electrical causes are a sense lead shorted to ground, an open fuse or resistor in the sense path, or a defective controller input. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM applies the same idea to channel A, where P0ABC sets below 24 V pack-side voltage for 1.6 s in a 2 s window, Type A. CARB calls for out-of-range monitoring of battery voltage sensors. The high counterpart is P0B1C and the plausibility code P0B1A. A pack voltage reading that is too low can prevent precharge and contactor closing, so the vehicle may not become ready to drive.

causes_en: Sense lead of channel C shorted to a higher potential
Evaluation error in battery controller software
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B1C.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense C Circuit High
P0B1C.desc: P0B1C reports that pack voltage measurement C reads above its plausible upper limit. Usually the measurement path is at fault, for example a sense lead shorted to a higher potential, a defective controller input or a software error in the evaluation, rather than a real overvoltage of the pack. No manufacturer documents P0B1C publicly. GM checks channel A against a 479 V limit on its BECM (P0ABD, Type A, 1.6 s in 2 s), and Mercedes-Benz logs the matching channel B fault P0B17 on the eSprinter. CARB requires out-of-range monitoring of battery voltage sensors. The low counterpart is P0B1B. The controller typically blocks or limits high-voltage operation.

causes_en: Loose or corroded sense connector or terminal
Chafed sense lead with intermittent contact
Controller software misinterprets transients
P0B1D.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B1D.desc: P0B1D stands for an unsteady pack voltage measurement C: the signal jumps, drops out for moments or changes faster than a real battery voltage can. Because the fault often clears itself, it is frequently found only as a stored code. No manufacturer documents P0B1D publicly; GM's published tables cover only channel A of this measurement (P0ABB to P0ABD). CARB requires circuit monitoring of battery voltage sensors in hybrid storage systems. Permanent faults of channel C are P0B19 to P0B1C, the same fault type on channels B and D is P0B18 and P0B22. Loose terminals, vibration and temperature changes are the usual suspects, so warnings tend to come and go.

causes_en: Voltage sense lead D or its fuse open
Sense connector loose or corroded
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B1E.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense D Circuit
P0B1E.desc: Voltage sense D is the fourth and last pack voltage measurement in the SAE J2012 scheme. P0B1E is its general circuit code: the battery controller treats this input as electrically faulty, for example open or without a usable raw signal. The assignment of D to a specific measuring point is manufacturer-specific. No manufacturer documents P0B1E publicly. GM illustrates the monitoring on channel A, comparing pack-side voltage with limits and with the summed cell voltages (P0ABB to P0ABD). CARB requires battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems to be monitored like other inputs. Detailed fault types of channel D are P0B1F to P0B22. High-voltage operation is usually restricted.

causes_en: Drift or calibration error of measurement channel D
Cell voltage acquisition faulty, reference sum wrong
Increased resistance at sense terminals
Battery controller software needs an update
P0B1F.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense D Circuit Range/Performance
P0B1F.desc: P0B1F says pack voltage measurement D is electrically present but disagrees with what the controller expects, typically the sum of cell voltages or a parallel pack measurement. It is a plausibility fault, not an open or shorted circuit. No manufacturer documents P0B1F publicly. GM's analogous channel A check, P0ABB, fails at a deviation above 12 V from the summed cell voltages for 20 of 25 samples at 25 ms, Type A, one trip. CARB requires rationality checks for battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems. Circuit faults of channel D use P0B1E, P0B20 and P0B21. With a doubtful pack voltage the controller narrows the usable battery window and limits power.

causes_en: Sense lead of channel D shorted to ground
Fuse or resistor in the sense path open
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B20.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense D Circuit Low
P0B20.desc: P0B20 sets when pack voltage measurement D falls below its plausible minimum. The cause is usually electrical: a sense lead shorted to ground, an interrupted fuse or resistor in the measurement path, or a damaged controller input. No manufacturer documents P0B20 publicly. GM shows the analogous check on channel A, where its BECM sets P0ABC once pack-side voltage stays under 24 V for 1.6 s within 2 s, Type A, one trip. CARB requires out-of-range monitoring of battery voltage sensors in hybrid storage systems. The high counterpart is P0B21, plausibility faults are P0B1F. An implausibly low reading can block precharge, so the vehicle may not become ready.

causes_en: Sense lead of channel D shorted to a higher potential
Evaluation error in battery controller software
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
P0B21.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense D Circuit High
P0B21.desc: P0B21 means pack voltage measurement D reports more than its plausible maximum. As with the other high codes, the measurement path is the main suspect, for example a sense lead shorted to a higher potential, a faulty input stage or an evaluation error in software, not an actual overcharged pack. No manufacturer documents P0B21 publicly. For channel A GM's BECM sets P0ABD above 479 V for 1.6 s in 2 s, Type A, and Mercedes-Benz records the channel B variant P0B17 on the eSprinter. CARB requires out-of-range monitoring of battery voltage sensors. The low counterpart is P0B20. High-voltage operation is usually blocked or limited until the fault is cleared.

causes_en: Loose or corroded sense connector or terminal
Chafed sense lead with intermittent contact
Controller software misinterprets transients
P0B22.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B22.desc: P0B22 completes the voltage sense D series and reports an intermittent or erratic pack voltage measurement D: the reading jumps, drops out briefly or changes implausibly fast, then recovers. Current code lists title it this way; the older label Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit does not belong to this number. No manufacturer documents P0B22 publicly; GM's published tables only cover channel A (P0ABB to P0ABD). CARB requires circuit monitoring of battery voltage sensors in hybrid storage systems. Steady faults of channel D are P0B1E to P0B21, the same fault type on channels B and C is P0B18 and P0B1D. Loose terminals or chafed sense leads are typical, so the warning comes and goes.

mfr.Audi: Battery contactor assembly failure, Battery Energy Control Module (BECM) failure

causes_en: Weak or failing cells or module in battery A
Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of battery A
Battery controller software or internal measurement fault
P0B23.desc: P0B23 is the general fault for the voltage of hybrid/EV battery A, the first of up to four sub-batteries or energy stores (A to D) that the battery controller evaluates separately; which physical unit carries the letter is up to the manufacturer. The code says that the measured voltage of this unit no longer fits the expected value, without the finer split into unstable (P0B24), low (P0B25) or high (P0B26). No manufacturer documents P0B23 publicly; Bentley and Stellantis bulletins only show the specific siblings. GM watches the comparable whole-pack voltage with P0ABB to P0ABD. CARB requires the voltage sensors and cells of the hybrid storage to be monitored, with fault codes that point to the smallest replaceable unit.

causes_en: Battery controller software (Jeep 4xe BPCM/HCP, Ford BECM updates)
Loose busbar, terminal or sense contact in battery A
Cell with rising internal resistance in battery A
P0B24.desc: P0B24 reports that the voltage of hybrid/EV battery A is unstable: it swings or jumps more than the battery controller accepts instead of staying steadily too low or too high (P0B25, P0B26). Stellantis lists P0B24-00 with MIL on the Jeep Wrangler 4xe and Grand Cherokee 4xe, together with pack voltage variation, cell balancing and state-of-health codes; the cure is new software for the battery pack control module or, on the 2025 Wrangler, for the hybrid control processor. Some of these Jeeps would not start or reported low 12 V batteries. Ford names P0B24 in the BECM of the 2025 Mustang Mach-E Extended Range, shown with the wrench lamp and fixed by reprogramming. Hardware causes are loose busbar or sense contacts.

mfr.Audi: Battery Energy Control Module (BECM) failure, High voltage battery assembly failure, Wiring issue

causes_en: Internal fault of the energy store, e.g. Bentley 48 V super capacitor
Aged or unbalanced cells pulling the unit voltage down
Deep discharge after long standstill
Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads
P0B25.desc: P0B25 sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery A drops below the window the controller expects. Bentley uses it in two different systems. In the 48 V Bentley Dynamic Ride anti-roll system it is stored in address 0021 (battery energy control module 2); if the highest and lowest cell readings differ by 0.5 V or more, an internal fault of the super capacitor is assumed and it is replaced. On the Bentayga and Flying Spur Hybrid the code appears in 008C, the high-voltage battery manager, with MIL and red battery warning, and the workshop must involve Bentley product support. GM checks pack undervoltage analogously with P0ABC (below 24 V). Unstable and high readings are P0B24 and P0B26. The driver loses roll control or battery power.

causes_en: Failing energy store, e.g. Bentley 48 V super capacitor
Cell group charged too high, balancing not effective
Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads
P0B26.desc: P0B26 means the voltage of hybrid/EV battery A is above the permitted value. Bentley documents it in the 48 V Dynamic Ride system of the Continental GT and Flying Spur, stored in address 0021 with symptom code 28672; the prescribed repair is replacing the super capacitor. On the Bentayga it appeared with P16C5, traced to a broken solder joint inside the capacitor; on the Bentayga and Flying Spur Hybrid it shows up in the high-voltage battery manager 008C beside P0B25, with MIL and red HV warning. GM monitors the analogous pack overvoltage with P0ABD (above 479 V, Type A). Typical reasons are a failing energy store, an overcharged cell group or a measuring fault. Low and unstable readings are P0B25 and P0B24. Charging and recuperation are limited.

mfr.Audi: Battery Energy Control Module (BECM) failure, High voltage battery assembly failure, Wiring issue

causes_en: Weak or failing cells or module in battery B
Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of battery B
Battery controller software or internal measurement fault
P0B27.desc: P0B27 is the general voltage fault of hybrid/EV battery B, the second separately monitored sub-battery or energy store. It covers a voltage that does not match expectation without saying whether it is unstable (P0B28), too low (P0B29) or too high (P0B2A). That battery B exists in production systems is shown by Stellantis, whose Jeep Wrangler 4xe bulletin lists P0B28; P0B27 itself is not documented publicly by any manufacturer. GM's analogous monitors of the whole pack are P0ABB to P0ABD, for example a pack reading more than 12 V away from the sum of the cells. CARB requires the voltage sensors and cells of hybrid storage systems to be monitored. The driver gets a hybrid warning and reduced battery power.

causes_en: Battery pack control module software (Jeep 4xe update)
Loose busbar, terminal or sense contact in battery B
Cell with rising internal resistance in battery B
P0B28.desc: P0B28 flags an unstable voltage of hybrid/EV battery B: the reading fluctuates beyond what the battery controller tolerates. Stellantis documents it with P0B28-00 on the Jeep Wrangler 4xe: the MIL is on, and the bulletin warns that after 49 days with this MIL lit the vehicle is no longer allowed to start. The remedy is new software for the battery pack control module, issued first as a rapid service update and later as a regular bulletin; recall 95B must be completed first. The same bulletin lists P0B24 for battery A and codes for voltage variation and cell balancing. Steady low or high voltages of battery B are P0B29 and P0B2A. Besides software, loose busbar or sense contacts can produce the same pattern.

mfr.Audi: Battery Energy Control Module (BECM) failure, High voltage battery assembly failure, Wiring issue

causes_en: Aged cells with lost capacity in battery B
Deep discharge or self-discharge after standstill
Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads
P0B29.desc: P0B29 sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery B stays below the range the controller expects for the present state of charge and load. It is the low counterpart to P0B2A; fluctuating readings belong to P0B28 and the general fault to P0B27. No manufacturer publishes a definition of P0B29; Jeep 4xe bulletins confirm the use of a separately monitored battery B only through P0B28. GM handles the analogous whole-pack undervoltage with P0ABC (pack voltage below 24 V). CARB requires battery voltage sensors and cells to be monitored and the fault to be narrowed to the smallest replaceable unit. Weak or deeply discharged cells in that unit are the usual reason, so the controller cuts discharge power and may block driving in EV mode.

causes_en: Cell group in battery B charged too high, balancing ineffective
Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads
Battery controller software fault
P0B2A.desc: P0B2A is stored when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery B rises above its permitted upper limit. It mirrors P0B29 (too low), while P0B28 covers fluctuation and P0B27 the general fault. No manufacturer explains P0B2A publicly; the closest documented case is Bentley's P0B26 for battery A, where a failing 48 V super capacitor reads too high. GM's analogous whole-pack overvoltage monitor is P0ABD (above 479 V, Type A). CARB demands monitoring of battery voltage sensors and cells in hybrid storage systems. Likely causes are a cell group charged too high because balancing fails, or a measuring fault. To protect the cells the controller restricts charging and recuperation and may open the contactors.

causes_en: Weak or failing cells or module in battery C
Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of battery C
Battery controller software or internal measurement fault
P0B2B.desc: P0B2B is the general voltage fault of hybrid/EV battery C, the third sub-battery or energy store that a controller can monitor on its own. It signals an implausible voltage of this unit without the detail given by P0B2C (unstable), P0B2D (low) or P0B2E (high). Which modules form battery C, and whether a vehicle has a third unit at all, depends on the manufacturer; no manufacturer documents P0B2B publicly. As a reference GM monitors the voltage of the whole pack with P0ABB to P0ABD, among them a plausibility check against the cell sum. CARB requires voltage sensors and cells of hybrid storage to be monitored and faults to point to the replaceable unit. Expect a hybrid warning and limited battery power.

causes_en: Loose busbar, terminal or sense contact in battery C
Battery controller software (pattern known from P0B24/P0B28)
Cell with rising internal resistance in battery C
P0B2C.desc: P0B2C indicates that the voltage of hybrid/EV battery C is unstable, meaning it changes faster or further than plausible for the current load, while a steady deviation would set P0B2D or P0B2E. No manufacturer documents P0B2C publicly. The pattern is known from the A and B siblings: on the Jeep Wrangler 4xe and Grand Cherokee 4xe, P0B24 and P0B28 were cured with battery controller software, and Ford fixed P0B24 on the Mach-E the same way. CARB requires the voltage sensors of the hybrid storage to be monitored for circuit and rationality faults. Physically, a loose busbar screw, a corroded sense terminal or a cell with high internal resistance can make the voltage of unit C jump, so the warning often comes and goes.

causes_en: Aged cells with lost capacity in battery C
Deep discharge or self-discharge after standstill
Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads
P0B2D.desc: P0B2D means the voltage of hybrid/EV battery C is too low compared with what the controller expects. High readings of the same unit are P0B2E, fluctuating ones P0B2C. No manufacturer documents P0B2D publicly; the nearest published case is Bentley's P0B25 for battery A, where a 0.5 V spread between highest and lowest cell points to a defective energy store. GM's corresponding whole-pack check is P0ABC (pack below 24 V). CARB requires that cells and voltage sensors of hybrid storage are monitored and that faults identify the smallest replaceable unit. A worn or deeply discharged module in unit C is the most likely reason. The controller lowers discharge power, so acceleration in electric mode suffers and the engine may run more often.

causes_en: Cell group in battery C charged too high, balancing ineffective
Drifting voltage measurement channel or sense lead fault
Battery controller software fault
P0B2E.desc: P0B2E is set when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery C exceeds its upper limit. It pairs with P0B2D for undervoltage; P0B2C covers unstable readings and P0B2B the general fault. No manufacturer publishes a description of P0B2E. GM's comparable monitor for the complete pack is P0ABD, which fails above 479 V and is Type A, so the MIL comes on at once. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid battery voltage sensors and cells and dedicated codes for the replaceable unit. An overvoltage reading usually comes from a cell group that ended up overcharged because balancing failed, or from a drifting measurement channel. The controller then blocks or reduces charging and regenerative braking; plugging in may be refused.

causes_en: Weak or failing cells or module in battery D
Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of battery D
Battery controller software or internal measurement fault
P0B2F.desc: P0B2F is the general voltage fault of hybrid/EV battery D, the fourth and last sub-battery in this code family. The controller reports with it that the voltage of unit D is implausible, without specifying unstable (P0B30), low (P0B31) or high (P0B32). Only packs that the manufacturer splits into four separately monitored units can set it, and no manufacturer documents P0B2F publicly. For orientation, GM checks the whole pack with P0ABB to P0ABD, including a comparison of the pack voltage with the sum of all cells. CARB requires voltage sensors and cells of hybrid storage systems to be monitored, with codes pointing to the smallest replaceable unit. The driver sees a hybrid or battery warning and reduced power.

causes_en: Loose busbar, terminal or sense contact in battery D
Battery controller software (pattern known from P0B24/P0B28)
Cell with rising internal resistance in battery D
P0B30.desc: P0B30 reports an unstable voltage of hybrid/EV battery D: the measured value fluctuates beyond the limit the controller allows. It differs from P0B31 and P0B32, which stand for a lasting low or high voltage, and from the general fault P0B2F. No manufacturer documents P0B30 publicly. The sibling codes for batteries A and B show the typical background: Stellantis and Ford corrected P0B24 and P0B28 by updating the battery controller software, and Jeep even blocks starting after 49 days with P0B28. CARB requires the hybrid storage voltage sensors to be monitored. Apart from software, poor contact at busbars or sense terminals and cells with high internal resistance make the reading of unit D jump.

mfr.Audi: Battery Energy Control Module (BECM) failure, High voltage battery assembly failure, Wiring issue

causes_en: Aged cells with lost capacity in battery D
Deep discharge or self-discharge after standstill
Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads
P0B31.desc: P0B31 is stored when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery D stays below the expected range. High voltage of the same unit sets P0B32, fluctuation P0B30 and an unspecified deviation P0B2F. No manufacturer publishes a definition of P0B31; Bentley's P0B25 for battery A is the closest documented example, with the energy store replaced once the cell spread reaches 0.5 V. GM uses P0ABC for an undervoltage of the whole pack (below 24 V). CARB asks for monitoring of cells and voltage sensors in hybrid storage and for fault codes that single out the replaceable unit. Typical is a module in unit D that has aged faster or self-discharged during standstill. Discharge power and electric range drop, and the controller may stop electric driving.

causes_en: Cell group in battery D charged too high, balancing ineffective
Defective module in battery D
Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads
P0B32.desc: P0B32 sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery D goes above its permitted maximum. It is the high counterpart of P0B31; P0B30 covers unstable readings and P0B2F the general fault. No manufacturer documents P0B32 publicly; Bentley's P0B26 for battery A, cured by replacing the 48 V super capacitor, shows the same fault type on another unit. GM's analogous whole-pack monitor is P0ABD (above 479 V, Type A, MIL at once). CARB requires hybrid storage voltage sensors and cells to be monitored and codes to identify the replaceable unit. Causes are an overcharged cell group when balancing fails, a defective module or a measuring error. Charging and recuperation are cut back, and the contactors may open to protect the pack.

causes_en: Service disconnect plug not fully seated or locked after service
Chafed, open or shorted detection loop wiring between plug base and battery controller
Corroded or spread terminals in the plug or its base
Battery controller input fault
P0B33.desc: The high-voltage service disconnect is the removable plug, usually fused, that splits the traction battery for safe servicing. A low-voltage detection loop runs through the plug, and the battery controller reads it to know whether the plug is seated; patents from Ford and Lear describe this loop, which opens before the main contacts part. P0B33 is the general circuit code for this detection input. No manufacturer documents P0B33 publicly. CARB requires such hybrid components to be monitored like any input. Performance, low, high and open have their own codes, P0B34 to P0B37; the separate high-voltage interlock loop uses P0A0A ff. Expect contactors to stay open: no ready mode, no charging.

causes_en: Battery controller software fault (Audi case under investigation)
Loose plug or worn contacts giving an implausible detection state
Increased resistance in the detection loop
Communication fault between battery controller and other modules
P0B34.en: High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit Performance
P0B34.desc: P0B34 covers a plausibility fault of the service disconnect detection: the signal is electrically within limits but does not match what the controller expects, for example a plug reported as removed while the high-voltage bus still shows voltage, or a state that changes without a matching event. Audi lists P0B3400 in the controller at address 008C of the 2025 Q5 e-hybrid, together with U029A00 and U059B00, and asks technicians to log the case in its pending service database; no threshold is published. CARB requires hybrid components to be checked for rationality as input devices. Pure circuit, low, high and open faults are P0B33, P0B35, P0B36 and P0B37. The car may refuse ready mode or charging.

causes_en: Detection loop wire chafed and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the plug base bridging to ground
Coding element in the plug shorted
Battery controller input stage fault
P0B35.en: High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit Low
P0B35.desc: P0B35 sets when the service disconnect detection signal stays below its lower limit. Where the loop is coded with a resistor in the plug, as in a Lear patent, a reading near zero typically points to a short to ground in the loop wiring; the exact meaning depends on how the manufacturer powers the input. Ford traced an intermittent short to ground in the low-voltage interlock wiring as the cause of its open-loop code P0B37 on the C-Max Energi, which shows how chafed harnesses act here. No manufacturer documents P0B35 publicly. CARB treats such signals as monitored hybrid inputs. High, open and performance faults are P0B36, P0B37 and P0B34. The contactors usually stay open.

causes_en: Detection loop wire shorted to a supply voltage
Open loop or missing contact read as high signal
Wrong or damaged service disconnect plug without proper coding
Battery controller input stage fault
P0B36.en: High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit High
P0B36.desc: P0B36 sets when the service disconnect detection signal stays above its upper limit. With a pulled-up input this usually means a short to a voltage source or a missing coding element in the plug; on some designs an open loop also reads high, so manufacturers separate it with P0B37 only where they can tell the cases apart. Patents from Ford and Lear show the detection loop as a low-voltage circuit that closes through the plug and is read by a battery or vehicle controller. No manufacturer documents P0B36 publicly. CARB requires such hybrid inputs to be monitored for out-of-range values. Low and performance faults are P0B35 and P0B34. The high-voltage system normally stays switched off.

causes_en: Low-voltage interlock wiring chafed with intermittent short to ground (Ford C-Max)
Service disconnect plug removed, loose or not locked
Open terminal in the plug base or interlock connector
Battery energy control module fault
P0B37.desc: P0B37 means the controller sees the service disconnect as open, either because the plug is really removed or because its detection loop is broken. Ford uses the code in the battery energy control module of the 2013-2016 C-Max Energi: bulletins SSM 46108 and TSB 17-0015 describe intermittent stalls or no crank with a Stop Safely Now message and MIL, stored with U3012 and, in another module, the interlock code P0A0A. The cause was an intermittent short to ground in the low-voltage interlock wiring, found by inspecting the harness for chafing. P0B33 to P0B36 cover circuit, performance, low and high faults. For the driver: the car shuts down or will not start.

causes_en: Pump connector loose, corroded or terminal pushed out
Open control wire between controller and pump
Pump electronics or motor failed open
Driver stage in the controlling module faulty
P0B38.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit/Open
P0B38.desc: Hybrid and electric drives cool the inverter and motor electronics with electric coolant pumps; J2012 numbers them A, B and C. P0B38 sets when the controller detects an open or general fault in the control line of pump B, typically by checking the driver output for missing load current. No manufacturer documents P0B38 publicly. FCA uses a pump B on the Jeep Compass and Renegade 4xe, where bulletins name its performance code P0C74, and Mercedes uses the pump A code P0A05 for an open control circuit of the low-temperature circuit pump on M264 engines. CARB requires output components of inverter thermal management to be monitored. Expect a coolant or hybrid warning and power reduction if electronics overheat.

causes_en: Control wire shorted to ground, often chafed at brackets
Pump electronics pulling the control input low
Coolant or water in the pump connector
Driver stage in the controlling module faulty
P0B39.en: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low
P0B39.desc: P0B39 sets when the control signal of motor electronics coolant pump B is lower than the controller expects, usually a short to ground on the command line or a pump input that pulls the line down. On a low-side switched or PWM line the module sees the voltage stuck low while it commands the pump off. No manufacturer documents P0B39 publicly. Pump B is in service at FCA (Compass and Renegade 4xe, performance code P0C74), and Ford stores the pump A codes P0A06 and P0A07 in the PCM of the 2020 Explorer and Aviator hybrids.
