GM's tables for sense Q, from the 2011 Volt to the 2019 battery controllers, list circuit, range, low and high monitors only, and the Ford Fusion bulletin ends four channels earlier at N. CARB 1968.2 forms the basis: it calls for monitoring of the battery voltage sensors in a hybrid energy storage system and for codes that lead a technician to the faulty part. Physically, an erratic Q reading would point to an unstable connection between tap and measuring chip, such as a cracked crimp, a damaged flexible circuit or a cold solder joint. The next channel, R, starts at P0B90.

causes_en: Loose, corroded or broken tap of sense lead R
Excessive resistance at a splice or busbar joint feeding channel R
Faulty measuring or balancing input on the cell monitoring board
P0B90.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit
P0B90.desc: P0B90 is stored when the battery controller concludes that the tap of sense R, the eighteenth cell channel, is open or too resistive. GM's 2019 battery energy control module runs seven cases for it: neighbouring cells 1.3 V or more apart, a reading under 36 mV while the balancing gate is on, or splice voltages above 0.1 V (0.5 V at a busbar splice). The fault has to be present for 0.8 s within a 1.6 s window and is Type A. The 2016 Volt and ELR use the same cases with a 0.6 s window. Oddly, GM's first-generation Volt tables of 2011 to 2015 contain no P0B90 at all, although they list the circuit codes of S to V. Range, low and high faults of R are P0B91 to P0B93.

causes_en: Measuring channel R reporting a stuck value
Outdated battery controller or hybrid processor software
Block 18 or 19 voltage drifting on two-mode NiMH packs
P0B91.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Range/Performance
P0B91.desc: Here the wiring of sense R is intact, but its value does not behave like a real cell. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain processor demands that cell R moves at least 0.005 V in the same direction whenever the cell average shifts by more than 0.022 V; 35 failures out of 40 samples at 100 ms give a Type A fault. The 2016 Volt allows 7 s of failure in an 8 s window, the ELR 20 of 40 samples at 200 ms. On the 2012 two-mode trucks R is nickel-metal hydride block 18: blocks 18 and 19 are each multiplied by twenty, and if both estimates miss the pack voltage by more than 70 V in 160 of 170 samples, P0B91 is set as Type B. A frozen measuring channel or controller software is the usual suspect.

causes_en: Sense lead R chafed through and touching ground or a lower cell
Failed input for channel R on the cell monitoring board
Cell or block on channel R genuinely collapsed
P0B92.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Low
P0B92.desc: P0B92 stands for an implausibly low reading on sense R. In GM's lithium-ion battery controllers of 2016 and 2019 the limit is 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s inside a 2 s window, Type A; the test is suspended while an open sense line fault is active, so a broken lead appears as P0B90 rather than P0B92. Programmes with a separate battery sensor module (GM 16OBDG02) use under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples. The eAssist mild hybrid applies 1.4 V, 7 of 10 samples, Type B. In the 2012 two-mode trucks R is NiMH block 18, and blocks 18 and 19 must both read under 2 V in 15 of 20 samples (Type B). A short of the sense lead to ground or to a lower cell is the classic cause.

causes_en: Sense lead R in contact with a higher cell potential
Damaged measuring input for channel R
Cell on channel R actually overcharged
P0B93.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit High
P0B93.desc: A reading on sense R above anything a healthy cell could produce sets P0B93. GM's lithium-ion battery controllers of 2016 and 2019 use 4.8 V or more, held 1.4 s within 2 s, as a Type A fault. The 16OBDG02 programme with its own battery sensor module draws the line at 4.90 V, 14 of 18 samples. GM's eAssist mild hybrid already reacts above 4.65 V (7 of 10 samples, Type B). On the 2012 two-mode trucks the channel is nickel-metal hydride block 18, which must exceed 23 V in 15 of 20 samples, Type B. Because a cell this high would be dangerous, an electrical fault is far more likely: a sense lead touching a higher potential, or a damaged measuring input on the monitoring board.

causes_en: Crimp or terminal of lead R opening under vibration
Hairline crack in the flexible circuit carrying channel R
Moisture or contamination in the monitoring board connector
P0B94.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B94.desc: No manufacturer documents P0B94 publicly. The code is reserved for a sense R signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing steadily. GM monitors channel R in six table sets between 2011 and 2019, but every one of those tables stops at the circuit, range, low and high monitors; an intermittent test does not appear. The legal basis is CARB 1968.2, which requires the voltage sensors of a hybrid energy storage system to be monitored like any other input and wants fault codes that point to the smallest replaceable unit. In practice such a fault would come from a connection that opens under vibration or heat, for instance a cracked crimp or a hairline crack in a flexible circuit.

causes_en: High resistance in sense lead S from corrosion or a loose terminal
Sense lead S broken at the cell connector
Defective input of the battery sensor module for channel S
P0B95.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit
P0B95.desc: P0B95 reports that the sense S lead, channel nineteen, no longer connects its cell reliably to the monitoring electronics. GM programmes with a separate battery sensor module (16OBDG02) measure this directly: after each normal reading the balancing gates switch in a test pattern, current flows through the sense wires and the voltage drop is turned into a line resistance. Above 30.00 (the table gives no unit) in 7 of 9 samples at 100 ms, the code sets as Type A. GM's eAssist mild hybrid instead needs lines N and N-1 both under 1.4 V plus a jump of more than 0.5 V in 200 ms, 7 of 10 samples, Type B, and stays quiet while P1B37 is active. The 2019 lithium-ion controller uses its seven cases with 0.8 s in 1.6 s.

causes_en: Measuring channel S frozen or lagging behind the other cells
Battery controller calibration requiring a software update
Block 19 or 20 out of step with the pack on two-mode NiMH batteries
P0B96.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Range/Performance
P0B96.desc: P0B96 is a plausibility code: the voltage of sense S looks electrically valid but fails to track the rest of the pack. GM's eAssist mild hybrid requires cell S to move at least half as much as the other cells once the average changes by more than 0.045 V, judged over 20 of 40 samples at 200 ms, Type B. The 16OBDG02 programme accepts a trend of 0.002 V and sets Type A after 35 of 40 evaluations, while the 2019 hybrid processor wants 0.005 V. On the 2012 two-mode trucks S is block 19, and the check scales blocks 19 and 20 by twenty and compares them with the pack voltage, with more than 70 V deviation in 160 of 170 samples leading to Type B. Circuit, low and high faults of S are excluded first.

causes_en: Sense lead S shorted to ground or to the next lower cell
Defective channel S input on the monitoring board
Cell or NiMH block on channel S actually discharged
P0B97.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Low
P0B97.desc: With P0B97 the controller sees sense S pulled close to zero. In the 2012 two-mode trucks, where S is the nickel-metal hydride block 19, the battery pack control module only sets it when block 19 and block 20 are both below 2 V in 15 of 20 samples, Type B, with the 12 V system between 9 and 18 V. GM's lithium-ion packs work cell by cell: 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s in 2 s on the 2016 Volt and the 2019 controller, Type A, and under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples in the 16OBDG02 programme. The eAssist mild hybrid sets it below 1.4 V, 7 of 10 samples, Type B. An open sense line fault takes priority, so P0B97 points more to a short than to a broken lead.

causes_en: Sense lead S shorted to a higher cell or busbar
Measuring chip reading channel S incorrectly
Real overvoltage of the cell or block on channel S
P0B98.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit High
P0B98.desc: P0B98 marks a sense S value that is too high to be a cell voltage. The thresholds vary with the battery chemistry and controller: GM's 2016 Volt and 2019 battery controllers flag 4.8 V or more after 1.4 s in 2 s (Type A), the 16OBDG02 programme 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples (Type A), and the eAssist mild hybrid more than 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples with the 12 V supply above 8.8 V (Type B). On the 2012 two-mode trucks S is NiMH block 19 and its limit is 23 V, 15 of 20 samples, Type B. Like the low test, the high test waits until open sense line faults are ruled out. The fix is usually wiring or the monitoring board; a truly overcharged cell is rare but must be excluded.

causes_en: Fretting corrosion on the terminal of sense lead S
Cracked solder joint for channel S on the monitoring board
Harness chafing that only shorts under movement
P0B99.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B99.desc: P0B99 is the erratic variant within the sense S group. A public manufacturer description does not exist. GM's tables cover channel S from the 2011 Volt via the 2012 two-mode trucks and eAssist to the 2019 controllers, yet only with circuit, range, low and high codes (P0B95 to P0B98). CARB 1968.2 obliges manufacturers to monitor battery voltage sensors of a hybrid storage system for circuit and rationality faults and to separate the fault codes by replaceable unit, which is why J2012 reserves this slot. Should a vehicle set it, the technician would look for a sense S connection that works most of the time but breaks briefly, typically a fretting terminal or a cracked solder joint on the board.

causes_en: Open sense lead T at the cell tab or connector
Poor busbar or splice joint in the channel T path
Monitoring board input for channel T failed
P0B9A.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit
P0B9A.desc: P0B9A is the open-circuit code for sense T, the twentieth cell channel. GM uses it only on lithium-ion packs. The 2011 Volt compares adjacent cells for a difference above 1 V and checks the busbar cap voltage against 0.7 V; the 2016 Volt and ELR raise the adjacent-cell limit to 1.3 V, add a balancing-gate test below 36 mV and decide within 0.6 s, and the 2019 controller keeps those values but stretches the window to 0.8 s of 1.6 s, Type A in both cases. The 2012 two-mode trucks also have a channel T, their last nickel-metal hydride block 20, yet their tables carry range, low and high codes for it and no circuit code. A genuinely open lead usually means opening the high-voltage pack.

causes_en: Channel T measurement stuck or sluggish
Block 20 voltage diverging from pack voltage on two-mode NiMH packs
Faulty pack voltage reference used for the comparison
P0B9B.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Range/Performance
P0B9B.desc: On the 2012 two-mode trucks sense T is block 20, the last of their twenty nickel-metal hydride blocks, and P0B9B shows how GM handles the missing neighbour: block 20 alone is multiplied by twenty and compared with the pack voltage, and a gap above 70 V in 160 of 170 samples sets the code as Type B. All other channels there use a pair of blocks. On lithium-ion packs the code means that cell T does not follow the pack average: the 2019 hybrid processor demands 0.005 V of movement when the average shifts by more than 0.022 V (35 of 40 samples, Type A), the 2016 Volt the same with a 7 s in 8 s window, and eAssist half the average movement in 20 of 40 samples, Type B.

causes_en: Sense lead T shorted to ground or a lower potential
Weak or discharged NiMH block 20 on two-mode packs
Failed measuring input for channel T
P0B9C.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Low
P0B9C.desc: P0B9C signals that sense T reads too low. On the 2012 two-mode trucks this is block 20, and because no block 21 exists the low test there looks at block 20 alone: below 2 V in 15 of 20 samples, Type B, while channels R and S each need their upper neighbour to read low as well. GM's lithium-ion controllers from the 2016 Volt to 2019 work with 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A, the 16OBDG02 programme with under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples, and the eAssist mild hybrid with 1.4 V in 7 of 10 samples, Type B. Open sense line faults are evaluated first. For the driver the result is a warning and reduced power until the cause is repaired.

causes_en: Sense lead T shorted to a higher cell or busbar
Measuring input for channel T drifting high
Cell or block T genuinely overcharged
P0B9D.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit High
P0B9D.desc: If sense T reports more voltage than its cell can hold, the battery controller stores P0B9D. GM documents it on several systems. The 2019 battery energy control module and the 2016 Volt set it at 4.8 V or above for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A, and only when no open sense line fault is pending. The 16OBDG02 programme with a dedicated battery sensor module uses 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples. The eAssist mild hybrid sets it above 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples, Type B. In the 2012 two-mode trucks the channel is block 20, the final NiMH block, with a limit of 23 V and 15 of 20 samples, Type B. Most such readings come from wiring touching a higher potential or a faulty measuring input.

causes_en: Loose or spread terminal in the channel T connector
Connection that opens with temperature changes
Electrical interference coupling into sense lead T
P0B9E.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B9E.desc: P0B9E would describe a sense T signal that flickers. It lacks any public manufacturer documentation. Even the 2012 two-mode trucks, whose last NiMH block is channel T, monitor it only for range, low and high, and GM's lithium-ion controllers add a circuit test but no intermittent one. The requirement behind the whole code family comes from CARB 1968.2: battery voltage sensors of a hybrid energy storage system are monitored components, and manufacturers must store separate codes that lead to the smallest part replaceable in service. A technician facing this code would wiggle-test the channel T wiring while watching the cell voltage live and look for a reading that dips or spikes for a fraction of a second.

causes_en: Sense lead U interrupted or detached from its cell
Corroded terminal raising the resistance of lead U
Fault in the balancing circuit used for the channel U test
P0B9F.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit
P0B9F.desc: P0B9F covers an open or high-resistance sense U lead, channel twenty-one. From U onward the 2012 two-mode trucks drop out, as their pack has only twenty blocks, so this code is a lithium-ion matter at GM. In the eAssist mild hybrid the test is the familiar one, lines N and N-1 both under 1.4 V with a change above 0.5 V within 200 ms in 7 of 10 samples, Type B, but it is now blocked by P1B38 instead of P1B37. The 16OBDG02 programme measures the sense line resistance and sets above 30.00 in 7 of 9 samples, Type A. The 2016 Volt and ELR decide in 0.6 s, the 2019 controller in 0.8 s of 1.6 s, both on adjacent-cell differences of 1.3 V and splice checks.

causes_en: Measuring channel U holding a fixed value
Software or calibration issue in the battery controller
Cell U behaving differently from its neighbours due to ageing
P0BA0.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Range/Performance
P0BA0.desc: P0BA0 tells the technician that channel U gives a number, but the number does not move with the pack. GM checks this rationality only on lithium-ion systems, since the two-mode NiMH trucks end at block 20. The Cadillac ELR of 2016 reacts to the smallest movement: when the average cell voltage changes by more than 0.006 V, cell U must follow, and 20 failures in 40 samples at 200 ms set a Type A fault. The Volt of the same year looks at 0.022 V of average movement and a 7 s in 8 s window, the 2019 hybrid processor at 0.005 V with 35 of 40 samples, and eAssist at half the average movement, Type B. Circuit, low and high faults are excluded before the test runs, so wiring is less likely than the controller.

causes_en: Sense lead U shorted towards ground or a lower cell
Dead measuring input for channel U
Cell U internally shorted or deeply discharged
P0BA1.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Low
P0BA1.desc: P0BA1 is stored when sense U reads close to zero. GM's lithium-ion controllers of the 2016 Volt and ELR and of 2019 treat 0.2 V or less over 1.4 s in a 2 s window as a Type A fault, provided no open sense line, lost slave communication or balancing fault is already active. The 16OBDG02 programme with its own battery sensor module uses under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples. GM's eAssist mild hybrid applies a much higher limit of 1.4 V in 7 of 10 samples, Type B. The two-mode NiMH trucks have no channel U. A short in the sense lead or a failed measuring input is the most likely finding.

causes_en: Sense lead U in contact with a higher potential
Measuring IC misreading channel U
Cell U actually overcharged
P0BA2.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit High
P0BA2.desc: P0BA2 flags an excessive voltage on channel U. GM's eAssist mild hybrid uses the lowest threshold of the documented systems: above 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples with the 12 V supply above 8.8 V, Type B. The 2016 Volt and the 2019 battery controller set it at 4.8 V or more held for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A; the 16OBDG02 programme at above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, Type A. As with the low code, the high test is held back while an open sense line or module communication fault is active. Channel U does not exist on the twenty-block two-mode trucks. Before replacing parts, the actual cell voltage should be measured, because a lead touching a higher potential is far more common than a real overcharge.

causes_en: Fatigued crimp on sense lead U
Loose fastener at the busbar tap of channel U
Vibration damage to the flexible printed circuit
P0BA3.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BA3.desc: Within the sense U group, P0BA3 is the slot for a signal that is present but unsteady. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM, the only maker whose tables cover channel U in detail, uses P0B9F to P0BA2 and nothing more. CARB 1968.2 demands monitoring of the hybrid storage system's voltage sensors and separate codes per repairable unit, and SAE reserves the intermittent code so that a manufacturer could report unstable sensing separately from a hard open or short. Physically this points to a connection that breaks for milliseconds, such as a fatigued crimp, a loose screw at a busbar tap or vibration damage to a flexible printed circuit. Repair follows the same path as for the circuit code.

causes_en: Broken or unplugged sense lead V
High-resistance splice or busbar joint on channel V
Cell monitoring board fault on channel V
P0BA4.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit
P0BA4.desc: P0BA4 reports an open or poorly connected sense V lead, the twenty-second channel and the last before W begins at P0BA9. GM's 2019 battery energy control module recognises it through seven cases, including 1.3 V between neighbouring cells, less than 36 mV with the balancing gate on and splice voltages above 0.1 or 0.5 V, with 0.8 s of failure in 1.6 s, Type A. The 2011 Volt already listed P0BA4 among its open sense line codes. In GM's 16OBDG02 programme a measured line resistance above 30.00 in 7 of 9 samples triggers it, in the eAssist mild hybrid low readings on lines N and N-1 together with a 0.5 V jump, Type B, gated by P1B38. Without a good sense lead the pack cannot balance or protect that cell.

causes_en: Channel V reading stuck while other cells move
Battery controller firmware needing reprogramming
Aged cell V responding differently to load
P0BA5.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Range/Performance
P0BA5.desc: P0BA5 describes a sense V value that stays within limits but fails a rationality check against the other cells. GM's 16OBDG02 programme demands a trend of at least 0.002 V in the same direction as the average whenever that average moves more than 0.022 V, with 35 failures in 40 evaluations giving Type A. The 2019 hybrid processor works the same way with 0.005 V. For the 2016 model year GM lists two variants: the Volt with a 7 s in 8 s window and the ELR with 0.006 V of average movement and 20 of 40 samples at 200 ms. GM's eAssist expects half the average movement, Type B. Since the test is skipped while circuit, low or high faults are active, P0BA5 alone points to the measurement rather than an open lead.

causes_en: Sense lead V shorted to ground or a lower cell
Monitoring board input for channel V failed
Cell V genuinely collapsed
P0BA6.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Low
P0BA6.desc: A sense V reading that collapses towards zero produces P0BA6. The threshold depends on the system: GM's eAssist mild hybrid uses under 1.4 V in 7 of 10 samples with at least 8.8 V on the 12 V side, Type B, while GM's lithium-ion battery controllers of 2016 and 2019 go down to 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A. The 16OBDG02 programme sets it below 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples. Because these tests are blocked by an active open sense line fault, P0BA4 would be reported first if the lead were simply broken; P0BA6 alone tends to mean a short to a lower potential or a failed input. The driver sees a hybrid or EV warning and reduced power.

causes_en: Sense lead V touching a higher cell tab or busbar
Measuring chip with faulty reference reading channel V high
Cell V really overcharged
P0BA7.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit High
P0BA7.desc: P0BA7 is the high-voltage plausibility code for channel V. The battery controller compares the measured value against a ceiling no healthy cell should reach: 4.8 V for 1.4 s within 2 s in GM's 2016 Volt and ELR and in the 2019 battery energy control module (Type A), 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples of 100 ms in the 16OBDG02 programme (Type A), and 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples in the eAssist mild hybrid (Type B). Each of these checks waits for the open sense line monitor to pass. A high reading usually comes from a sense lead V pressed against a higher cell tab or busbar, or from a measuring chip that has lost its reference, and only rarely from a cell actually overcharged.

causes_en: Contact of lead V lost intermittently under vibration
Joint on channel V opening with thermal cycling
Corroded connector pin for channel V
P0BA8.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BA8.desc: P0BA8 completes the five codes of channel V and is meant for an unstable rather than a failed sense V signal. There is no public manufacturer documentation for it. GM covers channel V in its 2011 Volt, eAssist, 2016 and 2019 tables but never with an intermittent monitor, only with P0BA4 to P0BA7. The code exists because CARB 1968.2 requires battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems to be monitored and fault codes to isolate the smallest replaceable unit, and J2012 provides an intermittent slot for every sense channel. A fault of this kind would typically be traced to a connection that loses contact under vibration or thermal cycling. Channel W follows from P0BA9.

causes_en: Broken, chafed or unplugged sense lead W
High-resistance busbar or splice joint at channel W
Failed input on the cell monitoring board for W
P0BA9.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit
P0BA9.desc: P0BA9 opens the W group, the twenty-third cell voltage channel, and flags a sense lead that is open or badly connected. GM's 2019 battery energy control module checks seven cases, ranging from a reading under 36 mV while the balancing gate of that cell is switched on to at least 1.3 V between neighbouring cells and splice voltages above 0.1 V or 0.5 V at busbar joints; 0.8 s of failure within 1.6 s sets it as Type A. The 2016 Volt module uses a 0.6 s window instead. GM's eAssist mild hybrid needs readings under 1.4 V on lines N and N-1 plus a change of more than 0.5 V within 200 ms in seven of ten samples, Type B. With the lead lost, the cell behind it can neither be balanced nor protected.

causes_en: Measuring input for W frozen at a fixed value
Battery controller software needing an update
Cell W reacting differently to load because of ageing
P0BAA.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Range/Performance
P0BAA.desc: Here the W reading is not missing but implausible: it fails to follow the rest of the pack. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain control processor 2 watches for the average cell voltage to move more than 0.022 V between samples and then expects channel W to trend at least 0.005 V in the same direction; 35 failures in 40 samples at 100 ms give a Type A fault. The 16OBDG02 programme applies the same logic with 0.002 V. The eAssist system is more tolerant and only asks the cell to move half as far as the others once the average shifts more than 0.045 V, 20 of 40 samples, Type B. In the 2011 Volt tables W appears as sensor 23 of the rationality check. Drivers often notice nothing beyond the warning lamp.

causes_en: Sense lead W shorted to a lower cell potential
Measuring input for W on the monitoring board failed
Cell W deeply discharged or internally shorted
P0BAB.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Low
P0BAB.desc: A W channel reading at or near zero sets P0BAB. How low is too low depends on the battery: GM's lithium-ion modules of 2016 and 2019 react to 0.2 V or less held for 1.4 s within a 2 s window, Type A, and the 16OBDG02 programme to under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples at 100 ms. The eAssist mild hybrid already fails below 1.4 V, seven of ten samples, as long as the 12 V supply exceeds 8.8 V and P1B38 is not active; that fault is Type B. All of these tests stand down while an open sense line fault is present, so a simply broken lead shows up as P0BA9. P0BAB on its own suggests a short towards a lower potential, a dead measuring input or a deeply discharged cell. Power and charging are usually restricted.

causes_en: Sense lead W in contact with a higher cell potential
Monitoring board input for W reading too high
Cell W actually overcharged after a balancing fault
P0BAC.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit High
P0BAC.desc: P0BAC is the upper counterpart to P0BAB: channel W reports more voltage than a single cell can plausibly hold. GM sets the limit at 4.8 V or more for 1.4 s within 2 s in the 2011 and 2016 Volt battery modules, which makes it a one-trip fault. The 16OBDG02 programme fails at above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, Type A, while the eAssist battery is stricter with more than 4.65 V in seven of ten samples, Type B. A high reading usually comes from a lead touching the potential of the next cell up or from a faulty input, less often from a genuinely overcharged cell. Because overcharging is a safety risk, the controller typically cuts charging and regeneration until the cause is found.

causes_en: Loose or fretting connector pin on lead W
Crimp on lead W opening with temperature changes
Cracked solder joint on the monitoring board input W
P0BAD.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BAD.desc: P0BAD is reserved for a W signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing outright. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. GM monitors channel W in several programmes, from the 2011 Volt to the eAssist and the 2019 tables, but only through P0BA9 to P0BAC; none of them contains an intermittent test. The slot exists because J2012 gives every sense channel five codes and CARB 1968.2 requires the battery voltage sensors of a hybrid energy storage system to be monitored with fault codes that point to the smallest replaceable part. If a vehicle did store it, the usual suspects would be a crimp or connector that loses contact under vibration or with temperature changes.

causes_en: Sense lead X broken or disconnected
Loose busbar fastener at the X sensing point
Sense harness X damaged during earlier battery work
P0BAE.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit
P0BAE.desc: Channel X, number twenty-four, starts with P0BAE, the open-lead code. The first-generation Volt of 2011 already detected it through several cases: two neighbouring readings more than 1 V apart, a busbar sense voltage above 0.7 V combined with an implausible cell voltage, or adjacent cells differing by more than 0.5 V on a shared supply line. GM's later 16OBDG02 programme measures the sense line resistance directly and fails it above 30.00 in seven of nine samples, Type A; the unit is not printed. In the 2019 battery energy control module the familiar 1.3 V and 36 mV criteria apply with 0.8 s in 1.6 s. Whichever method is used, the controller loses sight of one cell and normally restricts the battery.

causes_en: Sense X value stuck while the pack voltage changes
Calibration of the battery controller requiring reprogramming
Cell X with deviating internal resistance
P0BAF.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Range/Performance
P0BAF.desc: P0BAF covers a sense X signal that is electrically present yet does not behave like a real cell. For model year 2016 GM documents two versions in the same booklet. The Volt controller fails it when X moves in a different direction from the pack average, or by less than 0.005 V while that average moves more than 0.022 V, for 7 s within 8 s, Type A. The ELR variant samples every 200 ms, needs average movement above 0.006 V and fails after 20 of 40 samples, one trip. The eAssist hybrid asks for at least half of the average change, Type B over two trips, and GM's 2019 processor uses a 0.005 V trend test. Since the check pauses during circuit, low or high faults, P0BAF points to a stuck measurement rather than a broken wire.

causes_en: Short between sense lead X and a lower potential
Defective measuring channel X in the monitoring electronics
Cell X collapsed or internally shorted
P0BB0.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Low
P0BB0.desc: When channel X reads too low, P0BB0 is stored. In GM's eAssist mild hybrid the battery interface module sets it below 1.4 V in seven of ten samples at 200 ms, provided the 12 V system is above 8.8 V and the group fault P1B38 is not active, as a two-trip Type B fault. The 2011 Volt and the 16OBDG02 programme work with a far lower limit of about 0.2 V, the latter in 14 of 18 samples at 100 ms, Type A. That difference reflects the cell chemistry and how much voltage a healthy cell can lose. Because an open lead is caught first by P0BAE, a stand-alone P0BB0 is more often a short in the sense harness, a failed input or a cell that has collapsed. Expect reduced power and blocked charging.

causes_en: Sense lead X shorted to the next higher cell
Measuring input X drifting high
Cell X genuinely over voltage
P0BB1.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit High
P0BB1.desc: P0BB1 means the battery controller sees too much voltage on sense X. In GM's 2019 battery energy control module the threshold is 4.8 V or more, held for 1.4 s within a 2 s window, and the code is Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. The 16OBDG02 programme allows up to 4.90 V and needs 14 failing samples out of 18, while the eAssist battery treats anything above 4.65 V in seven of ten samples as a Type B fault. These tests are suppressed while an open sense line or a lost communication with the cell monitoring slave is active. A real cell at that voltage would be dangerously overcharged, so a wiring fault towards the neighbour cell or a defective input is the more frequent finding.

causes_en: Contact on lead X opening under vibration
Moisture or corrosion in the X sense connector
Harness X chafing against the module housing
P0BB2.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BB2.desc: Of the five X codes, P0BB2 is the only one without any public manufacturer description. It is intended for a sense X signal that flickers, drops out briefly or jumps between values. GM's Volt tables of 2011 and 2016 list channel X with circuit, range, low and high monitors, P0BAE to P0BB1, and no intermittent check. The code therefore rests on the J2012 structure and on CARB 1968.2, which requires hybrid battery voltage sensors to be monitored and the fault to be isolated to the smallest replaceable unit. In practice a technician would look for a contact that opens under vibration, moisture in a connector or a harness rubbing against the module housing.

causes_en: Open circuit in sense lead Y
Corroded or loose terminal raising line resistance at Y
Cell monitoring slave board fault on input Y
P0BB3.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit
P0BB3.desc: P0BB3 reports that the sense lead of channel Y, the twenty-fifth cell group, is no longer properly connected. GM's 16OBDG02 programme does not wait for odd voltages but calculates the resistance of the sense line and fails it above 30.00 in seven of nine samples, which is a one-trip Type A fault; the unit is missing in the table. The 2019 battery energy control module instead looks at the cell voltages themselves, for example 1.3 V between neighbours or a reading below 36 mV while that cell is being balanced, with 0.8 s of failure in 1.6 s. The eAssist mild hybrid sets it as a Type B fault when lines N and N-1 both read under 1.4 V and jump by more than 0.5 V. Low and high monitors for Y are blocked while P0BB3 is active.

causes_en: Analogue input Y frozen at one value
Battery controller software fault
Weak cell Y with sluggish voltage response
P0BB4.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Range/Performance
P0BB4.desc: P0BB4 is a plausibility code: the controller compares how the Y reading changes over time with the behaviour of all other cells. In the 16OBDG02 programme a sample counts as failed when the pack average moves by more than 0.022 V but Y has not trended at least 0.002 V the same way; 35 such results in 40 evaluations set a one-trip Type A fault. The 2019 hybrid powertrain control processor 2 uses the same frame with a 0.005 V trend. For the 2016 Volt the window is 7 s in 8 s. A frozen analogue input or a software problem in the battery controller are the typical findings, while a real cell defect is rarer. Unlike P0BB3, the signal is present, so the car usually keeps driving.

causes_en: Pinched sense wire Y shorting to a lower potential
Failed measuring channel Y
Cell Y severely discharged
P0BB5.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Low
P0BB5.desc: P0BB5 stands for a sense Y voltage below the plausible minimum. GM's 2016 Volt module and the 2019 battery energy control module both use 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s inside a 2 s window and flag it as Type A. Before testing, the 2019 module makes sure that no open sense line, no lost communication with the cell monitoring slave and no balancing or internal slave fault is active, and that the second protection self test is not running. The eAssist mild hybrid sets the code below 1.4 V in seven of ten samples, Type B. The likely culprits are a pinched sense wire touching a lower potential, a failed measuring channel or a cell that has really lost its charge. The driver sees a warning and reduced performance.

causes_en: Sense input Y bridged to the next cell potential
Defective input Y on the monitoring board
Overcharged cell Y after a balancing problem
P0BB6.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit High
P0BB6.desc: The battery controller logs P0BB6 when the Y channel climbs above a level no healthy cell reaches. GM's first Volt of 2011 put that limit at 4.8 V or more, 1.4 s within 2 s, with the MIL after one trip. The 16OBDG02 programme samples every 100 ms and fails above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, Type A; the eAssist battery fails above 4.65 V in seven of ten samples at 200 ms, Type B. A wiring fault that connects the Y input to the potential of the next cell is the most common explanation, followed by a failed input. Overcharging of a single cell is possible after a balancing problem and must be ruled out before the pack is charged again.

causes_en: Intermittent contact in the Y sense connector
Crimp or weld on lead Y opening when hot
Hairline crack in a solder joint of input Y
P0BB7.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BB7.desc: P0BB7 would describe an unstable sense Y signal, one that is mostly correct but drops out or jumps from time to time. No manufacturer publishes a monitor for it. Where GM covers channel Y, in the 16OBDG02 programme and the 2019 battery and hybrid processor tables, it does so with P0BB3 to P0BB6: line resistance, trend comparison, low and high limits. A brief interruption would there show up as a counted failure inside one of those tests rather than under its own code. P0BB7 thus exists as a J2012 placeholder that satisfies the CARB 1968.2 demand for monitored battery voltage sensors. Diagnosis would focus on connectors, crimps and solder joints that react to movement or heat.

causes_en: Sense lead Z interrupted
Excessive resistance at the splice or busbar of Z
Monitoring electronics input Z defective
P0BB8.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit
P0BB8.desc: P0BB8 is the open-circuit code of channel Z, the twenty-sixth and last cell channel with a generic P0 code. GM packs with more channels continue with manufacturer codes, for example P1B28 for the circuit of AA in the 2019 tables. The 2019 battery energy control module sets P0BB8 through the same seven cases as its neighbours, with 1.3 V between adjacent cells, under 36 mV on an active balancing gate or excessive splice voltage, 0.8 s in 1.6 s, Type A. GM's eAssist uses the voltage of lines N and N-1 below 1.4 V together with a change above 0.5 V in 200 ms, seven of ten samples, Type B and gated by P1B38. The 2011 Volt already listed P0BB8 among its open sense line faults.

causes_en: Z reading static despite changing pack voltage
Monitoring board or controller calibration fault
Cell Z with abnormal charge and discharge behaviour
P0BB9.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit Range/Performance
P0BB9.desc: With P0BB9 the controller says that sense Z does not track the pack: the value is within limits, but it stays still or moves the wrong way while the other cells change. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain control processor 2 enables the comparison once the system voltage is above 10.20 V and the average cell voltage shifts by more than 0.022 V, then demands a trend of at least 0.005 V on Z; 35 failures in 40 samples are Type A. The 2016 Volt variant fails after 7 s within 8 s. In the eAssist mild hybrid, Z has to follow at least half of an average movement above 0.045 V, 20 of 40 samples, Type B. A recalibrated controller or a replaced monitoring board is a more common fix than a new cell.

causes_en: Short in the Z sense wiring or connector
Failed channel Z on the monitoring board
Voltage collapse of cell Z
P0BBA.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit Low
P0BBA.desc: P0BBA is stored when the voltage measured on channel Z falls below the lower limit. In the 16OBDG02 programme the hybrid processor checks Z every 100 ms and fails it below 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples, a Type A fault, but only with a system voltage above 10.20 V and no open-circuit fault on the cell. GM's 2019 battery energy control module and the 2011 Volt use 0.2 V or less over 1.4 s within 2 s. This rules out a simple open lead, which would have set P0BB8 first. What remains is a short in the Z wiring or connector, a failed channel on the monitoring board or a cell whose voltage has actually collapsed. The battery is normally limited to protect the other cells.

causes_en: Sense lead Z shorted towards the higher neighbour cell
Faulty measuring input Z
Cell Z overcharged
P0BBB.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit High
P0BBB.desc: If the Z channel shows a cell voltage above the upper limit, the controller sets P0BBB. The 2016 Volt battery module uses 4.8 V or more for 1.4 s in a 2 s window, Type A, and checks first that the cell monitoring slave is communicating and no open sense line is reported. The 16OBDG02 programme fails above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, and the eAssist mild hybrid fails above 4.65 V in seven of ten samples with a healthy 12 V supply, Type B over two trips. Lithium-ion cells are not meant to exceed these values, so the reading normally points to a short towards the higher neighbour, a faulty input or a corrupted measurement, and only rarely to a truly overcharged cell. Charging is stopped as a precaution.

causes_en: Intermittent contact on sense lead Z
Joint at channel Z opening with heat cycling
Corrosion in the Z sense connector
P0BBC.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BBC.desc: P0BBC closes the generic block of 26 cell voltage channels from A to Z; after it J2012 moves on to pack-level codes such as P0BBD and P0BBE. The code is meant for a Z signal that is unstable rather than absent. There is no manufacturer documentation for it: GM monitors channel Z from the 2011 Volt to the 2019 battery energy control module, but always with P0BB8 to P0BBB only, and no table contains an intermittent monitor. Its basis is CARB 1968.2, which requires battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems to be checked and faults to be narrowed down to the smallest replaceable unit. Should it appear, contacts that fail under vibration or heat cycling are the logical starting point.

causes_en: Cells or modules with increased self-discharge or capacity loss
Controller software or cell capacity adaptation needing an update
Aged battery pack at end of life
Cell balancing unable to equalise the pack
P0BBD.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Variation Exceeded Limit
P0BBD.desc: P0BBD means the spread between cells or blocks of the pack has grown beyond what the controller accepts. GM used it on the two-mode hybrids, where a difference of more than 1.5 V between adjacent block voltages in three of three samples at 1 s, with battery current above 0.2 A, set a Type B fault labelled as end-of-life deviation. On the Chevrolet Bolt EV, bulletin 22-NA-151 links it to reduced propulsion and charging capped at 30 % and names cases induced by driving style that need reprogramming, otherwise a pack replacement. Volkswagen reports it on the ID.4 from cells with increased self-discharge, Audi on the Q4 e-tron with a drive system that cannot be activated, and Stellantis on the Wrangler 4xe.

causes_en: Cells drifted apart beyond what balancing can correct
Battery pack control module software needing an update
Defective or aged high-voltage battery pack
Faulty cell voltage measurement simulating a spread
P0BBE.desc: P0BBE watches the gap between the highest and the lowest cell voltage in the pack. GM's first-generation Volt sets it when that difference exceeds 0.3 V in 50 of 245 samples taken every 100 ms, provided the cell voltage rationality fault is not active; it is a one-trip Type A fault. Stellantis lists the code on the Jeep Grand Cherokee 4xe and Wrangler 4xe together with P0B24, P0DAB and a state-of-health code, where updated battery pack control module software is the remedy and an unresolved case can end in a no-start. Chrysler's warranty extension for the 2017 to 2021 Pacifica Hybrid replaces the whole high-voltage pack for this code. Its companion P0BBD reports a spread that has exceeded a set limit.

causes_en: Blown fuse in the battery fan feed
Fan relay contacts not closing or relay coil open
Open supply wire or loose terminal at the fan connector
P0BBF.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
P0BBF.desc: Air-cooled hybrid packs draw cooling air through a 12 V blower that is fed through a fuse and often a relay; the controller watches the voltage reaching the fan, and Toyota even uses that measured supply voltage to correct the fan duty. P0BBF means this feed is open or missing while the fan should be powered. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's Two-Mode hybrid monitors the same feed but reports only the high case, a welded relay, as P0BC1. CARB requires the electrical inputs and outputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. Low and high faults are P0BC0 and P0BC1, faults in the fan's own control line P0A81 to P0A85. Without power the fan stops, the pack warms up and the controller limits power.

causes_en: Fan supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Burnt fan relay contacts or corroded terminals causing voltage drop
Weak 12 V auxiliary battery or poor ground
Seizing fan motor pulling excessive current
P0BC0.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P0BC0.desc: P0BC0 reports that the voltage feeding the battery cooling fan is lower than expected while the fan is switched on. A short to ground downstream of the fuse, a corroded connector or a relay with burnt contacts drops the voltage, so the fan turns slowly or not at all. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Toyota's hybrid controller measures the fan supply on the auxiliary battery side and raises the duty when it is low, which shows why a sagging feed matters for cooling. CARB asks for circuit monitoring of all battery thermal management parts. The open case is P0BBF, the high case P0BC1 (GM: welded relay). A weak 12 V battery can cause a sag too, so check it first. Expect reduced power when the pack heats up.

causes_en: Fan relay contacts welded closed
Fan feed shorted to a constant battery voltage wire
Relay control output in the module stuck on
P0BC1.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit High
P0BC1.desc: P0BC1 flags voltage on the battery fan feed when there should be none, or more than expected. GM documents it for the battery pack control module of its Two-Mode hybrid SUVs and pickups (Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado, Sierra; 2012 and 2013 tables) as a welded fan relay: with the fan commanded off, a fan monitor voltage of at least 0.9 V in 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms sets it, provided the 12 V system is between 9 and 18 V and no fan circuit code (P0A81) is active. It is Type B, MIL after two trips. A stuck relay keeps the fan running with the vehicle off and drains the 12 V battery. The open and low cases are P0BBF and P0BC0; a fan that keeps turning without this fault is P0A83.

causes_en: Loose or corroded connector of sensor E at the sensing board
Failed thermistor E
Faulty input on the battery sensing board or module
P0BC2.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit
P0BC2.desc: Battery temperature sensor E is the fifth thermistor in the high-voltage pack; GM's Chevrolet Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the E codes as temperature sensor 5 of nine. P0BC2 is the general circuit code, used when the controller detects an electrical fault without classing it as low, high or erratic. GM's hybrid tables report only the specific siblings P0BC3 to P0BC6. NHTSA's summary of an Audi pending service solution for 2027 Q6 and A6 e-tron models names P0BC2 with a failure type byte among implausible temperature sensor errors. CARB requires battery temperature sensors to be monitored for circuit faults. With one value missing the controller limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits inside the pack, so checks call for high-voltage safety procedures.

causes_en: Sensor E drifting or poorly seated on its cell group
Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt)
Real local hot spot from a weak cell group or blocked airflow
P0BC3.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance
P0BC3.desc: P0BC3 is the plausibility check for battery temperature sensor E, GM's sensor 5: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors, which should agree closely. GM's 2016 hybrid table fails it when E is more than 25 °C away from the average of the others in 50 of 67 samples; the 2018 CT6 plug-in table more than 20 °C for 5 s within 6.7 s; the eAssist mild hybrid (13OBDG05C) allows only 8.55 °C, and only after the module has been off for more than six hours. All are Type B, two trips. The check is suspended while circuit codes are active, so it points to a sensor that reads wrongly but in range, or to a real hot spot. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 counts it among codes that set falsely in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming.

causes_en: Sensor E signal wire shorted to ground inside the pack
Internally shorted thermistor E
Moisture or contamination on the sensing board
P0BC4.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Low
P0BC4.desc: Sensor E is an NTC thermistor with a pull-up resistor, so its voltage falls as it gets hotter; a short to ground therefore looks like an extremely hot cell group. GM's 2016 table sets P0BC4 when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples; the 2011 Volt table and GM's 2019 battery module table use above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; the eAssist mild hybrid flags a sense voltage under 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 samples. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names it sensor 5 circuit low voltage. Its counterpart is P0BC5 (open circuit, reads very cold); a genuinely overheated pack is reported as P0A7E. Because the controller must assume heat, it cuts charge and discharge power and may run cooling at full speed.

causes_en: Open sensor E wire or backed-out pin at the sensing board
Cracked or open thermistor E
Module software misreading in the cold (GM Volt, reprogramming)
P0BC5.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit High
P0BC5.desc: P0BC5 reports that battery temperature sensor E delivers a voltage above its valid range. With GM's NTC sensors that reads as extreme cold, pointing to an open wire, a backed-out pin at the sensing board or a cracked thermistor. GM's 2016 table sets it below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the 2011 Volt table and GM's 2019 battery module table below -40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s, and the eAssist mild hybrid above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10 samples; all Type B, two trips. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links these codes to a Battery Too Cold message at ambient temperatures above -25 °C and prescribes reprogramming. Its counterpart is P0BC4. A pack the controller believes frozen gets strict charge and power limits.

causes_en: Loose terminal or unlatched connector of sensor E
Cracked or chafed sensor wire breaking contact intermittently
Sensing board fault affecting several temperature inputs
P0BC6.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BC6.desc: P0BC6 flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor E: the reading jumps far faster than the heavy battery mass could warm or cool. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 18OBDG02). Sampling every 100 ms, the controller adds up the absolute changes of the sensor value over a 10-sample window; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips, provided system voltage is above 10.2 V. The same logic covers the other pack sensors. The older Volt, Two-Mode and eAssist tables list no erratic code for sensor E. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a cracked wire or a connector not fully latched after pack work; if several sensors jump at once, suspect the sensing board.

causes_en: Open feedback wire or loose pin at the fan connector
Failed speed sensor or electronics inside the fan unit
Faulty feedback input in the controlling module
P0BC7.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit/Open
P0BC7.desc: Many battery cooling fans report their actual speed back to the controller as a pulse signal; Toyota patents describe a rotation sensor on the fan motor whose measured speed is compared with the target. P0BC7 means this feedback line for fan 1 is open or carries no usable signal. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables cover the same feedback only through P0BC8, P0BC9 and P0BCA. CARB requires the electrical inputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. The fan may still turn, but the controller can no longer confirm it and usually limits power to protect the pack. Faults in the drive circuit are P0A81 to P0A85; fan 2 feedback has its own codes P0D5F to P0D63.

causes_en: Dust-clogged impeller, blocked intake or worn fan bearing
Fan keeps running while commanded off (stuck drive or relay)
Fan electronics reporting a wrong speed
P0BC8.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Range/Performance
P0BC8.desc: P0BC8 compares the speed fed back by battery cooling fan 1 with what the controller commanded. GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables run two checks. With the fan enabled at 11 to 89 % duty for more than 11 s, the filtered difference between commanded and reported speed must stay inside calibrated limits; large errors fail within seconds, small ones after up to 43 s. With the fan off for more than 20 s, a reported speed above 120 rpm fails in 24 of 32 samples at 250 ms. It is Type B, two trips, and waits while drive or sense circuit codes are active. A dusty or worn fan that cannot reach its speed is the usual cause; a fan turning while commanded off points to a stuck drive. The circuit cases are P0BC7, P0BC9 and P0BCA.

causes_en: Fan seized, blocked or without power
Feedback wire shorted to ground or interrupted
Failed speed sensor inside the fan unit
P0BC9.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit Low
P0BC9.desc: P0BC9 means the speed feedback of battery cooling fan 1 is implausibly low while the fan is running. GM evaluates the feedback as a frequency: in its 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables the code counts a failure when the frequency stays below 8 Hz with the fan enabled at 11 to 89 % duty for more than 8 s and system voltage above 10.2 V; 16 failures in 20 samples at 250 ms set it as Type B, two trips. A frequency near zero comes either from a fan that is not turning or from a feedback line shorted to ground or interrupted. The high case is P0BCA, a speed that is merely too far from the target is P0BC8, and drive circuit faults are P0A81 to P0A85. Expect power limits when the pack warms up.

causes_en: Electrical noise on the feedback line from poor routing or a bad ground
Feedback wire shorted to voltage or another signal
Fan electronics sending an invalid speed signal
P0BCA.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit High
P0BCA.desc: P0BCA means the speed feedback of battery cooling fan 1 is implausibly high. GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables count a failure when the feedback frequency exceeds 290 Hz with the fan enabled at 11 to 89 % duty for more than 8 s and system voltage above 10.2 V; 16 failures in 20 samples at 250 ms set it as Type B, two trips. No real fan reaches that frequency, so the cause is electrical: noise coupled into the feedback line, a line shorted to another signal or to voltage, or fan electronics sending garbage. Check wire routing and grounds before replacing the fan. The low case is P0BC9, speed errors within range P0BC8, an open line P0BC7. While the feedback is untrusted the controller may limit power.

causes_en: Loose or corroded terminal in the feedback circuit
Chafed harness near the fan or battery case
Intermittent fault in the fan's speed sensor
P0BCB.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BCB.desc: P0BCB flags a speed feedback from battery cooling fan 1 that drops out or jumps in a way no rotating fan can, typically a loose contact in the feedback line. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables, which watch the same pulse feedback, list only performance, low and high (P0BC8, P0BC9, P0BCA). Toyota's battery cooling patents show the principle: the speed measured by a rotation sensor on the fan motor is compared with the target under steady command, so a jumping signal makes that comparison worthless. CARB requires the inputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. Wiggle-test the fan connector and harness. An open line is P0BC7; fan 2 has P0D63.

causes_en: Fault of the sensor or its circuit inside the inverter assembly
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter
Software fault in the inverter or hybrid control module
P0BCC.en: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0BCC.desc: In a two-machine hybrid one inverter feeds the traction motor and a second one the generator, the machine that is mainly driven by the engine to charge the battery or start it. Its power switches carry thermistors so the controller can cut current before they overheat. P0BCC is the general circuit code for sensor A of that generator inverter, used for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires hybrid components and their sensor inputs to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid reading the controller limits generator power, which can reduce charging and hybrid performance. The sensor normally sits inside the inverter assembly.

causes_en: Inverter controller software (Ford SSM 49120, Lincoln Aviator 2020)
Sensor drifting or stuck at one value
Uneven inverter coolant flow distorting the comparison
P0BCD.en: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0BCD.desc: P0BCD flags a generator inverter temperature sensor A whose signal is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state, for example a value stuck at one temperature or far from the other temperatures after a long soak. Ford documents this exact code: on 2020 Lincoln Aviator 3.0L hybrids built up to 18 July 2020, P0BCD stored in the inverter system controller (SOBDMC) lights the MIL and is caused by software; the fix is reprogramming that module. Patents by Hino and Mitsubishi Electric describe how such checks work, comparing heat generated in the inverter with the measured temperature change or detecting a stuck sensor. Circuit faults go to P0BCE or P0BCF instead.

causes_en: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the inverter assembly
Signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
P0BCE.en: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0BCE.desc: P0BCE means the signal of generator inverter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. Inverter thermistors are usually NTC types with a pull-up resistor, as GM's tables describe for the drive motor inverter sensors: a short to ground or a shorted element pulls the voltage down, which the controller reads as an impossibly hot inverter. GM sets the comparable drive motor codes at roughly 125 to 170 °C, depending on generation. No manufacturer documents P0BCE itself publicly; CARB requires this circuit monitoring for hybrid sensor inputs. The controller then protects the generator inverter with a substitute value and limits generator power. A real overheat is reported separately as P0A3E.

causes_en: Open sensor or circuit inside the inverter assembly
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
Lost sensor ground
P0BCF.en: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0BCF.desc: P0BCF reports a signal from generator inverter temperature sensor A above its valid range. With the usual NTC thermistor and pull-up, an open circuit, a lost sensor ground or a cracked element drives the voltage up, which reads as an extremely cold inverter. GM's comparable drive motor checks set below -40 to -58 °C and wait until the inverter has worked for about 90 s at 20 Nm or more, so a genuinely cold start does not trigger them. No manufacturer documents P0BCF itself publicly; CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid sensor inputs. Until the value is valid the controller uses conservative substitutes and may limit generator power. Check the inverter connectors before replacing the unit.

causes_en: Loose or corroded contact at the inverter connector
Intermittent fault inside the inverter assembly
Interference from the high-voltage circuit on the sensor signal
P0BD0.en: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BD0.desc: P0BD0 is reserved for a generator inverter temperature sensor A signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of failing for good. A liquid-cooled inverter changes temperature slowly, so sudden steps point to a contact problem or to interference: a Hitachi patent on inverter systems explains that the small sensor signal can pick up noise from the high-voltage main circuit and has to be filtered statistically. No manufacturer documents P0BD0 itself publicly; CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be checked for such faults as well. Permanent faults are reported as P0BCE or P0BCF. Freeze-frame data and a wiggle test at the inverter connector help find the cause.

causes_en: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
P0BD1.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0BD1.desc: Which thermistor is called sensor C depends on the maker. In GM's hybrid tables it is the second sensor of the motor A inverter: the phase V sensor in the 2016 to 2019 tables, labelled temperature sensor 2 in the Volt and ELR. P0BD1 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that is not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports only the specific siblings P0BD2, P0BD3 and P0BD4. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a valid value the controller cannot protect that phase and normally limits motor torque. The sensor sits inside the inverter, so repairs often mean replacing the assembly.

causes_en: Inverter module software (GM bulletin 18-NA-064, Bolt EV/Ampera-e)
Sticking thermostat in the power electronics coolant hose (Porsche Cayenne S E-Hybrid)
Inverter temperature sensor C drifting out of tolerance
Failing power inverter module
P0BD2.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0BD2.desc: P0BD2 checks whether inverter temperature sensor C, GM's second sensor in the motor A inverter, agrees with the other temperatures after a cold soak. More than 20 °C apart sets it: Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt; Type A in a 2019 table; Type A on the 2011 Volt and 2016 ELR, compared with coolant and transmission temperature after 6 h off. GM's 2012 and 2013 tables use 15 °C after 360 min. GM bulletin PIC6303A says that on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal the code alone needs no repair; the inverter is replaced only with P0AC4. GM fixes it by software on the 2017 Bolt EV and Ampera-e. Porsche replaces a coolant hose with a sticking thermostat on the Cayenne S E-Hybrid.

causes_en: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
P0BD3.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P0BD3.desc: P0BD3 means the signal of inverter temperature sensor C, the phase V sensor of GM's motor A inverter, is below its valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a short to ground reads as an impossibly hot inverter. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt and in a 2018 table; above 159 °C for 6.25 of 8.75 s, Type A, in a 2019 table; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt and 2016 ELR; above 125 °C, two trips, in the 2012 and 2013 tables. A genuine overheat of that phase is reported as P0C12. Since the sensor is part of the inverter, the usual fix is the inverter assembly.

causes_en: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
Lost sensor ground
P0BD4.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P0BD4.desc: P0BD4 reports a voltage from inverter temperature sensor C above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor this is an implausibly cold inverter, typically caused by an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked element. To avoid false alarms on a cold day GM waits until the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more. The 2016 Volt and a 2018 table then set it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, Type B, two trips; a 2019 table uses -50 °C with Type A. The 2011 Volt and 2016 ELR use below -58 °C, Type A; the 2012 and 2013 tables below -40 °C, two trips. Until the reading is valid the controller protects the inverter with substitute values and may cut motor power.

causes_en: Loose or corroded contact at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Interference from the high-voltage circuit on the sensor signal
P0BD5.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BD5.desc: P0BD5 is meant for an inverter temperature sensor C signal that jumps or drops out for short moments. Because the heat sink of a liquid-cooled inverter changes temperature smoothly, sudden steps point to a contact fault or to interference; a Hitachi patent explains that the small thermistor signal can pick up noise from the high-voltage main circuit. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM covers its sensor C, the phase V sensor of the motor A inverter, only with P0BD2, P0BD3 and P0BD4. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for erratic faults too. Freeze-frame data and a careful check of the inverter connector are the best starting points.

causes_en: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
P0BD6.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit
P0BD6.desc: Sensor D is, in GM's hybrid tables, the second thermistor of the motor B inverter, the counterpart of sensor C in the motor A inverter: phase V in the 2016 to 2019 tables, temperature sensor 2 of inverter B on the Volt. Other makers assign the letter differently. P0BD6 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports P0BD7, P0BD8 and P0BD9 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid sensor circuits. Without a valid value the controller cannot protect that inverter and usually limits the motor it drives. Read all stored codes, since several inverter codes often appear together.

causes_en: Inverter temperature sensor D drifting out of tolerance
Failing power inverter module
Uneven inverter coolant flow after soak
P0BD7.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P0BD7.desc: P0BD7 is the plausibility check for inverter temperature sensor D, GM's second sensor in the motor B inverter. After a cold soak its reading is compared with an average vehicle temperature; more than 20 °C apart sets the code, Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt and Type A in a 2019 table. The 2011 Volt compares with power electronics coolant and transmission temperature after 6 h off (20 °C, Type A); GM's 2012 and 2013 tables use 15 °C after 360 min, two trips. GM bulletin PIC6303A lists P0BD7 with the other inverter thermistor codes on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal: alone it causes no noticeable effect, and the inverter is replaced only if P0AC4 set at the same time.

causes_en: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the inverter (Jeep Compass PHEV bulletin)
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
P0BD8.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P0BD8.desc: P0BD8 means the signal of inverter temperature sensor D is below its valid range; with an NTC thermistor and pull-up that reads as an extremely hot inverter, usually from a short to ground or an internal sensor fault. GM sets it above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt, above 159 °C, Type A, in a 2019 table, above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt and above 125 °C, two trips, in the 2012 table. Stellantis lists P0BD8-11 for the 2026 Jeep Compass 1.6 PHEV outside the US among the codes behind a no-start with the message Electric Traction System Fault; the repair is the traction inverter of the hybrid dual-clutch transmission.

causes_en: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
Lost sensor ground
P0BD9.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P0BD9.desc: P0BD9 means inverter temperature sensor D delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor in the motor B inverter that equals an implausibly cold inverter, so an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked thermistor is likely. GM checks only after the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more, so a real cold start is excluded. The 2016 Volt then sets it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, Type B, two trips; a 2019 table uses -50 °C with Type A; the 2011 Volt below -58 °C, Type A; the 2012 table below -40 °C, two trips. Until the value is valid the controller uses substitute values and may limit motor B. Check the inverter connectors before replacing the unit.

causes_en: Loose or corroded contact at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Interference from the high-voltage circuit on the sensor signal
P0BDA.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BDA.desc: P0BDA covers an inverter temperature sensor D signal that changes in steps or drops out briefly. Real temperatures of a liquid-cooled inverter move smoothly, so such jumps suggest a contact problem or interference from the high-voltage switching, which a Hitachi patent on inverter systems names as a typical disturbance of the small sensor signal. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's tables cover sensor D, the second sensor of the motor B inverter, only with P0BD7, P0BD8 and P0BD9. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for erratic behaviour as well. Because the fault comes and goes, freeze-frame data and live data during a wiggle test are the most useful clues.

causes_en: Internal fault of the thermistor or its circuit inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
P0BDB.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit
P0BDB.desc: Which thermistor counts as inverter temperature sensor E is set by the manufacturer. In GM's hybrid tables it is the third sensor of the motor A inverter (PIM sensor #3), assigned to phase W in the 2016 to 2019 tables. P0BDB is the general circuit code for an electrical fault that is not classed as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM uses only the siblings P0BDC, P0BDD and P0BDE. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid reading the controller cannot protect the phase W power switches and usually limits motor torque. The sensor is built into the inverter, so the repair is often the inverter assembly.

causes_en: Phase W thermistor drifting out of tolerance
Uneven inverter cooling or residual heat after the soak period
Failing power inverter module (replace only with P0AC4 per GM PIC6303A)
P0BDC.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance
P0BDC.desc: P0BDC checks whether inverter temperature sensor E, GM's phase W sensor in the motor A inverter, agrees with the vehicle after a long stand. The 2016 and 2018 tables compare it after a cold soak with a calculated average temperature; more than 20 °C apart for 0.525 of 0.625 s sets Type B, two trips. A 2019 table uses the same 20 °C as Type A. The 2011 Volt compares it with power electronics coolant temperature (20 °C, Type A); the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks use 15 °C after at least 360 minutes off (Type B). GM bulletin PIC6303A says that on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal the code has no remedial action; the inverter is replaced only together with P0AC4.

causes_en: Shorted thermistor or signal line inside the power inverter module
Signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where the design has any
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
P0BDD.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Low
P0BDD.desc: P0BDD reports that the signal of inverter temperature sensor E, the phase W thermistor of GM's motor A inverter, sits below its valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a short to ground appears as an impossibly hot inverter. Thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, in the 2016 and 2018 tables; above 159 °C for 6.25 of 8.75 s, Type A, in a 2019 table; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks. A real overheat of that phase is reported separately as P0C13. With the sensor inside the inverter, the usual fix is the inverter assembly.

causes_en: Open thermistor or broken connection inside the power inverter module
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter
Lost sensor reference ground on the sensing board
P0BDE.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit High
P0BDE.desc: P0BDE means the signal of inverter temperature sensor E is above its valid range. For GM's NTC thermistor with pull-up that reads as an extremely cold phase W in the motor A inverter, typically an open circuit, lost reference ground or a failed sensor. GM sets it below -50 °C, but only after at least 90 s of inverter warm-up at 20 Nm or more, so a genuinely cold car does not trip it: 2.625 of 3.65 s, Type B, two trips, in the 2016 and 2018 tables, 6.25 of 8.75 s, Type A, in a 2019 table. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C (Type A), the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks below -40 °C (Type B). The controller usually limits power to protect the unmonitored phase.

causes_en: Loose, corroded or vibrating connector at the inverter
Cracked solder joint on the inverter sensing board
Ageing thermistor with unstable resistance
P0BDF.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BDF.desc: P0BDF flags an unstable signal from inverter temperature sensor E: the reading jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying out of range, typically from a loose connector, a cracked solder joint or an ageing thermistor. In GM's hybrid tables sensor E is the phase W sensor of the motor A inverter, but GM does not list this erratic code; no manufacturer documents P0BDF publicly. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be checked for circuit faults, which includes intermittent signals. Unlike P0BDD and P0BDE, the value returns to plausible levels between faults, so the code may come and go. Because the controller cannot trust the sensor, it usually reduces motor power while the fault is present.

causes_en: Internal fault of the thermistor or its circuit inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
P0BE0.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit
P0BE0.desc: Sensor F is, in GM's hybrid tables, the third thermistor of the motor B inverter (inverter B sensor #3), the counterpart of sensor E in the motor A inverter; the 2016 to 2019 tables assign it to phase W. Other makers may use the letter differently. P0BE0 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports P0BE1, P0BE2 and P0BE3 instead. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a valid reading the controller cannot protect that inverter phase and usually limits the motor it drives. Read all stored codes, since inverter faults rarely come alone.

causes_en: Phase W thermistor of inverter B drifting out of tolerance
Uneven inverter cooling or residual heat after the soak period
Failing power inverter module (replace only with P0AC4 per GM PIC6303A)
P0BE1.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance
P0BE1.desc: P0BE1 is the plausibility check of inverter temperature sensor F, GM's phase W thermistor in the motor B inverter. After the car has stood long enough, its reading must match a reference: in the 2016 and 2018 tables a calculated average after cold soak, with more than 20 °C difference for 0.525 of 0.625 s setting Type B over two trips, Type A in a 2019 table. The 2011 Volt compares against power electronics coolant temperature (20 °C, Type A), the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off with a 15 °C limit (Type B). GM bulletin PIC6303A lists P0BE1 for 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse, Velite and Regal: no customer-noticeable reaction, inverter replacement only with P0AC4.

P0BE2.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low
P0BE2.desc: P0BE2 is set when the voltage from inverter temperature sensor F, the phase W thermistor in GM's motor B inverter, drops below the valid window. Because GM pairs an NTC element with a pull-up resistor, a short to ground is converted into a temperature far above anything the inverter can survive. Limits found in GM's tables: more than 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips (2016 and 2018); more than 159 °C for 6.25 of 8.75 s, Type A (2019); more than 130 °C, Type A (2011 Volt); more than 125 °C, Type B (2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks). Genuine overheating of this phase has its own code, P0C16. The thermistor is part of the inverter, so it is rarely replaced on its own.

P0BE3.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit High
P0BE3.desc: P0BE3 is the high-signal fault of inverter temperature sensor F, GM's phase W thermistor in the motor B inverter. With an NTC element and pull-up, an open circuit or a sensor that has lost ground drives the voltage up, which the controller reads as an implausibly cold inverter. GM only judges this after the inverter has worked for at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more: below -50 °C for 2.625 of 3.65 s sets Type B, two trips (2016 and 2018 tables), or Type A for 6.25 of 8.75 s (2019). The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C (Type A), the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks below -40 °C (Type B). Expect limited output from motor B until the circuit is repaired.

Ageing thermistor with unstable resistance
P0BE4.en: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BE4.desc: P0BE4 stands for brief dropouts or jumps in the signal of inverter temperature sensor F, which GM's hybrid tables place at phase W of the motor B inverter. The reading returns to normal between events, which separates it from the steady low and high faults P0BE2 and P0BE3. GM does not list this code, and no other manufacturer documents P0BE4 publicly. CARB's monitoring requirement for hybrid sensor circuits covers such intermittent faults as well. Typical sources are a connector with poor contact, a cracked solder joint or a thermistor whose resistance has become unstable. While the signal is distrusted, the controller tends to cut motor B power, and the fault can disappear before the workshop sees it.
