Supply or signal fault on the inverter's sensor board
Software fault in the motor control processor
P0BE5.en: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit
P0BE5.desc: The inverter of drive motor A measures the current in each motor phase with a current sensor; the controller needs these values for torque control and overcurrent protection. P0BE5 is the general circuit code for the phase U sensor, used for an electrical fault that is not classed as offset, low or high. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables (2011 Volt through 2019) only use the siblings P0BE6, P0BE7 and P0BE8, and CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a reliable phase U reading the inverter typically switches to a reduced or alternate control mode, so motor A loses power. The sensor sits inside the inverter, which usually means inverter replacement.

causes_en: Hybrid control processor software (Jeep bulletin 08-056-21/08-057-21)
Zero offset of the phase U current sensor drifted beyond the limit
Faulty sensing electronics in the power inverter module
P0BE6.en: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0BE6.desc: GM uses P0BE6 as the offset check of the phase U current sensor in the motor A inverter. At every start, while no current flows, the controller learns the sensor's zero offset; if it exceeds 30 A (2011 Volt and 2016 tables, Type A; 2012 two-mode trucks, Type B) or 35 A (2019 table, Type A), the code sets. In GM's BAS Plus (eAssist) table a fault of this sensor makes current control switch to an alternate mode that does not use the current sensors. Jeep lists P0BE6 with the other phase current codes on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV for Europe, with the turtle and Service 4WD lights, and fixes it by reprogramming the hybrid control processors.

causes_en: Failed phase U current sensor inside the inverter
Sensor signal or supply pulled to ground on the sensor board
Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector
P0BE7.en: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0BE7.desc: P0BE7 means the output of the phase U current sensor in the motor A inverter has fallen below its valid range. GM converts the sensor voltage into amps and compares it with a limit: below -700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s in the 2016 tables and 0.1 of 0.15 s in a 2019 table, both Type A; below -700 A, Type B, on the 2012 two-mode trucks; below -440 A, Type B, two trips, in the BAS Plus (eAssist) table; the 2011 Volt uses 800 A limits for these sensors. Such values are far beyond real phase currents, so the cause is electrical, typically a sensor signal pulled toward ground. GM's eAssist controller then runs current control without the sensors, which costs motor A performance.

causes_en: Failed phase U current sensor inside the inverter

Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector
P0BE8.en: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit High
P0BE8.desc: P0BE8 is the high-side counterpart of P0BE7: the phase U current sensor of the motor A inverter reports a value above its valid range. GM's tables set it above 700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s (2016) or 0.1 of 0.15 s (2019), Type A, one trip; above 800 A, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 700 A, Type B, on the 2012 two-mode trucks; and above 440 A, Type B, two trips, in the BAS Plus (eAssist) table. A reading this high without matching battery current points to the sensor or its supply rather than real current; genuine excess current is covered by separate overcurrent codes such as P0C01. The inverter then uses a fallback control strategy and motor A delivers less torque.

Software fault in the motor control processor
P0BE9.en: Drive Motor A Phase V Current Sensor Circuit
P0BE9.desc: P0BE9 covers a general circuit fault of the phase V current sensor in the motor A inverter, meaning an electrical problem the controller does not narrow down to an offset, low or high condition. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's hybrid tables for the 2011 Volt, the 2012 two-mode trucks and the 2016 to 2019 models list only the specific siblings P0BEA, P0BEB and P0BEC; GM's BAS Plus (eAssist) table lists phase current codes only for U and W. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Because the three phase currents are used together for torque control and their sum is cross-checked (P0BFD), a lost V signal normally forces reduced motor A operation.

P0BEA.en: Drive Motor A Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0BEA.desc: P0BEA is the performance check of the phase V current sensor in the motor A inverter. GM implements it as an offset test: with no current flowing at start-up, the learned zero point must stay within 30 A (2011 Volt, 2016 tables, Type A; 2012 two-mode trucks, Type B, with P0BEB/P0BEC not active) or 35 A (2019 table, Type A, after a 0.4 s delay). A sensor whose zero has drifted would distort torque control and the phase current balance. Jeep names P0BEA among the phase current codes of the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV for EMEA markets, together with the turtle and Service 4WD lights; the remedy is a software update of the hybrid control processor and power inverter.

causes_en: Failed phase V current sensor inside the inverter

P0BEB.en: Drive Motor A Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0BEB.desc: P0BEB reports that the phase V current sensor in the motor A inverter outputs a signal below its valid range. GM compares the converted current with a lower limit: below -700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s (2016 tables) or 0.1 of 0.15 s (2019 table), Type A, one trip; below -800 A, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; below -700 A, Type B, two trips, on the 2012 two-mode trucks. Real phase currents never reach these values, so the code points to an electrical fault such as a sensor output pulled toward ground or a dead sensor. Unlike P0BEA, the sensor is not just shifted but out of its measuring range. Motor A is then run in a restricted mode.

P0BEC.en: Drive Motor A Phase V Current Sensor Circuit High
P0BEC.desc: P0BEC is set when the phase V current sensor of the motor A inverter reports a value above its valid range. In GM's tables the limit is above 700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s (2016) or 0.1 of 0.15 s (2019), Type A; above 800 A, Type A, on the 2011 Volt with PWM output disabled; and above 700 A, Type B, two trips, on the 2012 two-mode trucks. Because the check runs while the power stage is not switching or the value is far beyond any real current, it isolates a sensor or supply fault rather than an actual overcurrent. It pairs with P0BEB for the low side and P0BEA for offset. Expect reduced drive from motor A and further inverter codes in the memory.

P0BED.en: Drive Motor A Phase W Current Sensor Circuit
P0BED.desc: P0BED is the general circuit code of the phase W current sensor in the drive motor A inverter, for an electrical fault outside the offset, low and high categories. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables from the 2011 Volt to 2019, including the BAS Plus (eAssist) system, use P0BEE, P0BEF and P0BF0 instead. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Phase W matters even on systems with only two sensors: GM's eAssist table measures U and W and, if either sensor fails, runs current control in an alternate mode without the sensors. Expect reduced motor A torque, and check for related inverter codes before replacing parts.

P0BEE.en: Drive Motor A Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0BEE.desc: P0BEE checks the phase W current sensor of the motor A inverter for a plausible zero point. GM learns the sensor offset at each start while no current flows and sets the code above 30 A (2011 Volt and 2016 tables, Type A; 2012 two-mode trucks, Type B) or above 35 A (2019 table, Type A). In GM's BAS Plus (eAssist) table P0BEE is one of the faults that switch current control to a sensorless alternate mode, and it blocks the phase sum check P0BFD. Jeep lists P0BEE as Drive Motor A Inverter Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Performance on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV (EMEA), with turtle and Service 4WD lights, fixed by a hybrid control processor update.

Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector
P0BEF.en: Drive Motor A Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0BEF.desc: P0BEF indicates that the phase W current sensor of the motor A inverter delivers a signal below its valid range. GM's limits: below -700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s (2016 tables) or 0.1 of 0.15 s (2019), Type A; below -800 A, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; below -700 A, Type B, on the 2012 two-mode trucks; below -440 A, Type B, two trips, in the BAS Plus (eAssist) table. These readings lie far outside real phase currents, so a sensor output stuck near ground, a failed sensor or a supply fault is the likely cause. In the eAssist system this fault puts current control into a mode that ignores the sensors, and it disables the U-V-W correlation check P0BFD, so motor A runs with reduced output.

causes_en: Failed phase W current sensor inside the inverter

Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector
P0BF0.en: Drive Motor A Phase W Current Sensor Circuit High
P0BF0.desc: P0BF0 is the high-signal fault of the phase W current sensor in the motor A inverter. GM sets it above 700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s in the 2016 tables or 0.1 of 0.15 s in a 2019 table, Type A, one trip; above 700 A, Type B, two trips, on the 2012 two-mode trucks; above 440 A, Type B, in the BAS Plus (eAssist) table; the 2011 Volt uses 800 A limits for this sensor family. A value this high without matching battery current points to the sensor, its supply or an open reference rather than to real overcurrent, which GM reports separately (P0C01). With P0BF0 active, GM's eAssist logic switches to sensorless current control and suspends P0BFD, so motor A is limited until repair.

Software fault in the motor B control processor
P0BF1.en: Drive Motor B Phase U Current Sensor Circuit
P0BF1.desc: On hybrids with two electric machines, the inverter of drive motor B carries its own set of phase current sensors, which the motor control processor uses for torque control and to protect the power switches. P0BF1 is the general circuit code for the phase U sensor of motor B, meant for an electrical fault that is not classified as offset, low or high. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly: GM's tables for the 2011 Volt, the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks and the 2016 to 2019 models list only P0BF2, P0BF3 and P0BF4 for this sensor. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a valid phase U value, motor B is usually limited or switched off.

Faulty current sensing electronics in the power inverter module
P0BF2.en: Drive Motor B Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0BF2.desc: GM runs P0BF2 as the offset test of the phase U current sensor in the motor B inverter. Each time the vehicle is started, while no current flows through the motor, the controller learns the sensor's zero point and compares it with a limit: 30 A on the 2011 Volt (Type A) and in the 2016 tables (Type A, after 0.1 s), 30 A on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks (Type B, two trips, power stage open, P0BF3/P0BF4 not active) and 35 A in a 2019 table (Type A, after 0.4 s). Jeep lists P0BF2 on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV for Europe, together with the other motor A and B phase current codes, the turtle light and Service 4WD; the fix there is a software update of the hybrid control processors.

P0BF3.desc: P0BF3 is stored when the phase U current sensor of the motor B inverter reports a value below its valid range. GM converts the sensor voltage into amps and sets the code below -800 A on the 2011 Volt (Type A, 4 of 6 samples), below -700 A on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks (Type B, two trips), and below -700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s in the 2016 tables or 0.1 of 0.15 s in a 2019 table (Type A, one trip). The offset is learned at every start with no current through the motor and must stay within 30 A on the 2011 Volt (Type A, P0BEB/P0BEC not active, as printed in the table) and in the 2016 tables (Type A, 0.1 s), within 30 A on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks (Type B, two trips) and within 35 A in a 2019 table (Type A, 0.4 s). P0BF7.en: Drive Motor B Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0BF7.desc: P0BF7 reports that the phase V current sensor of the motor B inverter outputs a signal below its valid range. P0BFC.desc: P0BFC is the signal-high fault of the phase W current sensor in the motor B inverter. GM sets it above 800 A on the 2011 Volt (Type A, one trip), above 700 A on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks (Type B, two trips, 10 of 15 samples) and above 700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s in the 2016 tables or 0.1 of 0.15 s in a 2019 table (Type A). A reading this high with no matching battery current indicates the sensor, its supply or an open reference instead of actual current; true phase overcurrent of motor B is logged as P0C04, and the plausibility of all three phases together as P0BFE. With P0BFC stored the inverter derates motor B, and the hybrid system leans more on the engine and motor A.

causes_en: Hybrid control processor software (Jeep bulletin 08-056-21/08-057-21)
One motor A phase current sensor reading wrong but still within its own limits
Faulty current sensing electronics in the power inverter module
P0BFD.en: Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation
P0BFD.desc: In a three-phase motor without a neutral connection the three phase currents must add up to roughly zero. P0BFD checks this for drive motor A: if the absolute sum of the U, V and W readings exceeds a limit, at least one sensor is wrong. GM's limits: 156 A on the 2011 Volt and 110 A on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks (Type A, one trip), 110 A for 0.0032 of 0.0038 s in the 2016 and 2019 tables (Type A). GM's BAS Plus (eAssist) uses another balance, motor DC current plus accessory module current versus battery current, above 40 A, Type B, blocked while a phase sensor code is active. Jeep lists P0BFD on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV (EMEA), fixed by a software update.

causes_en: Hybrid control processor software (Jeep bulletin 08-056-21/08-057-21)
One motor B phase current sensor reading wrong but still within its own limits
Faulty current sensing electronics in the power inverter module
P0BFE.en: Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation
P0BFE.desc: P0BFE applies the phase balance test to drive motor B: the controller adds the U, V and W current readings, which should cancel out, and sets the code when the absolute sum stays above a limit. GM uses 156 A on the 2011 Volt and 110 A on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks (Type A, one trip, main relay closed) and 110 A for 0.0032 of 0.0038 s in the 2016 and 2019 tables (Type A). It catches a sensor that reads wrong while each signal alone stays in range, unlike the per-phase codes P0BF2 to P0BFC. GM's single-motor eAssist has no such code. Jeep lists P0BFE on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV (EMEA) with the turtle and Service 4WD lights; reprogramming the hybrid processors is the fix.

causes_en: Loose, corroded or damaged three-phase cable joint between inverter and motor A
Fault in the motor A inverter or its current measurement
Damaged stator winding of drive motor A
Motor control software fault
P0BFF.desc: P0BFF is the general code for the current flowing through drive motor A, the electric machine the manufacturer labels A. It covers a current fault that is not classed as too low (P0C00) or too high (P0C01). No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. CARB requires hybrids to monitor electric motor performance. The closest documented check is GM's P0C01, which compares the sensed phase current with a fixed limit, and Stellantis lists P0C01 on the 2026 Wagoneer S with damaged three-phase cabling as the cause. A stored P0BFF means the motor controller no longer trusts the motor current, so it usually reduces electric drive power. Check the three-phase connections, the motor windings and the inverter.

causes_en: High-resistance or loose three-phase connection at motor A or the inverter
Inverter power stage for motor A not delivering current
Open or damaged winding in drive motor A
P0C00.desc: P0C00 reports that the current of drive motor A is lower than the controller expects for the commanded torque, the counterpart of P0C01 (current high). No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM and Stellantis use only P0C01 from this group. CARB requires hybrids to monitor electric motor performance. Too little current points to a high-resistance three-phase joint, an open winding path or an inverter that cannot drive the phases. GM checks a missing phase separately as P0C05. The driver usually notices weak electric drive and a warning lamp; the vehicle may switch to engine-only or limp mode.

mfr.Audi: Drive motor generator power inverter control module failure

causes_en: Damaged or improperly torqued three-phase cable joints (Stellantis S2608000006)
Damaged stator winding of motor A (GM PIP5246)
Outdated hybrid control software (Jeep TSB 08-144-23)
Failing power switch or current measurement in the inverter
P0C01.desc: P0C01 is the overcurrent check of drive motor A, meant to protect the inverter's IGBTs. GM sets it when any phase current exceeds 725 A on the 2011 Volt, 600 A on the 2012 two-mode trucks and in the 2016 to 2019 tables, or 396 A on eAssist; since 2016 a too negative d-axis current (about -540 to -310 A, depending on stator temperature) also counts. A fast and a slow counter catch sudden and intermittent faults; Type A, one trip. GM PIP5246 links it on Volt and ELR to a damaged motor 1 stator. Stellantis lists it on the 2018/19 Wrangler eTorque (motor generator unit) and on the 2026 Wagoneer S and Cherokee, there caused by cross-threaded three-phase cable bolts. Expect limp mode.

causes_en: Loose, corroded or damaged three-phase connection of motor B
Fault in the motor B inverter or its current measurement
Damaged stator winding of drive motor B
P0C02.desc: P0C02 is the general current code for drive motor B, the second electric machine, such as the second motor of a two-motor hybrid or the rear motor of an electric all-wheel-drive system. It applies to a current fault that is neither classed as low (P0C03) nor high (P0C04). No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. CARB requires monitoring of electric motor performance. The documented relative is P0C04: GM checks the phase current of motor B against 600 to 725 A, and Stellantis lists P0C04 on the 2026 Wagoneer S and Cherokee with faulty three-phase cable joints. With P0C02 stored the controller usually cuts or limits the power of motor B. Inspect the phase cabling, the winding resistance and the inverter of motor B.

causes_en: High-resistance or loose three-phase connection of motor B
Inverter power stage for motor B not delivering current
Open or damaged winding in drive motor B
P0C03.desc: P0C03 indicates that drive motor B draws less current than the controller expects for the requested torque. It is the low counterpart of P0C04 and the motor B twin of P0C00. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly, and the GM hybrid tables use only P0C04 and P0C08 for motor B. CARB requires hybrids to monitor electric motor performance. Low current typically comes from a high-resistance cable joint, an interrupted winding path or an inverter stage that does not switch; a single missing phase is reported by GM as P0C08. In practice motor B delivers little or no torque, a warning lamp lights up and the system may fall back to the other motor or the engine.

causes_en: Cross-threaded or loose three-phase cable bolts with metal debris (Stellantis S2608000006)
Shorted or damaged stator winding of motor B
Failing power switch or current measurement in the motor B inverter
P0C04.desc: P0C04 is the overcurrent check of drive motor B and protects the IGBTs of its inverter. GM flags it when the highest phase current exceeds 725 A on the 2011 Volt or 600 A on the 2012 two-mode trucks and in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; the newer tables also fail a d-axis current below a stator-temperature curve of roughly -556 to -315 A. Fast and slow counters cover sudden and intermittent peaks, Type A, one trip. Stellantis names P0C04 with P0C01 on the 2026 Jeep Wagoneer S and Cherokee: cross-threaded or loose bolts on the three-phase cables between transmission and drive motor power inverter, checked by resistance against a 29 to 32 milliohm window. The car goes into limp mode with the MIL on.

causes_en: Loose or open three-phase terminal between inverter and motor A
Software fault, cured by update (Jeep TSB 08-144-23)
Internal fault of the motor generator unit or open stator winding
One-off event that does not return after clearing (Volvo TJ 36863)
P0C05.en: Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
P0C05.desc: P0C05 detects an open or missing phase between the inverter and drive motor A. GM checks each phase as the rotor passes its axis: if the peak phase axis current stays below 9 A while at least 23 A is commanded, with the rotor within 30 degrees of that axis and over 35 V on the inverter, about 200 failed samples set the code. It is Type A, one trip, on the Volt and two-mode trucks and Type B, two trips, on eAssist. Jeep lists it on the 2018/19 Wrangler eTorque with P0C01, curing it by software or a new motor generator unit. Volvo uses it in the rear axle inverter of 2020 to 2022 PHEVs and advises clearing it and test-driving before replacing parts. Expect reduced electric power.

causes_en: Phase cable or winding shorted to ground or housing
Shorted low-side power switch in the motor A inverter
Insulation damage from heat, moisture or chafing
P0C06.en: Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
P0C06.desc: P0C06 belongs to the phase circuit group of drive motor A and reports that a U, V or W phase line sits too low, typically a short to the negative high-voltage rail or to chassis ground. P0C05 covers an open or missing phase, P0C07 the opposite high state. No manufacturer documents P0C06 for a drive motor publicly; GM's hybrid tables use only P0C05 from this trio. CARB requires hybrid input and output components to be monitored for circuit faults. Such a short usually also trips the inverter's overcurrent protection, so P0C01 or insulation faults may appear alongside. The motor controller shuts down motor A, which leaves the driver with reduced or no electric drive and a warning lamp.

causes_en: Shorted high-side power switch in the motor A inverter
Phase cable shorted to the positive high-voltage path
Faulty gate driver holding a switch on
P0C07.en: Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit High
P0C07.desc: P0C07 is the high member of the drive motor A phase circuit group: a U, V or W phase line reads higher than it should, most likely through a short to the positive high-voltage rail or a power switch that stays on. Its siblings are P0C05 for an open phase and P0C06 for a phase pulled low. No manufacturer documents P0C07 publicly; among these three, GM uses only P0C05, which watches for missing phase current. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid input and output components. Because a stuck high phase drives uncontrolled current, the inverter normally disables motor A at once. The driver sees a warning lamp and loses some or all electric propulsion until the shorted part is replaced.

causes_en: Loose or open three-phase terminal between inverter and motor B
Open stator winding in drive motor B
Inverter stage for motor B not conducting
P0C08.en: Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
P0C08.desc: P0C08 is the open-phase check for drive motor B, the motor B twin of P0C05. GM runs it on the 2011 Volt and the 2012 two-mode trucks: each phase is checked as the rotor passes its axis, and a phase axis current below 9 A while at least 23 A is commanded, with the rotor within 30 degrees and over 35 V on the inverter, counts as a miss. Around 200 failed samples set it, Type A, one trip. Later GM tables up to 2016 keep the same logic. GM's eAssist has only one machine and no P0C08. The usual causes are a loose three-phase terminal, an open stator winding or an inverter stage that does not conduct. Motor B then delivers no torque, the MIL lights and drive power is reduced.

causes_en: Phase cable or winding of motor B shorted to ground or housing
Shorted low-side power switch in the motor B inverter
Insulation damage from heat, moisture or chafing
P0C09.en: Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
P0C09.desc: P0C09 marks a U, V or W phase line of drive motor B that is pulled low, for example by a short to the negative high-voltage rail, to ground or by a power switch that conducts when it should not. It is the motor B twin of P0C06; the siblings P0C08 and P0C0A cover an open phase and a phase stuck high. No manufacturer documents P0C09 publicly, and GM's hybrid tables use only P0C08 for motor B phase circuits. CARB requires circuit fault monitoring of hybrid components. A low phase usually causes overcurrent too, so P0C04 or insulation codes often accompany it. The motor controller switches motor B off; the vehicle continues with reduced power and a warning lamp.

mfr.Audi: Drive motor generator assembly failure, Drive motor generator power inverter control module failure

causes_en: Shorted high-side power switch in the motor B inverter
Phase cable of motor B shorted to the positive high-voltage path
Faulty gate driver holding a switch on
P0C0A.en: Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit High
P0C0A.desc: P0C0A reports that a phase line of drive motor B reads too high, typically a short to the positive high-voltage rail or a high-side power switch that stays on. It mirrors P0C07 for motor A and completes the motor B trio with P0C08 (open) and P0C09 (low). No manufacturer documents P0C0A publicly; GM only uses P0C08 for motor B phase circuits, based on missing phase current. CARB requires hybrid components to be monitored for circuit faults. A phase stuck high leads to uncontrolled current, so the inverter switches motor B off immediately and P0C04 may be stored as well. For the driver this means a warning lamp, reduced propulsion and, on electric all-wheel drive, loss of the driven axle.

causes_en: Failed gate-drive power supply inside the motor A inverter
Low 12 V feed, blown fuse or poor ground to the inverter control board
Open high-voltage feed to the inverter, e.g. in a belt starter-alternator (Mercedes LI15.40-P-077947)
P0C0B.en: Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit/Open
P0C0B.desc: P0C0B flags a lost or interrupted supply inside the motor A inverter. GM reads it from the IGBT module status: when the gate drive supply falls below its threshold, the module reports a bias fault; on eAssist the 5 V rail below 3.5 to 4.3 V or the 15 V rail below 10.4 to 12.6 V counts, with run/crank above 7 V. The 2012 trucks enable it between 9.5 and 18 V; the 2016 to 2019 tables need 0.002 to 0.168 s of fault within short windows, Type A, one trip. Mercedes applies the code to the high-voltage supply of the inverter in the belt starter-alternator of P3 hybrids (subtypes 16 and 17) and replaces that unit. Expect loss of electric drive or engine start.

causes_en: Internal fault of the drive power electronics (Audi TSB 2081725)
Weak 12 V supply, poor ground or high-resistance connector at the inverter
Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC converter output
P0C0C.en: Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit Low
P0C0C.desc: P0C0C reports that the supply voltage of the motor A inverter is present but too low, while P0C0B covers a lost or open supply and P0C0D a supply that is too high. Which supply is meant depends on the maker: GM ties its sibling P0C0B to the gate-drive supply of the IGBTs, Mercedes to the high-voltage feed. Audi documents P0C0C on the 2025 and 2026 A6 and Q6 e-tron family: stored in the electric drive modules together with P0E8D, it comes with a red high-voltage fault warning to stop safely, and the bulletin calls for replacing the affected front or rear power electronics. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid components. Without a stable supply the inverter cannot switch, so drive power is cut.

causes_en: Faulty voltage regulation of the gate-drive supply inside the motor A inverter
Excessive 12 V system voltage from the DC/DC converter or a charger
Supply or sense line shorted to a higher voltage in the harness
P0C0D.en: Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit High
P0C0D.desc: P0C0D reports that the supply of the motor A inverter is above its permitted range, while P0C0B stands for a lost or open supply and P0C0C for a supply that is too low. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's tables for the sibling P0C0B show what the supply is: the gate-drive rails of the IGBT module, on eAssist a 5 V and a 15 V rail that are each watched against limits. A rail running too high stresses the driver stage and can falsify the switching of the power transistors. CARB requires hybrid components to be monitored for circuit faults. Expect the inverter to shut down or derate, with reduced or no electric drive.

causes_en: Failed gate-drive power supply inside the motor B inverter
Weak 12 V feed, blown fuse or poor ground at the inverter control board
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the power inverter module
P0C0E.en: Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit/Open
P0C0E.desc: P0C0E is the motor B counterpart of P0C0B: the inverter for the second motor has lost the supply of its gate-drive board. GM documents it on the Volt and the two-mode trucks. The IGBT module reports a bias fault through its status line when the supply of phase A, B or C fails. The 2011 Volt checks with high voltage above 100 V, the 2012 trucks with run/crank voltage between 9.5 and 18 V, both after one count, Type A. The 2016 Volt needs 0.002 s of fault in a 0.024 s window, the 2018 table 0.02 s, the 2019 table 0.168 s, always Type A, one trip. P0C0F and P0C10 cover low and high supply. Motor B can no longer be driven, so propulsion is reduced.

causes_en: Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC converter output feeding the inverter electronics
Corroded connector or poor ground raising resistance in the inverter supply
Failing internal gate-drive power supply in the motor B inverter
P0C0F.en: Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit Low
P0C0F.desc: P0C0F means the supply of the motor B inverter is present but below its permitted range. P0C0E covers a lost or open supply, P0C10 a supply that is too high, and P0C0C is the same fault on motor A. No manufacturer documents P0C0F publicly. GM's tables for P0C0E name the supply in question: the power feed of the gate-drive board, checked phase by phase with run/crank voltage between 9.5 and 18 V on the 2012 trucks. A sagging rail can no longer switch the power transistors fully, so the inverter protects itself. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid components. The driver typically sees a warning and loses the electric drive of motor B.

causes_en: Faulty voltage regulation of the gate-drive supply inside the motor B inverter
Excessive 12 V system voltage from the DC/DC converter or an external charger
Supply or sense line shorted to a higher voltage in the harness
P0C10.en: Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit High
P0C10.desc: P0C10 flags a supply of the motor B inverter that is above its permitted range. Its siblings are P0C0E for a lost or open supply and P0C0F for a low one; P0C0D is the motor A version. No manufacturer documents P0C10 publicly. GM uses only the open-circuit code P0C0E for this supply and describes it as the power feed of the gate-drive board, monitored through the status line of the IGBT module. An overvoltage on that rail can damage the driver circuits, so the controller shuts the inverter down. CARB requires hybrid components to be checked for circuit faults. Expect a warning lamp and loss of the electric drive provided by motor B.

causes_en: Low coolant level or air in the power electronics cooling loop
Failed or weak electric coolant pump of the inverter loop
Clogged power electronics radiator or inoperative cooling fan
Sustained heavy load such as towing uphill in high ambient heat
P0C11.en: Drive Motor A Inverter Phase U Over Temperature
P0C11.desc: P0C11 is a protective code: the temperature sensor at phase U of the motor A inverter reads a valid but excessive value. GM uses it across its hybrids. The 2011 Volt reads PIM sensor A against 98 °C, the 2012 two-mode trucks against 88 °C with a reset at 85 °C, both Type A; the 2016 Volt sets it above 126 °C for 1.2 s within 2 s, the 2019 table above 128 °C, Type A, one trip. On eAssist the single inverter code P0C11 sets above 118.2 °C as Type B, two trips. Sensor faults such as P0AEE block it. Phase V and W are P0C12 and P0C13. GM advises finding the cause of poor cooling. The inverter cuts power to protect itself.

mfr.Audi: Coolant system leak, Drive motor generator power inverter control module failure, Engine cooling fan failure, Water pump failure

causes_en: Low coolant level or trapped air in the inverter cooling loop
Inoperative electric coolant pump of the power electronics
Blocked low-temperature radiator or failed cooling fan
Degraded thermal contact or failing power stage inside the inverter
P0C12.en: Drive Motor A Inverter Phase V Over Temperature
P0C12.desc: P0C12 sets when the inverter for motor A measures an excessive temperature at phase V while its sensor itself is plausible. In GM's 2011 Volt table that is PIM sensor C above 98 °C; the two-mode trucks of 2012 use 88 °C with an 85 °C reset, the 2016 Volt 126 °C for 1.2 s out of 2 s and the 2016 ELR 102.5 °C, all Type A, one trip. The sensor circuit codes of that thermistor, such as P0BD1 and P0BD2, have their own numbers and must be ruled out first. P0C11 and P0C13 are phases U and W, P0C15 is phase V on motor B. GM bulletin PIC6303A lists these overheat codes as a sign of insufficient cooling. Power is reduced while the inverter is hot.

causes_en: Coolant loss or air pocket in the power electronics loop
Electric coolant pump for the inverter stopped or running slow
Debris on the low-temperature radiator or cooling fan not running
P0C13.en: Drive Motor A Inverter Phase W Over Temperature
P0C13.desc: P0C13 covers phase W of the motor A inverter: the controller sees a credible sensor reading that exceeds the overtemperature limit. GM's 2011 Volt uses PIM sensor E with 98 °C, the 2012 two-mode trucks 88 °C, the 2016 and 2018 tables 126 °C for 1.2 s within a 2 s window and the 2019 table 128 °C for 1.5 s, always Type A, one trip, so the MIL comes on at once. The check is blocked while circuit or performance faults of the thermistor are active. Siblings are P0C11 for phase U and P0C12 for phase V; P0C16 is phase W on motor B. Because the code reports a real heat condition, the cooling system of the power electronics is the first place to look; output stays limited.

causes_en: Low coolant level or air in the power electronics cooling loop
Failed electric coolant pump of the inverter loop
Clogged low-temperature radiator or failed cooling fan
Long periods of high load on motor B, e.g. towing or steep climbs
P0C14.en: Drive Motor B Inverter Phase U Over Temperature
P0C14.desc: P0C14 is the motor B counterpart of P0C11: phase U of the second inverter has become too hot while its temperature sensor reads plausibly. GM documents it on the Volt and the two-mode trucks. The 2011 Volt compares PIM sensor B with 98 °C, the 2012 trucks use 88 °C with a reset at 85 °C, the 2016 Volt 131 °C for 1.2 s in 2 s and the 2019 table 131 °C for 1.5 s, all Type A, one trip. Sensor circuit codes such as P0AF2 or P0AF3 point to the thermistor instead and are checked first. P0C15 and P0C16 cover phases V and W. GM bulletin PIC6303A sends technicians to the cooling system when inverter overheat codes appear. Power from motor B is limited meanwhile.

mfr.Audi: Coolant system leak, Drive motor generator power inverter control module failure, Engine cooling fan failure, Water pump failure

causes_en: Coolant loss or air in the inverter cooling loop
Electric coolant pump of the power electronics not working
Blocked radiator for the power electronics or fan failure
Poor heat transfer or ageing power stage inside the inverter
P0C15.en: Drive Motor B Inverter Phase V Over Temperature
P0C15.desc: P0C15 reports overtemperature at phase V of the motor B inverter, based on a sensor reading that is valid but above the limit. GM applies it on the Volt and the two-mode trucks: PIM sensor D above 98 °C on the 2011 Volt, 88 °C on the 2012 trucks, 102.5 °C on the 2016 ELR, 131 °C for 1.2 s within 2 s on the 2016 Volt and in the 2018 table, every time Type A with one trip. It is a protective diagnosis, not a wiring check; the thermistor's own codes P0BD6 and P0BD7 handle sensor faults. Phase U and W are P0C14 and P0C16, phase V on motor A is P0C12. GM bulletin PIC6303A names P0C15 among the overheat codes that call for a cooling diagnosis. Motor B output is restricted.

mfr.Audi: Coolant system leak, Drive motor generator power inverter control module failure, Engine cooling fan failure, Water pump failure

causes_en: Low coolant level or air in the power electronics loop
Electric coolant pump of the inverter failed or blocked
Dirty low-temperature radiator or inoperative fan
P0C16.en: Drive Motor B Inverter Phase W Over Temperature
P0C16.desc: P0C16 is set by the motor B inverter when phase W runs too hot and the temperature sensor itself shows no fault. GM's tables give PIM sensor F above 98 °C for the 2011 Volt, above 88 °C with an 85 °C reset for the 2012 two-mode trucks, and 131 °C for 1.2 s within 2 s for the 2016 Volt, with 1.5 s in the 2019 table; each is Type A, one trip. Thermistor circuit codes such as P0BE0 and P0BE1 take priority and block the check. P0C14 and P0C15 are phases U and V, P0C13 is phase W on motor A. CARB allows some protective overtemperature strategies to run without MIL, but GM lights it here. Look for weak cooling first; until then motor B is derated.

causes_en: Offset learn not performed after replacing the inverter, motor or resolver
High voltage not reaching the inverter during the learn, e.g. contactor or HV cable fault
Loose three-phase ring terminals after a repair
Damaged motor stator winding (GM 21-NA-218)
P0C17.en: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Not Learned
P0C17.desc: P0C17 means the controller has no valid learned offset for the resolver of motor A, which it needs to align rotor position with the stator field. GM runs the learn at key-off and sets the code if it fails without a stored value: motor speed above 50 rpm, DC voltage below 192 V (200 V on the 2016 Volt), phase current below 15 A or a learn time over 1.4 s. The Volt is Type A, the 2012 two-mode trucks Type B. GM bulletin 21-NA-218 links it to missing high voltage or three-phase current, loose phase terminals or stator damage on Volt and ELR. Mazda requires the speed sensor learn on CX-90 and CX-70 PHEV after inverter or motor replacement. P0C4E reports a learned value out of range.

causes_en: Offset learn not completed after replacing the inverter, motor B or its resolver
No high voltage at the drive motor control module, e.g. contactor fault or disconnected HV cable
Control module needs reprogramming to enable a wide position sensor learn
P0C18.en: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Not Learned
P0C18.desc: P0C18 is the motor B version of P0C17: the resolver offset of the second motor has not been learned and no valid earlier value is stored. GM performs the learn at key-off; it fails if motor speed exceeds 50 rpm, DC voltage stays below 192 V, phase current stays below 15 A or the learn takes longer than 1.4 s. The Volt tables rate it Type A, one trip, the 2012 two-mode trucks Type B, two trips. GM bulletin 21-NA-218 notes that when P0C17 and P0C18 set together, a programming event is needed to allow a wide position sensor learn, and that missing high voltage at the drive motor control module can be the reason. P0C4F reports a learned value beyond its limit.

causes_en: Outdated power inverter module software (Stellantis 08-059-25, 08-231-24)
Implausible rotor position signal from the motor A resolver or its wiring
Faulty phase current sensing distorting the calculated torque
Internal fault of the inverter power stage or motor winding
P0C19.en: Drive Motor A Torque Delivered Performance
P0C19.desc: P0C19 is a plausibility check: the torque that motor A actually delivers, calculated by the motor control processor, does not follow the slewed torque command. GM sets it when the difference exceeds 123 Nm for 0.1875 s within 0.2 s on the 2016 and 2018 tables, Type A, one trip; eAssist uses 36 Nm as Type B, two trips. The 2012 two-mode trucks check whether the sum of the three phase currents exceeds 110 A for 200 ms. Stellantis lists P0C19 on the Jeep Wrangler 4xe and the Wagoneer PHEV with P1B03, a resolver rationality fault, and cures it by reflashing the power inverter module. The electric drive shuts down and the engine takes over.

causes_en: Short in the internal transmission wiring connector (Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid 21-008-23)
Implausible rotor position signal from the motor B resolver
Hybrid control or inverter module software requiring an update
Faulty phase current sensing for motor B
P0C1A.en: Drive Motor B Torque Delivered Performance
P0C1A.desc: P0C1A compares the torque command for motor B with the torque the motor control processor calculates as actually delivered. GM's 2016, 2018 and 2019 tables set it when the difference exceeds 132 Nm for 0.1875 s in a 0.2 s window, Type A, one trip, and only while listed resolver and motor control faults are inactive. The 2011 Volt and 2012 two-mode tables also list it, the trucks with a three-phase current sum above 110 A. Chrysler documents it on the 2017 to 2023 Pacifica Hybrid: with resolver codes P0A3F, P0A43 or P0A45 it points to a short in the internal wiring connector of the eFlite transmission, which is replaced. P0C19 is motor A. Expect limp mode.

causes_en: High transmission fluid temperature from heavy load, towing or a weak fluid cooler
Pump running against high resistance (binding, clogged filter) and heating its driver
Poor heat transfer from the module (mounting, contamination) or internal module fault
P0C1B.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Too High
P0C1B.desc: P0C1B is a protection code: the electronics that drive the auxiliary transmission fluid pump measure a valid but excessive internal temperature. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM shows the same function on the 2016 Cadillac ELR pump controller under its own code P1E37, an in-range overtemperature above 98 °C that could damage the inverter, checked only when the sensor itself is plausible. A Honda patent for a CVT pump explains the reaction: once the board temperature passes a limit, the control unit opens the pump relay and keeps the pump off until the fluid has cooled. The pump then stops, so start-stop and pressure support are lost. P0C1C to P0C1F cover faults of the temperature sensor itself and must be excluded first.

causes_en: Temperature sensor or its measuring circuit on the module board faulty
Unstable supply or ground of the pump module distorting the sensor reading
Moisture or fluid inside the module housing
P0C1C.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit
P0C1C.desc: P0C1C is the general circuit fault of the temperature sensor inside the auxiliary pump control module, used when the signal is invalid without fitting the low, high or range checks. No manufacturer documents it publicly. GM's 2016 ELR pump controller monitors its inverter sensor with own codes P1E34 to P1E36 instead, and the Honda CVT pump patent shows why the reading matters: it is the basis for switching the pump off before the board overheats. Without a valid value the controller cannot protect itself, so the pump usually runs restricted or stays off. CARB requires such sensors to be checked for circuit faults. Because the sensor is on the circuit board, the fix is normally the module or the pump assembly. P0C1D to P0C1F are the specific variants.

causes_en: Board temperature sensor drifted or measuring circuit out of tolerance
Reference value wrong because the transmission fluid or coolant temperature sensor is faulty
Internal fault of the pump control module
P0C1D.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0C1D.desc: P0C1D means the internal temperature sensor of the auxiliary pump module delivers an electrically valid value that does not fit the other temperatures in the vehicle. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's comparable check on the 2016 ELR pump controller, own code P1E36, runs after at least 6 hours of inactivity: the inverter reading is compared with the average of the power electronics coolant and transmission fluid temperatures, and a difference above 20 °C fails, Type B, MIL after two trips. A sensor that reads too low would let the board overheat unnoticed, which is why the Honda pump patent bases shutdown on this value. P0C1E and P0C1F cover voltage out of range, P0C1B real overtemperature.

causes_en: Board temperature sensor or its signal path shorted to ground inside the module
Measuring circuit of the pump control module faulty
Fluid or moisture on the module board
P0C1E.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P0C1E.desc: P0C1E reports that the signal voltage of the module's internal temperature sensor is below its valid range. With the usual NTC thermistor, low voltage corresponds to a very high temperature, so a short to ground looks like an overheated board. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM shows the scale on the 2016 ELR pump controller with its own code P1E35, labelled circuit low: a reading above 130 °C, near 0 V, for 250 of 350 samples at 10.4 ms sets a Type B fault, MIL after two trips. The Honda CVT pump patent uses this board value to cut the pump relay, so a shorted sensor can stop the pump although nothing is hot. P0C1F is the high side, P0C1B a genuine overtemperature.

causes_en: Board temperature sensor open or its solder joint cracked
Measuring circuit of the pump control module faulty
Ground offset at the pump module shifting the sensor voltage
P0C1F.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P0C1F.desc: P0C1F means the internal temperature sensor of the auxiliary pump module delivers a voltage above its valid range, which for an NTC thermistor reads as an implausibly cold board and usually indicates an open sensor path. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's ELR pump controller of 2016 shows the matching case under its own code P1E34, labelled circuit high: below -58 °C, near 5 V, for 250 of 350 samples sets the fault, Type B in the ELR tables. With such a value the controller loses its overtemperature protection; the Honda CVT pump patent shows that this protection is what keeps the driver board alive, so the pump is typically restricted. P0C1E is the low side, P0C1D the plausibility check, P0C1B real overtemperature.

causes_en: Motor connector of the pump not fully seated, or loose phase terminal
Open phase lead between pump inverter and motor
Power switch of one phase in the pump inverter not conducting
Open winding in the pump motor
P0C20.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
P0C20.desc: P0C20 means at least one of the three motor phases of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump carries no current, typically an open lead, terminal or winding. GM uses it in the pump controller of the Chevrolet Volt (2011-15 tables) and the 2016 Cadillac ELR: with the inverter in Run, high voltage above 35 V and the rotor within 30 degrees of a phase axis, the peak current of that phase is checked; below 1 A for 200 counts sets the code, Type A, MIL on the first trip. Each phase is tested in turn as the rotor turns. The pump cannot build torque, so pressure support and electric operation are lost. Later GM tables split the check into the per-phase codes P0B01, P0B04 and P0B07; P0C21/P0C22 are the low and high variants.

causes_en: Phase lead chafed through and shorted to ground or the transmission case
Transmission fluid or water in the motor connector creating a leakage path
Low-side switch or phase sensing in the pump inverter faulty
Motor winding shorted to the stator core
P0C21.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
P0C21.desc: P0C21 reports a low condition on the phase U, V or W circuits of the auxiliary pump motor, usually a phase lead shorted to ground or a voltage at a phase terminal that stays below what the inverter commands. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM watches the same wiring on the Volt and ELR with the open-circuit code P0C20 and catches shorts through overcurrent on P0C28 and its own phase current sensor codes P1E2A to P1E32. The Hitachi idle-stop pump patent shows that the inverter often reconstructs all phase currents from one DC-bus shunt, so a ground short and a sensing fault can look alike. The pump usually shuts down, auto-stop is blocked. P0C20 is the open circuit, P0C22 the high side, P0B01 to P0B08 the per-phase current codes.

causes_en: Phase lead shorted to supply voltage or to another phase
High-side switch of the pump inverter stuck conducting
Phase current sensing in the inverter reads too high
Shorted turns in the pump motor winding
P0C22.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit High
P0C22.desc: P0C22 reports a high condition on the U-V-W phase circuits of the auxiliary pump motor, for example a phase lead shorted to the supply or a phase voltage that stays high while the inverter should pull it down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. In GM's Volt tables the closest monitors are P0C28, which trips above 35 A on any phase within a few milliseconds to protect the IGBTs, and its own phase sensor codes P1E2B, P1E2E and P1E31 for readings above 30 A. The Hitachi sub-oil pump patent shows that phase currents are often calculated from a shared bus shunt, so a sensing error must be ruled out before the wiring is condemned. The pump stops and auto-stop is blocked. P0C21 is the low side, P0B02, P0B05 and P0B08 the per-phase high codes.

causes_en: Open command or enable wire between controller and pump module
Pushed-out or corroded terminal at the pump module or controller connector
Input stage of the pump control module faulty
P0C23.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit/Open
P0C23.desc: P0C23 is set by the controlling module, usually the PCM, TCM or hybrid controller, when the circuit to the auxiliary pump control module is open. J2012 does not name the line further; in practice it is the command or enable wire. Ford's 2016 F-150 2.7L bulletin shows such a command: the PCM drives the pump with a duty cycle that a scan tool can vary from 20 to 90 percent. GM's ELR pump controller only runs its phase tests while a wake-up signal is on. No manufacturer publicly documents P0C23 itself. With the line open the pump gets no command and stays off, so auto-stop is disabled and pressure support is missing. P0C24 and P0C25 are the low and high variants, P0C2B to P0C2E the feedback line in the other direction.

causes_en: Command wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed at the transmission case
Fluid or corrosion in the pump connector pulling the line low
Output stage in the PCM/TCM or input of the pump module faulty
P0C24.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit Low
P0C24.desc: P0C24 means the circuit from the controlling module to the auxiliary pump control module is held low, typically a short to ground on the command line. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. How the line is used is visible in Ford's 2016 F-150 2.7L bulletin, where the PCM commands the start-stop pump by duty cycle and the technician checks the pump by sweeping that command from 20 to 90 percent. A grounded line leaves the pump without a valid command or, depending on logic, permanently off. GM's ELR pump controller likewise depends on its wake-up signal to run. CARB requires output circuits of such components to be monitored. P0C23 is the open circuit, P0C25 the high side, P2796 to P2798 the classic pump control circuit codes.

causes_en: Command wire shorted to battery or another supply voltage
Output stage in the PCM/TCM stuck high
Input stage of the pump control module faulty
P0C25.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit High
P0C25.desc: P0C25 reports that the circuit from the controlling module to the auxiliary pump control module sits high, for instance a command wire shorted to battery voltage or an output that cannot pull the line down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Ford's 2016 F-150 2.7L bulletin shows the type of signal involved: a PCM duty-cycle command that can be swept from 20 to 90 percent to prove pump operation. A line stuck high can be read as a constant full command or rejected as invalid, so the pump may run continuously or be shut off. GM's ELR pump controller also uses a separate wake-up line as enable. CARB requires circuit monitoring of such outputs. P0C23 is the open circuit, P0C24 the low side, P0C2E the high fault on the feedback line.

causes_en: Low or aerated transmission fluid at the pump intake
Pump binding or contaminated, changing the motor load
Current sensing in the pump driver implausible
Outdated control software of the pump or controlling module
P0C26.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current
P0C26.desc: P0C26 is the general motor current fault of auxiliary pump A: the current drawn does not match what the commanded operating point should need, without clearly being too low or too high. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Its siblings show what is monitored: Ford stores P0C27, current too low, on 2014-16 Fusion and 2015-16 Edge with the 6F35 start-stop transmission when air enters the pump supply tube, and GM sets P0C28 on the Volt and ELR when any phase exceeds 35 A. CARB requires such components to be checked for rationality. A general current code therefore points to aeration, low fluid, a binding pump or current sensing errors. The pump may be switched off and auto-stop blocked; P0C27 and P0C28 are the specific variants.

causes_en: Air entering the pump supply tube (Ford 6F35, new tube with check ball)
Calibration of PCM and hybrid module (Ford Fusion/C-Max Energi)
Low transmission fluid level letting the pump draw air
High resistance or open circuit in the pump motor wiring
P0C27.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current Low
P0C27.desc: P0C27 means motor A of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump draws less current than expected, a sign that the pump is not loaded, for example because it sucks air or turns without delivering. Ford documents it twice. TSB 16-0111 covers 2014-16 Fusion and 2015-16 Edge with the 6F35 transmission and start-stop: MIL, P0C27 in the PCM and a harsh engagement after an auto-stop, caused by air entering the pump supply tube on transmissions built up to 26 February 2016; a new tube with a check ball fixes it. TSB 18-2282 for the 2013-17 Fusion Energi and C-Max Energi lists P0C27 and/or P0C28 and calls for reprogramming the PCM and hybrid module. P0C28 is the high side, P0C26 the general code, P0C2A a stalled motor.

causes_en: Pump control software faulty (Cadillac CT6 update 18199, Ford Energi TSB 18-2282)
Pump seized, contaminated or running against blocked flow
Short between motor phases or to ground
Current sensing or power stage in the pump inverter faulty
P0C28.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current High
P0C28.desc: P0C28 is the overcurrent protection of auxiliary pump motor A. GM uses it on Volt, ELR and later hybrids: the inverter trips when any of the U, V or W phases exceeds 35 A, in 2016 within about 4 ms of a 62 ms window, or when the d-axis current falls below a stator temperature limit, Type A, MIL on the first trip. GM service update 18199 for the 2018 Cadillac CT6 plug-in traces P0C28 to a faulty pump restart logic in the software. Ford's TSB 18-2282 lists P0C27 and/or P0C28 on the 2013-17 Fusion Energi and C-Max Energi, fixed by reprogramming the PCM and hybrid module; Ford also reports P0C28 in the SOBDMC of the 2024-25 Mustang Mach-E LFP, solved by software. P0C27 is the low side.

causes_en: Auxiliary hydraulic pump V475 of early production faulty (VW/Audi 0GC)
Poor contact at the pump electrical connection
Transmission control software not updated per service action
P0C29.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Driver Circuit Performance
P0C29.desc: P0C29 means the driver stage of auxiliary pump A does not behave as commanded, for instance the pump does not reach its target or the activation is reported as implausible. Volkswagen Group documents it on the 7-speed DSG 0GC (DQ381): VW lists P0C29 for the 2018 Golf R as implausible activation of auxiliary hydraulic pump 1 (V475), often with clutch and gear actuator codes as consequences; Audi's bulletin for the 2017-18 A3, A3 Cabriolet and S3 with gearbox dated up to 26 September 2017 calls for replacing the auxiliary hydraulic pump when only P0C29 remains. The customer sees a Gearbox Malfunction warning. VW improved the pump from October 2017 production. P0C2A is a stalled motor, P0C26 to P0C28 current faults.

causes_en: Auxiliary pump seized or jammed by debris (Ford F-150 2.7L replaces the pump)
PCM calibration causing false stall detection (Ford TSB 17-2056)
Very cold, thick fluid or wrong fluid type raising drag
Open phase so the motor cannot develop torque
P0C2A.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Stalled
P0C2A.desc: P0C2A means motor A of the auxiliary pump is commanded but does not turn, or turns far slower than required. Ford documents it in TSB 17-2056 for the 2016 F-150 2.7L with start-stop built from 1 May 2016: with the fluid above 38 °C the technician commands the pump through the PCM at duty cycles from 20 to 90 percent; if it runs, the PCM gets new software, if not, the auxiliary pump is replaced. GM shows how a stall is detected on the ELR pump controller, under its own code P1E3A: commanded minus actual speed above 200 rpm while more than 6.8 Nm is requested, Type A. Sensorless pumps cannot measure speed directly, so a stall shows up as a speed or current mismatch. P0C29 covers the driver stage, P0C28 overcurrent.

causes_en: Wiring or terminal tension fault between hybrid controller and pump control module
Early pump control module (GM date code 089-11 or older)
Key held in crank for a long time during a no-start
P0C2B.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal
P0C2B.desc: P0C2B concerns the status signal the auxiliary pump control module sends back to the controlling module. GM uses it on the Two-Mode hybrid trucks and SUVs (Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado, Sierra, 2ML70): the hybrid controller expects a complete fault status message from the pump controller every 1.5 s; if it is missing or incomplete for 9.75 s with the vehicle in Run or Crank, the code sets as Type B, MIL after two trips. GM preliminary information PIP4751G stresses that P0C2B, with or without P2797, rarely means a bad pump: check the wiring, replace the pump control module if its date code is 089-11 or older, and note that a key held in Crank during a no-start can set it. P0C2C to P0C2E are the specific variants.

causes_en: Electronics of the pump module reporting wrong status or speed
Intermittent contact on the feedback line distorting the signal
Pump not following the command mechanically, so feedback and command differ
P0C2C.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal Range/Performance
P0C2C.desc: P0C2C means the feedback signal from the auxiliary pump control module is present and electrically valid but does not make sense, for example a reported speed or status that contradicts the command. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Its siblings show the signal: on GM's Two-Mode trucks P0C2B watches a fault status message expected every 1.5 s, and on the 2021-23 Chevrolet Bolt EV and 2022 Bolt EUV GM bulletin 21-NA-148 pairs P0C2D with the pump performance codes P2797 and P2798, caused by bad solder joints in the low-voltage pump. CARB requires rationality checks for such inputs. Implausible feedback usually points to the pump electronics themselves. P0C2B is the general code, P0C2D and P0C2E the low and high variants.

causes_en: Faulty solder joints in the electric transmission fluid pump (Chevrolet Bolt, GM 21-NA-148)
Feedback line shorted to ground
Corroded or loose pump connector
P0C2D.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal Low
P0C2D.desc: P0C2D reports that the feedback signal from the electric transmission fluid pump module stays low, below its valid range. GM documents it for the 2021-23 Chevrolet Bolt EV and 2022 Bolt EUV in bulletin 21-NA-148: the driver sees Propulsion Power is Reduced and a Service Vehicle Soon lamp, with P0C2D, P2797 or P2798 stored. The cause is a part quality spill in the low-voltage electric transmission fluid pump on the driver side of the drive unit, where a soldering process was out of specification; the motor is not serviceable, so the complete pump is replaced. In this EV the pump supplies fluid for cooling and lubricating the drive unit. P0C2B is the general feedback code, P0C2C the plausibility and P0C2E the high variant.

causes_en: Feedback line shorted to supply voltage
Output stage of the pump control module no longer switching
Lost ground at the pump module letting the line float high
P0C2E.en: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal High
P0C2E.desc: P0C2E means the feedback line from the auxiliary pump control module sits above its valid range, for example shorted to supply voltage or no longer pulled down by the module. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's use of the siblings shows what the line carries: on the Two-Mode hybrids P0C2B watches a status message from the pump controller every 1.5 s, Type B, and on the Chevrolet Bolt EV and EUV bulletin 21-NA-148 links the low variant P0C2D to bad solder joints inside the pump. A stuck-high line can hide real pump faults, so the controller usually stops relying on the pump. CARB requires circuit checks for such signals. P0C2D is the low side, P0C2C the plausibility check, P0C25 the high fault on the command line.

causes_en: Control module software flagging the comparison falsely (Ford Mach-E, fixed by reprogramming)
Speed signals disagree because of a faulty input or a disturbed CAN signal
Internal fault of the hybrid control module
P0C2F.en: Internal Control Module Drive Motor/Generator - Engine Speed Sensor Performance
P0C2F.desc: P0C2F is an internal plausibility check of the hybrid control processor: the engine speed it reads through its own sensor path must match other speed information. In GM's Two-Mode truck tables (12OBDG06, 13OBDG06) the HCP compares its SPI-sensed engine speed with the calculated transmission input speed and with the engine speed received over CAN; a deviation beyond 250 rpm above 1500 rpm, with a wider band at lower speed, in 160 of 320 samples sets it as Type A, MIL after one trip. Ford uses it on the 2021–2023 Mustang Mach-E as P0C2F:92 in the secondary OBD module C, paired with a 1 Pedal Drive fault message; bulletin 24-2187 fixes it by reprogramming the powertrain modules. Real sensor circuit faults have their own codes.

causes_en: Wrong SOC estimate from a drifting pack current or voltage measurement
Battery or hybrid control software not drawing the charge down as intended
Electric assist blocked by another fault, so the pack cannot discharge
P0C30.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack State of Charge High
P0C30.desc: P0C30 is the counterpart of P0A7D: the battery controller finds that the state of charge of the high-voltage pack stays above its usable window. CARB requires hybrid OBD to flag a state of charge that can no longer be kept inside the manufacturer's range. GM's 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 describes the method: the SOC is checked once per drive cycle, the controller first allows time for the motor to draw the charge back down, then counts the distance driven with excessive SOC; if that share exceeds half of a trip longer than 50 km, at speeds above 15 km/h and pack temperature at least −10 °C, the code is stored as Type B, two trips. No other manufacturer documents it publicly. The car limits regeneration and charging to protect the cells, so braking feel and fuel economy can change.

causes_en: Low coolant level or air trapped in the inverter B circuit
Weak or failed electric coolant pump of the circuit
Clogged radiator or inoperative cooling fan
P0C31.desc: P0C31 reports that the cooling circuit of a second power inverter does not remove heat as expected; inverter A has its own code, P0A93. Vehicles with two separately cooled power electronics units, for example a front and a rear drive unit, need this second code. CARB requires hybrid OBD to monitor the parts used for inverter thermal management and, where feasible, to check the cooling performance itself. No manufacturer documents P0C31 publicly. For the analogous P0A93, Hyundai's 2011 Sonata Hybrid bulletin 14-HC-001 points to the electric water pump, and coolant pump faults of the B circuit are reported as P0B38 or P0C74. To protect the semiconductors the controller limits motor power. A low coolant level or trapped air is worth checking first.

causes_en: Battery cooling fan stopping at low 12 V system voltage (GM eAssist)
Low coolant, air or a weak pump in a liquid-cooled pack circuit
Blocked cooling air intake or ducts of an air-cooled pack
Failed pack heater or chiller valve
P0C32.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System A Performance
P0C32.desc: P0C32 is the functional check of the battery thermal system that CARB asks for. GM tunes it per vehicle: the 2012 Volt (12OBDG01A) fails it when the average pack temperature stays above 40 °C in active cooling or below −17 °C in active heating, after 4200 s or 9000 s, Type A, one trip. The Two-Mode trucks (12OBDG06) compare the hottest module with a limit that rises with inlet temperature, from 45 °C to about 65 °C, Type B. The air-cooled eAssist (13OBDG05C) models the power pack temperature after six hours off and fails above 15 °C deviation, Type B. GM bulletin PIP4992C links P0C32 on 2012–2016 eAssist cars to a pack fan that stops at low 12 V voltage and calls for reprogramming and fan replacement. B and C circuits use P2D3F and P2D40.

causes_en: Loose or corroded connector of sensor F at the sensing board
Failed thermistor F
Faulty input on the battery sensing board or module
P0C33.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit
P0C33.desc: Battery temperature sensor F is the sixth thermistor in the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the F codes under temperature sensor 6 of nine. P0C33 is the general circuit code for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly: GM's hybrid tables use only the more specific siblings P0C34 to P0C37. CARB requires battery temperature sensors to be monitored for circuit faults and, where possible, separate codes that point to the smallest replaceable part. With one temperature missing the controller has to assume the worst and limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits inside the pack, so checks need high-voltage safety procedures.

causes_en: Sensor F drifting or poorly seated on its cell group
Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt)
Real local temperature difference from a weak cell group or uneven cooling
P0C34.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance
P0C34.desc: P0C34 checks whether sensor F, GM's sensor 6, agrees with the rest of the pack. The controller compares its reading with the average of the other battery temperature sensors. GM's 2016 hybrid table fails it above 25 °C difference in 50 of 67 samples; the Volt and plug-in tables of 2016 to 2019 use 20 °C, in 2018 for 5 s within 6.7 s; the air-cooled eAssist (13OBDG05C) allows only 8.55 °C and tests only after more than six hours with the module off. All are Type B, two trips. Active circuit codes suspend the test, so P0C34 means a sensor that reads wrongly but within range, or a real local hot or cold spot. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names it sensor 6 performance among codes that set in cold weather without a hardware fault.

causes_en: Sensor F signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Internally shorted thermistor F
Faulty input on the battery sensing board
P0C35.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low
P0C35.desc: Sensor F is an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so its voltage drops as temperature rises; a short to ground looks like an extremely hot cell group. Low refers to the signal, not to the temperature. GM's 2016 table sets P0C35 when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples; the Volt battery tables of 2016 to 2019 use above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; the eAssist mild hybrid flags a sense voltage under 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 samples. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 calls it sensor 6 circuit low voltage. The opposite fault is P0C36; a pack that is really too hot is reported as P0A7E. Because the controller must assume heat, it cuts power and may run the cooling hard.

causes_en: Open circuit or unlatched connector of sensor F
Thermistor F open internally
Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt)
P0C36.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit High
P0C36.desc: P0C36 means the voltage from battery temperature sensor F sits above its valid range. With GM's NTC thermistor and pull-up, an open circuit, a broken wire or an unplugged connector pulls the input up and reads as an impossibly cold cell group. GM's 2016 table fails it below −69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the Volt battery tables of 2016 to 2019 below −40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s, and the eAssist table above 4.63 V, about −45 °C, in 7 of 10 samples, each as Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists it as sensor 6 circuit high voltage and links the F group to a Battery Too Cold message. The counterpart for a short to ground is P0C35. Expect limited power and possibly pack heating that is not needed.

causes_en: Loose terminal or connector of sensor F not fully latched after pack work
Cracked sensor wire with intermittent contact
Faulty battery sensing board, often with several sensors affected
P0C37.en: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C37.desc: P0C37 targets a sensor F signal that jumps instead of following the slow temperature change of a heavy battery. GM documents the logic in its 2016 to 2018 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 17OBDG02, 18OBDG02): every 100 ms the controller adds up the absolute changes of the sensor value over a window of 10 samples; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 set the code as Type B, two trips, with system voltage above 10.2 V and no communication fault active. The Volt, Two-Mode and eAssist tables have no erratic code for this sensor. Unlike P0C35 and P0C36, the signal stays inside its valid range, so the cause is usually a loose terminal or a cracked wire. If several sensors jump at once, the sensing board is the likelier suspect.

causes_en: Control unit software misjudging the sensor after long parking (Hyundai Palisade Hybrid)
Fault in the circuit of sensor A inside the converter or power control unit
Internal fault of the DC/DC converter requiring replacement
P0C38.en: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0C38.desc: The DC/DC converter steps the high-voltage battery down to the 12 V system and replaces the alternator in hybrids and EVs. Its power stage carries temperature sensors so the controller can derate before the semiconductors overheat. P0C38 is the general circuit code for sensor A. Hyundai documents it on the 2027 Palisade Hybrid as P0C381C (failure type 1C, voltage out of range): the hybrid warning light comes on after the car has been parked for a long time, and bulletin 26-01-071H and campaign 9D8 cure it with an HPCU software update that improves the detection logic, so the sensor itself is usually fine. CARB requires the converter's inputs to be monitored as comprehensive components. Low, high and erratic signals have their own codes P0C3A to P0C3C.

causes_en: Outdated hybrid control software (Ram 1500 eTorque, bulletin 08-037-21)
Sensor A drifting or with poor thermal contact to the power stage
Uneven cooling of the converter making the readings disagree
P0C39.en: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P0C39.desc: P0C39 is the plausibility check of DC/DC converter temperature sensor A: its reading lies within the electrical range but does not fit the converter's operating state or a second sensor. FCA uses it on the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid, where the code is called temperature sensor 1 performance. Bulletin 08-037-21 updates the HCP software and changes this code from a two-trip to a one-trip DTC, so the MIL can come on after a single fault. Sensor B, sensor 2 at Ram, has the matching code P0C3E. CARB requires rationality checks for such inputs. A drifting sensor or poor thermal contact is typical; outright circuit faults are reported as P0C38, P0C3A or P0C3B instead.

causes_en: Sensor A signal shorted to ground inside the converter or its harness
Shorted temperature element A, usually requiring converter replacement
Converter really overheated due to a cooling fault
P0C3A.en: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Low
P0C3A.desc: P0C3A means the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. Low refers to the signal voltage: with an NTC thermistor and pull-up, as GM uses for its hybrid temperature sensors, a short to ground or a failed element reads as extreme heat. No manufacturer documents P0C3A publicly. Mercedes-Benz shows the opposite case for the same sensor, P0C3B as a short to positive, on the EQB and the G-Class, and Ram the plausibility code P0C39. CARB requires the converter's inputs to be checked for out-of-range values. Because the controller must assume an overheated power stage, it limits or stops the converter output; the 12 V battery then supplies the car alone and a low-voltage warning may follow. The sensor is usually built into the converter.

causes_en: Faulty wake-up behaviour of the converter putting it into an error state (Mercedes 243/465)
Open circuit or short to positive in the sensor A circuit
Internal defect of the DC/DC converter
P0C3B.en: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A High
P0C3B.desc: P0C3B reports a signal from DC/DC converter temperature sensor A above its valid range, typically a short to positive or an open circuit pulled up by the input. Mercedes-Benz documents it on series 243 (EQB) and 465 (G-Class, including the electric G 580): information LI54.10-P-079533 describes P0C3B00 as a short circuit to positive of temperature sensor A, stored together with P0E9700, P0E5400 and P0C4000 after faulty wake-up behaviour of the converter. Drivers see a red 12 V battery message and white or yellow HV warnings. The remedy is a converter check in XENTRY, clearing the fault memory and a converter reset; parts are not replaced first. The low-signal sibling is P0C3A, sensor B's high code is P0C40.

causes_en: Loose terminal or moisture at the converter connector
Harness damaged by vibration with intermittent contact
Intermittent fault inside the converter
P0C3C.en: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
P0C3C.desc: P0C3C covers a signal from DC/DC converter temperature sensor A that drops out or jumps for short moments while staying mostly within range. The heat sink of a converter warms and cools slowly, so fast jumps point to the signal path rather than to real temperature changes. No manufacturer documents P0C3C publicly. The method is known from GM's hybrid tables for comparable thermistors, such as P0C37 for battery sensor F: the controller adds up signal changes in short windows and fails the test when several windows exceed a limit. CARB requires such inputs to be monitored for faults. Typical causes are a loose terminal, vibration damage or moisture at the converter connector. Unlike P0C3A and P0C3B, the fault may vanish between tests, so a wiggle test helps.

causes_en: Connector or wiring fault in the sensor B circuit

Converter or hybrid control software misjudging the sensor
P0C3D.en: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0C3D.desc: P0C3D is the general circuit code for the second temperature sensor of the DC/DC converter, which turns high-voltage battery power into 12 V supply. Converters with two sensors watch separate parts of the power stage or cross-check one sensor against the other. No manufacturer documents P0C3D publicly. Sensor B itself appears in bulletins: Mercedes-Benz lists P0C4000, a short to positive of sensor B, on the EQB and the G-Class, and Ram the plausibility code P0C3E as temperature sensor 2 on the 2021 1500 eTorque. Sensor A uses P0C38 for the same fault class. CARB requires such converter inputs to be monitored. A circuit fault makes the controller limit or stop the converter, so the 12 V battery may run down and warnings follow.

causes_en: Outdated hybrid control software (Ram 1500 eTorque, bulletin 08-037-21)

P0C3E.en: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance
P0C3E.desc: P0C3E flags DC/DC converter temperature sensor B as electrically valid but implausible, for instance when it disagrees with sensor A or with what the converter load should produce. FCA uses it on the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid under the name temperature sensor 2 performance. Bulletin 08-037-21 reflashes the hybrid control processor and changes P0C3E, together with P0C39 for sensor 1, from a two-trip to a one-trip code, so one failed test can light the MIL. CARB requires rationality checks for converter inputs. Typical causes are a drifting element, poor thermal contact or outdated software. Circuit faults of sensor B are reported as P0C3D, P0C3F or P0C40; a converter that is really too hot sets P0D32 instead.
